full_text:
The Falcons are confident DeMarcco Hellams can fill Jessie Bates' defensive role. Kevin C. Cox / Getty Images
FLOWERY BRANCH, Ga. — The words of DeMarcco Hellams’ college coach still echo in the Atlanta safety’s head. It’s unsurprising considering that coach was Alabama’s Nick Saban.
“He always said, ‘So what? Now what?’ ” Hellams said.
The gist is that no matter what happened, the response matters most, and it’s particularly fitting for Atlanta this week because there haven’t been many more “So what? Now what?” weeks in the Falcons defense’s recent history.
The team is coming off its fourth loss in five games; the defense’s early-season successes have disappeared. It just traded away its best defensive player, safety Jessie Bates, and Patrick Mahomes and the Kansas City Chiefs come to town Sunday.
There’s been a lot to process since Bates was traded Monday to the Jaguars in exchange for a second-round pick in 2027 and a fifth-round pick in 2028.
“Jessie is a special player, and as special a player as he is, the human being is even better,” Atlanta defensive coordinator Jeff Ulbrich said. “Everybody’s going to have to do a little bit more.”
The biggest weight will fall on Hellams, who is set to take Bates’ spot in the starting lineup. A seventh-round pick in 2023, Hellams started four games his rookie season and then missed all of 2024 with an ankle injury. He has only played 27 defensive snaps in the last two seasons, but he said this week, “This is something I’ve been preparing for; I feel like since I came in the league.”
“The thing that he will bring is a level of violence that is different,” Ulbrich said. “Whereas Jessie is very precise with the way he takes the ball off people, DeMarcco is gonna separate man from ball at times. So I’m excited about him getting an opportunity.”
Maybe that style of play will spark an Atlanta defense that is in a decided slump.
In the first four weeks of the season, the Falcons (3-6) were second in the NFL in defensive success rate (63.9 percent), fifth in yards per play allowed (4.9), eighth in defensive EPA (6.4 per 100 snaps) and first in quarterback pressure rate (46.3 percent), according to TruMedia.
Since Week 5, those numbers have plummeted to 30th (52.9), 26th (5.8), 22nd (minus-0.8) and 21st (33.7 percent).
“We haven’t played to our standard the last couple of weeks … and I think everybody is taking that upon themselves,” Ulbrich said.
The falloff has been starkest in the run defense. In the first month of the season, Atlanta led the league in yards per carry allowed (2.7) and ranked second in rush defense success rate (71.8 percent). In the past five games, it ranks 30th (5.1) and 32nd (53.4 percent) and has allowed 876 yards on the ground, the most in the league.
“We’re just not playing it well enough,” Ulbrich said. “That’s me from a scheme perspective, making sure that we’re getting guys in the right spaces to be successful, and at times we’ve done that and didn’t play well enough. We all have to do more and do better in regard to defending the run.
“I’ve never been a part of a great defense that didn’t defend the run well. That has to become part of our identity, and right now it is not.”
Ulbrich should be accustomed to replacing key pieces of this defense.
Last offseason, the Falcons let their most versatile defender, linebacker Kaden Elliss, leave in free agency. This preseason, they lost starting edge rusher Jalon Walker for the season with a torn ACL and last season’s sack leader, James Pearce Jr., for eight games because of an NFL suspension. This time it’s Bates, whom Ulbrich called last week “one of the best players, offense, defense, special teams that I have ever been around.”
“As long as you have Jessie Bates on your defense, you have a chance,” Ulbrich said before the Falcons played the Cincinnati Bengals in Madrid.
Bates’ loss “definitely hurts,” safety Xavier Watts said.
“He taught me so much more than about football,” Watts said. “It’s my first time with a guy being traded like that, especially with somebody I’m so close to … but I understand the NFL business.”
The last two years have “probably” been the most fluid in terms of personnel losses in Ulbrich’s career, he said.
“I wouldn’t say it’s a feeling of panic, but definitely you know it gives you another level of urgency to get things right and find the guys that can replace the guys you lost,” he said. “Guys always step up and emerge, and guys maybe that you didn’t see that had something special in them demonstrate it, so as challenging as it is, it’s an opportunity for some guys, too.”
“Opportunity” is also the word Ulbrich somewhat incongruously uses about facing the Chiefs (6-2), who are second in the league in yards per game (384.1) and fourth in EPA per play (.01), this week.
“You want to go up against the better teams to make sure that this is legit, and the guys that are stepping in are the right guys,” Ulbrich said.
The Falcons have their bye week after the Kansas City game, then face a Vikings team that just added their former quarterback, Kirk Cousins, and the Lions, who are third in the league in offensive scoring at 27.8 points per game.
“It’s a challenge anytime you go up against an NFL team,” Hellams said. “These guys are the best in the world.”

full_text:
The Bills are now a few days into having safety Amani Hooker on their roster, giving him a crash course in Jim Leonhard's defense and trying to get him ready for a full-time role. Stew Milne / Associated Press
After clinching their fourth straight victory and staying atop the AFC with a 7-1 record, the Buffalo Bills get back to their AFC East roots on a short week against the 2-7 New York Jets.
It’s only the second divisional game of the year for the Bills, with their first coming in a Week 4 loss to the New England Patriots in Orchard Park. The Bills will be on the road and will also be playing for the first time with trade deadline acquisition Amani Hooker.
What could be in store for Hooker’s role this week, what could be on the way for the Jets game, and how can we interpret some lingering trade deadline questions?
Here’s what stands out about the Bills heading into their Week 9 game against the Jets.
The Bills are a few days into having safety Amani Hooker on their roster, giving him a crash course in Jim Leonhard’s defense and trying to get him ready for a full-time role. General manager Brandon Beane called Hooker a “difference-maker.” Leonhard was equally as excited about Hooker’s fit in the defense and what it will allow the Bills to do.
“I’ve always felt he’s a complete safety,” Leonhard said Thursday. “I think he makes this defense better.”
Once a player is acquired at the deadline, it’s always a big question whether they’ll play just a few days after arriving at their new team. Hooker left nothing up for interpretation on his first day on the job.
“Oh, I’m gonna play on Sunday,” Hooker said definitively. “Yeah, I’ll be ready to go.”
But just how involved will he be on defense?
The way the Bills have talked about him since his arrival has been uniform. They remarked how bright he is and how well he’s taken to things, even on short notice. Previously, I thought they might take it slow with a player at a mentally demanding position, given all the things safeties need to be aware of, but based on how they’ve talked about him, Hooker could make his mark quickly. With only a handful of practices under his belt by Sunday, it wouldn’t be a shock if Hooker is out there as the starter and plays the majority of snaps in place of Damar Hamlin.
When the Bills released their initial injury report Wednesday, every member of the 53-man roster was projected as a participant of some kind. Though, because the Bills chose to do a walk-through to begin the week, that injury report can be taken with a grain of salt because it wasn’t an actual practice. When the team finally got on the field Thursday, there was one noteworthy development with a key part of their offense.
Starting right tackle Spencer Brown, who has been trying to play through a back injury he suffered against the Los Angeles Rams in Week 5, was not on the practice field at all. Brown wound up playing in Week 6 against the Las Vegas Raiders, sat out their Week 8 game against the Baltimore Ravens after their bye week, then played Monday night against the Minnesota Vikings. On top of that, Brown suffered an ankle injury early in Monday’s game and gutted through the rest of the evening. After practice, Brown was in the huddle with his teammates, but he was in sandals with a big wrap on his right ankle.
It wouldn’t be stunning if they are playing the long game to give him rest for the back and ankle injuries, given his importance and the Bills’ being on a short week. They also have another short week on the horizon, taking on the Kansas City Chiefs in Week 12 on Thanksgiving with only three days after their Week 11 game against the Miami Dolphins. Resting Brown could be important. Missing Thursday’s practice is usually not a good sign. There has been only one case this season of a player missing the first two practices of the week and still playing in the game that weekend. The good news for the Bills is reserve swing tackle Tylan Grable has performed admirably in spot starts the last two games.
When the Bills acquired Hooker from the Tennessee Titans, the remainder of his 2026 cap hit was $4.44 million. Though that isn’t a wild number, it was still too much for the Bills to absorb, with around $4 million in cap space heading into deadline day, according to the NFL Players Association’s daily salary-cap report Tuesday. To complete the deal, the Bills had to clear up cap space. Rather than going with a smaller restructure to save on outside linebacker Greg Rousseau, wide receiver Khalil Shakir and/or Christian Benford, the Bills opted for the maximum savings they could get in one move — restructuring left tackle Dion Dawkins’ deal to clear space. The Rousseau, Shakir and Benford restructures would have netted roughly $1.48 million, $639K and $532K, which, when combined, would have yielded $2.65 million in savings — more than enough to onboard Hooker and still have some breathing room. Even Rousseau by himself would have been enough and still left the Bills with breathing room.
The Dawkins restructure yielded $5.3 million in savings, but it raises more questions than Rousseau, Shakir or Benford would have. With the younger trio, there is no question any of them would be in Buffalo for this and the next two seasons, at least. However, with Dawkins turning 33 in April and his play having declined over the last two years, this restructure certainly has more strings attached. With this restructure, the Bills gave up the chance to save around $11 million in cap space if they moved on from Dawkins this offseason.
That is notable, given the Bills usually have cap-compliance troubles heading into the next offseason since Josh Allen signed his initial contract extension. However, it does not mean the Bills have to keep Dawkins on the team next year, and they will still have some optionality in the offseason regardless of the restructure. Because the Bills executed the move ahead of Week 10, half of Dawkins’ $15.465 million base salary had already been paid to this year’s salary cap, which lowered the amount they could restructure.
As a result, though the Bills won’t save the $11 million next year to move on, they’d still get around $7.6 million in savings because there is no more guaranteed money remaining on the contract and there isn’t a decision deadline for a roster bonus being due. If the Bills believed in Grable or Jude Bowry to take over the job, or they drafted a new left tackle in the first round, they could move on from Dawkins and save without hesitation.
The other piece of it is this: Why did the Bills feel the need to max out Dawkins’ cap space when smaller moves were available? They did so early into trade deadline day, which might insinuate the Bills were looking to do more than trade for Hooker, shopping for a second player at the deadline. Rather than piecing it all together one by one, the Bills instead opted to pull the biggest lever, which also maxed out how much they would owe to the 2027 salary cap.
The additional cap space gives the Bills some flexibility for the rest of the year if any veteran players are waived or become free agents to add to their 53-man roster. And if they don’t use any of that additional cap space, they can roll it over into the 2027 offseason, which would cancel out almost all of the cap they pushed down the road from the Dawkins restructure if they cut him. It wasn’t a move with dire implications, because they could only restructure half his salary, but it might make their cap-compliance journey in the 2027 offseason a bit more complicated.

Projected inactives vs. Jets: WR Skyler Bell, RT Spencer Brown, DL Greg Gaines, OLB Mike Danna, S Jalon Kilgore

full_text:
The Steelers and Bengals, both 6-2, will meet on "Sunday Night Football" with first place in the division on the line. Barry Reeger / Imagn Images
Each week during the season and occasionally during the offseason, our panel of AFC North writers tackles the issues, trending topics and looming decisions around the division. This week, we’re looking back at the trade deadline and ahead to “Sunday Night Football.”
Did the team you cover have to rescind a trade ahead of Tuesday’s deadline because it didn’t understand the NFL’s compensatory pick rules? Or was something else the barrier to real player movement?
Mike DeFabo (Steelers): Every time Steelers general manager Omar Khan talks publicly about his strategy, he says he’s trying to win now without sacrificing the future. That’s easier said than done in the new world where teams that believe they are contenders are doing everything in their power to make an aggressive push at the deadline.
Until Pittsburgh finds its future franchise quarterback, the Steelers have been especially reluctant to give up draft capital. The team also has some level of optimism that wide receivers Michael Pittman Jr. and Roman Wilson will return in the coming weeks to provide a needed boost in the passing game. That’s the company line. Personally, I see it as another risk-averse move from a franchise that often looks to minimize risk above all else.
Paul Dehner Jr. (Bengals): Can we insert the meme of the guy on the couch, puzzled and pointing to himself? That’s probably a better explanation than anything I would write here. Also, maybe the Bengals should hire that guy from the meme just to read Nick Korte tweets to them.
I don’t think whether the Bengals landed Arnold Ebiketie changed the potential for this season. It’s mostly embarrassing . But as somebody well-versed in embarrassment, I can tell you that will cycle out. The Bengals can win on Sunday, and nobody will care anymore. The real story will be whether their reluctance to part with any real draft capital for an addition will hinder this defense from reaching the level necessary to get to the Super Bowl.
Zac Jackson (Browns): I still think the Browns-Bengals/A.J. McCarron fax-machine thing, with Hue Jackson trying to be the boss, made for a better story. But what do I know? Anyway, the Browns are still mostly focused on the future, making it largely unsurprising that they stayed out of the deadline-related action.
Cleveland will be a team making plenty of headlines come March and April, and general manager Andrew Berry will likely be involved in trades then that include some of the 11 2027 draft picks the Browns currently own.
Jeff Zrebiec (Ravens) : One thing you don’t have to worry about is the Ravens understanding the compensatory rules. Those rules are like the Bible at their team facility. The Ravens made three trade acquisitions over the past two months despite the state of the team suggesting that they probably should have been sellers . Why weren’t they? They simply aren’t ready to give up on the season, and they are close enough to the wild-card mix that they felt it was premature to wave the white flag.
They also have a young coaching staff trying to establish itself, and stripping the team of talent in-season would have made it tough to make any notable progress in Year 1. But the biggest barrier of all was that they simply didn’t have many trade chips. Fans were screaming for them to deal vets Ronnie Stanley, Mark Andrews, Marlon Humphrey and Roquan Smith, but either their current form or the size of their contracts — in some cases, both — made trading those players nearly impossible.
Are you comfortable saying this division is a two-team race with nine weeks left? Or are Cleveland and Baltimore still not dead?
DeFabo: I’m 90 percent sure the Bengals and Steelers will be the two teams representing the AFC North in the playoffs. But you can never be 100 percent sure of anything in this division. Lamar Jackson is such a huge part of Baltimore’s ceiling. Without him for several weeks (or longer), I don’t know if the Ravens can keep pace. The Browns are showing some cracks. Their team, full of young talent, may be a year away from contending.
Dehner Jr.: I’m not counting the Browns out yet. Four in a row at home keeps the light of hope on in my eyes. Plus, they have two games with Cincinnati. If the Browns can find an answer for the Bengals’ offense and pull off the sweep, the entire dynamic of the race changes. Do I think it’s likely? No. I also didn’t think we’d still be talking about Deshaun Watson playing meaningful NFL snaps, so my mind is still adjusting to this Browns season. I just really like the roster around him and want to see the next two weeks before officially declaring them divisionally dead.
Jackson: I am comfortable saying that right now, with the main qualifier being that a lot can change in a week in the NFL. The Browns are mathematically alive and still will be when December begins, but they began Week 10 as a bottom-10 offense in scoring, first downs, success rate, sacks allowed and plays of 10-plus yards. The Browns can only keep up if things change drastically or if they start forcing five turnovers per game. Joe Burrow has more touchdown passes (16) in his last four games than the Browns have touchdowns (15) all season.
Zrebiec: The Browns and Ravens, assuming Jacoby Brissett brings competence to the quarterback position, may hang around for a little while. But yeah, I’m pretty comfortable in declaring this a two-team race. Any path to the Ravens getting back into this thing would probably require them to win four straight before their four-game division finish, and nothing they have shown over the last month suggests they have four straight wins in them.
Meanwhile, both the Bengals and Steelers are playing extremely well, and they’ve opened up some space. The Bengals’ schedule the rest of the way is extremely forgiving. I know this isn’t necessarily the question, but if the Bengals win Sunday, they could have the division wrapped up by Christmas.
Before it gets cold(er) and temporarily gloomy for some, specifically the loser of Sunday night’s Steelers-Bengals game, what’s the best case for optimism for the team you cover? Is there something that’s better or brighter than it might currently appear?
DeFabo: The Steelers are playing their brand of football, as the repeated investments in the trenches are finally paying dividends. Pittsburgh ranks second in total rushing EPA (11.84) and third in yards per carry (4.9). Defensively, the Steelers have allowed the fourth-fewest points per game (18.0) and rank fifth in EPA/play (0.11). To push them over the top, the Steelers badly need DK Metcalf to emerge from his slump and become the WR1 they’re paying him to be.
Dehner Jr.: The Bengals defense. I know, this take might be worse than my Browns opinion. We’ve seen an uptick from the linebackers in recent weeks, and Dexter Lawrence remains a game-changing disruption up the middle. More importantly, the Bengals have exactly one game left against an offense currently ranked in the top 12 in EPA/play (home against Kansas City). The degree of difficulty, plus the pressure the Cincinnati offense will put on a slate packed with flawed opponents, sets the defense up to post a productive second half —more importantly, one that provides momentum and confidence for a potential playoff run.
Jackson: The Browns have nice offensive pieces. They also have some good defensive pieces, and cornerback Denzel Ward is still as good as anyone at the position in his ninth NFL season. But optimism for Cleveland eventually building a legitimate, explosive offense lies in rookie wide receivers KC Concepcion and Denzel Boston and second-year tight end Harold Fannin Jr., all 22 years old and extremely gifted. None are finished products, but the collective arrow is pointing way up.
Zrebiec: I left M&T Bank Stadium last Thursday night after watching that Ravens-Jaguars…

full_text:
From left, guard Dalton Risner, center Ted Karras and left tackle Orlando Brown Jr. have been part of an offensive line that's provided top-tier pass protection this season. Thomas Shea / Imagn Images
CINCINNATI — Former Pittsburgh Steelers head coach Mike Tomlin was asked on NBC’s “Sunday Night Football” broadcast last weekend how exactly a team should attempt to stop the dominant Cincinnati Bengals offense.
His thoughtful schematic analysis started with a Tomlin-ism.
“First of all,” he said, “if you don’t have a four-man rush, you’re running on the beach trying to stop these guys.”
That’s the book, straight from Tomlin, but it could also come from just about any opposing defensive coordinator who’s likely hyperventilating while watching film of Joe Burrow, Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins this season. The weapons are too talented. The Bengals drop back more than any team in the NFL.
Get home with four or die trying.
Burrow is currently captaining the Death Star. Cincinnati isn’t merely the best offense in the NFL lately; it is lapping the field.
Highlights and fantasy points dominate news cycles. They thrust Burrow toward the top of the MVP conversation. His receiving duo has been compared to Marvin Harrison and Reggie Wayne, Randy Moss and Cris Carter. And they have Tomlin talking.
For all of the Bengals’ star power, the rise of their offensive line to one of the NFL’s best pass-protecting units unlocked a new stratosphere.
“Obviously, there’s been a lot of conjecture about (the offense) and the style,” offensive coordinator Dan Pitcher said. “The thing I come back to is: As insane as Tee and Ja’Marr have played and Joe is playing right now, the foundation for all of that is you have to keep him on his two feet.”
The Bengals’ offensive line ranks fourth in the NFL in pass-blocking efficiency, according to PFF. This is after holding the same ranking over the second half of last season, after Burrow returned from toe surgery. The unit ranked 27th in 2024, Burrow’s last full season.
After years of searching for answers in the draft and free agency, the Bengals finally found continuity and protection for the franchise quarterback.
Every Bengals opponent besides the Tennessee Titans and Baltimore Ravens has endured one of its three worst pressure-rate games of the season against Cincinnati.
“Those guys, No. 1, I think they’re all playing at a really high level,” Burrow said of the offensive line. “The cohesion that they have and the trust that they have and the relationships that they have upfront is fun to be around, and fun to watch and fun to be a part of. Our offense is open to so many different things. We’re more explosive than we have been in years, and that plays a huge part of it. It’s hard to push the ball down the field if you can’t protect for that extra second, second and a half in order to do it. You can find ways to do it, but it’s a lot harder. The guys that we have, I mean, they’re lights out; they’re playing some of the best football in the league.”
You can listen to the praise, but follow the reps for the proof.
The Bengals have the league’s most pass-heavy offense. They drop back 61 percent of the time on first downs, four percent more than any other team.
That’s also four percent more than any other season for coach Zac Taylor in Cincinnati.
Meanwhile, the Bengals rank fifth in the NFL in pressure percentage allowed against a four-man rush.
Taylor has always had trust in Burrow, but the trust established in this offensive line literally changed the game script.
“The amount of times we throw the football directly shows my confidence I have in our offensive line,” Taylor said. “Because if we weren’t, if I didn’t have that confidence, then we wouldn’t do that. We’d be looking at other ways to manufacture yardage and points. And we operate the way we do because I got a lot of confidence in how they do it.”
Right tackle Amarius Mims played the first half of the season at an All-Pro level, emerging as arguably the best right tackle in the NFL. He’s tied for the best pressure rate allowed among tackles, and he has pitched clean sheets against a who’s who of the league’s best edge rushers.
That includes T.J. Watt, in a September loss to the Pittsburgh Steelers. A rematch looms Sunday, with both teams tied for first place in the AFC North at 6-2.
A payday landing him at or near the top of the tackle market seems on the horizon for Mims, who is extension-eligible at the end of this season. He has become an organizational cornerstone in Cincinnati.
“You’ve got to put 71 in the 1, 5, 9, 97 conversation,” center Ted Karras said, referring to Mims alongside Chase, Higgins, Burrow and Dexter Lawrence, respectively, as the team’s top stars.
By bringing back the same five O-line starters for the first time in Burrow’s career, the Bengals trusted a collection of linemen at various career stages to create a unique chemistry that allows them to thrive in one of the NFL’s most challenging roles.
Right guard Dalton Risner found his home after spending the 2025 preseason practicing by himself in a park near his house. Karras, a five-time team captain, is the leader and soul of the group. Left tackle Dylan Fairchild is still looking to establish himself as a third-round pick in 2025. Veteran tackle Orlando Brown Jr. endured rough patches early in the season, but settled down on the left side. Even the ball carriers, Chase Brown and Samaje Perine, rate as two of the league’s best pass-protecting running backs.
“Every game that they play together, and every rep they take and every look they get together, they talk about it and they improve on it,” Taylor said. “And if they don’t get it right, it really bothers them. And it bothers them to their core. And it’s going to carry over to their Thursday night dinner and all the stuff that they do together. That’s going to be a big topic of conversation.”
The conversation starts with Burrow being on pace for the lowest sack percentage and highest completion percentage of his career.
That leaves opposing defensive coordinators scheming to always get home with the four-man rush while using extra bodies in the secondary to handle Higgins, Chase and Mike Gesicki.
The line’s performance is shutting that down and changing the math.
“If they have to pull resources out of coverage to generate a rush, then, if there’s any team in the league who dictates that the defense should be devoting as much or all their resources to coverage, it would probably be us,” Pitcher said. “So, if they feel like they have to pull resources out of coverage to generate a rush, then certainly they’re putting themselves in a difficult spot in the back end. … That’s the conundrum.”
The Bengals traditionally saw more two-high safety defense than any team in the league because of how the offense is built, but more recently opposing defenses have played more single-high and man coverage as they search for answers.
Knowing the Bengals will pass in situations normally pegged for run or pass plays adds to the offensive line’s challenge of keeping Burrow clean.
“We have one of the more unique situations for an NFL O-line,” Karras said. “We’ll get junk fronts on second-and-7. No one else has to deal with that in the NFL. We are trained very well to handle that.”
Opponents get desperate to stop this offense. The Titans tried more man coverage and single high. The Atlanta Falcons left A.J. Terrell in man against Chase on a deep touchdown pass to open Sunday’s 34-17 Bengals win. The Baltimore Ravens threw random blitzes that left Higgins and Chase in one-on-one coverage, which was the case on the fourth of five straight Bengals touchdown drives in a Week 7 win at Baltimore.
Burrow is a rhythm passer, and his line is helping him find his flow. That has created panic on the opposite sideline.

title: After Week 1 meltdown, the Packers are ready to handle Vikings defense The Vikings may have one of the league's best defenses, but the Packers have seen it before — and bulked up their offense in the meantime. Matt Schneidman
summary:

GREEN BAY, Wis. — Jordan Morgan was a disaster in Week 1 against the Minnesota Vikings at U.S. Bank Stadium.
The Green Bay Packers left tackle and 2024 first-round pick, starting his first meaningful game in the NFL at his college position, crumbled under the pressure of an incessant defense and arguably the toughest road environment in the league.

full_text:
Jordan Morgan and the offensive line have improved significantly since they were picked apart by the Vikings in Week 1. Stacy Revere / Getty Images
GREEN BAY, Wis. — Jordan Morgan was a disaster in Week 1 against the Minnesota Vikings at U.S. Bank Stadium.
The Green Bay Packers left tackle and 2024 first-round pick, starting his first meaningful game in the NFL at his college position, crumbled under the pressure of an incessant defense and arguably the toughest road environment in the league.
In a 39-22 loss that afternoon, Morgan surrendered five pressures (still tied for his season high), three quarterback hits (also a season high) and committed a false start on the third offensive play of the season, according to Pro Football Focus.
Entering Week 10 against the same opponent, this time at Lambeau Field, Morgan’s recent improvement is a microcosm of the offensive line’s growth since that fateful day in Minneapolis. Morgan’s last two games were his first two without allowing pressure, per PFF. In 79 combined pass-blocking snaps in wins over the Carolina Panthers and New England Patriots, Morgan has begun showing why the Packers entrusted him to protect quarterback Jordan Love’s blindside.
The Vikings still feature an unrelenting pass rush and probably the NFL’s best defense. But the surging Packers should feel much better about their left tackle and the others tasked with protecting the MVP candidate behind them against Minnesota defensive coordinator Brian Flores’ unit.
“Everybody’s confident,” Morgan said Thursday about the offensive line. “We’re 10 weeks in. We should be feeling good.”
The Packers felt anything but good after Week 1. They saw a 22-10 lead evaporate as the Vikings scored 29 unanswered points over the game’s final 18 minutes, largely because Love’s protection disappeared . That day, Morgan started his second career game at left tackle (the first came in a meaningless Week 18 game last season when backups played in the same stadium). Left guard Donovan Jennings and right guard Jacob Monk started their first career games. Right tackle Zach Bako-Bewele was still rounding into form from offseason knee surgery.
The result? Love weathered 15 quarterback hits. Morgan gave up those five pressures, Monk four, Bako-Bewele three, center Sean Rhyan three and Jennings two, per PFF.
Fast-forward nine weeks and the offensive line has improved vastly in pass protection. Morgan, the only constant on the offensive line this season, said he feels much more comfortable at left tackle now than he did facing the Vikings in Week 1 .
Over the first three weeks, the Packers ranked 31st in pressure percentage allowed (44.7) while Love took the most quarterback hits in the league (31, eight more than anyone else), according to TruMedia. From Weeks 4-9, the Packers ranked 13th in pressure percentage allowed (33.8) while Love took 26 hits, tied for 17th most over that span.
Tight end Tucker Kraft was asked Thursday where the Packers have grown most since Week 1.
“I’d say our offensive line, for sure,” Kraft said.
Morgan has stabilized his play lately, while veteran left guard (and now right guard) Laken Tomlinson has been a godsend since signing with the Packers after the Week 3 debacle against the Atlanta Falcons. Rhyan was sturdy at center, and 2025 seventh-round pick John Williams, who never played center in a game, has filled in admirably the last three games after Rhyan and Monk suffered injuries on the opening drive against the Detroit Lions in Week 7.
A combination of Travis Glover, Tomlinson and Kevin Zeitler has vastly improved Monk’s right-guard play, and Anthony Belton is finding his footing at right tackle after taking over for Bako-Bewele, who suffered a season-ending knee injury in Week 2.
Added experience at guard should help against Flores’ exotic pressure looks this time around. The Packers weren’t good enough mentally or physically before and after the snap in Week 1, so that will need to change to win their sixth game in the last seven and keep pace in a diabolical NFC North.
The Packers will start Morgan at left tackle, likely Williams at center (with Rhyan still not practicing) and Belton at right tackle. The guard spots will feature some combination of Aaron Banks, Tomlinson and Zeitler, veterans who have seen everything in the league. Packers coach Matt LaFleur wouldn’t divulge his plan to reporters this week, and understandably so.
Another variable that should help the Packers: no U.S. Bank Stadium crowd noise. Offensive coordinator Adam Stenavich said that building is one of the toughest to play in across the league. Pre-snap communication should be much easier for Love and his linemen without a silent count Sunday, which LaFleur said “makes a significant difference.”
“Oh, man. It makes a huge difference,” Love said Wednesday. “Silent count, it’s easier for D-line to get a little bit of a get-off. They kind of know what’s coming. But I think, too, just playing there, the environment, the noise, all those things, it throws communication off for an offense. We can’t hear each other communicating as well, so I think always playing at home, having our crowd, not dealing with crowd noise, not dealing with silent count, all those things, definitely make a huge factor.”
The Vikings lead the NFL with a 45.6 percent pressure rate, according to TruMedia. They blitz on 69.7 percent of dropbacks. Second place in the league is 42.2 percent. Flores specializes in presenting unique looks before the snap and doing something unexpected after. Love said this week that he’s mostly just guessing what the Vikings will do once the ball is snapped.
“You’ve still got to go execute,” LaFleur added. “This is … one of, if not the top defense in the league.”
Flores will get the better of the Packers’ offense sometimes, LaFleur said, adding that it’ll be key to survive those instances and not make a bad play worse, like fumbling or throwing up a prayer that gets intercepted.
Love will need to tap into his quick release, which he’s utilized effectively at times this season.
“When you know they’re coming, you’ve gotta find ways to get the ball out because they’re bringing extra guys every time and you know that,” Love said. “So we’ve got to have a great plan, and I think we do have that. It comes down to just seeing it, not panicking when you get those pressures and just getting the ball out quick.”
Love found success in Week 1 despite the late Vikings onslaught. He completed only 21 of 42 passes, but threw for 387 yards and two touchdowns, with a late interception. Nine weeks in, Love ranks eighth in passer rating when pressured, according to TruMedia, and has thrown for 115 more yards when pressured (919) than any other NFL quarterback.
To succeed against the Vikings on Sunday, it’ll require more of the same from the Packers’ MVP-caliber quarterback, but this time much better from an offensive line that now looks capable of delivering.
“Obviously playing them without the crowd noise is easier because you don’t have to deal with that,” Stenavich said. “That being said, they’re still very aggressive. They still present a lot of issues. That’s just who they are. They have really good players that are all tied together.
“It’s pretty impressive to watch, and it’s going to be a really big challenge.”

full_text:
Chiefs defensive tackle Chris Jones picked up his first two full sacks of the season on Sunday against the Jets. Denny Medley / Imagn Images
KANSAS CITY, Mo. — Kansas City Chiefs defensive tackle Chris Jones was in a good mood, so he decided to give team radio play-by-play announcer Mitch Holthus the scoop.
Minutes after Sunday’s blowout win over the New York Jets, Jones was asked about his second sack of the game, which took place when he lined up as a defensive end.
Jones smiled. He was out of position then … on purpose.
“I was supposed to be inside and Drue (Tranquill) was supposed to be outside. But I just refused to move inside,” Jones told Holthus on the team’s postgame video show . “It led to a sack, though.”
And likely some consequences afterward.
Jones predicted then that he was “going to get cursed out” by defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo in the meeting room for freelancing on a critical third down.
The result was the result, though. Jones picked up his second sack of the day, while part of his most productive outing of the season.
“I’m still Chris Jones, man. Don’t let it fool you,” Jones told Holthus. “I’m still Chris Jones.”
It was a welcome sight for a defense that had waited all season for the old Chris to arrive.
Jones, a seven-time Pro Bowler and three-time first-team All-Pro, hadn’t come close to that level of play during the Chiefs’ first seven games of 2026. In that time, he had just 0.5 sacks and also was posting career lows in pressure percentage.
That was before Sunday’s breakout. According to NFL’s Next Gen Stats, Jones had a season-high six pressures while contributing two sacks on 29 pass rushes. Three of those pressures were under 2.5 seconds.
For that effort, Jones was named the AFC’s defensive player of the week for Week 9.
Defensive line coach Joe Cullen, meanwhile, pointed to another play — one that didn’t show up on the stat sheet — when Jones impressed Sunday.
Late in the first quarter, with the Jets facing a third-and-6 just outside the red zone, Jones used a swim move to create pressure, then gave an extra burst of effort just before quarterback Geno Smith released the ball.
The result was a rushed throw — with Smith unable to hit receiver Adonai Mitchell down the sideline, despite Mitchell having a step on his defender for a potential touchdown.
Cullen complimented Jones’ strain to finish, describing it as a “great rush.”
“Obviously,” Cullen said, “he dominated in the game.”
The defense reached a different level because of it. The Chiefs’ 50 percent pressure rate against the Jets, per Next Gen Stats, was a season high, as were their five sacks.
Even that had some competition. Defensive end George Karlaftis — who also had two sacks Sunday — picked up his second sack early in the fourth quarter.
Jones said that only motivated him to not get one-upped.
“I told him I’ve got to get another one before this game ends,” Jones told Holthus. “So we were just having fun and feeding off of each other. I think in order for us to keep this defense going, it’s going to be up to George (and I) to set the tone of the defense.”
A few outside indications predicted Jones’ standout performance was coming. In fact, his Pro Football Focus defensive grade against the Jets (90.4) finished higher than his previous two game grades combined (36.1 and 51.7).
In fairness, Jones has been on previous injury reports with a calf injury. He played through it, though, and hasn’t had an injury designation the last two weeks.
On Thursday, Cullen disagreed with any suggestion that Jones needed outside motivation to jump-start his season.
“It’s like anything: When you have the opportunity to win a one-on-one, you’ve got to win it,” Cullen said. “But he’s a self-starter. Chris gets going.”
If Jones plays like this, the Chiefs have to be optimistic about their defensive prospects.
Young players like defensive linemen Ashton Gillotte and R Mason Thomas seem to be getting better each week. And 2026 first-round rookies Mansoor Delane (at cornerback) and Peter Woods (defensive tackle) didn’t even play this past week because of what are expected to be short-term injuries.
Even with a young lineup, the defense is trending toward a top-10 unit. FTN Fantasy’s all-encompassing DVOA metric ranks K.C. as the NFL’s 11th-best defense. Meanwhile, in expected points added per play, the Chiefs defense is eighth.
Combine that with a Patrick Mahomes-led offense, and the Chiefs could profile as a top AFC contender once the postseason starts.
A big part of that comes down to Jones, though — and what level of production the Chiefs get from him over the final few months.
“We always say he’s the piston that drives the engine,” Cullen said. “And as he goes, we go.”

full_text:
Kirk Cousins and Kevin O'Connell know each other's strengths and weaknesses, and their reunion in Minnesota has a chance to be special. David Berding / Getty Images
EAGAN, Minn. — Kevin O’Connell stepped into the media center in the basement of the Minnesota Vikings’ practice facility and smirked.
The coach couldn’t help himself. It was Wednesday, and reporters had filled most of the seats in the room. It was as packed as it had been in a long time, a window into what it meant for quarterback Kirk Cousins to return.
O’Connell’s smile, evident even before he sat behind the microphone, spoke to how much he understood this moment. After three years apart, the stars aligned to create an almost Disney-like level of theater. O’Connell acknowledged this. Then he arrived at the cold, hard reality: This injection of hope must bring about offensive improvement.
“We understand the point of the season that we’re at right now,” O’Connell said. “We need to specifically start playing better on offense to be the team that we can become.”
The Vikings’ offensive output has been jarring, to put it mildly. Completed forward passes and first downs feel like grand achievements. The statistics tell the same story.
Minnesota ranks 32nd in the NFL in offensive success rate at 33.9 percent, the lowest of any offense through nine weeks in the last four seasons. Inaccurate passes have been a theme. A tepid run game hasn’t alleviated the burden, either. Collectively, the unit has appeared to lack joy and cohesion.
Nine regular-season games remain to flip this script. The Vikings will play five of their final seven at home. Given their 6-2 start and the current bill of health for their championship-caliber defense and special teams units, these circumstances present a massive opportunity.
For Cousins, of course — but also for O’Connell.
The 41-year-old head coach is the team’s offensive play caller and chief play designer. For years, he has also been one of the franchise’s primary decision-makers, particularly regarding quarterbacks. O’Connell orchestrated the 2024 pre-draft plan that led to J.J. McCarthy’s selection. O’Connell helped shepherd Sam Darnold’s career revival. This past spring, O’Connell championed the signing of Kyler Murray.
Wednesday, when asked about the dynamic between Cousins and Murray, he referred to the offseason “competition” between Murray and McCarthy. It was almost a nod to all of the team’s quarterback uncertainty over the last three years, a smorgasbord of decisions worth second-guessing.
“I don’t think you can have a competition during the season,” O’Connell said. “I know it’s hard enough — well documented — during the offseason.”
Re-establishing a semblance of offensive momentum is not at all about validating the overused “quarterback whisperer” moniker for O’Connell. Instead, it is a chance for him to restore the widely shared belief among NFL colleagues and evaluators that his Vikings offense will produce with professionalism.
At its best, O’Connell’s system looks buttoned up. Play-action passes tie together with run concepts. Route distributions flow in concert with the quarterback’s footwork. Almost everything is purposeful. The Vikings throw over the middle with anticipation. They turn their backs to the defense. They disperse the ball to all areas of the field, ensuring that elite players such as Justin Jefferson and Jordan Addison have opportunities to create yards after the catch.
When the offense is working correctly, few elements of the Vikings’ attack capture the need for crispness better than its pre-snap operation. It matters how the players break the huddle. How the quarterback commands the protection adjustments requires a high level of detail. In fact, O’Connell’s offense reaches its fullest form when the quarterback has the acumen to assess the defensive picture and check into the best play.
Minnesota has not been able to do that for a season and a half, since Darnold left in the spring of 2025. Cousins offers that possibility. His shared experience with O’Connell, dating back to their time together in 2017 in Washington, helps fill the gaps of any unspoken preferences.
“Kevin knows me,” Cousins said. “He knows what I do well. He knows what I don’t do well. Kevin knows what I can handle. Kevin knows what I can’t handle. I think that helps. Not just that he knows your strengths, but that he also knows your weaknesses. As a result, he’s going to try to protect you — and not have you do things where he goes, ‘You know, that’s not how Kirk functions.’”
Likewise, Cousins knows O’Connell. He knows O’Connell’s strengths and weaknesses. As a result, he can cover for any blind spots in a way that might not be apparent to anyone besides the two of them.
This partnership has that potential. To push Cousins. To push the Vikings’ offense forward. And to push O’Connell toward a plan and a philosophy that adequately complement the Vikings’ defense and special teams.
History gives us a window into what it could look like. In Week 7 of the 2023 season, the week before Cousins tore his Achilles, he commanded O’Connell’s offense masterfully in a Monday night win over the San Francisco 49ers. He changed plays at the line of scrimmage. He threw the ball accurately. He ended up 35-of-45 passing for 378 yards, two touchdowns and an interception. He worked with O’Connell, and O’Connell worked with them.
Both received the credit on the national stage, another reminder that the most successful quarterbacks and coaches could not be special without one another.

full_text:
J.J. McCarthy (No.18) leaps alongside Malik Nabers after tossing a 66-yard touchdown pass to Isaiah Likely. AP Photo / Adam Hunger
EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. — It looked like the play of the game.
With the New York Giants down three to the Washington Commanders and facing a third-and-seven situation with a little more than halfway to go in the fourth quarter, Giants quarterback J.J. McCarthy took on the blitz. Commanders safety Nick Cross broke free into McCarthy’s face, but it didn’t matter as McCarthy fired a pass, splitting defenders and hitting a barely open Isaiah Likely.
The tight end caught the ball and took off running.
“J.J. threw a great ball,” Likely said. “I saw nothing but green grass, gave me a great open field block and at that point you’ve just got to just score.”
Likely did just that, turning what looked like a dead-in-the water play into a 66-yard touchdown. MetLife Stadium erupted as the Thursday Night Football crowd celebrated.
“The touchdown pass was just crazy good,” coach John Harbaugh said. “Isaiah obviously housed it. But that’s probably as good a play as you’re going to see in the National Football League all season, honestly.”
But because this is the 2026 Giants, that didn’t end up being the play of the game. There was still a half a quarter to be played and this year, that might as well be an entire new game with how much drama the Giants consistently pack into the final minutes. And unfortunately for Giants fans, that McCarthy dart will be included in a 24-21 loss rather than remembered in a victory.
But despite the final score and a final comeback drive falling short, that throw was as good an example as any this season of what McCarthy has brought to the Giants since they traded a 2027 fifth-round pick to the Minnesota Vikings in exchange for the 23-year-old quarterback.
McCarthy arrived at the end of September to a campaign on the brink following Jaxson Dart’s season-ending knee injury. The Giants turned to veteran backup Jameis Winston in the meantime but as soon as the trade happened, McCarthy was there waiting in the wings. Coaching staff finally put McCarthy in late in Week 6 and McCarthy nearly pulled off a comeback victory over the Saints. It was enough that the coaching staff stuck with McCarthy.
Through three starts, McCarthy has gone 2-1, steadying the season and keeping the Giants atop the NFC East with a 5-3-1 record.
It’s not all been pretty. McCarthy’s lone interception as a starter came at the worst time Thursday. A deep pass intended for Malik Nabers was picked by Rasul Douglas and ended up being the final offensive play of the game to seal Washington’s win.
“My thought process was pop it up to my playmakers,” McCarthy said. “Have them go make a play. Could have bought more time with a little bit more depth. But at the end of the day the thought process was, ‘Give it to one of my guys and have him go make a play.'”
McCarthy exited and later returned in Sunday’s win over the Eagles with a hip injury, completing just 12-of-19 passes and throwing no touchdowns. McCarthy then turned around on the short week to throw for a career-high 293 passing yards. McCarthy completed 23-of-36 passes, adding 34 yards on the ground on six carries.
“Man, resilience,” Winston said of what McCarthy showed Thursday. “He played well. He saw it well. They did some unique things on defense. He found a way to give us a chance to win, and as a quarterback, that’s the job.”
Can he keep doing it? After a long weekend, McCarthy and the Giants will get tested. In the next four weeks, the Giants will face three of the league’s top defenses: the Seattle Seahawks, the San Francisco 49ers and the Jacksonville Jaguars.
First up comes a 6-2 Jaguars team that just made a major investment in its defense, orchestrating three trades ahead of the trade deadline to boost the team’s Super Bowl hopes. The Giants won’t be in primetime but they will be in the 4 p.m. ET window after the game was flexed out of the 1 p.m. slot. It’s another opportunity for McCarthy to keep giving the Giants solid quarterback play.
Given McCarthy’s burgeoning consistency, the quarterback said he just feels good about his preparation going into each week and the intention behind every play.
“There is no gray-area going into each play and I just really appreciate the heck out of that,” McCarthy said.
“It is all about building, constantly growing, and that is what we are focused on. Being in the League for a little over two years now, seeing defenses that I have seen before and running concepts that I have run before, everything seems to be slowing down for me.
“Just being able to keep stacking and keep growing one percent every single day and I am just so blessed to be in this offense and so blessed to be a part of this organization.
“This football team is going to get better from this, I know that.”

full_text:
Despite some big plays, J.J. McCarthy lost his first home start in a Giants uniform as the Commanders snatched a late win. Robert Deutsch / Imagn Images
EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. — Thursday night’s game was following a familiar script. The gritty New York Giants held a narrow lead late over the Washington Commanders. They seemed to be making all the big plays to close out another win. Until they didn’t.
The Giants fell victim to the type of late-game gaffes they have avoided this season, stumbling to a 24-21 loss .
“It’s a missed opportunity, but like I told the guys, it would be great to win the game, but it doesn’t change our goals or our opportunity going forward,” coach John Harbaugh said. “It’s a tough loss. It’s the National Football League. You’re going to lose some games.”
The Giants dropped to 5-3-1, with the Commanders improving to 3-5-1 to pull within two games in the NFC East. The Commanders now have the tiebreaker over the Giants due to their tie in Week 5. The 4-5 Dallas Cowboys are also lurking.
“It’s disappointing, but you can’t let it bring you down,” Harbaugh said. “It would have been nice to open the lead in the division. We didn’t open it up as much as we could have if we had gotten the win. We’ve got a lot of tough games (left). It’s going to be (eight) dog fights.”
With the Giants trailing by three points midway through the fourth quarter, Giants quarterback J.J. McCarthy delivered a strike to Isaiah Likely with an unblocked blitzer in his face. The tight end snagged the pass between two Commanders defenders and raced 66 yards for the potential game-winning touchdown.
“(McCarthy) threw some dimes out there,” Harbaugh said. “The throw to Isaiah Likely with the blitz was just crazy good. That’s probably as good a play as you’re going to see in the National Football League all season.”
That’s when the script started to feel familiar, as the Giants defense intercepted Commanders quarterback Jayden Daniels on consecutive possessions to put New York in position to win another tight game. But the offense failed to close it out.
After safety Jevon Holland picked off a Daniels pass — the first interception of the season for Washington’s quarterback — the Giants faced a third-and-1 at their own 11-yard line. As has become the norm in short yardage, backup quarterback Jameis Winston came in to run a sneak. Winston was initially granted a first down, but he was marked short after the Commanders challenged the spot.
Facing fourth-and-inches from their own 11-yard line, Harbaugh sent his offense back onto the field. Harbaugh spoke after the game about how the team’s spirit is of courage and not fear, but he wasn’t willing to take that type of risk. Winston tried to draw the Commanders offside, awkwardly incorporating the song “Who Let the Dogs Out” into his cadence . It was unsuccessful and the Giants punted.
“I wasn’t seriously thinking about going for it there,” Harbaugh said. “I thought maybe we could draw them offsides.”
The defense responded by making another potential game-sealing play, as safety Ar’Darius Washington intercepted a fourth-down pass by Daniels with 2:15 remaining. But again, the offense couldn’t close the door.
Cam Skattebo picked up seven yards on two carries to set up a third-and-3 at Washington’s 39-yard line. Rather than giving the ball to Skattebo, who had 78 yards on 18 carries, offensive coordinator Matt Nagy made the odd decision to call a McCarthy keeper from an empty backfield. The Commanders weren’t fooled, as linebacker Sonny Styles burst through the line to drop McCarthy for a 2-yard loss while Skattebo watched from the sideline.
“It sucks, and I think part of it is I put myself in a situation last time we played these guys that kind of killed the trust in coach maybe a little bit, me giving up the ball last time,” Skattebo said of his overtime fumble in Week 5. “And maybe he didn’t want to give me the ball again. I don’t know. I’m not going to say that was something he was thinking. But I would think that as well.”
Punter Jordan Stout has been one of the Giants’ most reliable players, but he picked an inopportune time for a shank. His 12-yard punt after McCarthy got stuffed gave the Commanders the ball at their own 29-yard line with 1:46 remaining.
Daniels wasted no time attacking cornerback Deonte Banks, who has improved greatly but still doesn’t locate the ball consistently on deep passes. Banks got tangled up with Commanders wide receiver Treylon Burks to produce a 33-yard pass interference penalty. Washington was facing third-and-4 from the Giants’ 32-yard line three plays later. Giants defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson sent a blitz and Daniels responded by firing the ball to wide receiver Stefon Diggs on a quick slant. Diggs beat cornerback Dru Phillips, who took out Banks on his tackle attempt to clear the path for a walk-in touchdown with 57 seconds left.
The Giants had one last chance to get into range for a tying field-goal attempt. McCarthy started the drive by hitting wide receiver Malachi Fields for a 21-yard gain to Washington’s 48-yard line, but after an incompletion, the Commanders turned up the heat. McCarthy resorted to throwing the ball up for grabs as Washington sent all-out blitzes.
McCarthy was fortunate that Commanders cornerback Rasul Douglas failed to intercept a pass that fluttered after the quarterback’s arm was hit on second down. McCarthy wasn’t as lucky on third down, as a jump ball to wide receiver Malik Nabers was wrestled away by Douglas for a game-ending interception with 25 seconds remaining.
It was discouraging that Nabers couldn’t come down with the 50-50 ball, especially after all of his demands to get the ball. But it was puzzling that the Giants were throwing jump balls in that spot since they had two timeouts and only needed to gain about 10 yards to get into range.
“My thought process was pop it up to my playmakers, have them go make a play,” said McCarthy, who completed 23 of 36 passes for 293 yards, one touchdown and one interception.
It would have been hard to have confidence in Dominic Zvada to make the long field goal after he missed a 33-yarder in the first quarter. That came after the Giants elected to punt from Washington’s 37-yard line on their opening drive rather than attempting a 55-yard field goal.
It’s been a rollercoaster with the undrafted rookie — Zvada made all four of his field goals in last week’s win over the Eagles after making just 4-of-9 field goals in the previous three games — but Harbaugh remains committed to the ride.
“You can’t, as soon as a guy doesn’t make a play, start firing people left and right, especially your kicker, who’s a rookie,” Harbaugh said. “I’m confident that he’s going to become a good kicker. If at some point and time it doesn’t happen, it doesn’t happen. But I’m not going to panic halfway through the season with a guy who has made a bunch of kicks.”
The failed attempt to Nabers ended a quiet night. He had just five catches for 44 yards after having 11 catches for 121 yards and a touchdown in the first matchup with the Commanders. Nabers had a costly fumble at Washington’s 16-yard line as the Giants were driving for a score in the third quarter.
Likely was the focal point of the passing game, as McCarthy repeatedly found the tight end open in the middle of the field. Likely had nine catches for a career-high 127 yards, highlighted by the beautiful touchdown pass from McCarthy that somehow fit into a tiny window between Styles and linebacker K’Lavon Chaisson.
The inability to close the game on the ground was disappointing because the Giants had been effective running the ball. They leaned on lighter personnel much more than normal and the offensive lines opened holes for Skattebo, who rushed for two touchdowns. But the Giants couldn’t grind out the necessary yards to kill the clock at the end of the game.
“Very frustrating,” Likely said. “When you want to be one of the best teams in the league, you’ve got to be able to…

full_text:
The Steelers and Bengals, both 6-2, will meet on "Sunday Night Football" with first place in the division on the line. Barry Reeger / Imagn Images
Each week during the season and occasionally during the offseason, our panel of AFC North writers tackles the issues, trending topics and looming decisions around the division. This week, we’re looking back at the trade deadline and ahead to “Sunday Night Football.”
Did the team you cover have to rescind a trade ahead of Tuesday’s deadline because it didn’t understand the NFL’s compensatory pick rules? Or was something else the barrier to real player movement?
Mike DeFabo (Steelers): Every time Steelers general manager Omar Khan talks publicly about his strategy, he says he’s trying to win now without sacrificing the future. That’s easier said than done in the new world where teams that believe they are contenders are doing everything in their power to make an aggressive push at the deadline.
Until Pittsburgh finds its future franchise quarterback, the Steelers have been especially reluctant to give up draft capital. The team also has some level of optimism that wide receivers Michael Pittman Jr. and Roman Wilson will return in the coming weeks to provide a needed boost in the passing game. That’s the company line. Personally, I see it as another risk-averse move from a franchise that often looks to minimize risk above all else.
Paul Dehner Jr. (Bengals): Can we insert the meme of the guy on the couch, puzzled and pointing to himself? That’s probably a better explanation than anything I would write here. Also, maybe the Bengals should hire that guy from the meme just to read Nick Korte tweets to them.
I don’t think whether the Bengals landed Arnold Ebiketie changed the potential for this season. It’s mostly embarrassing . But as somebody well-versed in embarrassment, I can tell you that will cycle out. The Bengals can win on Sunday, and nobody will care anymore. The real story will be whether their reluctance to part with any real draft capital for an addition will hinder this defense from reaching the level necessary to get to the Super Bowl.
Zac Jackson (Browns): I still think the Browns-Bengals/A.J. McCarron fax-machine thing, with Hue Jackson trying to be the boss, made for a better story. But what do I know? Anyway, the Browns are still mostly focused on the future, making it largely unsurprising that they stayed out of the deadline-related action.
Cleveland will be a team making plenty of headlines come March and April, and general manager Andrew Berry will likely be involved in trades then that include some of the 11 2027 draft picks the Browns currently own.
Jeff Zrebiec (Ravens) : One thing you don’t have to worry about is the Ravens understanding the compensatory rules. Those rules are like the Bible at their team facility. The Ravens made three trade acquisitions over the past two months despite the state of the team suggesting that they probably should have been sellers . Why weren’t they? They simply aren’t ready to give up on the season, and they are close enough to the wild-card mix that they felt it was premature to wave the white flag.
They also have a young coaching staff trying to establish itself, and stripping the team of talent in-season would have made it tough to make any notable progress in Year 1. But the biggest barrier of all was that they simply didn’t have many trade chips. Fans were screaming for them to deal vets Ronnie Stanley, Mark Andrews, Marlon Humphrey and Roquan Smith, but either their current form or the size of their contracts — in some cases, both — made trading those players nearly impossible.
Are you comfortable saying this division is a two-team race with nine weeks left? Or are Cleveland and Baltimore still not dead?
DeFabo: I’m 90 percent sure the Bengals and Steelers will be the two teams representing the AFC North in the playoffs. But you can never be 100 percent sure of anything in this division. Lamar Jackson is such a huge part of Baltimore’s ceiling. Without him for several weeks (or longer), I don’t know if the Ravens can keep pace. The Browns are showing some cracks. Their team, full of young talent, may be a year away from contending.
Dehner Jr.: I’m not counting the Browns out yet. Four in a row at home keeps the light of hope on in my eyes. Plus, they have two games with Cincinnati. If the Browns can find an answer for the Bengals’ offense and pull off the sweep, the entire dynamic of the race changes. Do I think it’s likely? No. I also didn’t think we’d still be talking about Deshaun Watson playing meaningful NFL snaps, so my mind is still adjusting to this Browns season. I just really like the roster around him and want to see the next two weeks before officially declaring them divisionally dead.
Jackson: I am comfortable saying that right now, with the main qualifier being that a lot can change in a week in the NFL. The Browns are mathematically alive and still will be when December begins, but they began Week 10 as a bottom-10 offense in scoring, first downs, success rate, sacks allowed and plays of 10-plus yards. The Browns can only keep up if things change drastically or if they start forcing five turnovers per game. Joe Burrow has more touchdown passes (16) in his last four games than the Browns have touchdowns (15) all season.
Zrebiec: The Browns and Ravens, assuming Jacoby Brissett brings competence to the quarterback position, may hang around for a little while. But yeah, I’m pretty comfortable in declaring this a two-team race. Any path to the Ravens getting back into this thing would probably require them to win four straight before their four-game division finish, and nothing they have shown over the last month suggests they have four straight wins in them.
Meanwhile, both the Bengals and Steelers are playing extremely well, and they’ve opened up some space. The Bengals’ schedule the rest of the way is extremely forgiving. I know this isn’t necessarily the question, but if the Bengals win Sunday, they could have the division wrapped up by Christmas.
Before it gets cold(er) and temporarily gloomy for some, specifically the loser of Sunday night’s Steelers-Bengals game, what’s the best case for optimism for the team you cover? Is there something that’s better or brighter than it might currently appear?
DeFabo: The Steelers are playing their brand of football, as the repeated investments in the trenches are finally paying dividends. Pittsburgh ranks second in total rushing EPA (11.84) and third in yards per carry (4.9). Defensively, the Steelers have allowed the fourth-fewest points per game (18.0) and rank fifth in EPA/play (0.11). To push them over the top, the Steelers badly need DK Metcalf to emerge from his slump and become the WR1 they’re paying him to be.
Dehner Jr.: The Bengals defense. I know, this take might be worse than my Browns opinion. We’ve seen an uptick from the linebackers in recent weeks, and Dexter Lawrence remains a game-changing disruption up the middle. More importantly, the Bengals have exactly one game left against an offense currently ranked in the top 12 in EPA/play (home against Kansas City). The degree of difficulty, plus the pressure the Cincinnati offense will put on a slate packed with flawed opponents, sets the defense up to post a productive second half —more importantly, one that provides momentum and confidence for a potential playoff run.
Jackson: The Browns have nice offensive pieces. They also have some good defensive pieces, and cornerback Denzel Ward is still as good as anyone at the position in his ninth NFL season. But optimism for Cleveland eventually building a legitimate, explosive offense lies in rookie wide receivers KC Concepcion and Denzel Boston and second-year tight end Harold Fannin Jr., all 22 years old and extremely gifted. None are finished products, but the collective arrow is pointing way up.
Zrebiec: I left M&T Bank Stadium last Thursday night after watching that Ravens-Jaguars…

full_text:

Peak newsletter 🧠| This is an excerpt from The Athletic’s weekly newsletter covering the mental side of sports. Sign up here to receive the Peak newsletter directly in your inbox.
In my experience, NFL locker rooms are not the warmest places for reporters. The first time I stood in the Seahawks’ locker room as a young reporter for The Seattle Times, I heard the booming voice of a veteran defensive lineman:
Painfully naive and looking like a Harry Potter impersonator, I walked over with a big smile, introduced myself and stuck out my hand. The lineman’s reply, as he turned his back to me: “I don’t give a f— who you are.”
So let’s just say that I expected nothing from anyone in that locker room. But as I stood off to the side one day, struggling mentally and feeling detached from the world, linebacker K.J. Wright saw me and asked:
I lied and said I was fine, but here we are, a decade later, and I still remember how I felt walking out of the locker room that afternoon. My day wasn’t suddenly full of sunshine and butterflies. Nothing like that.
But it mattered to me that Wright noticed, that he asked.
Even in the cutthroat NFL, Wright always wanted to engage with people, and he always wanted to be liked. It made him a likable teammate, but it also became a fault once he entered a leadership position as a young coach for the San Francisco 49ers.
This is what Wright told me last May : “Something that I want to get better at: being honest. I like to sugarcoat a lot. … What I try to do is protect people’s feelings.”
And this is what he told me recently: “Oh, those days are over.”
I wanted to understand what had changed in those 18 months.
The most important thing that happened: Wright was promoted.
When we talked a year ago, he was a quality control coach for the 49ers, an entry-level job. Now he is the team’s linebackers coach, responsible for his own group of players.
The weight of that responsibility hit him when he stood in front of the linebackers’ meeting room: People are depending on me. They are literally depending on me to help them achieve their dreams.
It was an “a-ha” moment. Now 37 years old, Wright remembered how much he looked to his own coaches for answers during his 11-year playing career with the Seahawks and Raiders.
“So I’ve got to give them my time, my feedback, my honesty ,” he told me. “If I just bulls— and fluff around, the same stuff will keep happening. I don’t want to do that.”
Wright’s approach now can be boiled down to a few words: “Be direct and honest but calm and poised.”
Eye contact matters, he said. So does being concise. And he never wants to come across as if he’s talking down to his players.
“Tell them what they need to hear and do,” he said, “but tell them with poise and love.”
As much as anything, he tries to focus on his energy in those moments — his tone and demeanor. He gave an example.
Earlier this season, his linebackers started to push back on one of his coaching points.
Hold up, coach. That ain’t what I do.
It was a test. The 49ers linebacker group has a couple of highly decorated players who have been around a long time. Wright didn’t want to back down, but he also didn’t want to put his players on the defensive.
“I match their energy, but I’m not matching it to the point where I’m rattled or loose,” Wright said. “I’m convicted in what I say. I know that this is best. And so when I match you, I match you with calmness and poise.”
He still remembers the very first thing Johnny Holland, a longtime coach, told him when he joined the 49ers staff: “Whatever you do in this business, be honest with guys. Because 1) they appreciate it and 2) it makes them better.”
But here’s the part Wright didn’t know at the time: “I’ve realized,” he told me, “that it also makes me better.”
When he points out mistakes or offers blunt feedback, it’s not enough to tell a player what they did wrong. It’s Wright’s job (and the job of any leader) to provide the tools and guidance to do it right the next time.
To do that, he has tried to cut out all the sugar and fluff in his feedback. He has learned that direct, honest feedback, delivered with poise and intentionality, is enough.
I reminded Wright of what he said 18 months ago, when he told me he struggled with that part of leadership. He laughed and reiterated that those days are over, then added an important point:
“You’ve got to fight that doubt that pops in your mind.”

full_text:
Rasul Douglas (No. 29) picked off J.J. McCarthy deep in the fourth quarter to seal a wild win for the Commanders. Emilee Chinn / Getty Images
EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. — Jayden Daniels ripped his helmet off in frustration and took a seat on the bench.
His defense just handed him another chance to try to score and reclaim the lead as the clock neared the two-minute warning. But instead of capitalizing, his underthrown pass to tight end Chig Okonkwo was picked off near midfield. It was his second interception in as many drives and killed yet another for an offense that had started to unravel when it needed to be at its best.
Here we go again. The Commanders had a habit of making close and winnable games self-inflicted disasters this season, and this one — a must-win Thursday night matchup with the NFC East-leading Giants — was on the verge of becoming the latest. Owner Josh Harris, who typically comes down to the Commanders’ sideline to watch the final few minutes of games, again took his place for what could’ve been a slow, painful ending to his team’s season.
But these Commanders weren’t done.
When the clock hit two minutes, Washington came alive, much like it did a couple years ago when it took the NFL world by storm with its late-game heroics. In three drives — a defensive stand, a quick go-ahead touchdown and a game-sealing interception — the Commanders saved their season, and possibly their coach’s job, to collect its biggest victory of the year, a 24-21 win over the Giants .
It started with the rookie.
After safety Ar’Darius Washington picked off Daniels on a fourth-and-2 — Daniels was picked off by Jevon Holland on the previous drive — linebacker Sonny Styles knew the Giants were poised to run the ball on a critical third-and-3.
He saw this before in their first meeting, that Week 5 tie that Washington would love to forget . The Giants ran a crack toss in the back on a third down near midfield then so he had a feeling they’d do it again.
“Then when they went empty, kind of just looking at the tight end, like the way he was cracking,” Styles explained. “… Kind of had an idea it was QB run, so I just reacted.”
Styles kept his eyes glued to J.J. McCarthy as he took the snap and sprinted to the left. Then the rookie exploded through the line to chase him down from the back, tackling him for a loss of three yards to force a punt.
Giants punter Jordan Stout had booted a 68-yarder moments earlier, but he shanked his last attempt and it sailed only 12 yards before going out of bounds.
Then the Commanders feasted.
“I think you understand the magnitude of the moment, but you’re not really thinking about the season,” Daniels said. “In that moment, you’re really thinking about winning this game, and that’s kind of just the biggest thing for me. I didn’t want to let my team down in that moment, so when they gave me another opportunity to go out there and win the game, I didn’t want to let them down.”
Daniels quickly targeted Treylon Burks, who had a step on cornerback Deonte Banks and used his leverage to draw a pass interference flag. Another gift — a 33-yard gift — that Washington wasn’t going to waste.
Three plays later Daniels hit Stefon Diggs on a slant and the veteran wideout sprinted upfield, stopping inches before the goal line before turning and falling backward into the end zone, a la DeSean Jackson.
“Well, he probably could have waited some more,” Quinn joked afterward.
goodnight, dmv pic.twitter.com/PETWsZsXul
— Washington Commanders (@Commanders) November 13, 2026
It appeared that Daniels changed a signal on the play before the snap.
“Maybe, maybe not. You never know,” Diggs said facetiously.
Diggs said he and Daniels had worked on their communication throughout the week and this play ended up being one they needed against the Giants’ Cover 0 look.
“Baby Kobe,” Diggs said of Daniels. “He ain’t flinch. He’s going to be the same kind of player he is at the beginning of the game as he is at the end of the game.”
But the final piece of the Commanders’ rally was, fittingly, courtesy of its defense, a group that has found its rhythm in recent weeks and has repeatedly come up with big plays late.
Cornerback Rasul Douglas intercepted McCarthy on a deep, last-gasp attempt on third-and-10 with 34 seconds remaining.
Douglas nearly picked off McCarthy on his previous attempt, after safety Jeremy Reaves hit the quarterback’s elbow to send an errant throw right up the right sideline. The ball slipped through Douglas’ grasp that time, but not on the subsequent try. His eyes fixated on McCarthy, Douglas high-pointed the ball to grab it before receiver Malik Nabers could get his hands on it.
As Douglas headed for the end zone to celebrate with his fellow defensive backs, defensive coordinator Daronte Jones hugged Steve Wilks on the sideline. Wilks has joined the Commanders’ defensive staff as a part-time assistant, working primarily with the secondary.
“I think we bought in to what D.J. wanted us to buy in to this whole time,” Douglas said.
A few feet away from Jones and Wilks, Daniels flexed in celebration. Finally, after watching many games slip away by their own mistakes, the Commanders enjoyed a win they fought for until the end.
“We needed that,” Quinn said. “We needed every bit of it.”
