full_text:
Jayden Daniels hit Stefon Diggs late for a game-winning, season-saving score late in the fourth. AP Photo / Seth Wenig
EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. — Tired: Fire Dan Quinn, trade Jayden Daniels, don’t build the Washington Commanders their new stadium, send every ex-player and coach to the nearest available podcast/radio hit for their hot takes.
Wired: The Commanders live.
Washington’s season, four or five times in the fourth quarter Thursday, was teetering. The Commanders had battled, but they’d left enough on the table for the Giants to take a four-point lead with eight minutes to go. Then, Daniels threw his first two interceptions of the season, on back-to-back drives, the second giving New York a first down at Washington’s 45-yard line with 2:15 left.
Yet, in the gusting wind and rain at a stadium that has brought many miseries to the Commanders over the decades, Washington steadied itself. It didn’t get swallowed up whole by the finality of the last two minutes: the season is on the line . And, to be sure, Quinn’s future as head coach in D.C. was likely hanging in the balance, too. A loss to the NFC East-leading Giants would have all but eliminated Washington’s chances to get back in the division race, and given Josh Harris 11 long days before Washington’s next game, a week from Monday, against Cincinnati, to contemplate whether or not to pull the plug on his third-year coach.
But Washington endured. The defense stood tall and didn’t allow New York to get a first down, with first-round pick Sonny Styles flying to tackle Giants quarterback J.J. McCarthy on a designed quarterback run for a huge two-yard loss on third and 3 from Washington’s 37-yard-line. The offense, granted one last opportunity, drove 73 yards in 49 seconds with Daniels checking into a slant on an all-out Giants blitz to hit Stefon Diggs for 32 yards and the game-winning touchdown. And the defense, one last time, held up, with Rasul Douglas’ interception with 25 seconds left preserving a 24-21 Washington win .
After Sunday’s loss to the Rams, Daniels acknowledged that Thursday, here, was do or die. Washington did. The season, again meaningful, even at 3-5-1, continues.
“You understand the magnitude of the moment,” Daniels said. “And you’re not really thinking about, like, the season. I’m only really thinking about winning this game. That was kind of the biggest thing for me. I didn’t want to let my team down in that moment. So, when they gave me another opportunity to go out there and win the game, I didn’t want to let them down.”
The Commanders are, most assuredly, a flawed team this season. They make way too many mental mistakes. But they did cut those down Thursday, committing just four penalties for a total of 17 yards. They, most certainly, have trouble running the football. They had a grand total of 105 yards rushing against the Giants, on 33 carries. Tight end Ben Sinnott, dismissed as a bust well into his third season, scored his first touchdown of the season, with five seconds left in the first half, on a 1-yard catch to put Washington up at the half.
A month ago, Washington had a win over New York on its racket, only to, somehow, burn the last 51 seconds of overtime without getting its field goal unit on the field for what would have been a game-winning kick. It was shambolic, how everyone involved, from Quinn to offensive coordinator David Blough, to Daniels, screwed up an eminently unscrewable situation.
This time, this last time, the Commanders didn’t beat themselves when it most mattered.
“Going into it, we thought, this was going to be, all four quarters, all the way down,” Quinn said. “So there was not a spot of, like, ‘Let’s get them down early and finish it off.’ This was not that case. There have been too many close games (with New York). … to be behind, that was hard.”
Maybe the Commanders were talking themselves into believing, after McCarthy split Styles and K’Lavon Chaisson to hit tight end Isaiah Lively for a 66-yard body punch of a touchdown to put New York up 21-17 with 8.17 remaining. Maybe it was wishful thinking, the last, mournful hope of a condemned team that hasn’t been able to stay out of its own way much of this season. But they put together eight great minutes when they needed it most. The defense made three consecutive stops.
Daniels is, obviously, Washington’s North Star. But Styles, the seventh pick overall, is rapidly growing into everything the Commanders hoped he’d be. The speed and force is obvious; the reads are coming, rapidly. On that third and two, Styles’ film work, with a verbal assist from defensive tackle Charles Omenihu, indicated to him that the Giants were running a crack back run, with the tight end coming down the line to clear Washington’s edge defender, and give McCarthy enough room to get the first down. Styles brushed off Giants center Bryan Hudson, shot the gap, tackled McCarthy for the loss, and gave the offense the ball back.
(It helped Washington, immensely, that Giants punter Jordan Stout picked the next play to shankapotumus a 12-yard punt. Instead of pinning Washington inside the 10, the Commanders got the ball back at their 27 with 1:46 left.)
“I think, if you’re just the player you are, the moment can never be too big,” Styles said. “I think everyone understood in that moment, ‘We’ve got to get a stop right here.’ So guys just bowed up.”
Guard Sam Cosmi looked at his teammates as Washington huddled up.
“I have moments where I look, and everybody’s just locked in,” Cosmi said. “You have that, like, glare, where you know it’s game time, this is game time. We’re going to make big plays.”
Daniels drove Washington from the 27 to New York’s 32. On third and 4, Daniels knew New York was coming with a cover zero blitz — meaning one-on-one coverage for the receivers — and signaled the slant to Diggs, who beat Giants cornerback Dru Phillips. Phillips, inadvertently, then ran into teammate Deonte Banks, who was trying to come over to make the tackle, giving Diggs an unencumbered route to the end zone.
“Baby Kobe,” Diggs said of his quarterback.
First-year defensive coordinator Daronte Jones didn’t flinch, either. He kept dialing up blitzes on the Giants’ last series, not wanting to let McCarthy hit Likely or anyone else underneath to get in position to kick a game-tying field goal. Douglas had a shot at a McCarthy moon ball the play before, but couldn’t pull it in. On the next play, Jones called another blitz. Styles came free and got in McCarthy’s face. Forty yards downfield, Douglas was one-on-one with New York’s star receiver, Malik Nabers. But Styles’ rush made McCarthy’s throw hang just a bit. Douglas came down with it for the game-securing interception.
“When the ball’s in the air, I don’t even really see the receiver,” Douglas said. “I just know I’m going to get it. I trust my ability to play the ball, get the ball. I know some guys try to play the man. That’s not me. I want interceptions. I play the ball. That’s all I grew up doing. Me and Will (Gay, Washington’s defensive back coach) talk about it. If the risk is helpful for the team, take it.”
Washington is still two games behind New York, with eight to play. But the Commanders, now, have the tiebreaker with the Giants, if it comes down to that. If it comes down to that, though, this already wild ride of a season will have taken an even crazier turn than what happened here Thursday, when the Commanders merely saved their season. For a couple of weeks, at least.

title: 3 Biggest Things Carson Beck Said Before First Cardinals Start
full_text:
ARIZONA – The Carson Beck era is officially set to begin this weekend.
After the Arizona Cardinals announced Beck would be their starter in Week 10 , all eyes now gear towards the rookie third-round pick to finish out the season as the team's starting quarterback. How he performs in this final stretch will likely determine if he's sitting in the seat come 2027.
Beck met with reporters ahead of his first start — here's the three biggest things he said:
Beck when asked if he can carry confidence into his first ever start:
“Of course. I think the coolest thing about confidence is that confidence is a choice. With that also, I’ve said it before, it makes everyone else around you better as well. It exudes confidence into them when you’re showing that you’re confident.
"When you can choose that, again, you just have to go out there and execute. You have to go out there and do your thing and you have to go out there and be confident, have swag, and have moxie. Regardless of the circumstances, regardless of anything going on around you, regardless of maybe what happened the play before or maybe thinking about what’s going to happen the next play.
"You have to be in the present moment and that’s really all you can do and control.”
Beck on handling the spotlight of being a starting quarterback:
"I feel like I've done it for a long time. The past three years — having started at some of the biggest college programs in the country, having been a top five team (and) a number one team in the country —  you have the national spotlight. Obviously, it's a lot different now being in the NFL — (it) being such a huge product and what it is.
"Honestly, just be myself. Be there for my teammates, be selfless (and) do what I can for everyone around me. Then ultimately go out there and give my best effort, have confidence and just be relentless. I think that's how you handle that and there is really no more to it."
When asked if Mike LaFleur has given him any advice:
"There's this quote that (Head) Coach (Mike) LaFleur said — I don't remember if it was before a game or during training camp but he showed a clip of (Golden State Warriors Guard Stephen) 'Steph' Curry and he was essentially talking about the shot that he had in the USA versus France game. It's like, 'Being comfortable with not knowing what the outcome is going to be and then going out there and shooting your shot.' I think that's how you handle the emotions of it because obviously all of us care a ton.
"I care a ton, right? You want to go out there, you want to do good (and) you want to play your best but when you think too much about that and you fear failure or you fear not having the result that you want, that's when the emotions get in the way. I think just being comfortable with not knowing the outcome and then ultimately going and shooting your shot is how you handle those emotions."

title: Steph Curry's Influence Could Define Beginning of Cardinals' New Era

The third-round pick was confirmed to be the team's starter for Week 10's clash against the Los Angeles Rams. After sitting for the first half of his first NFL season, trades and injuries have opened the door for Beck to audition for what could be a bigger role past 2026.
There's a lot riding on Beck's performance and what it could mean for the Cardinals' future, but a gold medal piece of advice from head coach Mike LaFleur earlier this season has paved the path for Beck's mentality:
"There's this quote that (Head) Coach (Mike) LaFleur said — I don't remember if it was before a game or during training camp but he showed a clip of (Golden State Warriors guard Stephen) 'Steph' Curry and he was essentially talking about the shot that he had in the USA versus France game. Curry's one of the most talented players to touch a basketball court, though the overall message is to trust the talent, instincts and preparation with no hesitation.
That's something the Cardinals desperately need in their offense, and something that feels mandatory with Beck if he's going to play well enough to convince Arizona he's their franchise guy moving forward.
"I feel like I've done it for a long time," Beck said when asked about handling the spotlight.

title: NFL Insider Rips Cardinals' Surprising Budda Baker Decision
full_text:
ARIZONA — Arizona Cardinals safety Budda Baker was perhaps the biggest name that wasn't moved ahead of the league's 2026 trade deadline, ensuring the franchise legend remains with the team through 2026.
It wasn't for lack of suitors.
Baker had numerous teams that did extensive work on him at the deadline according to NFL insider Jordan Schultz.
"The trade that I thought had the best chance of happening in terms of a big name that didn't was Budda Baker to Buffalo. Now Jacksonville also made the big deal for Jessie Bates, the All-Pro from Atlanta, they also took a long look at Budda Baker. But Arizona, ultimately, was not willing to pull the trigger and it was a little hard for me to understand," said Schultz.
"They're going nowhere. The Cardinals are going nowhere this season. You have a Day 2 pick and probably more you could have gotten out of Buffalo. ... Budda Baker's given them everything. He's been there a decade. He's been to eight Pro Bowls, he's been an All-Pro. That's the type of thing where I just thought the organization should have done right by him."
The #Cardinals decided not to trade Budda Baker to the #Bills , and I struggle to understand why not. Great chopping it up with my guy @CSimmsQB today. https://t.co/2nOnucQvVS pic.twitter.com/nLf6SWOlon
The Bills' offer for Baker was reportedly around a second-round pick, which Arizona declined. Along with Jacksonville, the Detroit Lions were another team believed to be interested in Baker.
The 3-6 Cardinals ultimately didn't trade anybody at the deadline after previously dealing Jacoby Brissett and Marvin Harrison Jr. — Baker, Josh Sweat and even Garrett Williams were possible trade candidates.
Baker's one of the few players who (at least should) have the right to determine his future after spending the last ten seasons in the desert, emerging as a top player in the league and a pillar of a Cardinals franchise that hasn't seen much success since he arrived.
His name has always been involved in trade chatter, though 2026 felt like the most realistic possibility of a trade after Baker reportedly was open to a move to a contender, though he never officially put a trade request in and was open to whatever the future had in store.
Despite Buffalo being an ideal landing spot for Baker in terms of a win-now team along with the aggressive draft capital to make a deal happen, the Cardinals kept the face of the franchise around.
After 2026, Baker has one year remaining on his deal in Arizona. He will turn 31 in January.

title: Cardinals Finally Deliver Carson Beck News Fans Have Been Waiting For
full_text:
TEMPE — The Arizona Cardinals finally delivered the news fans have been waiting for.
Head coach Mike LaFleur confirmed on Wednesday that rookie third-round pick Carson Beck would start ahead of the team's Week 10 matchup against the Los Angeles Rams.
Beck gets the nod after the Cardinals lost previous starter Gardner Minshew to a season-ending UCL injury on Sunday.
"Go out and operate. Go operate this offense and go play," LaFleur said on what he wants to see out of Beck on Sunday. "Each play is his own. So do what he's been doing in practice. It's just an extension of the practice field. Obviously, it's live bullets, and go operate, go play his game."
The Cardinals are 3-6 on the season, and after the trade deadline has come and gone, they're officially turning the page towards the future with Beck — who will have the second half of Arizona's season as an evaluation for the front office ahead of a 2027 offseason where the Cardinals very well could pursue a quarterback.
Beck's extensive college experience at Georgia and Miami on top of successfully leading both programs to a national championship appearance made him an attractive late day two pick.
The plan wasn't initially for Beck to play this early in the season — especially against a loaded Rams defense with Aaron Donald and Myles Garrett — though LaFleur believes his passer is ready.
"You never really know until you get to the live bullets on Sunday," LaFleur continued on Beck.
"But just the way he goes about his business, whether it's been from OTAs through training camp before he got hurt, obviously seeing him operate there in that first half [preseason] plus the one you know possession there in the second half. So obviously we'll know more come that Sunday, but have all the confidence that he's ready to roll."

title: 3 Big Questions We Have After Cardinals' Trade Deadline
full_text:
The Arizona Cardinals have seen the NFL trade deadline come and go with a surprisingly silent Tuesday after previous activity earlier in the year.
The Cardinals move into the second half of the regular season with two of their hottest trade commodities in place.
Three big questions we still have:
The Cardinals are 3-6. They're clearly not going to be in position to win games the rest of the season while 2027 is an entirely different beast. As a result, Arizona found themselves in a tough position with a few veteran names — Josh Sweat atop the list.
The Cardinals' pass rusher is reportedly hoping to land a reworked deal next offseason, one that will assure him more than the $0 in guaranteed money in the last two seasons of his deal in 2027 and 2028 that he currently has.
That's not something the Cardinals should do given the current state of the team. And if Arizona's not going to comply, he'll likely try to force his way out — which will net the Cardinals bigger problems ahead instead of addressing it at the deadline.
If Sweat's future isn't here, why are we kicking the can down the road on his inevitable move?
Budda Baker is a franchise legend. Cardinals icon. Future Ring of Honor member.
With that said, Baker also reportedly was open for a trade this season. The Cardinals clearly aren't going to be competing for a Super Bowl soon, and Baker deserves the right to at least compete for one.
The Buffalo Bills reportedly offered a strong Day 2 pick for Baker, which Arizona declined.
For sentimental value, that can be applauded. For Arizona's locker room, that's a sign the Cardinals aren't just throwing the towel in despite the constant flow of injuries and losing.
Yet the Cardinals' refusal for a top pick for Baker feels like an extreme miss from general manager Monti Ossenfort , who had a golden opportunity to add to Arizona's stockpile of high draft picks in 2027.
Is keeping Baker, who has one year left on his deal, worth bypassing a second-round pick?
The Cardinals' general manager certainly operated like he was somebody on the hot seat this week.
Arizona had ample opportunity to strike a deal and build their chances of injecting massive talent to the roster in 2027. Unfortunately, the organization bypassed those opportunities — seemingly to keep its roster together here and now.
That very much reads like a general manager trying to save their job. It's no secret Ossenfort was under pressure after Arizona fired head coach Jonathan Gannon last offseason, as many wondered why Ossenfort — the architect of recently poor teams — stuck around.
2026 has been the same song and dance.
What's Ossenfort's ultimate job security entering the second half of the regular season?

title: The Good, Bad and Ugly From Cardinals Trade Deadline
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals' trade deadline mirrored much of their prior 2024 season — an exciting start with a flat ending.
After trading Jacoby Brissett and Marvin Harrison Jr. earlier in the season, the team's 3-6 record propped plenty of opportunities to sell more veteran names ahead of the trade deadline in hopes of truly stockpiling picks ahead of a loaded 2027 draft class.
That wasn't the case, as the Cardinals remained silent and passive as yesterday's 2:00 pm MST deadline came and went.
The good, bad and ugly from Arizona's overall body of work in the trade streets:
The Cardinals managed to flip Marvin Harrison Jr. for a second-round pick while upgrading themselves to a fourth-round pick for Jacoby Brissett.
Monti Ossenfort receives plenty of flack from Cardinals fans, and some of that is deserved, but that's truly a strong return for two players who simply weren't providing Arizona much — if anything at all.
Harrison had just five receptions this season prior to being traded for a second and some minor pick swaps. The Houston Texans have yet to see him break-out like they would have liked, and now some in H-Town are wondering if it might just be the player that was the problem all along.
Brissett, meanwhile, was benched last week and demoted to the bottom of the quarterback depth chart. He was set to be Arizona's inactive emergency passer — so really anything of value like a sixth or seventh-round pick would have been acceptable in a trade.
So when the trade was reported and the Cardinals ultimately sent a fifth-round pick to gain a fourth, it felt like a no-brainer.
Arizona, as a result of those two trades, has six picks in the first four rounds of the 2027 draft. Nice work.
Budda Baker has always found his name dangled in trade chatter. Such is life when you're a talented player on a typically not talented team. Yet this year felt different, as legitimate reports emerged on Baker's willingness to potentially find a fresh start on a competing team.
Not trading Baker isn't the bad part here. He's clearly a franchise icon and has plenty left in the tank.
However, reportedly refusing a second-round pick for Baker feels like bad business in declining a situation that is a rare win-win during the trade deadline.
If Baker himself shot down the trade — that's different. He deserves the right to dictate his future, and if he wants to stay in Arizona, that's perfectly fine. However, if Baker was indeed willing to be moved, and the Cardinals truly did say no to a Day 2 pick from the Buffalo Bills, that's simply not good business.
Baker's value will never be higher than now, and it would be a shame if at some point he's moved within the next 365 days for much less as a result of optics.
All signs point to a pending divorce between Josh Sweat and the Cardinals — it's just a matter of when.
Arizona understandably didn't give in to trade noise earlier this offseason/preseason when it was quite loud. However, Sweat clearly wasn't the player the Cardinals saw in 2025, and the feeling between the two sides isn't exactly romantic at this point in time.
Yesterday's trade deadline felt like a prime opportunity to offload Sweat while they could ahead of a 2027 offseason where one of two things is going to happen: The Cardinals will rework Sweat's deal to give him more guaranteed money on the final two years of his contract, or they'll trade him for what will likely be less than what he could have been had for now.
The trade deadline creates urgency and raises the price on players, as Super Bowl contenders are willing to spend more freely and seriously when they see their team's performance halfway through the year.
That didn't happen, and now the Cardinals practically kicked the can down the road on Sweat and the future problems that could create in the desert instead of handling it now.

title: Cardinals' Trade Deadline Said Everything About Monti Ossenfort's Job Security
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals' trade deadline has officially come and gone. All eyes in the desert were on the Cardinals and what they'd do after falling to 3-6 on the season. Injuries have decimated this year's iteration of Arizona football, and the Cardinals had plenty of talent available to fully establish themselves as sellers.
As fate would have it, despite all the noise, the Cardinals would stay pat and sidestep opportunities to bolster their 2027 stock of draft picks. The decision to retain veteran players while foregoing the chance to add more future ammo for team-building is one that will have ramifications for both present and future.
General manager Monti Ossenfort surprised more than some in the Valley when owner Michael Bidwill brought him back for a fourth season running the show, even in spite of firing head coach Jonathan Gannon.
His work — or lack thereof — spoke volumes today.
NFL general managers operate differently than most positions on an NFL team. Highly drafted rookies and freshly paid stars are often awarded greater lengths of time to succeed due to the capital invested in them. Coaches, meanwhile, are on the opposite end of the spectrum — a bad first season can immediately put their job in serious danger, as the Cardinals are all too aware with Steve Wilks nearly ten years ago.
Yet general managers fall somewhere in the middle of the spectrum of patience. It's hard to truly get a gauge for their impact until a few years down the road. As a GM, their job is to assemble and build talent. Barring a glaringly obvious hit or bust in either the draft/free agency, there's far too many variables to evaluate who is and isn't capable of running an NFL team.
Plenty in Arizona believed three years was more than enough to make a concrete decision on Ossenfort. After completely stripping Arizona's roster down to bare bones in 2023, the following season saw the Cardinals primed for their first playoff appearance since 2021 after entering their bye week at the top of the NFC West.
Yet the Cardinals crumbled, and 2025 brought no better results. Through three seasons, Arizona won just 15 games, and when Gannon was sent packing, many scratched their heads in disbelief as Ossenfort sat in his seat for another year in charge.
The first half of 2026 brought similar results, and for a general manager who very much was thought to be on the hot seat, the trade deadline presented a rare window of opportunity to potentially evaluate how Ossenfort personally viewed his job security.
A general manager offloading top assets for future draft picks just might signal their belief in job security entering the following offseason. Why would Ossenfort assemble loads of draft picks and sacrifice the rest of the Cardinals' 2026 season if he's not going to be the guy orchestrating their draft?
Conversely, you could make the argument that no moves would actually speak volumes for Ossenfort. He clearly had opportunities to continue adding to an impressive 2027 draft haul of six selections in the first four rounds, which includes two second-round picks. A general manager bypassing those opportunities very well could signal a win-now approach in order to save his job.
Many believed prior trades involving Marvin Harrison Jr. and Jacoby Brissett indicated the Cardinals were open for business. The reality sits a bit lower than that — Harrison hired agents for the first time in his NFL career and practically facilitated a way out while Brissett was quickly demoted to QB3/emergency duties.
Case in point, that didn't exactly signal the Cardinals as sellers ahead of the trade deadline — but it did leave the door open, and by Ossenfort shutting it, his silence spoke volumes.
Ossenfort's refusal to make trades does indicate he's a general manager whose job isn't guaranteed past this season. Arizona reportedly had an offer of a second-round pick for star safety Budda Baker while pass rusher Josh Sweat is clearly going to either demand a new contract next offseason or a trade elsewhere. His value won't be close to what it was at the deadline.
By all accounts, this will be a massively important second half of the season for the Cardinals. Perhaps Ossenfort's fate is already decided. Perhaps it all depends on how competitive the team can be. Perhaps injuries, yet again, could play a factor on who Arizona's general manager will be entering 2027.
However you read it, today's moves — or lack thereof — were a pretty big indication that winning is a priority here and now in the desert. The towel isn't being thrown in for anybody, regardless of how much stronger their 2027 draft could have been as a result.
And for a pretty banged-up 3-6 football team being coached by a rookie head coach, that's not good news for the future of its general manager.

title: Winners and Losers From Cardinals' Surprising Trade Deadline
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals didn't cash in on the bountiful number of trade rumors this week, standing still and not pulling the trigger on any moves as the league's trade deadline officially passed this afternoon.
That came as a surprise for most, as massive names such as Budda Baker and Josh Sweat (among others) were available.
The Cardinals failed to move off of both Budda Baker and Josh Sweat — arguably two of Arizona's top players on Nick Rallis' side of the ball. Arizona was facing the potential of selling both and fully hitting the reset button, which would have massively depleted the Cardinals' defensive talent.
Rallis — who was on the hot seat entering 2026 — keeps two established veteran talents, which should only help him down the stretch of the season. There's probably nobody happier than Rallis in the team's facility right now.
Welcome to the NFL, rook! To be clear, the Cardinals were not expected to make any trades to acquire players ahead of the deadline, though the fact still stands that Arizona didn't make any efforts to try and rescue offensive talent for a unit that's pretty gashed across the board in terms of injuries.
Beck will be tasked to prove himself as a potential franchise passer with little around him to work with, and while that was the expectation, it's now official as the Cardinals can't make any trades.
To read our grades for Arizona's trade deadline, you can click here .
This trade deadline was going to tell us a lot about how Cardinals general manager Monti Ossenfort viewed his job security, as it was unlikely he'd offload stars in Baker/Sweat to get top draft capital for picks he didn't believe he'd be making. Why set up another NFL GM for success if you're the one falling on the sword?
By not trading star players to position themselves better for the future, Ossenfort clearly is trying to maximize this season — one that some believe was already on borrowed time. Now, the Cardinals (as much as they could be) are hoping to win as many games as possible, and now Ossenfort hopes his gamble of silence at the deadline pays off to lend himself another season.
Williams found himself in trade rumors after apparently being in Rallis' doghouse, who has played Williams for just nine total snaps in the last two weeks despite being healthy. Williams is effectively benched for Max Melton, Kalen King, Denzel Burke and Kei'Trel Clark, and with his status as a pending free agent, it's unlikely he gets significant playing time for Arizona moving forward barring injury.
A fresh start would have been best for a player once considered to be one of the top slot corners in the game to contribute elsewhere — though that now isn't on the horizon.
Budda Baker is destined for the team's Ring of Honor after he retires. He's been a steady and powerful presence for the Cardinals during some dark times. Quite frankly, he's played his way into deciding what happens with his future. He appeared to be open to a potential trade, but when the Buffalo Bills came calling with a reported strong offer, the Cardinals declined. Who exactly made the call remains unknown, though we're on the fence on how Baker fares here.
On the plus side, he gets to continue his legacy in Arizona while his placement likely means the Cardinals are willing to pay his $20.8 million cap hit. On the downside, Baker clearly won't be competing for a championship soon despite having the door opened for that possibility. His legacy is cemented in Arizona and most here would have cheered him on elsewhere.
Truly mixed feelings for Baker.

title: Trade Deadline: Grading Every Move Cardinals Made — And Didn't
full_text:
ARIZONA — The NFL's trade deadline has officially come and gone.
The Arizona Cardinals opted for a shocking silence following multiple trades in the weeks leading up to today. With so much chatter, a deal for one of their top available players felt more likely than not.
Yet the dust has settled on Arizona's ability to make trades for the rest of the 2026 season, and the Cardinals must live with their decisions for the remainder of the year.
Grading every trade the Cardinals made — and didn't:
Deal : Marvin Harrison Jr. and a 2027 sixth-round pick for a 2027 second-round pick and 2027 seventh-round pick
Why it graded this way : The Cardinals ultimately notched a second-round pick for Harrison amid minor other picks swapped, which was incredible value for a receiver who caught just five passes for Arizona this season before departing. It was obvious Harrison wasn't going to flourish in the desert, and he hasn't done much since joining the Texans. The only thing holding this from being an "A" grade is Arizona's mountain of injuries at the receiver position after Harrison's departure.
Deal : Jacoby Brissett and a 2027 fifth-round pick for 2027 fourth-round pick and 2028 seventh-round pick
Why it graded this way : Listen, getting anything for Brissett after he was demoted to emergency quarterback status is a win. The fact that the Cardinals essentially jumped from a fifth to a fourth-round pick is a major win, especially for an aging veteran on an expiring deal who wasn't going to see the field again. While the bad contract extension still looms from the summer, we're grading the trade here — and Arizona batted well above expectations here for Brissett.
The stakes : Denver Broncos reportedly called on Trey McBride
Why it graded this way : Look, everybody would love to have a Trey McBride. And the fact that the Broncos inquired on McBride probably doesn't go far in the "Cardinals are doing things right!" playbook by not trading him. Still — even engaging in trade discussions for McBride at this point in time would have been pretty demoralizing for a Cardinals fan-base that's already suffered enough. Arizona's a much better team with McBride on the field, and unless a king's ransom was offered, that should have been a quick phone call.
The stakes : Sweat has been heavily tied in trade rumors since the offseason
Why it graded this way : I'd be very intrigued to hear the offers thrown around for Sweat, who clearly hasn't been happy since the Cardinals fired Jonathan Gannon. Quite frankly it's been an odd offseason/regular season for Sweat, who was MIA all summer and hasn't produced close to par based on his 2025 totals. Who knows if things have been smoothed over by now, though Sweat is looking for a restructured contract with more guaranteed money (since there's none remaining in his final two years) and that's not something the Cardinals should do based on their current timeline. It feels like we're pushing inevitable trade discussions to next offseason, but for now, Arizona retains its top pass rusher.
The stakes : The Cardinals reportedly declined a strong offer (Day 2 pick) from the Buffalo Bills for Baker
Why it graded this way : There's a lot to unpack here. The franchise icon wasn't exactly pounding the table for a trade, though he was reportedly open to a move towards a contender. That opportunity came knocking with what was a reported "strong push" by Buffalo with what's believed to be a second-round pick. Baker is a franchise legend and deserves to dictate his future, so if he was the deciding factor — so be it. However, Arizona is not going to get a stronger offer for Baker, who has just one year left on his current contract and will be turning 30. The Cardinals had a rare perfect opportunity to send Baker on a Super Bowl-contending team while getting top value for a non-premium position, and they declined. The love and respect for Baker is admirable, but the failure to stockpile more top draft capital for a loaded 2027 draft is eye-opening given Baker's age, contract and position. This move keeps the fabric of Arizona's defense in the building and continues a legacy of loyalty for Baker, but that's the only positive given how strong Buffalo's offer was.

title: Falcons Teammates Confident DeMarcco Hellams Can Fill Jessie Bates’ Role
full_text:
The Atlanta Falcons are counting on DeMarcco Hellams to help fill the void left by Jessie Bates III, and his teammates believe the young safety is ready for the opportunity.
Atlanta traded Bates to the Jacksonville Jaguars ahead of the NFL trade deadline, receiving a 2027 second-round pick and a 2028 fifth-round selection in return. While losing a three-time All-Pro defender is a significant blow to the secondary, the Falcons now have an opportunity to evaluate what Hellams can bring in an expanded role.
“We understand the business of the game, the nature of the game. That leaves guys in position to step up, which is me,” Hellams said. “I feel like I came into the league to take every day to prepare like a starter. And when my moment comes, to be ready for it.”
For Hellams, that moment has arrived. Through nine games this season, mostly on special teams, he has recorded 14 total tackles, including five solo tackles and nine assists. He also has one pass deflection and one tackle for loss.
The fourth-year safety has spent much of his career working behind established players in Atlanta’s secondary. Now, he has an opportunity to show that he can handle a starting role.
Hellams has the support of his teammates, including rookie safety Xavier Watts, who expressed confidence in his ability to step into the vacant position.
“I think ’Marco (Hellams) is going to come in and do a great job. Jammie Robinson, a couple other guys who might kind of bounce around in that position. But, next-man-up mentality,” Watts said.
Jammie Robinson, Sydney Brown, and Billy Bowman Jr. provide additional depth and flexibility in the secondary.
Head coach Kevin Stefanski has also expressed confidence in Hellams, identifying him as the next man up.
“DeMarcco is the next man up that we feel really good about,” Stefanski said. “He has played good football for us.”
Replacing Bates’ production and leadership will not be an easy task. However, Atlanta does not need Hellams to become Bates overnight. The Falcons need him to play confidently, communicate effectively and help stabilize the back end of the defense.
His first test will be a big one. Patrick Mahomes, Travis Kelce, and the Kansas City Chiefs will put a lot of stress on the perimeter of the defense with their ability to extend plays.
For Hellams, this is an opportunity he has spent years preparing for. Now, with the starting job within reach, he has a chance to prove his teammates and coaches right.

title: Ryan Neuzil Trade Leaves Falcons With a Big Question on the Offensive Line
full_text:
FLOWERY BRANCH – The Atlanta Falcons are 3-6, and they say the playoffs are still in reach. By Tuesday night, they had traded the center who started their last 26 games. On Sunday, his replacement will line up against Chris Jones.
Atlanta surprised many by trading center Ryan Neuzil at the deadline on Tuesday, flipping him to the Baltimore Ravens for interior offensive lineman Andrew Vorhees and a conditional 2028 draft selection.
Neuzil played five seasons with the Falcons and started the last 26 games (39 total). He was a solid center for Atlanta this season, allowing one sack and committing a single penalty, but the move makes it clear the team was ready to go in a different direction once he hit free agency this offseason.
In his place, Corey Levin will get the nod on Sunday.
“Obviously, love ‘Neuz’ [Ryan Neuzil],” Falcons head coach Kevin Stefanski said Wednesday when asked about the move. “Great person. Just felt like this was an opportunity for our football team and comfortable and feel good about Corey Levin stepping in.”
Levin joined the Falcons this offseason, following his former offensive line coach, Bill Callahan, from the Tennessee Titans. He has mostly handled special teams for the Falcons this season, but that will ramp up in the second half.
Stefanski expressed confidence in Levin’s ability to step in, perform snaps with Michael Penix Jr., and hold up as the team’s starter. The head coach confirmed that Levin had already been getting reps in practice and would be ready to go. Stefanski said he feels “really good” about where Levin is in understanding what the team is doing.
“He brings great energy into the locker room and onto the field,” Falcons running back Bijan Robinson said about his new center. “He doesn’t have an off switch. He’s already ready to go, always ready to play, no matter what the situation is. He just gives extreme effort.”
But the veteran has started only three games since the end of the 2022 season, and what’s waiting for him on Sunday would be a difficult challenge for even the most tenured center. For the Falcons, it is a massive question mark that could leave the heart of the offense exposed.
The Kansas Chiefs piled on five sacks and pressured Jets quarterback Geno Smith on half of his dropbacks. Defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo is renowned for his ability to send exotic looks at players, and All-Pro defensive tackle Chris Jones recorded two of those sacks last Sunday – Levin will be matched up with him on every snap.
“Corey Levin, being a veteran center and a guy who’s played in games and can think the game,” Stefanski said, “is important for a week like this.”
The Falcons are banking on it, especially given how he's the only rostered player with starts at center.
As for the additional piece of the deal, the Falcons are confident in what they have in Vorhees.
The interior offensive lineman was a projected day-two pick in 2023, but a torn ACL during the scouting combine tanked him into the seventh round. He started all 20 games from 2024-25, and made five more appearances (two starts) this season.
In Atlanta, he will likely fill a depth guard position alongside Kyle Hinton. At 6-foot-6 and 330 pounds, Vorhees adds immediate interior size and the traits Callahan loves.
“I've competed against him over the years, and he's a good football player,” Stefanski said about the plan for Vorhees. “Coach [Bill] Callahan and crew will get their arms around him and get him up to speed.”
Vorhees will be a free agent this offseason, so there is no guaranteed future even if he pans out as a player the Falcons can develop over the final weeks of the season.
The playoffs are still in reach for this team , especially in a winnable NFC South, but the deadline moves didn't get them any closer. If anything, they’re further away.
They moved two starters , and the question shifts to why the team felt so comfortable leaving an important position in question with half the season still to play. It’s a reasonable question, given how the Falcons dropped to 3-6 on Sunday, their fourth loss in the last five games, but Stefanski reiterated that the focus has not shifted in this locker room.
“We’re excited about the opportunities we have in front of us, but decisions that are made for our football team are always in the best interest of our football team,” Stefanski said. “We talked about it earlier this week – sometimes there is that tension [between] short-term and long-term, but I know the group we have of players. I know the group we have of coaches and staff. Our focus hasn't changed one bit.”
The Falcons’ center position might say otherwise, and Chris Jones will test it on the first snap.
Garrett Chapman is a sports broadcaster, writer, and content creator based in Atlanta. He has several years of experience covering the Atlanta sports scene, college football, Georgia high school football, recruiting for 24/7 Sports, and the NFL. You can also hear him on Sports Radio 92.9 The Game.

title: Falcons Still Have Path to NFC South Title Despite Sitting in Last Place
full_text:
The Atlanta Falcons are sitting at the bottom of the NFC South standings, but their chances of winning the division are far from over.
Atlanta enters Week 10 with a 3-6 record after losing consecutive games, including a disappointing 34-17 defeat to the Cincinnati Bengals. Despite the recent struggles, the Falcons remain within striking distance of the division lead in what is still a wide-open NFC South race.
All four teams have three victories through nine weeks, leaving plenty of uncertainty about how the division will ultimately shake out.
Here is a look at the NFC South standings entering Week 10:
Atlanta is tied with Tampa Bay in the overall standings but currently sits behind the Buccaneers because of its division record. Tampa Bay has won both of its NFC South matchups, while Atlanta is 1-2 against division opponents.
The Panthers have lost three consecutive games, opening the door for the rest of the division to catch up. New Orleans, meanwhile, has won two of its last three contests and was the only NFC South team to pick up a victory in Week 9.
Tampa Bay has won three of its last five games and will have a bye in Week 10.
Atlanta has a challenging schedule ahead, beginning with a home matchup against the Kansas City Chiefs in Week 10. The Falcons will then enter their bye week before traveling to face the Minnesota Vikings in Week 12.
The schedule continues with a home game against the Detroit Lions, followed by road matchups against the Cleveland Browns and Washington Commanders.
However, the most important stretch could come toward the end of the season. Atlanta closes its regular-season schedule with three consecutive NFC South matchups against Tampa Bay, New Orleans and Carolina.
Those games could ultimately determine whether the Falcons have a legitimate chance to win the division. That message may be a tough sell in Atlanta after the Falcons dealt Jessie Bates III and Ryan Neuzil this week, but head coach Kevin Stefanski remains adamant that the playoffs are still the goal.
The Falcons cannot afford to let their recent losing streak continue. With eight games remaining, Atlanta needs to find consistency on both sides of the ball and take advantage of opportunities against division opponents.
Fortunately, no team has established control of the NFC South. Atlanta may currently occupy last place, but the division remains competitive enough for a turnaround to change everything.
The upcoming schedule presents challenges, but it also provides opportunities. If the Falcons can get back on track, they could still make a push for the NFC South title and a postseason berth.

title: Updated Atlanta Falcons Draft Picks and Position after NFL Trade Deadline
full_text:
When Atlanta Falcons general manager Ian Cunningham was hired in January, he took the job knowing his team was low on available salary cap space heading into free agency and didn't have a first-round pick in the NFL Draft.
So it was no surprise that Cunningham and the Falcons took a conservative approach to free agency, with wide receiver Jahan Dotson getting the biggest contract at just two years for $15 million. The vast majority of the following moves were one-year deals .
They addressed a pair of needs with their first two picks in April's draft, selecting cornerback Avieon Terrell and wide receiver Zachariah Branch. They've gotten excellent value from linebackers Kendal Daniels and Harold Perkins Jr., selected in the fourth and sixth rounds, respectively.
The big moves the Falcons made in the offseason were in the front office, including Cunningham, and a coaching change.
Atlanta will not be quiet this offseason.
After trading safety Jessie Bates III and center Ryan Neuzil, the Falcons added a second-round pick in 2027 and a pair of Day 3 picks in 2028.
Sitting at 3-6, but losing strength-of-schedule tiebreakers, the Falcons currently have the No. 10 overall pick in the NFL Draft. They also have a pair of picks in the second round at No. 41 and No. 60 (from Jacksonville), a third, fourth, a pair of projected comp picks in the sixth, and a seventh, according to Tankathon .
The Falcons receive comp picks for running back Tyler Allgeier (Cardinals) and defensive tackle David Onyemata (Jets), but the Dotson signing canceled out a sixth for Kaden Elliss (Saints), according to Over The Cap .
However, before the draft, the Falcons will be big players in free agency. The Falcons have $143 million in available cap space, according to Spotrac , $38 million more than the Arizona Cardinals, who have the second most.
The Falcons' available space is so mind-blowing that there are 19 teams that don't have $38 million available for 2027 right now. In 2022, the Falcons had to cut salaries just to sign their draft picks. This team has come a long way when it comes to salary cap management.
With a full war chest of cash and picks, Cunningham and the Falcons will address several pressing needs, with offensive tackle, cornerback, and wide receiver being the biggest. Experience at linebacker and another starting safety will be big as well, but non-premium positions come cheaper than the big-ticket items.
The big question right now is still the big question at the start of the season: What about quarterback?
Michael Penix Jr. has shown flashes of being the long-term option for the Falcons, but has he shown enough to keep Atlanta out of the quarterback market in 2027? If the answer is yes, the team can spend significant resources building the team around the quarterback.
If the answer is no, the Falcons will need to spend significant resources to acquire a potential franchise player at the position.
Despite losing Neuzil, the Falcons' offense remains intact after the trade deadline, giving Penix a fair evaluation period over the next eight games to answer any lingering questions.

title: Who Will Be the Falcons' New Starting Center After Ryan Neuzil Trade with Ravens?
full_text:
The Atlanta Falcons have agreed to trade center Ryan Neuzil to the Baltimore Ravens in exchange for guard Andrew Vorhees and a 2028 sixth-round draft pick. With Neuzil heading to Baltimore, Atlanta now has an opening at center heading into Sunday's matchup against the Kansas City Chiefs.
Corey Levin is the most likely option to replace Neuzil in the starting lineup. The veteran offensive lineman has been listed as Neuzil's backup throughout the season and now has an opportunity to earn an expanded role.
Although Levin does not have an extensive history as a starting center in the NFL, he brings some experience to the position. He has made seven career starts in the league, giving Atlanta a player who has at least experienced the responsibilities of starting at the professional level.
He was originally selected in the sixth round of the 2017 NFL Draft by the Tennessee Titans. He's played six seasons with the Titans, not counting practice squad duty when he didn't make an NFL appearance, and joined the Falcons as a free agent in March.
The Falcons will need him to get comfortable quickly, particularly with the Chiefs coming to Atlanta this Sunday. Communication along the offensive line will be especially important as Levin takes on responsibility for identifying defensive fronts and helping keep the pocket clean for quarterback Michael Penix Jr.
Atlanta cannot afford to have communication issues up front, especially against a Kansas City defense capable of creating pressure in multiple ways.
Levin's familiarity with the offensive line and his experience serving as Neuzil's backup should help make the transition easier.
While Levin appears positioned to take over as the starter, the Falcons have also made a move to strengthen their depth at the position.
Atlanta signed center Gus Hartwig to its practice squad, giving the organization another option as it adjusts to life without Neuzil.
Hartwig brings considerable college experience, having made 48 starts at Purdue. He also spent time with the Detroit Lions and New York Jets before joining Atlanta.
His addition provides the Falcons with another developmental option at center while giving the coaching staff some insurance behind Levin.
It remains to be seen whether Hartwig will eventually receive an opportunity to compete for a larger role, but his experience at Purdue gives Atlanta another player familiar with the responsibilities of playing center.
Neuzil's departure marks the end of an important chapter for Atlanta's offensive line.
The Falcons originally signed him as an undrafted free agent following the 2021 NFL Draft. He gradually worked his way up the depth chart, appearing in 69 games and making 38 starts during his time in Atlanta.
The trade also reunites Neuzil with former Falcons offensive line coach Dwayne Ledford, who held that position in Atlanta from 2021 through 2025.
In return, Atlanta receives Vorhees, a former seventh-round selection who was considered a potential Day 2 pick before suffering an ACL injury at the 2023 NFL Scouting Combine. Since returning to full health, Vorhees has started 22 of 39 possible games.
The additional draft pick also gives Atlanta another asset as it continues reshaping its roster.
For now, however, the biggest question is whether Levin can provide the stability Atlanta needs in the middle of its offensive line.
With the Chiefs approaching, the Falcons will have little time to adjust. Levin appears to have the inside track to replace Neuzil, and his performance could play an important role in determining how well Atlanta's offense operates moving forward.

title: Falcons Make Shock Trade Deadline Deal with Ravens for Starting Center Ryan Neuzil
full_text:
The Atlanta Falcons are making another surprising move ahead of the NFL trade deadline, this time shaking up their offensive line by trading starting center Ryan Neuzil to the Baltimore Ravens. According to a source, Atlanta is sending Neuzil to Baltimore in exchange for offensive lineman Andrew Vorhees and a 2028 sixth-round draft pick.
The move is unexpected considering Neuzil's importance to Atlanta's offensive line over the past two seasons. He has played almost exclusively at center and has been the team's starter since 2025, becoming a familiar presence in the middle of the offensive line.
However, Neuzil is in the final year of his contract, giving Atlanta an opportunity to acquire assets rather than potentially lose him in free agency. He also has ties to Ravens offensive line coach Dwayne Ledford, who recruited him to Appalachian State before the two reunited in Atlanta.
This was the second move the Falcons have made on Tuesday. They also signed Jake Moody from the Ravens practice squad , while releasing Nick Folk in a corresponding move.
Falcons reporter Tori McElhaney also reported that the Falcons released edge rusher Drake Jackson from the practice squad and added former Denver Broncos safety Delarrin Turner-Yell and center Gus Hartwig to the
The trade is another indication of the direction general manager Ian Cunningham wants to take this organization as he continues reshaping the roster.
Atlanta's latest move comes just one day after trading veteran safety Jessie Bates III to the Jacksonville Jaguars in exchange for a 2027 second-round pick and a 2028 fifth-round pick.
The Falcons are clearly approaching the trade deadline with an emphasis on acquiring future assets rather than sacrificing draft picks to make a playoff push.
Cunningham has been vocal about his philosophy of accumulating draft selections. During his introductory press conference, he made it clear how much he values having additional opportunities to build through the draft.
"I love picks, man," Cunningham said.
He has also described draft selections as currency, explaining that accumulating more picks gives an organization additional opportunities to find impact players.
That philosophy is becoming increasingly evident in Atlanta. Cunningham previously helped oversee Chicago's draft strategy as assistant general manager, and he appears intent on bringing a similar approach to the Falcons.
The organization now has additional draft picks to work with as it looks toward the 2027 offseason.
In return, Atlanta receives Andrew Vorhees, a 27-year-old interior offensive lineman with starting experience.
Baltimore selected Vorhees in the seventh round of the 2023 NFL Draft out of USC. He started all 17 games for the Ravens in 2025 and provides Atlanta with another experienced option along the offensive line.
His arrival gives the Falcons flexibility as they determine who will replace Neuzil at center.
Ultimately, this is another significant roster decision from Cunningham. Between moving Bates and now Neuzil, Atlanta appears increasingly focused on building its future through the draft while adding players who fit its longer-term plans.

title: Falcons Poach Kicker from Ravens, Nick Folk Released, per Report
full_text:
The Atlanta Falcons are making a change at kicker, officially releasing veteran Nick Folk and signing Jake Moody off the Baltimore Ravens' practice squad, according to NFL insider Jordan Schultz . Moody will be added to Atlanta's 53-man roster and is expected to take over kicking right away.
The move comes after another disappointing performance from Folk in Sunday's 34-17 loss to the Cincinnati Bengals. The veteran kicker missed a 38-yard field goal in the fourth quarter, adding to a growing list of struggles that ultimately cost him his job in Atlanta.
Moody, meanwhile, is coming off a successful appearance for Baltimore. He connected on a 53-yard field goal against the Jacksonville Jaguars on Thursday, showing the leg strength Atlanta hopes to add to its special teams unit.
Folk entered the season with an impressive track record. He had been the NFL's most accurate kicker in each of the previous three seasons, missing just one field goal in each campaign. However, that consistency did not carry over to Atlanta.
His struggles became increasingly difficult to overlook over the past two weeks.
Against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers in Week 9, Folk missed a 53-yard field goal in Atlanta's 16-0 shutout loss. He followed that performance by missing a 38-yard attempt against Cincinnati, his first missed field goal from inside 40 yards in a regular-season game since 2017.
The miss against the Bengals snapped a streak of 107 consecutive successful field goals from that distance.
Falcons head coach Kevin Stefanski addressed Folk's struggles following Sunday's loss and offered a noticeably different response than he had in previous weeks.
"I'm very focused on this game," Stefanski said. "Obviously, I expect Nick to make his kicks. Nick expects to make his kicks, but really just focused on this game."
When asked whether he was concerned about Folk's performance, Stefanski added:
"He knows we're counting on him, and that's the nature of being a guy that you're counting on. But he's a pro."
Those comments represented a shift from the confidence Stefanski previously expressed in his veteran kicker. After Folk's missed 53-yarder against Tampa Bay, Stefanski said he was very confident in his abilities and would not think twice about putting him on the field.
That confidence ultimately did not prevent Atlanta from exploring other options. The Falcons have now decided to move on from Folk entirely.
Moody gives the Falcons a younger option with starting experience and the ability to connect on longer field goals.
The 26-year-old was originally selected by the San Francisco 49ers in the third round of the 2023 NFL Draft. He spent time with San Francisco and Washington before joining Baltimore's practice squad.
Moody most recently appeared for the Ravens against the Jacksonville Jaguars on November 5. He connected on his lone field-goal attempt, a 53-yarder, and converted his only extra-point attempt.
For his NFL career, Moody has converted 65 of 83 field-goal attempts, a 78.3 percent success rate. He also has experience making kicks from beyond 50 yards, including a career-long 57-yard field goal.
The Falcons are hoping Moody can provide more consistency at a position that has become an unexpected problem this season.
Atlanta has dealt with several issues throughout its disappointing campaign, and missed kicks have only added to the frustration. With Folk unable to deliver the reliability the organization expected, the Falcons have decided it is time for a different direction.
Moody now gets an opportunity to establish himself as Atlanta's kicker moving forward, while Folk will look for his next opportunity after his release.

title: Falcons Earn High Marks for Jessie Bates III Trade with Jaguars
full_text:
The Atlanta Falcons made headlines yesterday when they traded All-Pro safety Jessie Bates III to the Jacksonville Jaguars for a second-round pick in April's NFL Draft and a fifth-round pick in 2028.
The Falcons were busy in the offseason with multi-year contract extensions for their young nucleus of players , but Bates was left without a new deal. Bates turns 30 in February, and his not getting a new contract was a harbinger of things to come by Tuesday's trade deadline.
From the Falcons' point of view, they are 3-6, paying a significant salary to a non-premium position to an aging player who is on the final eight games of his contract.
Despite denials from Kevin Stefanski on Monday , it's definitely a signal that the Falcons are focused on 2027, loading up on draft picks and sitting on the most available salary cap in the NFL.
To Falcons fans, it's a sign of another lost season from a franchise that has had eight-straight losing seasons.
But what did the national media think about the deal? Looking from the outside in, ESPN's Seth Walder, who hated pretty much every move the Falcons made over the last five seasons, loved the move, giving the Falcons a B+ on their return.
Walder rightly points out that keeping Bates and trying to get a comp pick for him wasn't going to work in Atlanta. They have $150 million in available salary cap space, and it's likely they'll sign multiple free agents who would cancel out the Bates loss in the formula.
"If the Falcons were not going to be contenders this season, then they almost had to deal Bates for the most they could get for him," Walder wrote on ESPN . "And while the 3-6 Falcons are still in the race in the lowly NFC South, they had to ask themselves: Is this team really going to make a run in 2026? It seems they answered that question honestly."
The Jaguars may have overpaid on the surface, but if they let Bates walk at the end of the season, they could get up to a third-round draft pick in return via the comp formula. The Jaguars are sitting $20 million over next year's cap already and aren't expected to be players in free agency.
After the trade, the Falcons are sitting on picks No. 10, No. 41, No. 60, and No. 72 in next year's draft. They can address a plethora of needs with those picks , including offensive tackle, wide receiver, and cornerback, among others.
It also gives them another pick to add to a package should they decide to trade up into the top five for a quarterback if they deem that's the move to make.
From all of the one year contracts to the salary cap hoarding, the Falcons indicated they were pointing towards 2027 as a re-tooling year for the franchise.
An excellent return on the Bates trade further indicated their intentions.

title: Falcons QB Michael Penix Jr. Flashes Rarely Seen Skill Amid Performance Drop-Off
full_text:
Michael Penix Jr. isn’t a scrambling quarterback by any means.
Entering this season, he had just 81 career rushing yards.
“I get that a lot about me not really scrambling much,” Penix said.
The third-year Atlanta Falcons quarterback is a pocket passer relying on processing defenses and a strong arm.
But that doesn’t mean the 6-foot-3, 220-pounder doesn’t possess the athleticism and wheels to elude opposing defenses if a play breaks down.
“That’s definitely part of Mike’s game,” Falcons head coach Kevin Stefanski told reporters Monday. “He’s plenty big and fast enough, and I thought those were excellent moments where he could move forward and make plays with his legs.”
In Atlanta’s NFL Madrid game debacle that was a prelude to a roster shakeup , Penix rushed for a career-high 50 yards on three carries in the 34-17 Week 9 loss to the Cincinnati Bengals at Santiago Bernabéu Stadium. He had 15 yards on the ground before the breakout performance.
His top rush was for 23 yards in the first quarter. Look too fast, and you’d think it was another left-handed Falcons quarterback named “Michael”.
The run put Atlanta in position to take a 10-7 lead on a 31-yard Nick Folk field goal.
“I felt good out there,” Penix said, discussing his mobility at Sunday’s postgame press conference. “I was able to scramble – get a couple of first downs. That’s what I felt we needed in those situations, so I took advantage of it.”
Penix finished the game with 20-for-31 passing for 162 yards, a touchdown, an interception, and 50 yards on the ground, second on the team behind running back Bijan Robinson’s 100 .
Penix’s running was a silver lining as his performance has dwindled the last two games, with one being a four-interception outing , after back-to-back three-touchdown pass games and an NFC Offensive Player of the Week award .
It could potentially introduce a new layer to offensive coordinator Tommy Rees’ scheme.
Knowing Penix can willingly pull the football and make a run for it can keep defenses honest as they’ve begun stacking the box on Atlanta to stop Robinson and the Falcons’ rushing attack .
“That adds a different dimension to your offense when your quarterback is getting out of there,” Stefanski said. “Those happen when you have really good pocket movement, when you have good decisions, when you’re listening to your feet.”
After losing four of their last five, the Falcons’ (3-6) upcoming schedule is unrelenting.
Up next is a Week 10 home game as Atlanta hosts the Kansas City Chiefs (6-2) and their three-time MVP and Super Bowl champion quarterback Patrick Mahomes.
Kansas City hosted and defeated the New York Jets 35-12 in Week 9 behind standout performances from Mahomes and running back and reigning Super Bowl MVP Kenneth Walker III, formerly of the Seattle Seahawks.
Kickoff is at 1 p.m. from Mercedes-Benz Stadium on CBS.

title: Kevin Stefanski Sends Message to Falcons Fans After Jessie Bates Trade
full_text:
The Atlanta Falcons are insisting they are not giving up on the 2026 season, despite making a significant move that suggests the organization is also looking toward the future.
Atlanta traded veteran safety Jessie Bates III to the Jacksonville Jaguars on Monday, a move that could be interpreted as a sign that the Falcons are shifting their focus toward 2027 rather than making a push for the playoffs this season. However, head coach Kevin Stefanski pushed back against that notion during his Monday press conference.
Stefanski acknowledged the difficulty of moving on from Bates.
“You guys know how I feel about Jessie, the person, Jessie, the player,” Stefanski told reporters. “But at the same time, this is football, where sometimes you have one foot in the short term, one foot in the long term. There's things like this that make your team better in the long run. Draft picks are the lifeblood of an organization. That's something we believe in.”
The decision to trade Bates is significant considering his importance to Atlanta's defense. He has been one of the team's most recognizable leaders and an important piece of the secondary. Losing him creates another challenge for a Falcons team that has struggled to find consistency this season.
Still, Stefanski wants fans to understand that the trade does not mean Atlanta is abandoning its postseason aspirations.
When asked whether the organization was essentially punting on the season, Stefanski made his position clear.
“Our fans are smart enough to know that in no way, shape, or form would we punt on this season. We have three wins, just like the rest of our division. Obviously not where we want to be, we want to play better, but we're very much in the thick of this thing and we trust in the guys that we have,” Stefanski said.
There is some truth to Stefanski's argument. The NFC South remains wide open, and Atlanta is still within reach of the division title despite sitting at 3-6. The Falcons have an opportunity to make up ground if they can turn things around over the second half of the season.
However, there is a difference between remaining mathematically competitive and making moves that suggest an organization believes it can contend right now.
Trading Bates sends a complicated message. Atlanta is collecting valuable draft picks for the future while simultaneously asking its current roster to find a way to compete without one of its most important defensive players.
Stefanski also emphasized that replacing Bates will require a collective effort.
“It's not just one person that has to step up. It's all of us that have to step up,” Stefanski said.
The Falcons can insist they are not giving up on 2026, and technically, they remain in the NFC South race. But Monday's trade raises legitimate questions about the organization's priorities.
Atlanta may still have a chance to win one of the weakest divisions in football, but trading away a player of Bates' caliber is not necessarily the move expected from a team that believes it is positioned to make a serious postseason run.
Stefanski can say the Falcons are not punting on the season. Now, the team will have to prove it on the field.

title: Ravens Provide Clarification On Surprising Last-Second Trade Acquisition
full_text:
It's rare to see a team make a trade for two starters at the same position where only one player can be on the field at a time without there having been a significant injury occur between the time both were acquired.
However, after losing all three of their top centers that they added during he offseason to major injuries before Week 4 rolled around, who can blame the Baltimore Ravens for wanting to upgrade and bolster the depth of their interior offensive line with another center?
Nonetheless, general manager Eric DeCosta's decision to pull the trigger on a trade right at the deadline for former Atlanta Falcons starting center Ryan Neuzil , barely over a month after trading a 2028 second-round pick to the Philadelphia Eagles for two-time Pro  Bowler Cam Jurgens , was a little puzzling for fans and pundits to take in .
Instant reactions to the move ranged from speculating whether Neuzil was coming in to be inserted into the starting lineup sooner rather than later, whether it be at center and slide Jurgens over to left guard, or if he'd straight up replace inconsistent veteran John Simpson at guard. He has started each of the last nine games at center for the Falcons and came into the league as a former All American at guard.
"I think he brings versatility," head coach Jesse Minter said. "I don't anticipate anything changing with Cam [Jurgens] and what position he plays, and we think he's the future of our offensive line. I think it's just a piece that adds depth, and I do think he'll have some position flexibility as he gets here and as he gets going. Wherever that leads, I think we'll see as we go."
Before becoming a Raven, Jurgens was playing out of position at guard for the Eagles and experienced some struggles. He is glad to be back in this natural position on a new team and welcomes Neuzil's arrival and what it means for the overall quality and depth of his unit.
"It's never a bad thing to have more guys that can snap," Jurgens said. "Ryan's a guy that's played a lot of football. I'm excited to have him in the room."
By adding a player of Neuzil's experience, versatility and pedigree, the Ravens won't find themselves in a position of having to slide stud first-round rookie Vega Ioane over to center again and leave them with another subpar combination at guard. It also gives them another option to turn to at left guard if Simpson's play doesn't improve.
To go from starting nearly 30 straight games to being relegated to a high-value backup is not what Neuzil envisioned for himself when the season started, and he was the anchor in the middle of his own unit, but he's willing to play whatever role is required of him.
"I'm not sure really the plan right now," Neuzil said. "I'm just here to get better and fill in wherever they need me to...I played a little bit of guard my first year, and then transitioned to center, but just wherever they need me."
The last few days have been a bit of a whirlwind for the sixth-year veteran and his family as he went from returning home from playing in the Falcons' international matchup with the Cincinnati Bengals in Spain on Sunday to hopping on a plane to Baltimore late Tuesday night.
Unlike most players who are brought in from another team in the middle of the season, Neuzil has a strong foundation in the type of wide-zone blocking schemes that he'll be executing in Baltimore. He spent the first four years of his career being groomed by Ravens offensive line coach and run game coordinator Dwayne Ledford, who was likely consulted by the player personnel department in before the trade was made.
"It definitely helps a lot," Neuzil said. "I was with [Ledford] for five years in Atlanta, so [I] understand what he wants and what he sees in offensive linemen, so it's definitely a plus."
