title: Bills' Amani Hooker Trade Grades: Not Everyone Loved Buffalo's Deadline Day Deal
full_text:
The Buffalo Bills made one of the biggest trades on deadline day when they swung a deal with the Tennessee Titans for safety Amani Hooker.
The trade saw general manager Brandon Beane give up a second-round pick in exchange for Hooker and a fifth-round pick.
Buffalo had a clear need at safety and needed a big move. Hooker is not a superstar player, but he is on that next tier and should prove to be a very nice upgrade for the Bills' defense that desperately needed a boost.
Now, let's see how experts from different media outlets graded the move. We've also provided our grade beneath those.
Walder comes in with the lowest grade in our round-up. His biggest issue with the Bills' trade is the price.
"So Hooker is an upgrade at a position of need for a Super Bowl-contending team and will save them a few million per year relative to the market. But is that worth a second-round pick? It strikes me as rich. Hooker is a good player but not a star -- he has never been a Pro Bowl selection or All-Pro and only snuck into Jeremy Fowler's NFL evaluator survey of top safeties in the 'also receiving votes' category. As a result, the compensation here is a bit steep," Walder said.
A second-round pick is expensive, especially for a safety who is very good but not elite. However, we also have to remind ourselves that the pick is going to be late in the second round, which basically makes it a third-round pick, so there's that.
Adding to that, the Bills received a fifth-round pick back, and we also know that Hooker is under contract for two more years following this one, so that also softens the blow.
Patra was a fan of the deal because of the fit with Hooker. He didn't think the price was too much.
"I love the fit. Buffalo can now become much more multi-faceted on the back end with Hooker’s arrival," Patra explained. "The price wasn’t exorbitant for a player still under contract for two additional years with no guaranteed money. Yes, giving up a Day 2 pick is tough, but assuming it’s at the back of Round 2 while the Titans pick is at the front of Round 5, it’s not that far of a fall to get a potential difference-maker come January."
The Bills had one of the worst pass defenses in the NFL and that's something Hooker will help with given his strength is playing on the back end.
Hooker's ball-hawking ability is huge, also, as the Bills had just one pick from their safeties combined this season and C.J. Gardner-Johnson, who is no longer with the team , had the pick.
Pereles thinks the trade for the Bills was "expensive," but all of the positives Hooker brings to the table is enough to justify the price, as is the Bills keeping up with other Super Bowl contenders who made big trades.
"The Bills saw several other Super Bowl contenders making significant win-now moves and decided to make their own on deadline day, acquiring safety Amani Hooker and a 2027 fifth-round pick from the Titans for a 2027 second-round pick," he explained.
"It's a big move for a player in the middle of his best year: Hooker has five interceptions this year, including three off Joe Burrow in one game. Other Bills safeties have one pick combined. He is a versatile defender who's willing to tackle -- a strong addition to a Bills secondary that needed help. It was expensive, but worth doing. Buffalo got significantly better Tuesday," Pereles added.
Reports suggested the Titans weren't interested in trading Hooker ahead of the deadline, so Beane was going to have to overpay a bit to pry him away from Nashville.
I'm pretty sure that if Bills fans had to choose between the trade that went down and nothing at all, they would choose the former. Fans have been wanting Beane to do something significant for years now and he finally did it.
I love this trade for the Bills.
Yes, a second-round pick is a lot, but it's basically a third-round pick because the Bills' selections are going to be at the end of rounds. Buffalo also got a fifth-round pick back, and they are getting a player who is under contract for two more years .
Hooker is also a well-rounded player with his ability to play strong or free safety, and even in the slot. He is also good in coverage and against the run, as evidenced by his Pro Football Focus grades of 75.2 in coverage and 83.9 in run defense, ranking 10th and 13th among safeties, respectively.
Hooker thrives most at free safety and has a nose for the football. As we previously noted, the Bills had just one pick from safeties in 2026, and we know also sports one of the worst pass defenses in the NFL and the defense has given up 28 plays of 20-plus yards, an issue Hooker can definitely help fix.
The Bills needed a big trade to help their defense and this was as close to one as Buffalo could get. Hats off to Beane for getting it done.
Daniel Popper, The Athletic: A-
Walter Cherepinsky, Walter Football: A
Eric Edholm & Frank Schwab, Yahoo Sports: B+

title: Carolina Panthers Mailbag: No Trades, First-Place Matchup, and More
full_text:
The Carolina Panthers did not have a busy week, but there's plenty going on with them. It's an important week moving forward, and there are some key storylines coming up. Here's what you need to know.
This, to me, feels very much like the Panthers using a cop-out. The NFC South is abysmal, and the day before the deadline, both the New Orleans Saints and Atlanta Falcons offloaded good players. That leaves the Panthers and Tampa Bay Buccaneers at even strength.
The Panthers have lost three in a row and obviously feel no sense of urgency. They are going to get healthier, but until then, how much longer can they keep losing? The Panthers don't have a ton of flexibility to make moves, so it's not all that surprising. It is a little disappointing, though.
A team in a tight divisional race, with the ridiculous number of injuries the Panthers have sustained, should be adding players to offset the losses and keep them in the race. Instead, the Panthers seem to be banking on everyone else being just as bad. It may well work out, but they could've taken matters into their own hands and probably should have.
When the Panthers were 3-2 and in first place, life felt so good. It felt like they were about to really seize control and take a huge step forward as a franchise. Three losses later, life does not feel good, but they incomprehensibly remain in first place.
That is, until Sunday. A fourth straight loss, this time to the New Orleans Saints, would hand the division lead to the Saints. It's only the middle of the season, but this is a monumental matchup. It is borderline must-win.
The Panthers have overlooked the Saints far too much over the last couple of seasons. Dave Canales-led teams often come out flat when there's a moment like this. Hopefully, that won't be the case this week, but it's hard to have much confidence there.
On paper, though, the Panthers should be slightly better than the Saints here, but that really hasn't mattered before.
Reports suggest that the Panthers and Bryce Young are on their way to an extension worth over $50 million. This is both fair and unfair, appropriate and inappropriate. The report came out during that brutal two-week stretch in which he took 11 sacks, but he's back on the upswing again.
The version of Young we've seen this year, including those two awful games, is absolutely worth $50 million. He's made the most porous offensive line work to the tune of the fourth-most yards per game. He's had to endure receivers coming in and out of the lineup with injuries and a rookie play-caller.
The "problem" is that it's a small sample size. I fully believe this version of Young is here to stay, and that he will never again be questioned as a starting-level QB. The thing I wish would happen is the Panthers using his bad first two years and mediocre third year as a way to get a discount.
Sadly, it doesn't work like that, but it would help the team out a lot. But ultimately, Young has earned a lucrative extension with his play, and that's really all anyone can ask for.
The defense under Todd Wash for his first game as coordinator was not night and day from Ejiro Evero's, but it was better. It's going to take some time for the players to adjust to a slightly new system, so we still saw some lingering Evero things last week and may this week.
What we didn't see, though, were third-and-long conversions (excluding pass interference conversions, but when you're working with practice squad cornerbacks, that's what happens) due to inexplicable coverages. They stopped the run pretty well, too.
They flocked to the ball and played downhill a lot more. The system still needs to be ironed out, but Wash has the players playing hard, and there's not much more we can ask for in the wake of firing a coordinator.
Zachary Roberts is a journalist with a wide variety of experience covering basketball, golf, entertainment, video games, music, football, baseball, and hockey. He currently covers Charlotte sports teams and has been featured on Sportskeeda, Yardbarker, MSN, and On SI.

title: Winners and Losers From Panthers’ Silent Trade Deadline
full_text:
Carolina Panthers GM Dan Morgan has decided to stand pat at the NFL trade deadline for the second consecutive year. The decision by Morgan not to add any pieces to the current roster to help the team in the second half of the season will likely be scrutinized by fans, as the Panthers have lost three straight games and are dealing with injuries to several key players.
But with Carolina sitting at 3-5 on the season, the Panthers are still very much in the NFC South division race. So, while some players on the roster could benefit from Morgan’s decision to stay put, others are sure to have a tougher go of it in the second half of the season.
The biggest winner of the deadline for Carolina is defensive tackle Derrick Brown. According to reports, several teams were calling Morgan regarding the defensive tackle, but the GM was not interested in moving one of the top defensive players on the roster.
But there’s also the fact that Brown is a player the Panthers have invested a lot of money in. So unless someone was offering up a king’s ransom for the defensive tackle, it makes sense that the Panthers would hold on to him.
Players who could benefit from Carolina’s decision to stay put include those on the injured list who are slowly but surely making their way back to practice. Cornerback Mike Jackson, wide receiver Xavier Legette, and running back Jonathon Brooks have all had their 21-day practice windows opened.
The Panthers are hoping that with the return of Jackson and Horn, the Carolina secondary will be able to play at a high level for the rest of the season.
Another winner is Carolina’s future draft capital. The Panthers didn’t give up any draft picks to acquire a player for the remainder of this season.
There are currently eight picks that the Panthers have in the 2027 NFL Draft. Carolina still has plenty of needs to fill, and Morgan will have plenty of opportunities to do that in the offseason.
Of course, that doesn’t mean the Panthers will find great players with those picks. But the GM will have the opportunity to address the team’s needs in the offseason.
The biggest loser of the Carolina Panthers trade deadline is likely going to be quarterback Bryce Young. Carolina’s offensive line has been very inconsistent this season, and the offense has struggled to string together consistent drives.
Young was sacked 11 times in losses to the Buccaneers and Packers. While the Panthers’ offensive line showed some improvement against the Broncos, Young was stripped of the football on a sack during the team's final offensive possession.
Another offensive lineman or even another weapon in the passing game would have been nice for Young. Instead, he will have to continue to rely on the players currently on the roster to get the job done and hope for more consistency from the offense.
One area of the team that could have used some help is the cornerback position. The Panthers have been hit hard by injuries in the secondary as of late, and that was on full display against Denver.
When the Panthers’ cornerback depth is tested, it’s not always pretty. Against the Broncos, the Panthers relied on a bunch of guys who weren’t expected to see much action this season. Marco Wilson and Corey Thornton combined for four accepted pass interference penalties, with another flag against Wilson declined in favor of a taunting penalty.
This could be an issue for the Panthers as they are trying to win the division. Hopefully, the Panthers will get Jackson and Horn back soon, but until then, they will have to rely on their current depth.
The Panthers could have addressed the cornerback position with a trade, but instead, Morgan chose to stand pat with the players currently on the roster. This means that if another injury were to occur in the secondary, the team would have to rely on that same depth.
The silent trade deadline also did not bring any players to Carolina who could help the team’s chances of winning the NFC South.
Despite having a 3-5 record, the NFC South is still there for the taking for the Carolina Panthers. Right now, the Panthers are tied with the New Orleans Saints at 3-5, while the Falcons and Buccaneers are both 3-6.
The decision not to make a trade is an interesting one. Morgan had the opportunity to explore acquiring a player who could help the Panthers now, but decided to keep the draft picks instead and wait for the injured players to return to the field.
There are good arguments for both sides of the decision. Carolina is not a team that is one player away from winning a Super Bowl. Trading away valuable draft picks for a short-term solution is not the way to build a team for the long term.
But there is also something to be said for taking advantage of an opportunity when it presents itself. Carolina doesn’t know how often it will be in a position to win the division with a losing record.
Morgan made his decision, and now the Panthers have to make it work. If the Panthers can find a way to win the NFC South, then standing pat at the deadline will have been the right move.
But if the injuries continue to pile up and Carolina misses the playoffs, then there will be questions about why Morgan didn’t make a trade when he had the chance.
Mark Livingston is a South Carolina native and recent Penn State graduate with a degree in Digital Media and Journalism. He previously wrote for Greenville Sports Media, where he covered various sports and teams across the Carolinas. His experience includes game coverage, feature stories and interviews.

title: 3 Panthers Opponents Who Got Better or Worse at the NFL Trade Deadline
full_text:
Carolina Panthers didn’t make any moves at the NFL trade deadline. But other teams did. Some of the Carolina Panthers opponents in the NFC South made moves by trading away some of their veteran defensive players. Also, the Minnesota Vikings made a move to bring back a familiar face to play quarterback for them.
The Carolina Panthers are fighting to win the NFC South this year. But with so many injuries in their secondary they can’t make too many mistakes on the field. Also, their offense hasn’t been able to consistently move the ball down the field in games.
There could be some value in some of the trades that were made at the NFL trade deadline for the Carolina Panthers. But there could also be some trades that make things a little more difficult for the Panthers. Here are three trades that could make an impact on the Panthers remaining schedule.
The Vikings made a move to trade a 2027 third-round pick to the Las Vegas Raiders for the rights to bring back the veteran quarterback Kirk Cousins to Minnesota. Cousins left the Vikings for the Atlanta Falcons two years ago.
But does it matter for the Panthers? Will Cousins be able to produce enough in the offense for Minnesota to make them more difficult to defend than they already were before the trade?
Cousins can run the offense of Minnesota’s head coach Kevin O’Connell already. He also has the current star receivers on the team in Justin Jefferson and Jordan Addison. He can come in and run the offense immediately. But there won’t be much time to work out the kinks since the Vikings are in the middle of a season.
For the Panthers the biggest concern would be how Cousins will handle the pressure that the Panthers defense can bring. The Carolina secondary has been hit hard with injuries. The last thing the Panthers need is a QB that can recognize coverage and get the ball out before the defense can recover.
The Panthers hope that Cousins can’t get the football out of his hands before the Panthers secondary can recover from coverage errors. He is a QB that doesn’t need to extend the play with his feet. If the Panthers can’t affect his timing then Minnesota can attack the Panthers defensive backfield.
Of course the Vikings have to prove that this move makes them better. Cousins hasn’t played in O’Connell’s offense since 2023. He knows the offense. But that doesn’t mean that he’ll automatically pick up where he left off.
It will be interesting to see if the Vikings made the right move when the Panthers travel to Minnesota on December 6th.
Atlanta Falcons made a move to trade away safety Jessie Bates III to the Jacksonville Jaguars for a 2027 second-round pick and a 2028 fifth-round pick. This is a very good return for the Falcons. But for the remainder of the season the move can only hurt the Falcons chances of winning the NFC South.
The Falcons got the best of both worlds by dealing Bates III. But more the latter than the former. He’s a veteran safety that can read the eyes of a quarterback to make plays in the secondary. He can also recognize an offense’s scheme and then react to it. He’s the type of player that can make a quarterback hesitate when deciding whether or not to throw into a certain area of the field.
The Panthers already have had their fair share of issues this season in regards to pressure and turnovers. Having another less experienced player in the secondary for the Panthers to have to worry about would be a plus for Carolina. Especially in a game that could come down to the wire in which the Panthers would have to throw the ball.
There are still other defensive players that Atlanta has on their roster. So it is not as though their secondary is going to be easy to beat in the upcoming games for the Panthers.
This is a very interesting trade because it’s being made by a team that is currently in the hunt for the NFC South. But they are dealing away one of their better defensive players for future draft capital.
The trade will likely be better for Atlanta in the long run. But for the remainder of this season it is hard to see how losing Bates III can help the Falcons defense.
If the Falcons are still in the hunt for the NFC South title in Week 18, the Panthers will be glad that they do not have to play against one of the best safeties in the league.
The Saints made a move to trade defensive tackle Davon Godchaux to the Jacksonville Jaguars.
In return for the veteran defensive tackle, New Orleans received a conditional 2028 NFL Draft pick in the 6th round. While Godchaux was not a stats-sheet-filling defensive tackle, he provided much needed size and veteran presence on the interior of the Saints’ defensive line.
This matters against a team like Carolina. Especially if the Panthers want to establish the running game.
If the Panthers can get four yards or more on first down, that opens up a lot of things for the offense. And takes pressure off of Bryce Young.
Does losing the veteran defensive tackle make it any easier for Carolina to find yards in the running game?
One defensive tackle does not make a whole team’s defense against the run. There are other players on the Saints’ defense that can be used to stop the run. It will be interesting to see if New Orleans can replace what Godchaux brought to the defense.
If Hubbard is able to consistently find yards between the tackles then the Panthers can keep feeding him the ball. And force the Saints to make adjustments on defense. If the middle of the Saints defensive line is able to stop the Panthers then they will have to find other ways to move the ball down the field.
This trade will be worth watching in the short term as the Panthers take on the New Orleans Saints on Sunday.
While the Panthers didn’t make any trades at the deadline. There are several trades from other teams that could be of value to the Panthers.
The only other opponent on the remaining schedule of the Panthers that could have gotten better is the Minnesota Vikings. By bringing back Kirk Cousins, Minnesota has a veteran QB that knows several of the players on the team as well as several of the coaches.
The Falcons and Saints have gone in the other direction by trading away experienced defenders for draft picks. Carolina is more concerned with how the defenses will look for the remainder of the season than with the draft picks that were received in return for those players.
This trade will have the biggest impact on the NFC South race. As long as the Falcons are still in the hunt for the division title in Week 18, Carolina will be glad that they do not have to play against one of the best safeties in the league in Jessie Bates III.
However, the Godchaux trade is the one that will have the biggest impact on the Panthers’ remaining games. As they will test the Saints’ defensive line on Sunday.
While none of these trades guarantee the Panthers can win more games. The trades do provide the Panthers with more advantages as they try to win the NFC South.
But with the NFC South still up for grabs, Carolina will take any advantage it can get.
Mark Livingston is a South Carolina native and recent Penn State graduate with a degree in Digital Media and Journalism. He previously wrote for Greenville Sports Media, where he covered various sports and teams across the Carolinas. His experience includes game coverage, feature stories and interviews.

title: Panthers Did Nothing at Deadline, but Several Reinforcements Are Coming
full_text:
The Carolina Panthers are currently on a nosedive , losing three straight after starting the year 3-2. A huge piece of that nosedive has been injuries on both sides of the ball. The defense has been ravaged ; both starting corners, Jaycee Horn and Mike Jackson, have been on IR since Week 3.
Not only have Jackson and Horn been out, but their replacements, Will Lee III and Akayleb Evans, have been as well. That's left Carolina with Marco Wilson and Chau Smith-Wade as the starting corners. Sunday's loss to the Broncos made it evident that those two aren't a winning solution.
Panthers' premier pass rusher Jaelan Phillips, who signed a four-year $120 million deal with Carolina in free agency, has been out since Week 7 with a hamstring injury.
On offense, the injuries are just as bad. Right tackle Taylor Moton is on IR after fracturing his fibula; WR Xavier Legette hasn't played since Week 2, after suffering a knee injury in a win against the Atlanta Falcons. Another injury from that game: RB Jonathon Brooks injured his groin and went on IR.
The injuries have piled up worse than Carolina can imagine, yet the Panthers didn't address any of the depth concerns at the trade deadline.
With no moves made, the Panthers are heavily relying on the return of their starters, and head coach Dave Canales gave an update on some potential returns happening sooner rather than later.
Speaking to the media on November 9th, the day before the NFL trade deadline, Canales provided updates on several key starters . His quote is as follows.
"It's getting very exciting with some of the guys that are close. And those are conversations were having today, tomorrow, as we have these days to evaluate them. We're talking about Jaycee, Mike, we're talking about Jonathon Brooks. [They're] all going through their processes to see when they're ready to come back."
"Xavier is another one, and I'm so excited for where they are. We got to take in these next two days to see what it's going to look like going into the weekend."
As positive as Canales sounds, it's highly unlikely all of those players will be back on Sunday for a pivotal division game against the Saints. Mike Jackson returned to practice on Wednesday, which is a phenomenal sign.
Horn is still on IR; Legette and Jaelan Phillips have returned to practice, so Carolina will certainly have more reinforcements entering Sunday in New Orleans. If they all play and produce, then Carolina won't look as bad for not making any deadline moves.
Preston is an experienced sports writer focusing on NFL, College Football, NBA, and MMA topics. He is a passionate Charlotte and Oklahoma sports fan and graduated from the University of Science and Arts Oklahoma in 2025 with a Bachelor of Arts in Communications degree with a focus in journalism.

title: Mike Jackson's Return Could Be His Final Audition With the Panthers
full_text:
The Panthers may have another starting cornerback on the field as the team tries to push for the NFC South title. On Wednesday, Mike Jackson returned to practice after missing the last five games with a groin injury that required surgery.
However, Jackson is trying to prove more than just that he can help the Panthers win in the next few weeks. He is trying to prove that he is worth a new contract and that the Panthers should keep him around after this season.
Even though he has been one of the Panthers’ top defensive players for the last two seasons, Jackson has missed a lot of time this season with the groin injury. He will be a free agent after this season, so the remaining games could be his last chance to prove to the Panthers that they should keep him around.
The 21-day practice window for Jackson was opened by the Panthers on Wednesday, allowing him to practice with the team while he tries to get activated off injured reserve.
Jackson hasn’t played in a game since Carolina’s Week 3 loss to the Cleveland Browns. With Jaycee Horn also sidelined, the Panthers have been relying on several lesser-known cornerbacks to get through the season.
The Panthers’ secondary had its share of problems in the team’s 26-21 loss to Denver on Sunday. There were several penalties and other issues on the back end of the defense, and Jackson could provide another veteran presence for the Panthers as they prepare to face the New Orleans Saints in what is sure to be a tough divisional battle.
Jackson has not yet been cleared to play in the Panthers’ game on Sunday against New Orleans. However, getting back on the field for practice is a step in the right direction for him to prove to the Panthers what they have been missing while he was out with the injury.
Jackson joined the Panthers in a trade with the Seattle Seahawks before the 2024 season. He has been a reliable starter for Carolina the last two seasons and has put up some big numbers for the Panthers.
Jackson had 36 passes defended and six interceptions in the 2024 and 2025 seasons . His 19 pass breakups in 2025 led the NFL.
Jaycee Horn was given a big-money contract by the Panthers last year. He’s been a great player opposite Jackson, and that is certainly a factor that the team will take into consideration when deciding whether or not to spend big money on another cornerback.
But Jackson still has some things to prove. He’s coming off surgery, and he hasn’t played in a game for Todd Wash yet. That’s something the Panthers couldn’t have anticipated when they signed Jackson to his current contract.
Now Todd Wash is the defensive coordinator, replacing Ejiro Evero. Jackson has not played in a defense similar to Wash’s before.
Jackson thinks that he can take some of the things that he’s learned from Evero and apply them to Wash’s more aggressive style of defense .
How he performs in the new system is going to be something to watch for the rest of the season.
It will be interesting to see how things play out for Jackson and the Panthers.
This year, the cornerback is playing on the second year of a two-year, $10.5 million contract with the Panthers . The contract carries a salary-cap figure of $7.8 million for 2026, according to Over the Cap.
Jackson’s production was great for the Panthers prior to his injury, so they will certainly look to see what kind of value they can get from him based on his current production.
Spotrac previously projected that Jackson could receive a three-year contract worth approximately $40 million .
That would put his next contract at about $13.3 million per season, which is a big jump over what the Panthers have been paying him.
But should the Panthers spend that kind of money on a cornerback who turns 30 in January and has missed much of the season due to injury?
Jackson has played at a high level when healthy, but the Panthers have other needs on their roster. If they were to pay Jackson more than $13 million a season, it would limit what they could do to fill other holes on the roster.
A shorter contract in the $10 million range per year would be better for the Panthers. This would recognize his previous play and give them some protection in the event of injury or decline in play.
If the Panthers can keep Jackson, they should. However, they should not pay him any more than they have to.
The Panthers don’t have to make a decision on Jackson right now. He still has games left to play and can help out a battered secondary.
But Jackson’s return will also give the Panthers a chance to evaluate the cornerback in a different light. They will be able to see how he is recovering from surgery, how he is fitting into Wash’s defense and if he is able to return to his form prior to the injury.
Jackson’s play over the past two seasons has earned him consideration for another contract, but the Panthers must be able to sign him for a fair price.
The Panthers should try to bring him back, but not at any cost.
If Jackson returns and plays like he did before he got hurt, he’ll make that decision a lot harder for Morgan. And with free agency coming up, Jackson knows these final games could have a big impact on what happens next.
Mark Livingston is a South Carolina native and recent Penn State graduate with a degree in Digital Media and Journalism. He previously wrote for Greenville Sports Media, where he covered various sports and teams across the Carolinas. His experience includes game coverage, feature stories and interviews.

title: 3 NFL Trade Deadline Deals the Panthers Should've Been All Over
full_text:
The Carolina Panthers did not make any moves at the NFL trade deadline on Tuesday. Instead, the team is going to use the players on the current roster and hope that some of the injured players can return in time to make a run at the end of the year.
The Carolina Panthers have plenty of needs on their roster. While they’re still in contention to win the NFC South, general manager Dan Morgan stood pat at the deadline.
Not every team in the NFL was giving up a first-round pick for a player to help them immediately. Some teams were giving up late-round picks for a player.
The San Francisco 49ers on Tuesday traded for wide receiver Keenan Allen from the Indianapolis Colts in exchange for a 2027 sixth-round draft pick.
That is not much to give up for a veteran wide receiver who is so good at getting open against NFL defenses.
In eight games with the Colts, Allen had 40 catches for 351 yards and one touchdown.
While the Panthers have several young receivers on the roster in McMillan and Coker, adding another experienced target for Young would have helped the offense move the chains for the rest of the season.
The Panthers would have had to deal with Allen’s contract for the remainder of the season, but for a sixth-round pick in 2027, he could have been a nice addition for the rest of the season.
The Panthers are still in contention to win the NFC South, and adding another offensive weapon to help them make a run for the rest of the season would have been a good move.
The Detroit Lions traded for safety Andre Cisco from the New York Jets on Monday for a 2028 sixth-round pick.
With several of Carolina’s corners on IR, a veteran addition to the secondary would have been a good move for the Panthers.
The Panthers are down several players in the secondary due to a rash of injuries.
The veteran safety would have added another experienced player to the Panthers’ secondary, although not necessarily as a direct replacement for one of the injured cornerbacks.
This would have been a good trade for the Panthers because they would have been getting a player of value and giving up very little in terms of future draft picks. His contract would also have to be considered.
While the San Francisco 49ers made a trade for a veteran wide receiver in Keenan Allen, the Kansas City Chiefs made a trade for a younger wide receiver in Josh Downs. The Chiefs gave up a 2027 fourth-round pick and a 2027 fifth-round pick to the Indianapolis Colts for Downs and a 2027 seventh-round pick.
While Keenan Allen is a veteran, Downs is a younger player that the Panthers could keep for future years. However, his contract expires after this season.
There are still many opportunities for Carolina to add talent to the receiving corps. Downs would have been a great addition to the offense in several ways, giving Young another target in the passing game, especially in the short area of the field.
Downs had 33 receptions for 354 yards and one touchdown in nine games with the Colts this season.
Downs would have cost more in terms of draft capital than Allen, but not to the extent of multiple first-round picks.
There are several reasons why the Panthers did not make a trade before the trade deadline. Most of the players who are currently on the Panthers’ roster and on the injured list are expected to return to the team in the near future. This would allow the Panthers’ front office to make moves for the future rather than just trying to keep up with other teams in the league.
There are many positions on the team that could use an upgrade, but the Panthers are in a position to win the NFC South right now.
The Panthers have little space under the salary cap and so would have struggled to take on another player’s contract.
Of course, not every traded player would have been a good fit for Carolina, and Morgan could not assume that other teams would have been as willing to make the same trade with the Panthers.
There were many other players traded on Tuesday, and several of those could have been players that the Panthers would be interested in.
While Morgan did not make a big trade, there were plenty of smaller deals that could have been made to help the Panthers down the stretch of the season.
Mark Livingston is a South Carolina native and recent Penn State graduate with a degree in Digital Media and Journalism. He previously wrote for Greenville Sports Media, where he covered various sports and teams across the Carolinas. His experience includes game coverage, feature stories and interviews.

title: Tackle? Cornerback? Panthers Pass on Most Glaring Needs in Latest Mock Draft
full_text:
The NFL trade deadline has come and gone , featuring huge moves across the league. The trade deadline is one of the most anticipated points on the NFL calendar; rosters can change dramatically, and with that, the focus on roster building shifts to the offseason.
The NFL Draft becomes even more important for some teams after the deadline. This is especially true for teams that either stock up on draft picks, like the Philadelphia Eagles, or just aren't active and keep theirs, like the Carolina Panthers .
Carolina was dead silent at the trade deadline. GM Dan Morgan made zero moves despite clear holes on the roster caused by injuries. Carolina has to figure out how to turn around its season still, with a division title on the line, but the NFL Draft looms large.
Even at full strength, this roster is flawed and could see major changes due to expiring contracts and underperformance by players. That said, it's never too early for mock drafts, and one of the latest has Carolina making a questionable pick.
Bleacher Report's Brent Sobleski dropped his NFL mock draft after the trade deadline . In that mock, Sobleski has the Panthers picking 19th in the draft for the second straight year, not to bring in help in the secondary or offensive line, but to draft Oregon TE Jamari Johnson.
This is far from the first time the Panthers have been linked to an Oregon tight end. Look back at any mock draft before the 2026 NFL Draft; many featured Kenyon Sadiq going to Carolina.
Sadiq ended up with the New York Jets, and Carolina drafted Monroe Freeling. After last season, tight end felt like more of a need, Carolina's offensive line played well and both corners were outstanding.
That's not the case this year; Jaycee Horn and Mike Jackson have barely played, both placed on IR after Week 3. Jackson is also a free agent after this season, which means Carolina may need a replacement corner.
As for the offensive line, injuries have been an issue, primarily to Taylor Moton and Damien Lewis.
However, the offensive line issues don't start and end with injuries; this unit has been the most disappointing position group in the NFL.
Rasheed Walker at left tackle and Luke Fortner at center have both been abysmal. Entering Week 9 against the Broncos, both have led the league in pressures allowed at their positions.
Based on this mock draft, there are much smarter choices on the board at 19th overall. USC's Eligah Page is a prime example: a big left tackle with good footwork who has thrived against Big Ten competition this season.
At 19th overall, Carolina will miss out on some cornerbacks such as Notre Dame's Leonard Moore and Clemson's Ashton Hampton, but other names are still viable selections, such as Alabama's Zabien Brown and Mississippi State's Kelley Jones.
If Carolina has the 19th pick, it likely means the season has turned around somewhat, because right now, things are trending in the wrong direction.
Preston is an experienced sports writer focusing on NFL, College Football, NBA, and MMA topics. He is a passionate Charlotte and Oklahoma sports fan and graduated from the University of Science and Arts Oklahoma in 2025 with a Bachelor of Arts in Communications degree with a focus in journalism.

title: NFL Week 10 Expert Picks: Will Panthers Hold Off Saints for First Place?
full_text:
The Carolina Panthers still hold the lead in the NFC South race despite losing three games in a row . They are 3-5, which is the same record as the New Orleans Saints.
Those two teams will not have the same record this week, barring a tie. They'll face off in New Orleans for the first time this season. You'll recall that the Saints' peskiness made the division title a lot harder to come by for Carolina last season.
A win keeps the Panthers in first. A loss drops them out for the first time in a long time and it would bring up even more questions.
CBS Sports analyst John Breech predicts a narrow Panthers victory, 23-20. These two teams played two relatively tight games last year, and with how evenly matched they seem right now, this is unsurprising.
His CBS colleague, Pete Prisco , has picked the Panthers in one game all year, and it was the ugly loss to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. Big shocker: Prisco is going with the Saints in this one, 24-21.
"This is an enormous game in the division, even though both teams have just three victories. The winner will be in first place. The Saints beat the Browns last week, while the Panthers have lost three straight. The Saints make it four in a row as Tyler Shough has a big day," he wrote.
Sporting News' Vinnie Iyer is keeping the field-goal difference here, predicting the Saints to emerge victorious, 27-24. "New Orleans dug deep to outlast Cleveland last week and found some needed rushing juice with Audric Estime. They also have the receivers around Tyler Shough to duel Bryce Young and his weapons well. Both defenses have been maligned, but toss a coin toward Brandon Staley," he wrote.
Sports Illustrated's Iain MacMillan isn't willing to make a prediction on the tight matchup, instead saying the best pick is to take the over, thanks to two horrible defenses.
Jeremy Cluff of Arizona Republic thinks the Panthers win a little more handily than others, 28-20. "Bryce Young and the Panthers have lost three straight games, but are still right in the thick of the NFC South race. New Orleans is 1-4 at home. Carolina ends its skid with a big win on the road," he said.
Sports Betting Dime's model predicts a 30-26 win for the Panthers. Dimers' model predicts a 25-24 victory for the Panthers.
What does this tell us? That the margins in this game are unbelievably thin. It's going to be an extremely close contest, with some experts leaning one way and others leaning the other.
The Panthers need to turn the tides, but they have their work cut out for them.
Zachary Roberts is a journalist with a wide variety of experience covering basketball, golf, entertainment, video games, music, football, baseball, and hockey. He currently covers Charlotte sports teams and has been featured on Sportskeeda, Yardbarker, MSN, and On SI.

title: Dan Morgan's Seat Should Be Getting Hotter After Panthers' Quiet Trade Deadline
full_text:
The Carolina Panthers did nothing at the NFL trade deadline on Tuesday. For a team battling injuries and poor depth in the secondary, that was not the move that most fans were hoping for from the Panthers.
But that is not the only issue. The Panthers' secondary has been a problem for several seasons, and general manager Dan Morgan has not done enough to address it.
The problem with the Panthers' roster extends beyond what Morgan did not do on trade deadline day. It extends to what he has not done to fix the team's secondary in the past.
At some point, the GM needs to be held accountable for the roster he has put together.
Horn and Jackson can play when healthy, but that isn't the issue. The problem with the Panthers' secondary is that there isn't enough depth at cornerback for when those two players are injured.
The Panthers have had some good performances from Horn when he is healthy. Jackson is also a good player for the Panthers. However, as is the case in the NFL, injuries happen and the Panthers should have been better prepared for Horn or Jackson to miss time.
The Panthers have a secondary that is too thin, and Carolina cannot rely on that secondary to get them through any tough spots.
As previously discussed in Panthers on SI's report on Carolina's cornerback injuries, the injuries have exposed how little depth the Panthers have behind their starters.
Morgan had numerous chances to add to the Panthers' secondary in free agency, the draft and now at the trade deadline. Instead, the problems that the team is experiencing in the secondary are the same problems that have existed for several seasons.
That's difficult to overlook.
Morgan can be forgiven for not giving up a lot of assets for a short-term fix to the secondary problems, but it does not mean there are no other holes on the Panthers' roster to fill in order to become a Super Bowl contender.
The Carolina Panthers entered the trade deadline with a 3-5 record but were still leading the NFC South. Carolina still had a chance to win the division, but the team needed to start winning games.
While Carolina did not need to make a blockbuster trade, Morgan could have looked to bring in a solid veteran cornerback to provide some depth at the position.
The Panthers did sign veteran cornerback Jakorian Bennett to their practice squad on November 6, but that doesn't mean the team's depth problems have been solved.
The asking prices on some of those players might have been too high for Morgan's taste, but the Panthers' secondary has been a problem for a while now, and that needed to be addressed long before the trade deadline on Tuesday.
In addition to not making a trade, Morgan's offseason decisions will also be put under a microscope.
The Panthers can't keep blaming injuries for certain positions on the field.
As discussed in Panthers on SI's earlier trade deadline analysis, Carolina couldn't afford to sacrifice valuable draft picks just to make a short-term move. But that doesn't excuse the front office for not having enough dependable options at cornerback.
And if Carolina's secondary is still in trouble and the Panthers can't capitalize on their opportunity to win the NFC South, Morgan will have to answer more than just why he didn't make a trade at the deadline.
Why weren't the Panthers better prepared at certain positions on the field?
Mark Livingston is a South Carolina native and recent Penn State graduate with a degree in Digital Media and Journalism. He previously wrote for Greenville Sports Media, where he covered various sports and teams across the Carolinas. His experience includes game coverage, feature stories and interviews.

title: Eagles' Jordan Davis Trade Raises Big Question About Panthers Keeping Derrick Brown
full_text:
The Philadelphia Eagles received a massive return for defensive tackle Jordan Davis prior to Tuesday’s NFL trade deadline. Jacksonville sent the Eagles a 2027 first-round pick and a 2029 second-round pick for the defensive tackle that the Eagles selected in the first round of the 2022 NFL Draft.
This move should be of interest to Carolina Panthers fans, considering that defensive tackle Derrick Brown was mentioned in various trade rumors prior to the deadline. Reports stated that several teams had inquired about the Panthers’ best defensive player.
While the Eagles received an offer that was too good to turn down, the Panthers decided not to move on from Derrick Brown. General manager Dan Morgan chose to keep one of the Panthers’ best players on the team.
Did the Panthers miss out on an opportunity with Derrick Brown after seeing the return that the Eagles got for Jordan Davis? There are some differences between the two players and the situations of the two teams that must be taken into consideration.
The Eagles received two valuable draft picks from Jacksonville for Davis, who had become an important part of their defensive line.
Davis was a member of the Eagles’ Super Bowl-winning team and was named a team captain in 2026, according to Philadelphia’s official announcement of the trade.
But Philadelphia had other players on the defensive line that it could use as well.
The Eagles have several other good defensive players on the team, including former first-round pick Jalen Carter, Moro Ojomo, Byron Young, and Ty Robinson. The Eagles had the depth at the position to make trading Davis an option.
The Eagles were 2-7 before the trade deadline. Adding future draft picks makes sense for a team that is in a difficult position right now.
Carolina wasn’t in quite the same position.
While Brown’s name was mentioned prior to the trade deadline, the Panthers were clear that they were not interested in trading the defensive tackle.
According to Athlon Sports' reporting on NFL insider Jordan Schultz, several teams inquired about Brown, but Carolina wasn't looking to move him.
The organization clearly believes in Brown.
The Panthers are already struggling with issues in the secondary due to injuries, and Carolina’s defense is not consistently putting pressure on opposing quarterbacks. Removing Brown would create another hole on Carolina’s defensive line.
The Panthers already have Brown under contract through the 2028 season, and he can be part of Carolina’s core of players as the team continues to build around him.
The Panthers have been trying to build a complete team for years, and trading away one of the team’s best defensive players would be a huge risk. There is no guarantee that a first-round pick would turn out to be as good as Brown.
While the Eagles had several options to replace the production of defensive tackle Jordan Davis, the Panthers do not have the same luxury with Brown.
There is still a legitimate argument that Morgan should have at least considered what another team might have offered for Brown. Jacksonville gave up two premium picks for Davis, and Brown is one of Carolina's best players.
There was interest in Brown from other teams, but that doesn't mean Carolina would have received the same offer Philadelphia got for Davis.
While Carolina received calls on Brown, there has been no confirmed report of a team offering a first-round pick and a second-round pick in a trade for him.
Another problem with trading Brown is that it would have left the Panthers with approximately $33.15 million in dead money on their 2026 salary cap, according to Athlon Sports, citing Over the Cap . That is roughly $22.2 million more against the cap than keeping Brown.
That’s a lot of money for a team that was already working with limited salary cap space.
Carolina entered the trade deadline leading the NFC South with a 3-5 record. While the Panthers have a lot of work to do, they are still in a position to compete for a division title.
Morgan would have had to compare the value of the future draft picks to the value of having Brown on the team, as well as the salary cap hit the team would take on by trading him.
The Panthers have eight picks in the 2027 NFL Draft to add young talent to the team, so the need to trade away one of the team’s best defensive players is not as great as it would be for the Eagles.
The Eagles made a good move by trading Davis for two valuable draft picks. But Philadelphia was in a better position to absorb the loss of a starting defensive tackle.
For Carolina, the decision wasn't quite that simple.
Unless another team was willing to offer something that Morgan simply couldn't refuse, keeping Brown was the better decision for the Panthers.

title: 8 Biggest Trades Bears Made Under Ryan Poles, Ranked By Significance
full_text:
The Chicago Bears are now two weeks removed from the earth-shattering Jeffery Simmons trade that unlocked their defense. They sent two first-round selections and a fourth-round pick to the Titans for Simmons and a fifth-round pick. If his first two games donning the blue and orange are any indication, they definitely underpaid .
Acquiring Simmons was one of Bears general manager Ryan Poles' best moves since taking the helm in 2022. It was far from his only consequential trade, though. He's always kept the phone lines open when it comes to trade conversations.
Here are the eight biggest trades Poles has made, ranked from eight to one in terms of significance.
A draft-day trade that saw them move down one spot might not seem as significant as other moves Poles has made, and it didn't include as much draft capital as others, but it was still monumental. Many believed DT Jalen Carter was the best player in the 2023 NFL Draft, and the Bears could've landed him with the ninth overall pick due to character concerns.
Poles trusted his judgment because he knew he had an ace in the hole . They instead drafted Darnell Wright, who has arguably become the league's best right tackle. They also knew the Eagles wouldn't take him, so they moved down one spot and picked up a fourth-round pick. They turned that extra pick into punter Tory Taylor, who has developed into a weapon in his third season.
Carter is a great player, but it's safe to assume they don't have any regrets at Halas Hall.
Khalil Herbert showed legit flashes over his first three years in Chicago after the team selected him in the sixth round of the 2021 NFL Draft. However, largely got phased out in year four, carrying the ball only eight times over the first six weeks. They shipped him to the Bengals for a seventh-round pick ahead of the trade deadline.
Why does this one rank so highly in terms of significance? The butterfly effect, of course. The Bears drafted Kyle Monangai with the pick they received for Herbert. Monangai was one of the biggest steals of the 2025 NFL Draft , and he picked up right where he left off this year before suffering a turf toe injury in Week 4.
The other DJ Moore trade (more on the first one later, obviously). They shipped Moore and a sixth-round pick to Buffalo for a second-round selection this offseason. With the depth that the Bears accumulated at receiver, many saw it as a necessary evil to create some cap space ahead of free agency.
Very few expected them to receive a second-round pick for Moore, though. Not after putting up a career-low 682 yards last season. Even fewer expected the Bills to inherit his four-year, $110 million contract. The Bears wound up trading the pick down, and eventually turning it into Sam Roush and Malik Muhammad II (after trading up to select him). All things considered, this was a great deal for Chicago .
Not all significant trades work out in Chicago's favor. Roquan Smith was one of the league's best young linebackers in 2023, but he seemingly wasn't happy with the Bears' new regime after Ryan Poles took over. He briefly requested a trade ahead of training camp before eventually being a good soldier.
Poles decided the damage had been done, though. They traded the then three-time All-Pro to the Ravens for a second-rounder, a fifth-rounder, and AJ Klein, who only lasted two weeks in Chicago. The Bears turned those picks into two contributors, Gervon Dexter Sr. and Noah Sewell. It was still a bad move, though.
Sure, they didn't want to pay Smith $20 million per year. However, they didn't mind paying Tremaine Edmunds $18 million per year the next offseason. Only one of them has come close to living up to that contract, and it wasn't the one who was cut before he could finish it.
Mismanagement by former GM Ryan Pace left Chicago's salary cap situation in ruins when Poles took over. They were a team going nowhere fast, and they needed to tear it down to build it back up. Poles knew liquidating Mack's massive contract was the quickest way to provide a jolt to the rebuild. They traded him to the Chargers for a second- and sixth-round pick in his first significant move on the job.
Did the trade age well? Not really. Mack was his usual dominant self over the next two seasons, accumulating 25 sacks. It's worth noting that Mack would've been rotting with a massive contract on a rebuilding Bears team (like he is now on a stingy and underwhelming Chargers team) over the next few years if they hadn't pulled the trigger, though.
Meanwhile, the Bears turned the picks into Jaquan Brisker, Elijah Hicks, and Trenton Gill (they turned the 2023 sixth-round pick into two 2022 seventh-rounders). Again, significant isn't always good.
To Poles' credit, he seemingly figured the whole trading thing out by year three. His ties to Kansas City might've helped him land a future Hall of Fame guard for a fourth-round pick in the 2025 offseason.
Thuney didn't allow a single sack last season, and he went on to be named the NFL's inaugural Protector of the Year for his efforts. He's also picked up right where he left off over the first half of 2026.
Their decision to trade a sixth-round pick to the Rams for Jonah Jackson (literally one day before acquiring Thuney) is a noteworthy honorable mention . Both players have fortified the interior of Chicago's o-line.
Speaking of Poles' ties to Kansas City, that connection also helped acquire Jeffery Simmons. He previously worked with Titans GM Mike Borgonzi in Kansas City, and the trust between the two is not only what got the deal over the finish line, but it's what got it over the starting line. Well, that, and Poles offering up two first-round picks right off the jump.
The trade could be a rare win/win for both sides. Simmons has completely unlocked Chicago's defense. It's obvious how this trade helps them . From the Titans' perspective, they now have ample draft capital at their disposal (and more cap space) to accelerate their rebuild.
Was there ever any doubt as to which trade would take the top spot on this list? Their decision to move off the first overall pick in 2023 largely shaped the Bears' current roster. Sure, Carolina being a dumpster fire that season (and subsequently helping Chicago get the first pick in 2024) helped, but that was still a calculated move by Poles. Acquiring Moore was a huge factor in their struggles, as Bryce Young had no reliable pass-catchers to throw to.
The Bears turned that one pick into Darnell Wright, Tory Taylor, Caleb Williams, Tyrique Stevenson, Luther Burden III, Sam Roush, Malik Muhammad II, and three years with DJ Moore. Hang it in the Louvre.
Jerry Markarian has been an avid Chicago Bears fan since 2010 and has been writing about the team since  2022.  He has survived the 2010 NFC Championship Game, a career-ending injury to his favorite player (Johnny Knox), the Bears' 2013 season finale, a Double Doink, Mitchell Trubisky, Justin Fields, and Weeks 8-17 of the 2024 NFL season. Nevertheless, he still Bears Down!

title: Another Last-Ditch Stadium Idea to Sell Bears on Hospital Site Arises
full_text:
When the Illinois legislature convenes next week for its lame duck session and considers Bears stadium legislation , it's possible they could be looking at a different suggestion.
It's an old idea somewhat altered, and there's no guarantee the Bears are even going to rate this as an option based on what they've said in the past.
The Capri Investment Group and GRIT Chicago is proposing a 75,000-seat indoors stadium at the old Michael Reese Hospital site in the Bronzeville neighborhood, 2.3 miles south of Soldier Field and at the lakefront. It would be connected to McCormack Place.
The Bears currently have said they're considering Hammond for their stadium but are willing to weigh an Illinois option.
Developers on Thursday unveiled a $10 billion proposal for a large-scale development district in Bronzeville that would include a domed stadium for the Bears. https://t.co/hBwAx1Ip1A
The Illinois funding mechanism being considered later this month or in early December in Springfield was developed after Gov. J.B. Pritzker and some Chicago area politicians put it together, and is based on the Bears constructing the stadium but selling it back to the local government. The team would  then lease it for a nominal fee to avoid paying taxes. However, they would have to pay taxes on any property where they build hotels, restaurants or other businesses near the stadium.
The plan is meant for an Arlington Heights project, but could also apply to a Chicago-based plan.
An early look at the Titans’ new $2.2B Nissan Stadium, aimed for completion in February 2027. pic.twitter.com/bjvo7ZFXSu
This newly proposed project is for an estimated $10 billion stadium a bit west of the previous Michael Reese Hospital plan that was discussed. It keeps the Bears playing within the city limits, but there are problems with it.
For one, the property was deemed too small in the past by both Bears ownership and NFL commissioner Roger Goodell. The new plan addresses this somewhat, but in the process also demolishes six buildings where people currently reside.
This is to be built on 100 acres of property and that's larger than the original plan for a stadium at this site, however it's nothing compared to the 326-acre Arlington International Racetrack site the Bears currently own.
The new plan includes hotel and businesse. The company's proposal includes 2,000 hotel rooms, 300,000 square feet of retail/restaurants, 400,000 square feet of office space, a 500,000-square-foot youth sports complex, and a 400,000-square-foot wellness center.
🚨EVERY #NFL STADIUM RANKED🚨 1: Allegiant 2: Arrowhead 3: US Bank 4: Mercedes Benz 5: Lincoln Financial 6: SoFi 7: Lumen 8: Empower 9: Lambeau 10: Superdome 11: NRG 12: Gillette 13: Ford 14: State Farm 15: AT&T 16: Hard Rock 17: M&T 18: Paycor 19: Lucas Oil Thoughts on this…? pic.twitter.com/sE6ALI6Fi4
It includes some changes to Chicago public transportation to let fans get to the facility and 3,500 structured parking spaces, which seems entirely inadequate. They would need to build a 29th Street Metra station and a CTA Green Line station that would be half a mile from the stadium.
Another potential draw for the Bears is that the company is offering to buy the Arlington Heights property if the Bears pursue this Chicago option.  The Arlington Heights property is 326 acres, though, which doesn't quite sound like an even trade off.
This entire plan sounds like another one of Chicago's half-baked ideas thought up quite often during the Brandon Johnson and Lori Lightfoot mayoral administrations for hanging onto the Bears.
There's another new proposal in the Bears' stadium saga, this one relating to Bronzeville, as @leilarahimi and @LouCanellis discussed. pic.twitter.com/60gisAYCTV
The site has already been studied and rejected for good reasons. It's much like the Johnny-come-lately idea of putting a stadium near the point where the Calumet River and Lake Michigan meet at the site of the old U.S. Steel South Works, or even the idea from the village of McCook to put one there. While there would be advantages to the Michael Reese property over some other sites suggested in the past, the Bears have already drawn up and have plans for the stadium in Arlington Heights on their own property and the Indiana offer is probably the best overall because of cost and taxes.
Getting their act together has been a problem in Chicago for years no matter the project or change. This one looks no different. The state needs to consider that legislation so the Bears can get their Arlington Heights stadium construction started as soon as possible.
The only real obstacle will once again be Chicago politicians, who can't accept the fact the team is owned by someone else and they've already decided to move it outside the city. This stadium plan released by Capri is going to provide fuel for those Chicago politicians to argue against Arlington Heights once again.
Any emerging, attention-grabbing Bears stadium proposals should face this question first … Is the Bears organization actually invested or engaged at all in said proposal? If not … 🤔 Question 2: Can the Bears, with patience thinning and other league owners seeking clarity,…

title: Chicago Bears Trades That Should Have Been Made at the Deadline But Weren't
full_text:
The Chicago Bears made one of the biggest trades of not only 2026, but in NFL history when they acquired Jeffery Simmons after reaching a deal with the Tennessee Titans.
It was one of the biggest trades in NFL history because the Bears became the first team in the common draft era to trade multiple first-round selections for a defensive tackle .
But when the trade deadline rolled around on Tuesday, the Bears did not make another deal despite rumors suggesting they were still in the market for a cornerback , even after the Simmons deal.
We can't say we're disappointed after the blockbuster Simmons trade, but here's the moves we would have liked to see general manager Ryan Poles pull off before the deadline passed.
The Bears have a serious concern at the cornerback position, but it's not at the spot we thought it would be.
Entering the year, we assumed the spot opposite Jaylon Johnson would be the concern, as the team was set to start either rookie Malik Muhammad or the perennially-disappointing Tyrique Stevenson.
However, it has been Johnson who has been the biggest issue with his lackluster coverage and tackling, along with Stevenson. Meanwhile, Muhammad has been sensational and the Bears can only hope that will continue the rest of the season.
We would have loved to see either Woolen or Wright added to the Bears' defense.
Woolen was the preferred option because of his past success and ability to thrive in man coverage. Wright, who played for the Bears last season, would've been a solid fallback option to give Chicago's defense the depth it needs.
Both players made sense as trade candidates, too, as they're on teams going nowhere and both have a one-year contract. Wright seemed even more primed to get traded thanks to his not having any role in the Jets' defense.
Few teams in the NFL utilize 12 and 13 personnel as much as the Bears do. According to Sumer Sports , Chicago deploys those groupings at the fourth-highest rate in the NFL.
So, if you're the Bears, you need to make sure you have reliable, well-rounded tight ends. The Bears did have that before the Cole Kmet injury, but things are a lot shakier now that he's out for the season .
Sam Roush has the makings of a good dual-threat tight end, but he has been about as inconsistent as you'd expect from a rookie and there have been definite growing pains. It's hard to rely on someone like that in a big spot.
Then we have Stephen Carlson, who doesn't do much more than block, so defenses don't really have to worry about him being deployed as a pass-catcher when he's on the field.
Goedert would have been the dream addition here because he's a huge threat in the passing game as well as a good blocker. Alie-Cox would have made for a fine consolation prize with his solid blocking and serviceable pass-catching ability.
We thought both players had a good chance to get moved with the situations their teams are in, and with both players north of 30 and in the final year of their deals. We were wrong.
A few weeks before the deadline, FOX Sports' Jay Glazer reported that the Bears had put in a call for Mack , so there was at least some interest in him on the Bears' part.
Edge rusher probably wasn't the biggest need the Bears had, but there is no doubt Mack was the one trade Bears fans wanted most and it all seemed perfectly set up for a Mack-Bears reunion.
The Bears had a need for more depth at edge rusher and the Chargers are in the midst of a nightmare season that has them sitting at 0-8 and going nowhere.
Teams in Los Angeles' situation would normally be heavy sellers, and a veteran like Mack who could retire at any moment would normally want out of that situation.
But, neither of those things turned out not to be the case, as the Chargers were unwilling to trade Mack and, more importantly, Mack wanted to stay with the Chargers .
The real roadblock for the Bears, assuming they were still wanting to make a deal, was Mack because if he had requested a trade, the Chargers would have done it. Instead, he'll be riding it out with the Chargers, who will need the miracle of all miracles to make the playoffs.

title: 4 Bears Offseason Trade Candidates Now That the Deadline Has Passed
full_text:
The NFL trade deadline has passed, and the Chicago Bears did not acquire any more players after their blockbuster trade for Jeffery Simmons two weeks ago, nor did they send away any players, despite trade rumors around involving Tyson Bagent . If the Bears are going to win a Super Bowl, they're going to have to do it with the roster they now have.
That said, making it past the trade deadline doesn't mean there aren't certain players who could be dealt once the season is over. There are four in particular who may be strong trade candidates by the time March rolls around, including one obvious name and one that may come as a surprise.
Credit where credit is due: Jaylon Johnson was instrumental to the Bears' win last Sunday. However, his stellar performance in that game, and his timely pick-six, should not be enough to overwrite what has been a terrible season for him. The former two-time Pro Bowler is a shell of his former self, and 2027 will be the last year of his four-year, $76 million contract.
The Bears have to get out of that deal any way they can, especially with Jeffery Simmons' 2027 cap hit now on Chicago's books. That makes Johnson their top trade candidate, though they'll almost certainly release him if they can't find a partner, and that could severely limit any return the Bears get in a trade.
Yes, the Bears did just sign D'Andre Swift to a three-year extension in August, and he started the year with a bang in the Bears' 59-point Week 1 win. But he's been downright awful ever since Kyle Monangai was sidelined with a turf toe injury. Swift is averaging just 3.0 yards per carry in five games without Monangai, and that calls into question whether he's even the Bears' top running back.
Sure, the Bears' most recent games have included a gauntlet of good and great defenses, but guess what kind of defenses the Bears will face in the playoffs? If Swift isn't able to handle that kind of competition, then he may become a valuable trade piece in March. His new contract is very reasonable, and the Bears could add some badly needed draft capital after sending two firsts and a fourth to the Tennessee Titans.
This one hurts, but the fact of the matter is that we may have seen the last of Cole Kmet in a Bears jersey. Colston Loveland's explosive entrance into the NFL last year had already relegated Kmet to the TE2 spot, and if rookie Sam Roush can put together a solid second-half of the season, we're talking about potential TE3 duties for the longest-tenured member of the offense.
That, obviously, would force the Bears to find a trade parter for Kmet. The 2027 season would be the last year of his contract, and he's coming off of a major knee injury, so the return for Kmet would be limited. But if they don't deal him away in a trade, the Bears may have to simply release him.
This may come as a surprise to Bears fans but hear me out. Trapilo's improbable return from injury was a fantastic story at the start of the season, but he has struggled mightily in his limited number of snaps thus far. Meanwhile, Theo Benedet has quietly taken strides in his development since last year, earning a respectable 79.9 impact grade from Pro Football Network .
If Benedet continues to impress and Trapilo cannot get back to pre-injury form, there's a scenario where the Bears may try to flip Trapilo for draft capital to restock their warchest. I won't say it's probable or even very likely, but it's a scenario for general manager Ryan Poles to consider.

title: 3 Cornerbacks Bears Can Sign Right Now After Not Addressing Need at Trade Deadline
full_text:
In the weeks leading up to the NFL trade deadline, there were no shortage of rumors saying the Chicago Bears were in the cornerback market .
And it's not hard to see why. While rookie Malik Muhammad has been better than expected, Jaylon Johnson has been far worse than expected and Tyrique Stevenson has shown zero signs of improvement.
Making matters worse of late, Muhammad has missed two games in a row with a toe injury and Stevenson got banged-up yet again this past week against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers.
But the Bears didn't make a trade at the deadline for a cornerback, which leaves them with a need for more depth at the position.
Here's a look at three players they could sign right now.
Early in his career, Lattimore was viewed as one of the best at his position in the NFL after notching a Defensive Rookie of the Year award and four Pro Bowls over his first five seasons — and those showings came under current Bears defensive coordinator, Dennis Allen, so he has a connection in Chicago.
However, injuries have derailed him significantly since then, and he suffered yet another in 2025, when he came down with a torn ACL that ended his campaign early.
When on the field, Lattimore has usually been at least serviceable in recent years. Even before his injury last season, the veteran was giving up a completion rate of 59.5% and a passer rating of 93.0, which amounts to better coverage numbers than Johnson's in 2026.
Assuming he's healthy, which he should be now that a year has passed since his torn ACL that he suffered in November of last year, the Bears should kick the tires on Lattimore.
A former first-round pick of the Tennessee Titans, Jackson has not met expectations during his career, but he has still proven to be a serviceable starter, which makes him a very good backup, and that's exactly what the Bears need him to be.
Jackson's best attribute is his speed that allows him to keep up with faster receivers down the field, and on top of his ability to play on the boundary, he also has played snaps in the slot. Jackson has return experience as well to give him some added value.
In 2025, Jackson permitted a 62.7% completion rate and an 87 passer rating when targeted. In the season before that, he was even better, with a 48.8% completion rate and a 85.2 passer rating.
To compare, those numbers are better than what Johnson is putting up this season.
Another cornerback with a Bears connection, the best years of Diggs' career came while working under Chicago's defensive backs coach, Al Harris.
Harris coached Diggs from 2020 through 2024, and in that span Diggs notched two Pro Bowls and one All-Pro nod and looked to be on a superstar trajectory before injuries derailed him.
There is no doubt that Diggs is no longer that guy, but maybe a reunion with Harris can get him back to respectability.
Diggs is on the Seattle Seahawks' practice squad, but Chicago can poach him if it signs the veteran cornerback to the active roster.

title: Chicago Bears' Most Disappointing Players at Halfway Point of 2026 Season
full_text:
As the Chicago Bears enjoy their bye in Week 10, they are also at the midway point of the 2026 season, so it's a perfect time to reflect on what has transpired through nine games.
As a whole, the Bears are having a great season. Chicago sits in first place in the NFC North at 7-2 and has looked like one of the very best teams in the NFL, and the Bears have seen Caleb Williams take the step forward they were looking for.
However, not everyone has lived up to the hype in 2026.
With that in mind, here's the five Bears players who have been the most disappointing going into the bye.
Johnson's struggles date back to last season, but the belief was that those struggles were a result of him not being 100%.
So, there was renewed hope for him in 2026, especially after he put together a strong training camp. But, through nine games, Johnson looks like a shell of the player who was formerly considered an elite cornerback in the NFL.
Johnson is giving up a completion rate of 67.4% and a passer rating of 107.5, and there has been multiple occasions where Johnson's tackling has left a lot to be desired, to put it nicely. Johnson's 23.7% missed tackle rate is the highest of his NFL career.
There is hope after his last game, though. Johnson enjoyed his best showing in coverage in Week 9 after giving up a completion rate of 20% and a 0.0 passer rating, per Pro Football Focus , and Johnson recorded a clutch pick-six that might have saved the game for Chicago.
The Bears can only hope that performance will be a turning point for Johnson, who is hugely important to Chicago's defensive success the rest of the way.
If the Bears cornerback doesn't rebound in a big way in the second half of the season, he's likely going to be cut in the offseason.
We normally wouldn't have had high expectations for a sixth-round pick like van den Berg, but after he had a strong preseason and was one of the reasons why the team felt comfortable trading Gervon Dexter, expectations rose significantly.
Since then, van den Berg has not lived up to the hype. The rookie has notched overall and run defense grades of 39.2 and 42.1, and he has been a non-factor in the pass-rush with just one pressure.
The Georgia Tech product's playing time has decreased, also, with van den Berg seeing no more than 11 snaps since he played 22 in Week 1. And, since those 11 snaps, van den Berg has played eight, five and three snaps in each of his last three games, and he was a healthy scratch in Week 8 .
Now with Jeffery Simmons in the mix, van den Berg's opportunities to see the field have taken another hit.
Odunze entered the season with a loose grip on the No. 1 receiver title going into the season, but he has since lost that to Luther Burden, who has been better in 2026.
Drops have been an issue for Odunze, who has three through nine games, which is one more than he had in 12 last season. Two of those drops were egregious ones in the end zone.
We wanted to see Odunze become more consistent and cement himself as the No. 1 wide receiver the Bears thought they were getting when they drafted him No. 9 overall in 2024.
Instead, Odunze has been inconsistent and is on pace to fall just short of 1,000 yards.
After his impressive second half of last season, we had Loveland pegged for superstardom . Instead, the second-year tight end has been disappointing and is actually on pace to finish with less receiving yards than he had in 2025.
One problem has been Caleb Williams simply not seeing him open on several occasions this season. But the other issue has been drops, with Loveland notching four through nine games. The Michigan product had just one last season.
Loveland has been more consistent of late, with 54 or more yards in each of his last four games and two touchdowns in that span, but he still hasn't posted more than 69 yards in any game and that's well below expectations.
Sweat had one of his most productive seasons in 2025, when he tallied 10 sacks. Through seven games this season, Sweat has three, which puts him on pace to finish with about seven.
Aside from his disappointing sack production in 2026, Sweat also got himself suspended for two games for violating the league's performance-enhancing drugs policy.
One reason to be optimistic for Sweat the rest of the way is the addition of Simmons, who is drawing a ton of attention that is freeing his teammates up for more one-on-ones.
While that takes more pressure off Sweat on a snap-by-snap basis, it also increases expectations because Sweat should be taking advantage of the Simmons effect en route to more sacks.
