title: Joey Porter Jr. Addresses Concerning Absence From Dallas Cowboys Practice
full_text:
The Dallas Cowboys could potentially be without standout cornerback Joey Porter Jr. for a second straight game as he continues to deal with an ankle/foot injury ahead of Week 10's matchup against the San Francisco 49ers.
Porter Jr. was once again listed as a DNP on the injury report during Thursday's practice after missing last week's win over the Indianapolis Colts.
While meeting with reporters afterwards, Porter Jr. finally cleared the air when it comes to the question that every Cowboys fans is asking: is his absence contract-related?
Porter Jr. said that he doesn't pay any mind to the concerns fans have about his absence and that he's focused on getting healthy and returning to action as soon as possible.
“I don’t know where that narrative came from," Porter Jr. said, per Joseph Hoyt of The Dallas Morning News. "I mean, I get it, it’s the internet, but I don’t really pay no attention to that or do I really care. My goal is to win games and play football.”
Well, to be fair, that narrative came from his preseason absence with the Pittsburgh Steelers due to a back issue, an injury that suddenly healed once he was traded to Dallas.
That's not saying his current injury isn't legitmate; it certainly is. But it's hard for fans not to latch onto that narrative when it
It turns out that Porter Jr. has been dealing with this injury longer than most Cowboys fan realize.
Porter Jr. told NFL insider Jane Slater that he originally injured his foot during his Cowboys debut against the Houston Texans in Week 4 and that he's been playing on it ever since.
“Tweaked it, Houston game, and I just kept playing on it," Porter Jr. told Slater. "My 70% looks good. You know, that's what I think. So it just got worse, as I kept playing on.”
He ended up missing Week 5's loss to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers due to illness and returned to action the following week against the Green Bay Packers. Despite Dallas suffering another primetime loss, Porter Jr. played arguably his best game of the season at Lambeau Field, finishing with three solo tackles and two pass breakups.
Based on his comments and latest injury designation, it's looking like Porter Jr. will be watching from the sidelines as Dallas looks to upset San Francisco on Sunday.
And regardless of what he says, Cowboys fans will continue to have their concerns that his absence is tied to a potential contract extension until he returns to action.

title: George Pickens Injury Update & Everything Else From Cowboys' Thursday Practice Report
full_text:
The Dallas Cowboys have put out their second injury report of the week ahead of the Week 10 game against the San Francisco 49ers.
The Wednesday injury report was loaded, with 16 players listed on it, and six of those players, including cornerback Joey Porter Jr., didn't take part in practice for an injury-related reason.
Three players were listed as limited, also, including wide receiver George Pickens, linebacker DeMarvion Overshown and wideout KaVontae Turpin, all of whom didn't play last week. Turpin has missed multiple games with his injury.
Now, let's see if any of those players were upgraded on Thursday.
Alijah Clark and Juanyeh Thomas are new additions to the injury report, but Clark only has an illness, so no real concern there.
Now, for some good news: linebacker DeMarvion Overshown was upgraded to full after being limited on Wednesday, so he's now trending toward playing.
Overshown told reporters he expects to suit up on Sunday and went into detail about what happened with his hamstring.
"It was just some ongoing stuff that we didn't... I ain't going to say properly address the first round, but it was just like the hamstring. It happens that you really don't know when it's all the way healed," Overshown said, per Calvin Watkins of The Dallas Morning News.
"So I was feeling good. And next thing you know, I got blood and fluid just clogged up in there," he added. "So that was something that we wasn't expecting, but the problem is fixed now and I'm ready to get back to it.”
As for every other player on the injury report, it was status quo.
With Pickens being listed as limited once again, this keeps his status for Week 10 up in the air after Pickens was limited all throughout last week before being inactive .
We'll see if Pickens is capable of turning in a full practice on Friday, but if not, he will likely be listed as questionable once again.
Pickens missed a game last week for the first time since being traded to the Cowboys.
If Pickens sits out, the Cowboys could be very short-handed at wide receiver, as Jonathan Mingo has not practiced this week.
Porter was a non-participant once again at practice on Thursday.
Porter told Jon Machota of The Athletic that his foot is "jacked up," and he denied that his absences for the Cowboys this season have anything to do with his contract.
“My goal is to win games and play football. If there’s any chance I can get on the field, I’m gonna get on the field and do what I do best," he said.
The Cowboys will drop their final injury report on Friday, so we'll likely have a clearer picture of Porter's status then. But, at this moment, it looks like he's not going to play again.
If Porter can't go, the Cowboys will deploy Cobie Durant in his spot opposite DaRon Bland.

title: Injuries Forcing Dallas Cowboys to Give Benched Rookie More Playing Time
full_text:
The Dallas Cowboys have been no stranger to injuries this season, especially on defense. These issues are continuing headed into Week 10's home matchup against the San Francisco 49ers.
These ailments certainly haven't helped an already struggling defense find its stride under defensive coordinator Christian Parker. But despite a 4-5 record, the Cowboys are still well within range of winning the NFC East and securing a playoff spot.
With the trade deadline having come and gone , the Dallas defense has no choice but make do with what it's got, regardless of who's healthy or not.
As a result, Cowboys rookie linebacker Jaishawn Barham is set to receive more playing time as Dallas deals with injuries at edge rusher, Parker told the media on Thursday.
Barham played just three snaps on defense in Week 9 against the Indianapolis Colts. This comes after he saw snap counts of just 21 and 16 in Weeks 7 and 8, respectively. Despite starting six games this season at off-ball linebacker, his playing time has decreased significantly in recent weeks.
But with Donovan Ezeiruaku dealing with an ankle injury in danger of missing Sunday's game, the Cowboys set to use Barham at outside linebacker against the 49ers.
"Next man up, we have some guys who have played significant steps throughout the year," Parker said, per ESPN's Todd Archer. "That's a rotational position. Then we'll get Jaishawn more involved there. He's kind of been involved there in some spotlight duty already with some different packages we've had throughout the season. We'll be able to deploy him there some too."
Barham impressed during the preseason before showing flashes early on in the regular season. Through nine games, he's tallied 35 total tackles (20 solo), four tackles for loss and one quarterback hit on 325 defensive snaps.
It's clear that Barham hit a rookie wall. With the Dallas defense struggling, the coaching staff had no choice but to push him further down the depth chart.
Perhaps a solid showing as a pass rusher could give Barham fewer responsibilities to worry about and allow him to play a bit looser. Sacking Niners quarterback Brock Purdy would certainly boost his confidence while giving Dallas' defense the boost it needs to help upset San Francisco in Week 10.

title: George Pickens Injury Scare Surfaces After ESPN App Update Despite Practice Progress
full_text:
The Dallas Cowboys are finalizing preparations for a Week 10 showdown against the San Francisco 49ers , and many have been monitoring the health of star wide receiver George Pickens and cornerback Joey Porter Jr.
Both men have missed time at practice throughout the week due to nagging injuries that kept them out of last weekend's win over the Indianapolis Colts, and are now working their way back to the field.
On Thursday, however, Cowboys Nation received a bit of a scare and conflicting messages when Pickens popped up as "OUT" for Sunday evening's game against the 49ers. There is one problem: he was actually out on the field practicing.
Cowboys WR George Pickens (hamstring) participating in practice for the second day in a row pic.twitter.com/MKGyJGYLVJ
Pickens was limited at practice on Wednesday, but on Thursday he was back going through drills throughout the afternoon.
Despite what seems like the progress for Pickens, the ESPN app appeared to glitch which led to a brief moment of panic for fans who were hoping to get Pickens back on the field for Sunday's crucial game at AT&T Stadium.
Literally while he was practicing lol. Has to be a glitch. https://t.co/hTuQ3gOszS
While Pickens is listed as out on the app, it shows his estimated return date for November 15, which will be Sunday when kickoff is scheduled for 4:25 p.m. ET. So, despite the hamstring and shoulder injuries that forced him out of action, Pickens is inching closer to a return.
The injuries that have plagued Pickens all season long have forced him into a smaller role in the Cowboys' offense this season after his breakout 2025 campaign. They also appear to have limited Dallas' opportunities to pull off a trade ahead of Tuesday's trade deadline , despite some speculation that the Cowboys could look to move the pass catcher.
Instead, Dallas apparently received no calls for Pickens , and he will now suit up for the remainder of the season under the franchise tag. Hopefully, he can find his way back to full health and find a way to step up his game and his role in the offense as we prepare for a key stretch of the regular season.
This season, Pickens has hauled in just 39 catches for 533 yards and two touchdowns. We'll see if he can add to those totals on Sunday when the Cowboys and 49ers face off at 4:25 p.m. ET on FOX.

title: Super Bowl-Winning Head Coach Eyeing NFL Return and Cowboys are Perfect Fit
full_text:
When this season comes to a close, it will likely end with the Dallas Cowboys missing the playoffs for a third straight year.
We hate to be so pessimistic, but let's just face facts: Dallas does not look like a playoff team and we find it hard to believe they'll navigate what is a fairly tough schedule the rest of the way to make it to the postseason.
If that happens, the Cowboys must fire Brian Schottenheimer. Now, to be clear, we'd fire him today if given the opportunity, but it's going to take more to convince Jerry Jones to pull the trigger.
Missing the playoffs should be enough, but never say never.
Here's a fun name to throw into the mix: Bruce Arians.
The Super Bowl-winning coach recently told NFL insider Jordan Schultz that he has the "itch" to get back into coaching.
"Now that I'm all healthy again, I got the itch again, so, we'll see," Arians said of the possibility he could return to coaching. "Yeah, we'll see. Never say never."
Arians explained that he had a slew of health issues that led to him leaving the Bucs, where he won the aforementioned Super Bowl.
Arians revealed he was dealing with a torn Achilles, back issue and a heart problem during his last season in the NFL, which was 2021. But Arians said those issues are now behind him, which is why he's eyeing a return to the NFL.
Along with his Super Bowl in 2020, Arians is a two-time Coach of the Year winner and is one of the most well-respected offensive minds in the sport.
Arians would be just what the doctor ordered for the Cowboys if they fire Schottenheimer this coming offseason .
For starters, he's an experienced head coach with a Super Bowl ring and those are two qualities Schottenheimer did not have when Dallas hired him.
Arians is also a great offensive mind and we know the Cowboys' strength is their offense. Arians-led offenses routinely ranked inside the top 10 from 2015 through 2021.
Arians likely wouldn't call plays, but he's going to hire an offensive coordinator who shares his offensive vision. Arians didn't call the plays in his three seasons as the Bucs' head coach, but Tampa finished third, third and second in points.
Perhaps the most important thing Arians would bring is discipline, something we know this undisciplined Cowboys team needs.
The former Arizona Cardinals head coach is the perfect blend of players' coach and disciplinarian. Players love playing for Arians, but he also holds his players accountable, something Schottenheimer doesn't do enough — and it shows .
The downside to Arians is obvious: he's 74 years old and could retire again in a few years, which would be a problem for most teams.
But with the Cowboys in win-now mode, Arians' age is irrelevant. If he can deliver a Super Bowl in a year or two and then rides off into the sunset, nobody will be complaining.

title: Cowboys Named Post-Trade Deadline Landing Spot for Ex-Bills Pro Bowler in Free Agency
full_text:
The Dallas Cowboys stood pat at the trade deadline on Tuesday, which wasn't all that surprising because owner Jerry Jones had hinted he didn't expect anything to happen .
The reason the Cowboys didn't make another move , according to head coach Brian Schottenheimer and ESPN's Adam Schefter, is that the Cowboys feel they have enough talent on the defense already to right the ship.
"Last year, they made a number of moves. Earlier this season, they traded for Joey Porter Jr. That was a big move at the time. There's only so many big moves a team can make," Schefter said. "Dallas felt like it was aggressive in upgrading its roster. The Cowboys still believe they have the talent they need to make a late second half of the season push here. Let's see if they can get it done."
With the trade door now closed, Bleacher Report's Moe Moton thinks the Cowboys should dip into free agency for help.
Moton suggests the Cowboys sign ex-Buffalo Bills Pro Bowl linebacker Matt Milano.
"Dallas Cowboys' oft-injured linebacker DeMarvion Overshown sat out Week 9 with a knee injury," Knox said. "Milano could give one of these teams quality snaps at linebacker."
It's true Overshown sat out in Week 9 , but with hamstring and back injuries. It's also true that Overshown has missed six games in total and is proving to be injury-prone once again.
But that's not the only issue the Cowboys have.
Dallas has also seemingly lost faith in rookie linebacker Jaishawn Barham, who has seen his snaps decline in each of the last three games en route to seeing just three in Week 9. That has forced Dallas to lean more on Shemar James in recent weeks.
Safe to say, the Cowboys might want to explore adding more depth at the position in free agency.
At 32 years old and after not having played a snap in the NFL this season, the veteran linebacker is a total wild card in terms of what to expect if he signs with the Cowboys.
During his career, Milano has amounted to a highly-effective pass-rusher when asked to blitz and can play sound run defense and about average coverage.
His tackling isn't that great, but he would fit in perfectly with the rest of the Cowboys' defense. We also know that Milano has had issues staying healthy, but he would likely be a rotational player, which will help him stay out of the trainer's room.
Even if Milano isn't what he once was, the veteran can still provide adequate depth in what is a shaky linebacker's room.
We suspect the Cowboys will wait to see how things play out with Overshown's latest injury before they consider bringing in another linebacker.
But if he remains absent for another game or gets hurt again after his next return, Dallas has to seriously consider making a move.

title: Updated 2027 NFL Draft Order: Where Dallas Cowboys Stand After Trade Deadline
full_text:
The Dallas Cowboys sat idle at the NFL trade deadline , so the team will now ride out the rest of the 2026-27 campaign with the current roster. Dallas' next opportunity will be during the offseason, when they can address holes on the roster through free agency and the NFL draft.
Unfortunately for the Cowboys, they will be sending their highest of two first-round picks to the New York Jets as part of last year's trade deadline deal for Quinnen Williams .
Currently, that would be the No. 13 overall pick. The Cowboys will still own one first-round pick barring any offseason trades before the draft. The lower of Dallas' two first-round picks would currently be No. 21 overall, but there is still plenty of football left to play this season.
At No. 21 overall, the Cowboys may not be able to land one of the marquee prospects in this year's draft, but they could still take advantage of a deep draft class and land a promising talent on the defensive side of the ball.
In a post-trade deadline mock draft, that player is Oregon Ducks star defensive tackle A'Mauri Washington , who stands 6-foot-3, 325 pounds, and can bolster the team's defensive line against both the run and the pass.

title: Everything Dallas Cowboys Have to Fear About San Francisco 49ers in Week 10
full_text:
When the Dallas Cowboys take on the San Francisco 49ers in Week 10, the matchup will present one of the toughest the Cowboys have faced this season.
Entering this contest, the Niners are without a doubt one of the best teams in the NFL as they sit with a 7-1 record and atop the NFC West, one of the best divisions in the league.
Meanwhile, the Cowboys have had difficulties beating some of the league's bottom-feeders this season, as we saw in Week 9 , and that does not bode well for their chances versus San Francisco.
Even owner Jerry Jones admitted his team faces a tough task in this contest on Sunday.
"And overall, we’re not playing very good. And we’re sure going to have to take what we’ve done over the last several weeks, put the best parts of it together, because we’ve got a real challenge coming up this weekend with San Francisco," Jones said .
Now, a look at everything the Cowboys have to fear about the 49ers ahead of their Week 10 matchup at in Dallas.
There has been a lot of talk about the Cowboys' lack of motion on offense this season, but we haven't seen much attention paid to how bad Dallas' defense is against motion.
The Cowboys have allowed +0.11 EPA (expected points added) per play against motion this season, which ranks dead last, according to DLLS Cowboys' John Andersen .
Meanwhile, the 49ers have used motion on a whopping 71.5% of offensive plays this season, the highest rate in the NFL.
As if the Cowboys' putrid defense didn't have enough to worry about, add this onto the list.
The Cowboys enter this game against the 49ers with the second- worst run defense in the NFL, with Dallas defense giving up a ridiculous 147.4 rushing yards per game.
Knowing that, the 49ers present a nightmare matchup, with San Francisco sporting the seventh-best rushing attack in the league.
Everyone knows how good Christian McCaffrey is and that hasn't changed this season. But the Niners actually have a very good one-two punch with rookie Kaelon Black, who is ripping off an impressive 4.5 yards per carry.
Just because McCaffrey isn't on the field, don't think the Cowboys are going to be catching a break. Black has been a fantastic option to spell McCaffrey in 2026.
The Niners have been good at stopping both the pass and run in 2026. San Francisco enters this game ranked eighth against the pass, second against the run and sixth in points allowed.
The Niners have also done a good job taking the football away, as evidenced by their 12 takeaways (six interceptions, six fumbles recovered), which rank tied for ninth-most.
One positive for the Cowboys is the Niners blitz at an average rate, which is notable because Dallas has had issues handling the blitz. The Niners also don't have a potent pass-rush with their 15 sacks and 72 pressures, which rank as the fifth- and tied for the 15th-fewest in the NFL.
But clearly that has not prevented San Francisco from playing defense at a high level. The Cowboys are going to need a lot of points to make up for what we suspect will be another terrible defensive showing and that's a major problem in a matchup against a top-notch defense like the Niners'.

title: Adam Schefter Explains Why Cowboys Stood Pat on Trade Deadline Day
full_text:
After all of the moves the Dallas Cowboys made during the offseason to try and fix their defense, none of it worked.
So, owner Jerry Jones decided to spring for a trade for Joey Porter Jr. late in September, but that hasn't worked, either.
Then, the trade deadline came on Tuesday, and despite owner Jerry Jones saying he wanted to do more , the Cowboys did nothing and will instead hope what they have on the roster currently will be enough to right the ship.
ESPN's Adam Schefter was asked why the Cowboys didn't make a move on Tuesday and the answer was simple: Dallas thinks it has enough talent on the roster for this team to succeed.
He also noted that the Cowboys were never close to making a deal.
"It never sounded like they got close to making any big deals," Schefter said.
"I know there's a lot of chatter out there about George Pickens. Never sensed any movement towards a George Pickens trade. Never sensed any movement about Dallas making a big move," Schefter added.
"Last year, they made a number of moves. Earlier this season, they traded for Joey Porter Jr. That was a big move at the time. There's only so many big moves a team can make," he said. "Dallas felt like it was aggressive in upgrading its roster. The Cowboys still believe they have the talent they need to make a late second half of the season push here. Let's see if they can get it done."
Schefter briefly mentioned the chatter surrounding Pickens. Well, ESPN's Jeremy Fowler reported on Wednesday that the Cowboys were never going to trade Pickens, and Pickens didn't want to be traded, either. Fowler also noted that the Cowboys didn't receive any calls about Pickens.
"The Cowboys did not receive any trade calls on receiver George Pickens, who is happy in Dallas and didn't want to be traded," he said. "Teams in the receiver market weren't shopping in the high-end aisle, either, so the idea of a Pickens trade was a nonstarter. Plus, Dallas had no plans to deal him."
Schefter's report echoes what head coach Brian Schottenheimer said on Wednesday. The Cowboys head coach said the team believes it has enough talent to get the job done.
“It shows you that we’re confident in our roster and our best football is still ahead," Schottenheimer said, according to The Athletic's Jon Machota .
Schefter's report and even Schottenheimer's comments are both damning for the coaching staff.
If there is enough talent on the roster — which we would agree there is, at least to avoid being this terrible — and the Cowboys aren't playing good football, especially on defense, we can only blame the coaching staff from there.
Even if you want to say there are effort issues on both sides of the ball, as some former Cowboys have pointed out , that points to a culture problem that is also on the coaching staff.
And with the Cowboys' insistence on not making any changes to the group, it's hard to have any hope for the rest of this season.

title: Broncos Fire Back at Chargers' Accusations Over Failed Daiyan Henley Trade
full_text:
The Daiyan Henley trade is off.
Late Wednesday night, the Denver Broncos made the announcement , shocking fans and media alike. The Los Angeles Chargers posted a welcome-back meme for Henley around the same time, confirming there was no trade.
We learned on Thursday that it was officially due to a failed physical. Adam Schefter reported that the Broncos had concerns about Henley's knee after his physical, but they still wanted him — just not at the price of the previously agreed-upon 2027 fourth-round pick and 2028 fifth-round pick, given what they discovered during the physical.
Pro Football Talk 's Mike Florio reported that Henley's physical in Denver revealed some arthritis in one knee. That didn't match up with the picture of health that L.A. reportedly presented of Henley to the Broncos.
But Denver was still interested in keeping Henley. According to 9NEWS ' Mike Klis , the Broncos went back to the Chargers to negotiate a different price. L.A. didn't budge, so the trade was canceled.
Chargers GM Joe Hortiz claims that he was transparent about Henley's health status and that the Broncos were aware of the veteran linebacker's situation before agreeing to terms on the trade. Every team evaluates injuries differently, which is why these transactions come with the caveat of "pending a physical."
According to ESPN 's Lindsey Thiry , Hortiz wouldn't confirm Schefter's report that it was Henley's knee that failed to pass Denver's physical, let alone Florio's report of finding arthritis, but the Chargers GM claims he shared any health concerns with the Broncos before they agreed to the trade.
"We came to terms on it, made the agreement, they called us up and were asking us to amend the trade based on the physical," Hortiz told Thiry. "And in our minds, the physical's a binary thing. It's pass or fail. And they wanted the player still. They wanted to change the terms. They used it, and we weren't going to do it."
Henley has dealt with a knee and shoulder injury this season, though he's played through both. Hortiz was adamant that the Broncos were aware of Henley's health status.
"Yep, absolutely," Hortiz told Thiry when asked whether he was transparent with Denver about Henley's health. "'Hey, he's dealing with this, but he's expected to practice and play for us this week.' And I think that was their plan. They certainly wanted him still."
As for Chargers head coach Jim Harbaugh, he expressed his frustration with how the botched trade unraveled and why he believes the NFL should close the "loophole" that allows a buying team the prerogative to ask for different compensation after the deadline passes.
"The Broncos based a pass-fail on a medical grade on whether we would take less compensation, and we wouldn't, and we didn't," Harbaugh said. "In my opinion, it's one of those loopholes the league should really look into because it sets a bad precedent, [and it] continues to set a bad precedent."
According to Klis, when Henley's knee turned out to be a bit more concerning than the Broncos had been led to believe, the Chargers "brushed off concerns." The Broncos reached out to the NFL, and the league confirmed that, given the failed physical, Denver could approach the Chargers about changing the compensation if they still wanted Henley.
"Per league source, it was only after Henley flunked his physical — in which several medical opinions were sought — [the] Broncos got [the] NFL involved and received confirmation it was OK to revisit the compensation, as there is precedent for these situations," Klis reported on X.
Harbaugh and the Chargers are trying to present this as Denver basing the pass-fail of Henley's physical on whether L.A. would renegotiate the compensation, but the Broncos are pushing back on that through Klis, even going so far as to reveal that they reached out to the NFL about it, after the linebacker's physical produced results that didn't match what they'd been told when they agreed to send a fourth- and fifth-round pick for him.
The Broncos claim they had a "long-term view of the player," per Klis, which is why they were still willing to make a trade with the Chargers even after Henley failed the physical. The Chargers wouldn't accept any new terms, so that was that.
"Regardless of compensation, it was well within Broncos rights to simply flunk him on physical and move on. Instead GM George Paton tried to find a solution for a difficult situation. Again, within the Broncos rights and the NFL aware every step," Klis reported on X.
Now, some people around the NFL are using the botched Henley trade as a referendum on the "loophole" within league rules that allows for teams to change the terms of a deal, pending the physical, even after the trade deadline has passed. For the seller, the argument is that it puts them at a disadvantage because, with the deadline passed, it's not like they can go back to other interested suitors.
For the buyer, as the Broncos were in this scenario, the loophole offers protections and flexibility in the event that a physical uncovers conditions that may not have been disclosed when the trade was agreed upon in principle. That allows the buyer to seek value commensurate with what their physical evaluation found, in the event that it doesn't line up with how the seller presented the player's bill of health.
Some people believe that the rules should be based 100% on the physical: if the player passes, the trade goes through at the agreed-upon price. Period. End of story. If the player fails his physical, then the buyer has only one recourse: cancel the trade.
There are two sides to every story. We've reported both sides, leaving it up to you to decide what really happend.
Did the Chargers try to pull a fast one on the Broncos and sneak an injury past a division rival? Or did the Broncos try to leverage a failed physical in bad faith to strong-arm a better deal for Henley after the deadline had passed?
A third possibility is that the Chargers were transparent with the state of Henley's health, but that the Broncos' medical standards were different, or they could have even discovered more in the physical than the Chargers were aware of.
Teams can view the severity of a player's injury differently. That's why some teams will spend money on a given player in free agency who may have a checkered injury jacket while other teams won't even consider signing them.
Add into the botched Henley trade the rariety of it being between two division rivals, and perhaps we shouldn't be all that surprised that it fell through in spectacular fashion, with both sides pointing the finger.

title: Broncos at the Bye: 5 Warning Signs That Could Derail the Playoff Push
full_text:
The Denver Broncos are halfway through their bye.
Sitting at 7-2, the Broncos have to feel great about navigating their initial gauntlet of a schedule as well as anyone could have predicted. That doesn't mean there aren't things to improve, though.
Coming out of the bye, the Broncos have only one plus-.500 opponent on the schedule until Week 16's Christmas Day bout with the Buffalo Bills. Already winners of five in a row, the Broncos have a great chance to extend their winning streak, and really go on a run.
All of Denver's 2026 goals are still on the table, including a second straight AFC West crown, the No. 1 playoff seed in the AFC, and a potential Super Bowl berth. But if the Broncos don't address these five warning signs at the bye, the season could potentially swerve off the rails.
Let's break down what Sean Payton must fix before hosting the Las Vegas Raiders in Week 11.
The Broncos' offense has been one of the worst this season, but it has steadily improved since Payton took back the play-calling duties in Week 5. The one lingering problem, though, remains the run game.
Jonah Coleman's return from injured reserve three weeks ago was a godsend, but the rookie alone hasn't been enough to elevate the Broncos' ground game out of the doldrums. Fans hoped that a running back trade ahead of Tuesday's deadline could change things, but the Broncos made no such move.
The reason Denver stood pat and didn't trade for a running back? The coaches know that it's not a running back issue; it's a blocking issue , as Payton himself pointed to on Wednesday in an appearance on The Herd with Colin Cowherd.
Payton also hinted that personnel changes could be coming up front, so that's something we'll be watching for over the next few days. But Payton and run game coordinator Zach Strief have to look at everything, including personnel and blocking concepts, to figure out how to spark this ground attack.
Coleman can do a lot of heavy lifting, as he's already proven over the past three weeks. But he can't do it alone. The Broncos have to get to the bottom of why their offensive line and tight ends are performing so poorly as run blockers.
The Broncos currently field the 27th-ranked rushing offense, averaging 91.4 yards per game. Coleman has elevated that average by about 10 yards per game, but it's not enough.
At some point, veteran running back J.K. Dobbins has to start carrying his fair share of the water, too. The only thing the Broncos have going for them on the ground is Coleman and the continued excellence of All-Pro left tackle Garett Bolles and All-Pro right guard Quinn Meinerz.
Offensively, the Broncos ranked 31st in third-down efficiency, converting just 32.4% of their attempts. Defensively, it's far from ideal: Denver ranks 21st, allowing conversions on 41.2% of opponent attempts.
If you can't stay on the field as an offense, the points aren't going to come. If you can't get off the field on third down as a defense, you'll allow too much yardage and put yourself in unfavorable red-zone situations.
Offensively, the Broncos took a big step in the right direction in Week 9's road win over the Carolina Panthers, convering 60% of their third-down attempts. That was great to see, and it was due to the Broncos executing better on first and second down, which set up more favorable third-down situations.
The Broncos' defense also did much better on third down against the Panthers, allowing just 3-of-10 to be converted, so both units showed progress in this area before hitting the bye. Let's hope the coaches can get to the bottom of this issue and keep the Broncos' third-down efficiency improving down the stretch.
The Broncos' scoring has improved dramatically over the past three weeks, averaging 28 points per game. It has helped them climb out of the bottom three scoring teams, putting them at No. 20 this season, averaging 22 points per game.
As quarterback Bo Nix's confidence has flooded back and the Broncos have moved past the brutal defenses they had to face through the first eight weeks, which included Steve Spagnuolo and the Kansas City Chiefs twice, the Jacksonville Jaguars, the Los Angeles Rams, and the San Francisco 49ers, the offense has begun to climb out of its shell.
The Broncos definitely have offense moving in the right direction at the bye, but there's still plenty of work to be done to bolster this unit as a bona fide playoff-caliber force to be reckoned with. One week might not be enough time to solve all the problems, but just fixing the run game/blocking issues will have a major trickle-down effect on the Broncos' third-down efficiency and scoring.
The Broncos started off the season with one of the most historically bad tackling showings ever. It has improved, but it's still far from where it needs to be.
The 2026 Broncos' defense hasn't been on the same level as it's 2025 counterpart, and its tackling woes are one of the reasons why. It comes out in the wash against the run and pass, allowing teams to pick up free yardage by simply making the first guy miss.
The Broncos have missed a whopping 102 tackles this season, the most in the NFL. Their 13.7 missed-tackle percentage leads the league, too, according to SFData9ers on X .
It's not the mark of a playoff-worthy defense. The Broncos' one saving grace has been their situational defense. When the chips are down in end-of-game sequences, this defense has continued to answer the bell, and it's still rushing the passer among the best in the NFL.
But if the Broncos can't shore up their tackling issues, playoff opponents like the Bills, Chiefs, Bengals, and others will have a heyday.
The Broncos' defense has been inexplicably leaky this season. Granted, they've faced a who's-who list of some of the NFL's best quarterbacks, but even against Bryce Young last week , the Broncos allowed five explosive plays — three through the air and two on the ground.
We can chalk some of that up to the injuries Denver has dealt with in the secondary, with starting safety duo Talanoa Hufanga and Brandon Jones ruled out in Carolina, and cornerback Riley Moss suffering a concussion early on, but it's not the whole story.
Yardage-wise, the Broncos' defense has allowed 2,076 yards through nine games. Only three teams have been worse than Denver in this area; it's not a winning stat.
So how do the Broncos keep coming out on top in these games? Again, it comes down to Nix's fourth-quarter magic and the defense's clutch-time composure.
If defensive coordinator Vance Joseph can get to the bottom of the explosives, and that includes on the ground, where Denver is allowing 124.3 yards per game, the Broncos could become a juggernaut. As the schedule continues to open up for them, I have a feeling the Broncos' defense will show some major signs of improvement, but Joseph has to batten down the hatches on some of these fundamental flaws.

title: Insider Provides Context to Botched Broncos Trade for Daiyan Henley
full_text:
The Denver Broncos stunned the NFL world late Wednesday night by announcing that their trade for inside linebacker Daiyan Henley has been called off . The team did not specify why it was backing out of the pact it made Tuesday with the Los Angeles Chargers.
Hours after the dust settled, ESPN NFL insider Adam Schefter provided a bit of clarity, reporting that Denver had medical concerns over Henley — specifically, his knee — that Los Angeles didn't share.
The Broncos, after flagging the issue, attempted to negotiate a revised trade deal, presumably without the 2028 fifth-rounder included in the original agreement. The Chargers rebuffed, and the deal was dead.
"It is not uncommon for one team to have some medical concerns about a player while another does not. In this case, Denver had concerns about Henley following his physical," Schefter wrote on X. "Even then, the Broncos still wanted Henley with Denver and LA discussing revised trade alternatives throughout the day, taking into account those concerns. In the end, no agreement was reached. The deal was off."
Pro Football Talk's Mike Florio later noted that Denver discovered arthritis in Henley's knee, which explains why the club got cold feet at the eleventh hour.
“The Broncos discovered an issue with Henley’s knee,” Florio wrote Thursday . “It has, we’re told, arthritis.” He added that a source with neither the Chargers nor the Broncos told PFT that most, if not all, starting linebackers in the NFL have some degree of arthritis in their knees.
Henley has appeared in all eight games for the Chargers thus far this season, notching 51 total tackles (21 solo), two passes defensed, one interception, a forced fumble, and a half-sack. He was limited prior to Week 6 with a listed knee injury; he was designated as questionable but ended up playing.
Obviously, the Broncos prefer to have Henley on the roster today rather than the prospect of facing him again later this season. They made a purposeful acquisition in the hopes of improving the pass coverage within their linebacker corps — something Henley excels at .
It's a bummer in that sense, but the Broncos obviously felt that Henley's condition could have long-term ramifications and wasn't worth the capital they agreed to surrender for him. How that ends up shaking out will be determined.
Moving forward, however, is the status quo: Alex Singleton and Justin Strnad as the starting ILBs, with Karene Reid and Jordan Turner as the primary backups. The Broncos also have seventh-round rookie Red Murdock on the practice squad; Murdock may eventually see playing time now that Henley is no longer in the picture.
Denver also has an open spot on the 53-man roster after waiving defensive back Sean Fresch Jr. to initially make room for Henley.

title: Ben Powers Isn't Broncos' Biggest OL Problem, But He Could Pay the Price
full_text:
With the Denver Broncos on bye, head coach Sean Payton appeared on The Herd on Wednesday.
Among other things, Payton expressed his dissatisfaction with the Broncos' blocking up front and hinted at potential personnel changes during the bye.
Looking at the Broncos' offensive line this season, it obviously hasn't been good enough. The unit could do with a shakeup, given that the Broncos still rank in the bottom 10 in rushing.
Not everyone on the unit is playing poorly, as left tackle Garett Bolles and right guard Quinn Meinerz have been among the NFL's best at their respective positions. You'd hope that would be the case, though, given that they're both first-team All-Pros.
That leaves left guard Ben Powers, center Luke Wattenberg, and right tackle Mike McGlinchey as the options to consider benching over the bye. Of those three, none has drawn as much vitriol from fans and some Broncos media members as Powers has, but it's not deserved — not fully, at least.
This isn’t to say Powers has played particularly well, but he hasn’t been the biggest culprit behind the O-line's failure to launch. That would be McGlinchey, followed by Wattenberg, then Powers.
Before getting into the data, there's an argument that Powers makes the most sense to bench because of extenuating circumstances. Of the three, he's the only one in the final year of his contract .
Denver also has better options to replace Powers, making him easier to bench than McGlinchey or Wattenberg, especially factoring in their respective contracts.
Behind Powers is Kage Casey, whom the Broncos drafted this past April to be their starting left guard in 2027, and they seemed pleased with his development in practice this past summer. The Broncos could decide to make the switch, see if Casey can handle it, and get answers for next year, though that could be tough to balance with their Super Bowl aspirations if it doesn't go swimmingly.
The Broncos also have Alex Palczewski, their sixth offensive lineman, who stepped in for an injured Powers at left guard for much of last season. While fans seemed to love Palczewski, he was vastly overrated and finished the season among the bottom 10 worst guards in nearly every offensive-line metric.
Also, Palczewski has performed better on the right side than on the left. Keep in mind that he currently fills the sixth O-line spot, which means that moving him into the starting lineup at left guard would mean replacing two players in the team's top six.
If it wasn’t for McGlinchey’s contract, or if Denver wasn’t afraid to bench him and could break free of the sunk-cost fallacy, Palczewski at right tackle would make sense. It would be better than Matt Peart or Frank Crum at right tackle (if Crum comes off injured reserve). Denver could consider benching McGlinchey and putting Casey at right tackle, too, though it would be extremely unlikely.
However, regardless of who replaced him, the first obstacle to benching McGlinchey would be overcoming the sunk-cost fallacy, believing that because he has one of the highest cap hits on the team, he should be on the field. His play has not been anywhere close to commensurate with his contract.
As for Wattenberg, the Broncos just gave him a four-year, $48 million extension a year ago, and are likely stuck with him through the 2027 season. The team could view Alex Forsyth — who's in the last year of his deal — as an upgrade in run blocking, but his pass protection has been a massive downgrade whenever he's been called upon.
After going over the tape again, Powers gets a lot more hate than he deserves. Is he great? No. He's an average player playing at an average level, while Wattenberg and McGlinchey are playing among the worst at their positions in the NFL.
This season, Powers has allowed a 2.7% blown-block rate with 14 blown blocks, while McGlinchey is at 18 blown blocks and a 3.5% blown-block rate, and Wattenberg is at eight blown blocks and a 1.6% blown-block rate, though Wattenberg has faced nearly 1/8th of the one-on-one blocks that Powers and McGlinchey have.
Digging deeper into run-game-specific metrics, since the Broncos' lack of a ground attack has become such an issue, Powers has just four blown blocks, as does McGlinchey, while Wattenberg has five. That means 10 of Powers's blown blocks have been in the passing game, compared to 14 from McGlinchey and three from Wattenberg. Remember, again, though, Wattenberg is rarely asked to block one-on-one, which is important context.
In other run-game metrics, like yards before contact, with each player as the lead blocker, and forced bounces allowed (where the lineman doesn't clear the lane and the back is forced to bounce to another hole), Powers ranks among the top 20 guards in the NFL in each category.
At the same time, Wattenberg ranks in the bottom six, with McGlinchey in the bottom eight in both categories. Again, Powers hasn’t been great, but he's not the worst player on the O-line. Sorry, Broncos fans.
There is even an adjustment for the quality of defensive linemen faced, and the Broncos have gone against some serious talent this season. With those adjustments, Powers ranks higher than he does without them, while McGlinchey is the same, and Wattenberg is actually worse.
While I haven't gotten into it much, Powers is also dealing with a Lisfranc injury he suffered against the Jacksonville Jaguars last season, which required offseason surgery. For offensive linemen, returning to normal play after an injury takes about 11 months, and Powers had surgery in February or March, but he doesn't get the same benefit of the doubt that other Broncos do.
So, one last time, I ask: does Powers deserve to be benched?
The answer is no, but Powers is the most likely option to bench because of the Broncos' lack of reliable depth at the other positions and because sitting him down wouldn't force the team to confront the sunk-cost fallacy, as it would with Wattenberg or McGlinchey.
There are risks to benching Powers, as chemistry and communication are vital on the offensive line, but the Broncos' starting five hasn't been good enough, so we could see changes, whether they're fair and just to the individual or not.
After this season, the Broncos should strongly consider finding three new starters and significantly upgrading their O-line depth.

title: Broncos' Daiyan Henley Trade With Chargers Falls Through in Stunning Reversal
full_text:
The Daiyan Henley trade has been called off.
The Denver Broncos made the announcement late Wednesday night, saying the Henley deal with the Los Angeles Chargers had fallen through. It was due to a failed physical.
"The proposed trade involving Chargers linebacker Daiyan Henley will not be finalized. We have great respect for Daiyan as a player and person, and we wish him all the best moving forward," the statement read.
pic.twitter.com/vFJ7MYS2UN
The Chargers responded by posting a "Welcome back, Daiyan" meme on their X account.
https://t.co/Ewbs7j6Yga pic.twitter.com/QzaZ40ZFF7
The deal for Henley, agreed to in principle ahead of Tuesday's NFL trade deadline , would have sent the Broncos' 2027 fourth-round pick and 2028 fifth-round pick to the Chargers in exchange. The Broncos will obviously be holding onto those picks.
Henley is about to turn 27 and is in the fourth and final year of his rookie contract. He's a two-time team captain in L.A. and is poised to lead the Chargers in tackles for the third straight season.
Broncos fans were excited about the prospect of Henley working into the linebacker rotation with Alex Singleton and Justin Strnad, especially given his coverage chops. Alas, unless the Broncos seek to sign him as a free agent in the spring, we'll never know how Henley would have fit in.
The Broncos are on bye, with their next game not until November 21, when they'll host the Las Vegas Raiders at Mile High. The Raiders have a new starting quarterback — Fernando Mendoza — and a pair of tight ends who've combined for over 1,000 receiving yards and seven touchdowns already this season.
Let's hope the Broncos have a better answer for Brock Bowers and Michael Mayer than they have the tight ends they faced in their last three games, to whom they allowed 330 yards and three touchdowns.
Apparently, the Broncos weren't as copacetic with Henley's knee issue as the Chargers were, and sought different compensation. In the end, the Broncos and Chargers couldn't come to an agreement and the trade was off.
That's what we know. It's a shocker, but the Broncos weren't comfortable giving up a fourth- and a fifth-rounder for a linebacker they like, but whose knee may have been suspect.

title: Sean Payton Puts Broncos' Starting OL on Notice With Bye Week Warning
full_text:
Since Sean Payton took back the play-calling entering Week 5, Bo Nix and the Denver Broncos' offense have been much better.
It was a gradual burn, and that build-up is still ongoing, but Payton has the Broncos back to playing a semblance of winning offense. Most importantly, Nix's confidence has returned — flooding back in Week 7 after his 62-yard touchdown run.
Each week since then, Nix has looked a little bit better, and after beating the Carolina Panthers on the road last Sunday, I don't think too many people are still worried about his football psyche. He's hunting with the football again , challenging defenses vertically, and playing with confidence.
Payton is happy to see the improvements on offense, but with the Broncos hitting their bye at 7-2, there are still several things he wants to clean up.
"I'm pleased with some of the change. Some of the things we're doing better," Payton told Colin Cowherd during an appearance on The Herd . "There's still that yellow tape around the offense that says 'work in progress.' It just is. And yet, I would say this: so much of what we're able to do offensively—run the ball, have balance—can really make what Bo has to do, make his job easier."
What exactly does Payton want to fix over the Broncos' bye? He pointed to the blocking up front, and even hinted that he and the coaches could consider making changes to the starting five, given the offensive line's ongoing struggles and the unit's depth.
"Now, getting specific, like, man, I'm watching the cut-ups from the game we just played, and we didn't block them very well. I'm just being honest, so that has to improve," Payton told Cowherd. "We've got plenty of depth on the offensive line, so during this bye, we're going to look at all those little things closely because the tape that's surrounding the offense needs to come down and the family needs to move in. So that's kind of where we're at."
You've got to love Payton likening the Broncos' offense to a domicile that's under construction, with the yellow cautionary tape surrounding it and whatnot. As he said, the work on the building has been done, and it's time for the family to move into its new home, meaning that it's time for the Broncos to move beyond the struggles they've had with even the most fundamental things on offense.
Thankfully, the Broncos' bye came as close to the midway point of the season as it gets, giving them plenty of tape to self-scout and enough games left to make the type of meaningful changes that could propel them into the playoffs.
"That's the cool thing about the bye right now is you really get this chance to take a zoom and look real close at what's been going well, what hasn't, why hasn't it been, and let's not kid ourselves," Payton said.
It sounds like Payton and his coaches will be brutally honest with themselves about what they've seen on tape. That being said, I wouldn't expect to see Payton make wholesale changes to the offensive line.
If the Broncos do anything, though, they might want to look at making a change at center. Luke Wattenberg has been one of the NFL's worst centers this season, and as frustrating as that is one year removed from the Broncos giving him a four-year, $48 million extension, they can't "kid" themselves.
Wattenberg has been a liability, and he's made life much more difficult for left guard Ben Powers and All-Pro right guard Quinn Meinerz, who have had to cover for his miscues, mishaps, and mental errors, leading to some social media backlash. The Broncos have Alex Forsyth under contract through this season, and he's got plenty of starting experience and time with Nix, so it might make sense to let Wattenberg sit for a spell to see if things improve.
Jonah Coleman has sparked the Broncos' run game, but it hasn't led to a sudden reversal in fortunes. The Broncos only rushed for 82 yards as a team last week in Carolina, with an average gain of 3.0 yards, compared to the Panthers producing 96 yards on the ground with an average gain of 4.8 yards.
Coleman can create on his own, and that's a blessing, but he can't do it all by himself, and Payton knows that. Payton and run game coordinator Zach Strief must figure out how to get this O-line rowing in the same direction, but that's partly what the bye is for.
In that same conversation with Cowherd, Payton went to bat for his quarterback, making it clear that the Broncos believe Nix to be their franchise quarterback and pushing back at the critics who question his arm strength.
"I know we have the right quarterback in the building," Payton said of Nix. "In other words, I've just seen it. I've seen the behavior, the things that you need in clutch moments, the arm strength. That was probably the biggest false narrative relative to him coming out was his arm strength, and he's got a way-above-average arm talent."
During Nix's early-season slump, the Broncos reportedly became " concerned " with his hesitancy, but they never lost faith in him as their current and future franchise quarterback. Payton wanted to see Nix " let 'er rip ," and that tide began to turn in Week 7 in the Broncos' road win over the Arizona Cardinals.
Over the past three weeks, Nix has exceeded the 200-yard passing mark in each game, and he's been using his legs more often. The assumption was that Nix's early-season slump was a combination of his psyche healing from his ankle injury suffered last January and the Broncos' brutal initial schedule.
Nix looked spooked and overwhelmed at times, but that was punctuated by outbursts of tremendous quarterback play, as seen in Week 2 against the Jacksonville Jaguars, Week 3 against the Los Angeles Rams, and in the first half of Week 6 against the Seattle Seahawks. Nix's pocket presence was terribly inconsistent; his footwork and technical foundation were out of whack, and he looked like he was pressing.
Entering the Week 10 bye, though, all of that feels like ancient history. And despite the obvious mental struggles Nix was going through in his recovery from ankle surgery, he still found ways to win games, even against some of the NFL's tier-one competition.
Nix's resilience and ability to overcome adversity are two of the intangible traits that drew Payton and the Broncos to him, and they likely play a big part in the club's ongoing faith in him as its franchise quarterback. During the period when Nix was struggling, Payton pulled him aside and talked to him, pointing to the enormity of the schedule the NFL gave the Broncos to start this season.
And yet, Nix prevailed — far more often than not, defeating some great teams.
"The quarterback thing, he's going to be outstanding," Payton said of Nix. "And I shared with him, I said, 'Hey, week to week in our league,' I said, 'Do you realize in three weeks, no one will have a clue—last year, no one could tell you about the Jet game last year. No one's going to be able to tell you one thing. Now, you've just gone through a gauntlet of some of the better defenses in football. You've seen the Chiefs twice, you've seen Jacksonville, you've seen Seattle, like, that's a stretch.'"
It hasn't been easy for Nix, but he has found his footing. The resistance training of the first eight games has built up one heck of a football callus.
Nix is playing with great confidence again, and his aura feels no different than it did last year against Josh Allen and the Buffalo Bills in the divisional round. Despite all the imperfections, despite all the obstacles of the schedule, Nix has the Broncos at 7-2, leading the AFC West, and in position to wrest the No. 1 playoff seed away from the Bills.
"We're at 7-2, and that's the positive," Payton told Cowherd.
Given the schedule Denver has faced, 7-2 is a triumph of willpower and fortitude. Payton deserves a lot of credit, and so does Nix. But the job isn't done yet.
Payton's got to fix this run game. And as he's said, it's long past due.

title: 7 Things to Know About New Broncos LB Daiyan Henley
full_text:
And just like that, the NFL trade deadline has come and gone.
After weeks of speculation and rumor, the Denver Broncos made a move — but not the one fans were expecting — acquiring fourth-year linebacker Daiyan Henley from the Los Angeles Chargers for a 2027 fourth-round pick and a 2028 fifth-round pick.
The Broncos had the vision last year of a three-man linebacker rotation, and it was realized in the form of Alex Singleton, Dre Greenlaw (when healthy), and Justin Strnad. Due to the amount of time Greenlaw missed, though, Strnad saw the field way more than even the Broncos anticipated.
After the 2025 season ended, the Broncos made the tough decision to part with Greenlaw after one injury-riddled season, and reupped with Singleton and Strnad, re-signing both to multi-year extensions. That made Strnad an undisputed starter, but the Broncos didn't have the three-man rotation at linebacker.
What should Broncos fans know about a veteran who, until Tuesday, had been nothing but a divisional enemy? Here are seven things to know about Henley and the trade.
Intra-divisional trades are rare, especially in the AFC West. The Chargers had multiple suitors for Henley ahead of the trade deadline, but the Broncos were reportedly the only team knocking on L.A.'s door that was willing to offer a fourth-round pick plus additional compensation.
Part of the Broncos' rationale was surely the 2027 fourth-round compensatory pick they expect to be awarded for the free-agent departure of defensive lineman John Franklin-Myers. Denver entered the trade deadline with a full complement of 2027 draft picks, but with that comp pick coming back, it'll still end up with a fourth-round selection, provided it isn't traded.
Henley was born and raised in Los Angeles and is the youngest son of Eugene "Big U" Henley, a famous hip-hop influencer and former shot-caller of the notorious Rollin' 60s Crips in Crenshaw . Big U played a part in the success of several famous hip-hop artists, like Nipsey Hussle and Kurupt, and was called the "Godfather" of rap music by Wiz Khalifa.
Big U spent a good chunk of Daiyan's childhood behind bars, which helped to keep the youngster on the straight and narrow. Once freed, Big U went on to coach Daiyan in Pee Wee football, guiding him to success and helping him to avoid the same pitfalls and mistakes he made on the streets.
Henley's family is royalty in South Central L.A., which made his selection by the Chargers so fitting. Big U named Daiyan (pronounced DAY-on), which means "mighty ruler" or "protector" in Arabic.
Henley played most of his collegiate career at Nevada before transferring to Washington State for his red-shirt senior year.
Henley is in the fourth and final year of his contract as a 2023 third-round draft pick. According to The Athletic 's Noah Furtado , the Chargers began extension talks with Henley, but no agreement materialized.
The soon-to-be 27-year-old Henley is nearly four years younger than Strnad. The Broncos wanted to get younger at linebacker, and Henley is another step in that direction.
Time will tell exactly what Henley's role will be with the Broncos, but he will see the field. There's a very good chance the Broncos' front office will look to extend him, maybe even before the 2026 season is over.
On Wednesday, Denver restructured safety Talanoa Hufanga's contract to free up nearly $4 million in cap space, so whether it comes during the Week 10 bye or after the season, look for Henley to be re-signed.
With half the season in the books, the Broncos are only on the hook for $1.84 million, per The Denver Post 's Parker Gabriel . That makes the move even more of a home run for Denver.
The Broncos is getting a three-down linebacker with 41 career starts (Strand only has 28) for under $2 million. Even the draft capital relinquished for Henley will be inconsequential, especially if the Broncos are able to get him extended.
That could come sooner than some people might realize.
Henley was a two-time team captain with the Chargers. He was viewed as the most important voice in that locker room, which is one of many reasons why Chargers fans and L.A. media were so surprised by this trade.
On top of that, Henley also wore the green dot on his helmet, signifying that he had the radio on the field. Only one defender can wear the green dot on the field at one time, and the defensive coordinator relays the plays to that player.
Henley was a team captain in L.A. and the Chargers' defensive signal-caller. His football IQ is off the charts, and he's one of the most athletic linebackers in the NFL, even if he isn't the biggest (6-foot-0, 225 pounds).
Henley led the Chargers in tackles in 2024 and 2025, getting well over the century mark both years. His 51 tackles this season led the Chargers, so he was on pace to lead the team in tackles for a third straight season.
His size can be a detriment at times; Henley can struggle to get off blocks and sort through the trash, but he makes up for it with his smarts, instincts, and explosiveness. He's a reliable tackler, but staying out of the paws of the NFL's big interior offensive linemen will be key.
The Broncos might not use Henley right away on first and second down, but as we'll discuss next, they'd be remiss not to use him in obvious passing situations.
Henley has four career interceptions and 15 pass breakups. The Broncos have been in desperate need of a coverage linebacker for years, and he checks that box as a three-down player with coverage chops and a nose for the ball.
The Broncos have struggled mightily this season to cover tight ends and running backs out of the backfield. Denver has allowed the most receiving yards in the NFL to running backs and the second-most to tight ends.
Over the last three games alone, the Broncos relinquished 330 receiving yards and three touchdowns to tight ends. Coming out of the bye, the Broncos will host the Las Vegas Raiders at home.
The Raiders' two tight ends — Brock Bowers and Michael Mayer — have already combined for 1,046 receiving yards and seven touchdowns this season. Granted, a new quarterback — Fernando Mendoza — will be throwing them the ball when the Broncos meet the Raiders in Week 11, but getting Henley in the fold should be a timely buffer.
Henley wore the No. 0 jersey in L.A., but that belongs to Jonathan Cooper in Denver. At Washington State, Henley wore No. 1 — but that's currently occupied by Evan Engram — and he wore the No. 11 at Nevada — but that's Troy Franklin's number.
It'll be interesting to see what jersey number Henley ends up with, but there aren't too many available, let alone the desirable ones that are often rocked by linebackers. There are no single-digit numbers available, and none in the teens, but No. 56 could be had, with Levelle Bailey on injured reserve.

title: What Could Be Coming After Broncos Restructure Hufanga's Contract
full_text:
The Denver Broncos took care of some necessary bookkeeping almost immediately after acquiring inside linebacker Daiyan Henley from the Los Angeles Chargers.
According to Spotrac , the Broncos have restructured the contract of starting safety Talanoa Hufanga, converting $4.89 million of his current salary into a signing bonus. The move created $3.9 million in salary cap space.
This slightly altered the future ramifications of Hufanga's deal, which runs through next season. He now carries cap hits of $9.5 million, $7.6 million, and $14.8 million for 2026, 2027, and 2028, respectively — the latter technically a void year.
An excellent addition since joining the club, Hufanga has been especially impactful thus far this season, winning Defensive Player of the Week honors following his two-interception effort amid Denver's Week 3 upset of the Los Angeles Rams.
"I mean, that’s who he is. He finally caught the ball," defensive coordinator Vance Joseph said on Oct. 1. "That could have been him last year a couple of times, but he worked really hard on his ball skills. He really did, seriously, over the spring and the summer. So it’s paying off. He’s trusting the system, he’s trusting his leverage. When he came to us, he wasn’t a match or man-cover player. He was more of a spot drop, vision and break player. So he’s learned how to play in this system, and the weak part of his game was his coverage, but now it’s a strong part of his game."
Hufanga, who's missed the last four games due to an ankle injury, is likely to be back in action when Denver returns from its Week 10 bye to host the Las Vegas Raiders, who'll be starting first-overall pick, quarterback Fernando Mendoza, in the Mile High City.
Since the Broncos were already under the cap when they landed Henley — and they're only taking on less than $2 million in this year's salary — logic would dictate that the brain trust has another transaction up its collective sleeve.
That transaction is likely to be an extension, and that extension is likely to go to slot cornerback Ja'Quan McMillian, who's among a handful of Broncos players in the final year of their contracts, along with fellow corner Riley Moss, safety Brandon Jones, and wide receiver/returner Marvin Mims.
One of the league's best nickels, McMillian has notched 21 solo tackles, seven pass deflections, three sacks, and an interception in 2026. He's playing on a one-year, $5.76 million restricted free-agent tender ahead of what's scheduled to be his first career foray into an unrestricted market.
The former undrafted defender has objectively earned an extension — and he just may get it in the days ahead.

title: Film Room: Bo Nix Is Finally Hunting Again—and Broncos Are Better for It
full_text:
The Denver Broncos set an NFL record against the Carolina Panthers on Sunday by winning their 16th consecutive one-score regular-season game. It was closer than it should have been, but there was a lot of promising stuff on tape this week.
Bo Nix had a great game , even if the box score doesn’t bear the fruit most fans would expect from elite-level quarterback play. It was abundantly clear that the Broncos' offensive game plan was to push the ball against a banged-up Panthers secondary unit, and that aggression with the vertical passing game helped open things up underneath.
It also didn’t matter that a lot of the shot plays ended in incompletions, either. Denver attacked Carolina’s depth cornerbacks at will, drawing a handful of defensive pass-interference penalties along the way.
That’s the great thing about being aggressive and hunting with the football. You don’t always need an explosive completion to affect the defense and move the football. There are four outcomes to a passing play, and three of them are good for the offense.
Denver’s offense had rhythm against a bad defense in the first half, mounting a handful of scoring drives early and having another cut short by a Nix interception in the red zone. More on that here in a minute.
But the best thing I noticed came on four incomplete passes and that red zone interception. Let’s look at the film.
I love how Payton started the game with shot plays. I wish Bo puts this ball closer to the "red line", because it gives Sutton more space to work his feet, but its still a great ball. Just missed on this one. pic.twitter.com/yRlEZpxSvD
Knowing that the Panthers were down to their fifth- and sixth-string cornerbacks, Sean Payton called a shot play with three vertical routes to open the game. I love this play call because it gets Nix to be aggressive right away and sets the tone for the offense.
Carolina is in Cover 6, playing quarter-quarter-half on the back end, giving Nix a one-on-one shot to Courtland Sutton down the left sideline. Nix sets his feet and lets this thing fly, giving Sutton a great opportunity to make a play at the highest point.
Unfortunately, Sutton landed out of bounds, but the aggressive nature of this play is what I’ve been asking for over the past handful of weeks.
If I had to be critical of anything here, it would be the placement of this ball. This isn’t a bad throw, but I would like to see this put a little closer to the “red line, " which is an imaginary line running five yards parallel to the sideline. That would give Sutton more room to work his feet on the boundary, but that’s just nitpicking.
2nd play of the game. Take another shot. Being aggressive draws DPI, which is just as good as a completion. pic.twitter.com/BdyOWUCwtF
On the next play, Nix stays aggressive with another shot to Troy Franklin. Carolina comes out in a two-high shell, but rotates into a single high man-coverage. Nix sees safety Nick Scott patrol the deep middle as Franklin works the boundary against cornerback Corey Thornton.
Nix lets it fly as soon as he hits his back foot, putting another nice ball out there for Franklin to try to make a play. Thornton is flagged for pass interference on this play, which is one of the three positive outcomes for the offense on a passing play.
Targeting Thornton, who was called up from the practice squad for the game, was a great decision here. Putting pressure on depth pieces to perform early in the game can, and will, lead to positive outcomes.
I like Bo trying to fit the hole shot here. Stay aggressive. A little more air under this and it's completed instead of picked off. Kudos to Thornton for one heck of a play. The other team gets paid to play, too. pic.twitter.com/K0HksfRilW
Some people are going to disagree with me on this play. This is that red-zone interception that took points off the board. While I agree you can’t make a mistake like that, I like how aggressive Nix was with the football on this throw.
Denver runs Sutton on a corner route into Carolina’s Cover 2 defense, and Nix tries to layer a “hole shot” to the boundary. Thornton makes an incredible play by getting great depth in his flat zone to undercut the throw and pick it off.
The reason why I like this play is that Nix is taking a chance with the football, and it’s actually there for the taking. If he gets a little more air under this ball, this could have set the offense up inside the 5-yard line.
Sometimes you win, sometimes you lose. The other team has players who get paid to play the game, too. Chalk one up for the bad guys and move on.
All Go Special on the last play before Half. Bo rips this john to Franklin. Great play by Chau Smith-Wade. Bo likes to rip these seam shots. He needs to do it more. pic.twitter.com/D9R8S1ZS0Z
That interception was critical. Carolina would go on to score a touchdown on their ensuing possession, ultimately taking the lead. But Nix responded on the next Denver drive, operating a nice two-minute drill to get points on the board.
Our next play is an “All-Go Special," with five vertical routes on what was essentially a Hail Mary attempt. But Nix doesn’t throw it up for grabs. He rips a seam shot to Franklin, and it’s broken up at the last second by cornerback Chau Smith-Wade.
This is a great play by Smith-Wade, because this throw is right on the money for a touchdown. You could argue that Nix could put a little more air under this throw, too, but that's nitpicking the result of a great defensive play.
Denver's offense hasn't had these tight-window throws all year, but Nix has had success throwing these seam shots for years. He hit tight end Adam Trautman for a one-handed touchdown catch against the Panthers two years ago on a very similar throw to this one.
This throw is similar to the Franklin seam shot. It's from Bo's rookie year against Carolina. A little more air under it and a great catch by Trautman. pic.twitter.com/LVbnnl6RUX
Glance post to Engram. Love the aggression here. Just another great play by Smith-Wade. Right ball placement and pace. Can't win them all. pic.twitter.com/TlLML0LWYj
Nix tried it again later in the game as well.
During Denver’s first scoring drive of the second half, Payton calls a glance-post route for tight end Evan Engram in the red zone. Nix had to evade pressure from his left and throw this ball on the run, but he rips this ball perfectly.
Nix gets it above the head line, in a place where only Engram can catch it. But Smith-Wade plays it perfectly again, knocking away a touchdown pass.
This is good stuff, even though the pass falls to the turf at the back of the end zone. Denver scored on a nine-yard touchdown run by Jonah Coleman two plays later.
Outside of the Arizona Cardinals game a few weeks ago, Nix hadn’t been pushing the ball vertically all year. He wasn’t hunting with the football like this, and it was causing major issues with the passing game and bleeding into the run game. Denver’s offense was stagnant, even putrid at times.
Taking chances and making teams honor the vertical passing game opens up everything else. You don’t need to complete every one of these plays to make teams have to respect you.
You also get the added benefit of sometimes drawing penalties downfield, which is just as good as a completed pass. Carolina was flagged five times for pass interference, and every one of them was justified.
When Nix is operating within the scope of the offense and taking chances with the football, the Broncos look much better. I hope this is a sign of things to come following the bye week.

title: Broncos' New Linebacker Pecking Order After Daiyan Henley Trade
full_text:
The Denver Broncos made a move ahead of Tuesday's NFL trade deadline, acquiring linebacker Daiyan Henley from the Los Angeles Chargers.
Denver sent a 2027 fourth-round pick and a 2028 fifth-rounder to its division rival for Henley, but that's no skin off GM George Paton's teeth, given that he expects to get a fourth-round compensatory pick back for John Franklin-Myers's free-agent departure.
We've covered the Broncos' biggest winners and losers of the Henley trade and graded the move . Now it's time to examine how the fourth-year veteran's arrival could shake up the Broncos' linebacker depth chart.
The Broncos finally have a coverage linebacker. As exciting as Henley's arrival is, I don't anticipate him replacing either of the starters out of the gates.
Singleton and Strnad will remain the Broncos' starting linebacker duo, but unlike Turner and Reid, Henley is going to play. Much like last season, when Dre Greenlaw was healthy, the Broncos will implement a three-man rotation at inside linebacker, based on down and distance.
It might not happen right away, but I'd love to see Henley start eating into Singleton's coverage snaps. Coverage isn't Singleton's strong suit, and yet, he's played 365 so far this season, the most of any NFL inside linebacker.
Meanwhile, Strnad has played 280 coverage snaps, the seventh-most among NFL linebackers. On one hand, you'd like to tip your cap to Singleton and Strnad for playing so many snaps against the pass. On the other, neither is doing a good job.
The best reflection of that is the amount of yardage the Broncos have hemorrhaged to tight ends this season. In just the past three games alone, they've allowed 330 passing yards and three touchdowns to tight ends.
The Broncos had to do something, and they did, adding Henley just as they hit their bye. That gives him time to settle in and assimilate the playbook on the fly.
Since the Broncos won't be playing again until Week 11's home game against the Las Vegas Raiders, I like Henley's chances of being ready to contribute. I hope we see him early and often because the Raiders have All-World tight end Brock Bowers and Michael Mayer, two tight ends who've combined for 1,046 yards and seven touchdowns already this season.
Granted, the Raiders will have a different quarterback throwing them the ball when the Broncos see them, as Kirk Cousins was traded to the Minnesota Vikings on Tuesday. But No. 1 overall pick Fernando Mendoza shadowed Cousins through the first nine weeks, and even though he's a rookie, he's smart enough to know how the Raiders' bread gets buttered.
As for the bottom two linebackers on the depth chart, the Broncos opted to cut defensive back Sean Fresch Jr. to make room for Henley, instead of one of them. Both Turner and Reid are key special teams contributors, so they'll be sticking around the active roster for the foreseeable future.
Henley begins his Broncos tenure as the third linebacker on the depth chart, but he's started 41 career games since entering the league as a Chargers third-round pick in 2023. He's a two-time team captain and L.A.'s green-dot wearer, meaning he called the signals for the defense. He was also the Chargers' tackles leader twice and was on pace to do it again this year before his trade.
Strnad has been in the league since 2020, and has 28 career starts, just to put things in perspective. Henley has seen a lot of football, and he's played well in all facets of the game.
Henley is going to see the field out of the gate, even if he doesn't replace Singleton or Strnad as a nominal starter. The Broncos traded for him for a reason, and their desperate need to stanch the bleeding in the middle of their passing defense dictates he sees the field in obvious passing situations.
It's going to be interesting to see just how the Broncos balance their new three-man linebacker rotation.
