title: Packers Sign Defensive Tackle-Turned-Tight End to Practice Squad
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The Green Bay Packers filled an opening on their practice squad on Tuesday by signing rookie tight end Kenny Fletcher Jr.
Fletcher was part of a Tuesday workout that included four tight ends and two quarterbacks. One of the tight ends was Zack Kuntz, who was drafted by the Jets in 2023. One of the quarterbacks was rifle-armed Jalen Morton.
The Packers opted to go with Fletcher, who went undrafted this year out of Rutgers. He spent the offseason and training camp with the Buccaneers but didn’t catch any passes in the preseason and failed to make their 53-man roster. He spent the start of the season on the Colts’ practice squad.
Fletcher caught 46 passes for 373 yards and two touchdowns in 2024, a season cut short by an injured wrist, and 2025. He spent the 2022 and 2023 seasons at defensive end, where he had 2.5 sacks among 10 tackles.
“Believe it or not, Kenny came in, he was frustrated, he wasn't getting enough playing time at defensive end,” then-coach Greg Schiano said . “We were discussing maybe a transfer and I said, ‘Kenny, I don't want you to transfer. You belong here.’
“I said, ‘Look, you played wideout in high school. Why don't you give tight end a try? I got a funny feeling you're going to be pretty good at this.’ And in whatever it was, 15 practices, he got himself ready. I think literally we've just scratched the surface with Kenny as a tight end. And he's another guy that I expect to see in that league and he's talented enough to do it for a while.”
Fletcher embraced Schiano’s idea.
“As soon as he told me that [moving to tight end was in the best interests of he and the team], I was ready for the change. I played wide receiver in high school, so that was cool. As soon as he brought up tight end, I knew I could do the job. It really wasn’t hard for me after he told me that was our best chance of winning. After he told me that, it was great.”
Fletcher made an instant impact. He caught four passes in his first game at the position and touchdowns in each of his first two games. He added seven catches against Virginia Tech. He had 19 catches in the first six games before the injury against Wisconsin.
The ability to catch the ball was easy because he played receiver in high school. How about as a blocker?
“I love blocking because of the violence in it,” Fletcher said in 2024 . “You can use some of your defensive violence and techniques and transfer it to tight end.”
“Blocking, I feel like I’m a violent football player,” Fletcher added . “So blocking, the violence in me helps me block. It’s second nature, again.”
Fletcher measured 6-foot-2 7/8 and 250 pounds at this year’s pro day. He ran a 4.71 in the 40 but put up some strong numbers in other tests for a Relative Athletic Score of 8.26 .
The Packers have four tight ends on their 53-man roster with Tucker Kraft, Jonnu Smith, Mark Redman and Josh Whyle. With Whyle out with a concussion, they promoted their practice squad tight end, Drake Dabney, to the gameday roster for the win at New England.
Luke Musgrave remains on the physically unable to perform list with a neck injury.
Fletcher will embrace the opportunity.
“It means the world,” Fletcher said while at Rutgers. “It’s my dream playing football. Whatever comes with it, I’m going to take it and roll with it.”
The Packers have a full practice squad.
Offense: QB Cam Miller, G Dillon Wade, T Dalton Cooper, TE Drake Dabney, TE Kenny Fletcher, WR Isaiah Neyor and WR Quincy Skinner.
Defense: DT Mazi Smith, DT David Blay Jr., edge Nyjalik Kelly, edge Arron Mosby, edge D.J. Johnson, LB Jack Dingle, CB Domani Jackson, CB Elijah Culp, S John Saunders Jr.
International: K Lenny Krieg.
Wade, Cooper, Dabney, Neyor, Kelly, Mosby and Jackson spent training camp with the Packers.
“You’ve got to try to get this guy up to speed in regards to our offense and all that as soon as possible, which is always a little bit more of a challenge in-season,” coach Matt LaFleur said of Miller last week. “So, he’s going to have to learn a lot on his own and pay attention and we’re going to have to find time to devote to him, as well.”

title: Packers-Vikings Matchups: Who Has Advantage in Love-Flores Showdown?
full_text:
It’s redemption weekend in Green Bay, Wisconsin.
The Green Bay Packers are about to play what is, to date, their biggest game of the season. Kick-started by their Week 1 win over the Packers, the Minnesota Vikings started the season 6-0. They looked poised to run and hide from the Packers, who lost two of their first three games.
On Sunday at Lambeau Field, the Packers have a chance to avenge their season-opening loss while tying the Vikings in the standings.
Can they? Here are our weekly matchups.
Justin Jefferson is awesome. The analysis on him as a player can start and stop there.
But who is going to be throwing him the ball?
Minnesota opened training camp with four quarterbacks. Kyler Murray was signed to be the starter but is on the sideline with a strained hamstring. With the addition of Murray, former first-round pick J.J. McCarthy was traded to the Giants in late September. The backup, Carson Wentz, started in place of Murray on Monday night but looked lifeless in the process of losing to the Bills. Max Brosmer got some time last year when injuries struck the position, but he’s not a sound solution.
So, the Vikings were forced to make a move at quarterback. At Tuesday’s trade deadline, they sent a third-round pick to the Raiders to reacquire Kirk Cousins. Cousins is a four-time Pro Bowler, including three selections during his time in Minnesota. He starred under Kevin O’Connell from 2022 until he suffered a torn Achilles at Lambeau Field in 2023.
With experience in the offense, Cousins is the odds-on favorite to start against Green Bay.
Meanwhile, the Packers’ defense is coming off one of its best games of the season. It picked off Drake Maye three times, sacked him four times and pressured him on 18 of his 38 dropbacks.
Outside of a game at Ford Field in Detroit, the Packers’ defense has mostly been excellent since the calendar turned to October.
The Packers’ defense, until further notice, is good. Minnesota’s offense is a mess.
Bijan Robinson ran wild on the Packers in Week 3. Outside of that, the Packers have done a good job of keeping opposing ground games under control. Jahmyr Gibbs ran for more than 100 yards against them, but it took him 29 carries to get to his 116 yards.
The Packers are familiar with the backfield that the Vikings will bring with them this weekend. Aaron Jones and Jordan Mason spearhead this attack. Jones leads the Vikings with 474 rushing yards and is averaging 4.1 yards per carry. He’s not the same player he was during his prime seasons with the Packers, but he is still good.
The Packers’ defense, however, is rolling.
Here’s the matchup of the game. The last time these teams played, Jordan Love threw for 387 yards on 21 completions. He was sacked four times and threw one interception and lost two fumbles.
He was under siege essentially from the beginning of the game to the end, when the game got out of hand. The Packers’ offensive line that day was Jordan Morgan at left tackle, Donovan Jennings at left guard, Sean Rhyan at center, Jacob Monk at right guard and Zach Bako-Bewele at right tackle.
This week, the Packers will have a new starting five with the interior certain to be three new players and Anthony Belton playing at right tackle. The offensive line has gotten better from the first game of the season but is still prone to blown blocks and missed assignments.
Minnesota’s blitz-happy defense sacked Buffalo’s Josh Allen four times on Monday and has brought pressure all season.
The difference this time around is that Love is playing as well as he ever has in his career.
Is he ready for the No. 1 defense in the NFL? Minnesota is allowing just 14.5 points and 161 passing yards per game. It’s suffocated everyone all season.
So, why does the edge go to Green Bay?
Jordan Love is on a heater. His performance against New England may have been the best of his career. He was excellent for three quarters against Carolina before one bad interception started to turn the tide.
He has been very good against almost any defense he has faced this season. That includes Flores’ group in Week 1 before he got snowed under by a defense that smelled blood.
The Packers’ defense should be better prepared for Minnesota’s quarterback situation this week. They’re also at home, which means their offensive line won’t be behind the gun of having to deal with Minnesota’s crowd noise.
Great quarterbacks can overcome almost anything. Love has been great the last few weeks, and that gives him the nod against a great defense.
Does Green Bay have a run game now? OK, that’s probably a step too far. However, the ground attack had by far its best performance on Sunday against the Patriots.
Josh Jacobs dropped out of the game with a fractured finger that will require surgery and won’t play on Sunday, but perhaps they found something with Kaleb Johnson. Johnson ran for a season-high 68 yards. That’s a season high for the Packers, not just Johnson.
Will Johnson get more run this week with the team they are playing? That remains to be seen. Chris Brooks and Pierre Strong are better in pass protection and that could play a big role against Brian Flores’ nasty defense.
Despite the improvement last week, the Packers are a bad run offense until further notice.
One thing to keep an eye on as the game gets into the fourth quarter: The Vikings’ defense was on the field for more than 40 minutes against Buffalo and will be playing on a short week. Will they wear down late?
Green Bay’s special teams is coming off what was perhaps its best game of the season.
Trey Smack, the embattled kicker, was asked to put the ball through the uprights seven times on Sunday. He booted all seven right down the middle, looking as confident as he has all season. Bo Melton returned a kickoff to the midfield, and the kick coverage was solid.
Can the Packers repeat that performance this week in a bigger game?
On Minnesota’s side, kicker Will Reichard is a legitimate weapon. He made 11 kicks of more than 50 yards a season ago, including a 62-yard bomb. He has missed just two field goal attempts this season, and both came from more than 50 yards.
Myles Price will handle return duties. He is averaging 29.9 yards per kickoff return. He almost took two kickoffs back for touchdowns against Green Bay, including a 68-yarder. He is averaging 17.5 yards per punt return, as well, with an 86-yard touchdown against Tampa Bay.
The Packers’ special teams has had its moments but is too up-and-down to be trusted in this spot.

title: Texans' Injury Report Raises Concerns on Woody Marks, Marvin Harrison Jr.
full_text:
The Houston Texans have released their second of three injury reports of the week heading into their upcoming matchup against the Cleveland Browns.
And for one of the few times this season, the Texans' Thursday injury report happened to showcase a few more concerns from what was shown on the first day of practice –– particularly in the case of two key offensive pieces: running back Woody Marks and wide receiver Marvin Harrison.
Let's take a look at the latest on the Texans' injury report only a few days away from Week 10's matchup
LB Azeez Al-Shaair (groin/personal) RB Woody Marks (knee) TE Brevin Jordan (finger/foot) WR Marvin Harrison (hamstring) OL Keylan Rutledge (neck/shoulder)
RB David Montgomery (groin) DE Will Anderson (ankle) DE Danielle Hunter (hamstring)
WR Tank Dell (hand/shoulder) S Reed Blankenship (hand/concussion) CB Jaylin Smith (hamstring) LB Jake Hummel (groin) OL Blake Fisher (thumb)
Something that immediately sticks out from the Texans' Thursday injury report that wasn't present on their previous one: both Marks and Harrison Jr. were DNP in practice with their respective issues.
It'd be a noteworthy, but also rare absence for both players in the event they were set to miss this weekend's action in Cleveland.
Marks (knee) has been active in every game for the Texans so far this season. Throughout the past three weeks since David Montgomery has been sidelined with his groin issue, Marks has been the leader in Houston's backfield, claiming a lion's share of the offensive reps.
During last week's game against the LA Chargers , Marks put together 18 carries for 70 yards (3.9 yards per carry), making it his fourth-straight game logging over 70 all-purpose yards.
If he were to miss any time at all for Week 10, his absence could wind up being significant for a Texans backfield that's been stuck without Montgomery, and could continue to be against the Browns, depending on how his status shifts heading into the weekend.
In the event both were to miss out on Sunday, the Texans would be down to just two players in their running back room: veteran Dare Ogunbowale and recently-signed Emari Demercado.
In Harrison Jr.'s case, he also has yet to miss a game for the Texans this season since his arrival. His only missed game of the season came back in Week 5 when he was with the Arizona Cardinals and was left to sit out knowing that a trade to send him out to Houston was imminent .
His absence––if he were to miss this week with a hamstring ailment––would slim the Texans' receiver room down once more, considering they just had to deal with the loss of Jaylin Noel after Week 7 against the New York Giants .
That means more involvement for Nico Collins, Tank Dell, Xavier Hutchinson, and Kayshon Boutte, and especially so if the Texans' backfield is without its top two contributors in Marks and Montgomery.
Another injury to keep an eye on for someone who still practiced in limited capacity? Defensive end Danielle Hunter, who was not listed on the injury report on Wednesday, yet popped up as a late entry on Thursday with a hamstring issue.
Perhaps it's nothing to worry about for the veteran defender. But those hamstring injuries can be tricky depending on the severity, especially for a 32-year-old edge rusher. So he'll remain a name to monitor alongside Marks and Harrison Jr. as the Texans release their final injury report after Friday's practice.

title: Texans' C.J. Stroud Faces Long Odds in MVP Race at Midseason Mark
full_text:
The first half of the Houston Texans' 2026 season has been filled with some really solid play from quarterback C.J. Stroud .
Stroud is throwing for a career-high 281.4 yards per game on a 64.2% completion rate, along with a 16-2 TD-to-INT ratio. He has the sixth-best passer rating in the NFL at 104.8 and is one of five quarterbacks in the NFL to have thrown two or fewer picks on the season (min. 5 GP).
It's gotten to the point for Stroud where, if he keeps up this same level of production, there might be real questions around whether or not he could enter some MVP discussions as we get deeper and deeper into the season.
However, when looking at his odds heading into Week 10, there's certainly some more work to do before Stroud is considered anything close to true MVP consideration, let alone being a frontrunner for the award.
According to odds from FanDuel Sportsbook , Stroud is currently tied for the eighth-best odds at taking home this year's MVP award (+6000) right alongside Kansas City Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes.
Seven other quarterbacks find themselves ahead of Stroud's own odds: including Caleb Williams (+5000), Kirk Cousins (+4000), Jordan Love (+750), Trevor Lawrence (+550), Brock Purdy (+550), Josh Allen (+370), and the current frontrunner for the award, Joe Burrow (+145).
It's some pretty nice company for Stroud to be surrounded by. And at the very least, being within those MVP discussions in any capacity is great for his stock this offseason when he's set to hit the negotiation table for his next contract .
However, if Stroud really wants to make a push for that MVP trophy this year–– rather than simply just be in the talks for it–– it's going to take a really dedicated effort over the second half of the schedule to make it happen.
And really, a lot of Stroud's chances simply come down to team record.
At 3-5 for a Texans team that's currently out of the postseason picture, it's really hard to consider the signal-caller of that offense a true MVP candidate, at least at this point in the year.
Now, could the Texans stack up a few wins and change the narrative just a bit ? Most definitely. With nine games left on the regular season schedule and several winnable games ahead for Houston, getting onto the right side of .500 can be within arm’s reach in no time.
But Stroud will need to continue playing at an elite level throughout that timeframe while the Texans are stacking up multiple wins; a task that's been much easier said than done through the first eight games of the year.
At the very least, Stroud deserves to remain on the MVP radar for as long as the Texans still have a fighting chance in the regular season. And if Houston climbs into the playoffs with a 12-5 or 11-6 record on the back of his production, it'll be hard to completely disregard him for the discussion.
So right now, Stroud might be falling a bit behind in the race. But give it a few more weeks, and things might shift for the better to potentially put him within reach of being the Texans' first-ever MVP in franchise history.

title: Texans Rookie Could Be in Line for Increased Usage in Week 10
full_text:
Through the first half of the 2026 season, the Houston Texans' rookie class has been a bit... underwhelming.
While yes, Keylan Rutledge has emerged as a pleasant surprise on the Texans' offensive line, others around the rookie class have either underperformed, or simply haven't gotten utilized as a part of the game plan on a week-to-week basis.
However, for Week 10 against the Cleveland Browns , there's a chance that the Texans could be handing over an increased workload to one member of their rookie class––and that's none other than second-round tight end Marlin Klein.
Throughout most of the season so far, Klein––the Texans' 58th-overall pick in the second round of this past draft––has been a bit of a non-factor within the Texans' offense, or even on the special teams side.
The 6-foot-6, 250-pound tight end out of Michigan played a combined 22 offensive snaps from Weeks 1 to 3, was inactive on game days from Weeks 4 to Week 7, and that was up until he was able to get a few more reps his way after the bye in Week 9 against the LA Chargers.
Klein saw 19 offensive snaps come his way, which was over double his season-high to that point. He also saw nine special teams snaps. The Texans, for the first time this season, made a more concentrated effort to get him involved.
It didn't result in any stats coming Klein's way, and that's certainly something the Texans want to see trend in a different direction. However, knowing he got involved in the offense much more than the prior eight games is certainly a success in itself.
Texans offensive coordinator Nick Caley also made it known that Klein has made "a lot of progress" ahead of the Texans' game against the Chargers, and will look for different situations to put him in moving forward.
“Yeah, no, he's made a lot of progress," Caley said ahead of Week 9. "I mean, all those guys, I feel, have done a good job. [Tight Ends Coach] James Ferentz does a really good job with those guys. He's getting better every single week."
"And again, like anything else, it's about focusing on the process, trying to get better, putting him in different situations, getting him exposure to different areas in the C-gap or off the ball in the run game, and then being able to move him around. It's like anything else. It's a continuous build for a guy like him, but it is for all of us.”
Having five tight ends on the 53-man roster does make the road a bit tougher for Klein to get involved on a consistent basis, which became clear during the first eight games on the schedule.
But now that he's continued to make noticeable progress in the eyes of the coaching staff, it becomes simpler to entrust a bigger workload in him on a week-to-week basis. And that seems likely to continue in Week 10 against the Browns.
That's especially so if one of the Texans' regular tight ends winds up missing any time. On Wednesday's injury report after practice , Brevin Jordan was a DNP due to a finger/foot issue. As it pertains to Klein's role against Cleveland, his status will certainly remain one to keep close watch on.
So looking ahead for Klein, expect to see much more of him within the Texans' offense as the season goes on, which might be able to provide their scoring attack a bit more versatility thanks to his upside as a blocker and a vertical threat in the passing game.

title: Deshaun Watson Downplays Texans Reunion Ahead of Week 10 Matchup
full_text:
The Houston Texans will get to see a pretty familiar face on the opposite sidelines this weekend as they'll be traveling to face the Cleveland Browns in Week 10 , and that's former Texans quarterback Deshaun Watson.
Watson, who was drafted to the Texans back in 2017, spent the first four years of his career in Houston en route to two playoff appearances, three Pro Bowl nods, and at the time, quickly rose up as one of the more talented young signal-callers in the NFL.
But since those four years that we saw Watson as a part of the Texans, a lot has changed.
Between his 2021 trade request and lengthy legal investigations , the trade that sent him from Houston to the Browns in exchange for three firsts, a third, and a fourth round pick, multiple up-and-down years with Houston, and a 2024 Achilles injury, we now find ourselves to Week 10 of the 2026 season.
Watson will be starting for the Browns, facing up against his former team for just the second time of his career thus far, while also marking the first time that he'll be up against C.J. Stroud on the other side.
However, even with this game being just the second time that Watson has been facing the Texans, he doesn't seem to be focusing on the reunion aspect much at all.
"You know, going against my former team, that stuff was in the past," Watson said of facing the Texans. "Four or five years ago, yeah, it was a big deal, but now I think both sides have moved on."
"We're just both trying to find ways to win and continue to put ourselves in position for later on down the road."
The last time that Watson was up against the Texans back in 2022, things didn't fare too well for Houston's side of the equation.
The Texans fell in a pretty one-sided loss on their home field, 14-27 in a game led by quarterback Kyle Allen, while the Texans had four total team turnovers and went a brutal 1-12 on third down.
Watson didn't have a particularly strong game, as he completed just 54.5% of his passes for 131 yards and an interception. But regardless of his individual performance, there's no doubt that the Texans will be hungry to find their way to a different fate for themselves this time in 2026.
Yet, don't expect the Texans to be focusing much on the fact that Watson will be playing his former team once again–– and that's especially so for quarterback C.J. Stroud.
Stroud spoke about how he's feeling ahead of his first matchup facing Watson, where he similarly shrugged off any notion that this game meant any more than the next.
"It's a football game in the NFL. I really don't think about that," Stroud said of facing Watson. "I have a lot of appreciation for Deshaun. He was good to me when I was in college, and I've been a big fan of his when he played here as well..."
"There's a couple other guys that I played with in college who have been on the Texans. That's every week in the NFL; usually playing against former players and guys you grew up watching. So, it's nothing different."
The most important aspect of this game for the Texans simply might revolve around how important getting a win would be. At 3-5 with their backs against the wall, this game becomes extremely critical to take advantage of , especially knowing that the Browns are also in the AFC Wild Card hunt like Houston is.
Time will tell if the Texans can take care of business in Week 10. And for fans that have been along for the ride since the Watson days, getting a victory against him and this Browns team might offer a nice sense of revenge from the last go-around.

title: Texans Week 10 Consensus Power Rankings: Optimism Starting to Build
full_text:
The Houston Texans sit at 3-5 with nine games to go on their 2026 regular season schedule. And while they might still be sitting under a .500 record, it seems that the stock for this Texans team is on its way up after their latest win over the LA Chargers .
Now of course, a win over the 0-8 Chargers shouldn't completely change the narrative about Houston . But there's reason to believe that another second-half season run could be in store for the Texans moving forward.
The offense has been playing well as a unit. C.J. Stroud could find his way into some MVP discussions soon (if he hasn't already), and if the defense can just find some type of consistency down the stretch, this Texans roster will be a hard group for any team to stop throughout the second half of the season.
With that in mind, let's sort through a new batch of consensus power rankings to see just where the Texans stack up around the league as they head into their Week 10 game against the Cleveland Browns:
Sports Illustrated 's Conor Orr does highlight that the Texans' latest loss is against the 0-8 LA Chargers. However, he doesn't fail to note that C.J. Stroud has been playing lights out throughout this season.
"Yes, it’s the Chargers. But L.A.’s defense isn’t the problem (and is actually pretty good). So you can take that C.J. Stroud top 10 talk very seriously. Five touchdowns. Three hundred eighty-four yards. Mercy."
NFL.com 's Nick Shook allows the Texans to climb up a few spots in his rankings thanks to a 44-point performance against the Chargers, which also came with Tank Dell's first touchdown score in a game dating back to 2024.
"A 44-point outburst and dominant win over the lowly Chargers had to be as cathartic as it was enjoyable for these Texans -- especially for Tank Dell, who scored his first touchdown since returning from a lengthy injury absence. It should also remind us that, while 3-5, Houston's not out of the running for the playoffs yet and might only be just getting started."
ESPN 's writers were polled on their power rankings this week, where the Texans climbed an impressive five spots. D.J. Bien-Aime was asked about Houston's most important game left on the schedule, which actually happens to be right around the corner: Week 10 against the Browns.
"The Texans are trying to finish the 2026 season like how they ended 2025, when they started slow and still got into the playoffs. A loss to the Browns could mean their season is unofficially done, as they're currently 3-4 against AFC opponents. Making the postseason would become difficult due to tiebreakers, and losing head-to-head to a team in the wild-card hunt also wouldn't be ideal. With the Jaguars at 6-2, there's almost no way for the Texans to reach the playoffs by winning the AFC South."
The Athletic's Josh Kendall and Chad Graff have the Texans at the lowest point in our consensus rankings at 22nd––which comes largely because of the type of competition Houston just faced. However, they still gave credit where it's due for the offense.
"Even after an easy win against the Chargers, it’s hard to give the Texans too many flowers because of their 0-4 start. Since then, however, the Texans have the second-best offense in the league based on EPA per play, behind only the Bengals. C.J. Stroud lit up the Chargers for 384 yards and five touchdowns on Sunday."
CBS Sports ' Pete Prisco doesn't think the Texans are out of the hunt just yet, especially when C.J. Stroud is playing at the level he has been over the coming weeks.
"With a soft schedule the next few weeks, they can get back into playoff contention. They aren't dead yet. C.J. Stroud is playing great football."
FOX Sports ' Ralph Vacchiano ties for the highest ranking for the Texans on this list. And if their defense ends up turning around in the next few weeks, they could quickly find their way into some Super Bowl conversations.
"If the Texans hadn’t stumbled in overtime against the Giants before their bye, they’d be riding a four-game winning streak, sitting at .500, and the entire NFL would be talking about how dangerous they are. Truthfully, though, even at 3-5, they’re dangerous and a playoff berth isn’t far out of reach. What makes this run weird, though, is that they’re doing it with their revived offense and on the shoulders of QB C.J. Stroud, who is making a hell of a contract push. If their defense was even close to what it was the last few seasons, we might be talking about the Texans as a Super Bowl-bound team."

title: Texans Injury Report vs. Browns Week 10: Multiple Starters Miss Practice
full_text:
The Houston Texans have wrapped up their first day of practice ahead of their Week 10 matchup against the Cleveland Browns.
And following that practice session for the Texans, we've gotten a glimpse of the injuries that this roster is dealing with in the days ahead of this weekend's contest––where in Houston's case, there's a chance that they could be forced to play without one or more of their typical starters.
Let's break down the latest from the Texans' Wednesday injury report before facing the Browns in Week 10.
LB Azeez Al-Shaair (groin/personal) TE Brevin Jordan (finger/foot) RB David Montgomery (groin) OG Keylan Rutledge (neck/shoulder)
WR Tank Dell (hand/shoulder) RB Woody Marks (knee) S Reed Blankenship (concussion/hand) WR Marvin Harrison (hamstring) CB Jaylin Smith (hamstring) LB Jake Hummel (groin) OG Wyatt Teller (illness)
DT Tommy Togiai (elbow/shoulder) OT Blake Fisher (thumb)
The most notable takeaways from the Texans' first injury report of the week surround the four names who were listed as DNPs; three of them being starters.
David Montgomery is the least surprising of the four, who has missed each of the Texans' team practices since leaving Week 5's game against the Tennessee Titans with a groin injury, and has gradually been working his way back to the lineup.
Texans head coach DeMeco Ryans made it known that Montgomery's status has improved from last week ––when he was ruled out with a groin injury on Wednesday––but said he would continue to be evaluated throughout the week. It remains to be seen if he ends up playing once the weekend rolls around.
The Texans also ended up seeing rookie offensive lineman Keylan Rutledge pop up as a rare entry on the injury report, as Coach Ryan’s noted that he had suffered a stinger during practice and would be listed as day-to-day.
The stinger doesn't initially seem like something that would inhibit Rutledge's status for Sunday, but he'll have two more practices to go in order to see whether or not he'll be able to suit up.
If Rutledge is indeed sidelined for whatever reason this weekend, veteran Wyatt Teller could be the primary name to look towards as Houston's next man up at left guard. He's started two games already this season in place of Ed Ingram at right guard, and he might be fit to do the same on the other side of the line, if prompted.
Azeez Al-Shaair might be a name to keep an eye on, as he was a DNP with seemingly the same groin injury that's restricted his availability in practice as of late . However, given that he also had a personal designation, there's a better chance that he'll be good to go for either Thursday or Friday's session.
Tight end Brevin Jordan also wound up as a DNP in practice with a finger/foot issue. If he's unable to go against the Browns, Houston has four other tight ends on the roster to turn to instead, including second-round rookie Marlin Klein, who was active on the gameday against the LA Chargers for the first time since Week 4.
The Texans' final status for everyone on the roster will become clearer after Friday's practice. But until then, keep a close watch on those four who didn't practice, while also not losing sight of anyone who was limited for Wednesday’s action.

title: Texans' Latest Update on RB David Montgomery Isn't Too Promising
full_text:
The Houston Texans have been left with a lingering injury within their running back room in the form of David Montgomery's groin issue.
Montgomery, who the Texans first brought onto the roster via trade earlier this offseason, has been sidelined since Week 5 with said injury . He's missed the following three games of Houston's season and hasn't suited up for a single team practice since.
It's led to many wondering exactly what's going on with Montgomery, and how much longer he could be expected to be out moving forward.
The Texans wasted no time ruling out the veteran back this past week on Wednesday before facing the LA Chargers, but no ruling has been made for Week 10 against the Cleveland Browns.
Yet, while no ruling has been made on Montgomery's status for this coming weekend in Cleveland, the latest update from Texans head coach DeMeco Ryans isn't exactly the most optimistic for his status against the Browns.
Ryans was asked about the status of those injured around Houston's roster heading into Week 10's game vs. the Browns–– and surrounding the latest on Montgomery, the Texans head coach said that he was getting better, yet still "going through the process."
"David Montgomery's still going through the process. He's getting better. We're encouraged by his progress so far. We'll see when he's able to get back out on the field."
Now, on the surface, that update for Montgomery's health long-term could be worse. After all, he's still progressing positively according to Ryans, and he hasn't been ruled out for Sunday, which was a different story this time last week .
But what Ryans didn't say is anything about Montgomery's participation in practice on Wednesday.
﻿ According to KPRC2's Aaron Wilson , Montgomery was attending the Texans' Wednesday practice, but he wasn't dressed and didn't participate.
His status hasn't changed from the week-to-week designation he saw upon first going down with the injury, but logging a DNP the first day of practice after missing the last three games might not be the most optimistic sign.
Of course, there are two days of practice left for the Texans before they're set to hit the road for Cleveland. So there is ample time for Montgomery to improve his status in time to play on Sunday for Week 10.
When reading the tea leaves, though, it does feel as if Montgomery could ultimately be forced out for one more week before he's able to officially make his return to the lineup–– which would then come in Week 11 against the Indianapolis Colts.
If Montgomery is forced out for the Texans this week, that means Houston's running back room will once again be held down by Woody Marks as the leader in the backfield, paired with veterans Dare Ogunbowale and Emari Demercado as his primary backups.
The Texans' run game has been able to stay afloat with Marks leading the way, yet having a healthy Montgomery as a piece of the puzzle to handle some of the work in the backfield could be a nice floor raiser for Houston's offense to lean on.
Keep an eye on Montgomery's status and whether or not he's able to practice with the team as we creep further into the week. But if he's unable to suit up for either of Thursday or Friday's sessions, don't hold your breath that he'll be back on the field for Week 10 against Deshaun Watson and the Browns.

title: Texans' Winners and Losers After Staying Quiet at Trade Deadline
full_text:
The Houston Texans' trade deadline was a quiet one.
While the Texans were involved in a slight bit of trade chatter before Tuesday's deadline , the 3 p.m. cutoff inevitably came and went without Houston shaking up their roster at all.
And with that decision from the Texans, a couple of names around the existing roster tend to come out on the other side of the deadline, seeing their stock trending in the right directions. Others, who might've benefitted from a move one way or another, might not be feeling the same way right about now.
Knowing that, let's sort through a couple of the Texans' biggest winners and losers from their lack of trade deadline activity, and what it may mean for those same guys moving forward:
The Texans had been linked to rumors surrounding potential interest to add onto two positions of need on their roster: running back and safety. And after the 3 PM buzzer sounded, Houston wound up adding neither onboard.
And that seems like it should be a vote of confidence in not only this Texans' run game to at least remain afloat for the remainder of the season, but also in Woody Marks (and perhaps a slight bit of David Montgomery) being strong enough to help sustain and build on their current production in the backfield.
Will Marks and Montgomery be able to help lead the Texans to a top-15 rushing attack in the NFL? Probably not. But if they can stay within the middle of the pack while still boasting a strong passing offense and overall defense, Houston will be in good shape.
These two offensive linemen feel like an easy package to put together here, because each found themselves in a pretty similar spot at the trade deadline .
The Texans signed both Teller and Smith in free agency. They haven't cemented themselves as starters since then and could've been dealt at the deadline for a small return to find that next opportunity elsewhere.
Those potential deals to send them out, though, did not end up coming to fruition.
So now, both Teller and Smith are stuck on the Texans' bench until further notice for the remainder of the season. While the Texans' offensive line has been stable without either of them claiming a big role, it's certainly not the ideal vision that either had for their time in Houston upon signing here this past offseason.
Another similar case to the Texans' running back situation at the deadline here: Houston was rumored to add a safety via trade, and ultimately decided not to. Instead, they'll be moving forward with their current safety unit led by Calen Bullock, and likely when healthy, Reed Blankenship.
And that's some big news for someone like Blankenship; someone who's struggled to adjust within the defensive scheme with some inconsistent performances, and has recently suffered from a hand injury and concussion during his early time with the Texans.
Clearly, though, Houston didn't feel the need to upgrade the back-end of their secondary, and is confident to roll with Blankenship––or perhaps his backup, M.J. Stewart––for the rest of the year. Time will tell if that bet ends up paying off for them.
The Texans walked into the trade deadline with five tight ends on their roster––just as they did to kick off Week 1 of the season. And there seemed to be a slim possibility that Houston would shed one of those names, and thus open up a roster spot and, more importantly, expanded opportunities for rookie Marlin Klein.
Houston didn't take that approach, however. They still have five tight ends on the roster, likely for the remainder of the season, and that leaves Klein in a bigger uphill battle to get consistent playing time within the Texans' offense.
The good news is that Klein did manage to finally be activated to the gameday roster against the LA Chargers for the first time since Week 4.
He played over 20 snaps for zero recorded stats, but seeing him on the field in a bigger capacity is a good sign for his stuck. Things might just look better had someone like Brevin Jordan or Cade Stover gotten dealt.

title: Why the Texans Chose to Stand Pat at NFL Trade Deadline
full_text:
The NFL trade deadline has officially come and gone. And over the course of Tuesday's action up until the buzzer, we saw a few deals around the league go down for teams to either buy or sell some talent for the second half of the season.
However, the Houston Texans were not one of those teams.
The Texans seemingly looked around the market to find anything that made sense for them, might've talked to multiple teams in the process, but decided to hold off on adding or subtracting any pieces to their current roster.
The rest of the AFC South, though? They weren't shy to get to dealing . The Jacksonville Jaguars made multiple additions like Jordan Davis and Jessie Bates, while the Tennessee Titans and Indianapolis Colts continued their selling sprees surrounding guys like Amani Hooker and Josh Downs.
So why did the Texans decide to take their conservative approach as opposed to others that might've not been as gun-shy?
Really, it comes down to just where the Texans stand at this particular point in the season, paired with the amount of assets they have on hand to deal.
When taking a step back to look at the Texans' trade deadline situation, it was pretty tough to diagnose the team as true buyers or sellers.
On one hand, the Texans are coming off a resounding win over the LA Chargers this past weekend that injected a bit of hope that this group could make a late-season run.
Their offense was firing on all cylinders, their defense was looking back to their 2025 selves, and one final addition to the roster at the deadline could've gotten Houston one step closer to their ultimate goal.
But the Texans also had reason to hold off on adding a starting-level player to their roster as well.
After all, Houston is still stuck at a 3-5 record with work to do before they're deemed true playoff contenders, meaning a move to "buy now" could only take a couple of weeks, and a couple of losses could turn sour pretty quickly.
On top of that, the Texans have already made a couple of trades to upgrade their roster–– they just didn't happen during the trade deadline.
Houston made a deal heading into Week 6 with the Arizona Cardinals to bring in Marvin Harrison Jr. for a second-round pick and a late-round pick swap, and they also made a trade before Week 1 to add Kayshon Boutte to their receiver room for Jaylen Reed and another late-round pick swap.
The Texans have made moves to get this roster better. They've spent draft capital to make even more upgrades. And really, Houston's roster as currently constructed still has a reasonable amount of life left in their season to consider themselves right within the playoff hunt, even two games back from .500.
So could the Texans have gotten better by making a trade deadline addition to the roster? Sure, every team in the league could have that argument.
But a deadline move just didn't make a ton of sense for the Texans to execute without a truly tantalizing package.
No running backs were on the market that were realistic to acquire and moved the needle in the backfield from where things stood as is, and the same can be said about Houston's other rumored interest in safety.
Without any solid pieces up for grabs, and the lack of urgency from the Texans' side of things to pull the trigger on a deal, it's led to the end result looking like this at the deadline: quiet, without any shakeups, and thus puts a bit more pressure on this current roster to turn things around for a postseason appearance.
Based on their latest win against the Chargers , there's a good amount of optimism in the air that the Texans can make that climb up the standings happen. However, there's a lot more work to do in the weeks ahead for that to become a reality.

title: Which Texans Players Could Get Dealt on Trade Deadline Day
full_text:
The Houston Texans have just a couple of hours to go until they're on the other side of the NFL trade deadline.
﻿ To this point, things have been pretty quiet in H-Town . And that's led to the belief that the Texans could simply let this deadline come and go without making a move to their roster— which is a very real possibility.
But when taking a step back to look at the Texans' roster ahead of the trade deadline, a select few players around the building might make sense as a potential name to ship out for one reason or another.
Whether it be because that player might have value on the trade market if they were shopped, or if they might simply be a better fit in another situation, four players onboard the Texans feel as if they're the most likely names to be on the move, if a trade really is in play before 3 PM CT.
With that in mind, let's take a look at four Texans players that have the most realistic shot of being traded on deadline day:
The Texans' offensive line has taken a bit of a different shape from the state it was expected to be coming out of the offseason.
Back in the summer, the Texans were expected to start free agent signing Wyatt Teller at left guard in hopes that he would be an upgrade for a struggling unit upfront.
But he's only started in two games this season because of an injury to Ed Ingram, and has instead found his role as a bench contributor that might be better suited for a change of scenery at the deadline.
The Texans could find a suitor that has a starting spot in mind for Teller, get minimal draft capital in return for him, but also salvage a bit of their offseason investment that hasn't panned out quite as well as the front office would've hoped.
It's a win-win for the Texans and Teller, if he's looking for a bigger opportunity heading into the second half of the season. And in reality, this feels like it could be the most likely move of all that we see Houston end up making.
A very similar case here for Braden Smith: someone who the Texans signed to a two-year deal earlier in free agency expected him to start on their new-and-improved offensive line, yet hasn't found a consistent role as a starter since beginning the first four weeks of the season on injured reserve.
At most, Smith has filled in as a contributor in the Texans' jumbo looks on offense. But on a line that also has a solid backup swing tackle in Blake Fisher behind their starting duo of Aireontae Ersery and Trent Brown, Smith's presence in this offensive line room becomes a bit redundant without a clearly determined role.
So rather than let Smith sit in the Texans' offensive line room as a backup for the rest of the season, the Texans could strike on a deal for more value than someone like Teller could be worth, reshuffle their tackle room without Smith, and have a better set of draft assets to build with for this offseason.
Could the Texans value Smith more as a depth piece on their offensive line? Might teams be wary about trading significant assets to an injury-prone veteran tackle? Yes and yes. And those two factors might be what hold up a move getting done here. But it's an idea that's worth considering from Houston's lead decision-makers.
It's always fair to question whether or not a quarterback-needy team could be in the market to add Davis Mills; someone who many consider to be one of the more reliable backups in the NFL. And the idea isn't too outlandish to consider here for the Texans .
C.J. Stroud is playing lights-out through eight games of the season. He's going to get a new contract this offseason, and so is Mills, who's currently in the last year under contract and is due to be an unrestricted free agent in 2027.
If the Texans didn't intend on paying Mills another contract, a deadline move would make sense. Houston can cash in on an expiring contract in the form of a draft pick, and send out a backup who's gotten barely any playing time this year anyways.
However, the Texans could still go out and re-sign Mills this summer. And even if they aren't, the front office may simply see more value in Mills as a backup on their roster compared to whatever they could get back in return via trade. And if that's the case, then they might not deal Mills out at all.
This is simply a case of the Texans suffering from an overabundance at a certain position. And in this case, Houston might have one too many tight ends currently on their roster.
And the one name within that group of tight ends that makes sense to ship out would be Cade Stover.
He was just deemed a healthy scratch just last weekend against the LA Chargers, and with the increased involvement of Marlin Klein in the game plan moving forward, it'll be even harder for Stover to make an impact moving forward.
The solution? The Texans could trade away Stover now, get a minimal return for him, and move forward with a slimmer tight end room that opens up more involvement for Klein, as well as Brevin Jordan and Foster Moreau.

title: Colts vs. Dolphins Preview: Can Indy Finally Stop the Slide?
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts are back home Sunday, and if you’re looking for a matchup between two teams fighting for their season, this probably isn’t it.
Indianapolis enters Week 10 at 2-7 on a five-game losing streak. Miami comes to Lucas Oil Stadium at 1-7.
We’ve got the Colts’ 28th-ranked defense in yards allowed against Miami’s 31st-ranked scoring offense. What a barn burner.
But forget the season outlook for a minute. The Colts should still win this football game, and there are a few things they absolutely have to do to make sure that happens.
The trade deadline has passed, the smoke has cleared, and Keenan Allen and Josh Downs are gone. Those two accounted for 70% of the Colts’ wide receiver receptions and 61% of their receiving yards before being traded Tuesday.
That leaves Daniel Jones throwing to a depleted receiver room, with Tyler Warren standing as the only proven option left.
Jonathan Taylor needs to look like Jonathan Taylor again. He has 656 rushing yards and eight touchdowns this season, but has totaled just 69 rushing yards over the last two games.
If Indianapolis is going to move the ball consistently, Taylor has to produce even when Miami knows the run is coming. I would expect the Dolphins to make Jones find someone other than Warren.
Defensively, this is where I want to see the young guys take another step.
Adetomiwa Adebawore had four pressures and three quarterback hits against Dallas, while Hunter Wohler finished with 16 tackles, Bryce Boettcher had 12 and CJ Allen added 10. Caden Curry and Jaylahn Tuimoloau each added a sack, as this defense is finally giving its young players opportunities to make an impact.
And there really isn’t a better chance to build on it.
Miami will start Kyle McCord after Malik Willis was placed on injured reserve with a groin injury. McCord has yet to throw a regular-season NFL pass, meaning the Colts will be facing a first-time starter at home.
That doesn’t guarantee anything with this defense, but the game plan should be pretty simple: stop the run, make McCord beat you, and don’t give away explosive plays.
This game screams low-scoring. Then again, both teams have shown enough offensive struggles and defensive breakdowns that a couple of mistakes could turn an ugly game into something much more chaotic.
This matchup should also serve as a reminder of the expectations surrounding this franchise. Eight or nine wins in Indianapolis usually has this fanbase calling for everyone's job, but even during a fire sale and a five-game losing streak, this is still a game Colts fans expect to win.
Losing at home to a 1-7 Dolphins team starting a quarterback making his first NFL start would be a new low.
Sunday should be about putting the trade deadline behind them, feeding Taylor, and seeing whether this young defense can finally start building something.
Michael Greene is a graduate of Indiana University and the Scouting Academy. He's in his first year covering the Indianapolis Colts and NFL, with a unique focus on fantasy football.

title: 3 Draft Receivers Who Fit the Bill for Colts After Josh Downs Trade
full_text:
It's fair to say the Indianapolis Colts' wide receiver position is incredibly underwhelming following the team trading away Josh Downs .
The Colts traded Keenan Allen too, but he wasn't expected to play beyond this season; Downs looked like a piece of Indy's future.
Add on that Alec Pierce is dealing with more injuries than expected, and suddenly the future at the position is in question.
With the team committing to rebuilding and losing Downs, a wide receiver is a must-draft in 2027.
It's never too early to talk about the draft, so with that in mind, here are three prospects to keep an eye on next April for the Colts to select as offensive weaponry for the future.
For quick reference, these wide receivers are projected Day 2 or 3 prospects since Indy has no first-round pick.
Why not start with a hometown hero like Indiana University's Nick Marsh?
Marsh and fellow dynamic pass-catcher, Charlie Becker, have formed one of the deadliest wide receiver duos in college football.
Marsh would factor in as an immediate starter for the Colts, and while he stands around 6'3" and weighs a robust 210 pounds, he is incredibly explosive and has grit as a blocker.
Through nine games this year, Marsh has put up 669 receiving yards on 38 catches and eight touchdowns. The most impressive stat for Marsh is his yards per reception, which stands at 17.6.
Indiana’s Nick Marsh is such a violent player. Violent blocker, violent after the catch, and violent with his route running. Marsh is top 20 nationally in yards per route run (3.23) pic.twitter.com/C0xYTMoo0X
Indianapolis needs another top wide receiver to pair with Pierce for the future, and Marsh not only embodies what you want at the position, but he's also a fantastic route-runner with blazing speed and the willingness to do the dirty work.
A versatile weapon as a slot operator is just what the doctor ordered for Indianapolis, and there may be no more explosive variation of that than Texas A&M's Mario Craver.
Craver can operate as both a quick-win receiver and a deep threat, and his career college numbers reflect that. Below are the catch totals by season.
Craver is lightning in a bottle; he can soak up catches inside while also being a danger to take it to the house anytime he touches the football.
Mario Craver had the entire defense in a BLENDER pic.twitter.com/ka0jZDpGiJ
Indianapolis can use a multi-role receiver like Craver, and while he'll factor more into the slot than anything else, he'll always keep a defense on its toes.
Cooper Barkate is a technician at the position, and he can serve as an ultra-reliable pass-catcher that Indy's next franchise QB can lean on.
Barkate started his college career at Harvard (2022-2024), but transferred to Duke in 2025 and immediately produced.
He played 14 games and hauled in 72 catches for 1,106 receiving yards and seven touchdowns.
Barkate would ultimately end up with the Miami Hurricanes for the 2026 campaign, operating in the offense with one of the most electrifying pass-catchers in Malachi Toney.
Barkate took on the role as the number two option in the passing game, but after Toney sustained a high ankle sprain in practice on November 4th, things changed.
Immediately, this thrust Barkate into the WR1 role against the Notre Dame Fighting Irish. Expectations were high, but not only did Barkate answer the call, he aced the test.
Barkate finished with nine catches for 75 receiving yards and a pair of critical touchdowns to keep the Hurricanes close. He'll likely be the top option in the Hurricanes' wide receiver room going forward.
Cooper Barkate refuses to let Miami go away. The Hurricanes WR scores his second TD of the night to make it 24-31 against Notre Dame. pic.twitter.com/Tz2yJMUhWk
Barkate is looking like a Day 3 pick, which Indianapolis has accumulated plenty of for the 2027 draft. That type of projection means the Colts shouldn't rely on Barkate to be a top pass-catcher, at least not right away.
Regardless, Barkate is a high-IQ and efficient receiver who can make plays when they matter most, secure catches consistently, and be a reliable weapon.

title: Every Pick Colts Added at Trade Deadline (and Who They Should Target in Draft)
full_text:
As 4 PM Eastern came and went Tuesday afternoon, the Indianapolis Colts' 2027 roster remained entirely intact. No player with a contract stretching beyond the maligned 2026 season was shipped off for draft capital of any kind.
Carlie Irsay-Gordon is seemingly wiping the slate entirely clean for whoever is chosen to shepherd in the next era of Colts football. The trade deadline was about ensuring that was the case while maximizing the value of players the next general manager would have no input on.
The remaining parts of the roster however, will be under the proverbial microscope.
Holding on to Jonathan Taylor guaranteed the Colts wouldn't be receiving a first-round pick (or, of course, an equivalent) to add to their armada of 2027 draft capital, but they are still well stocked with a projected 12 picks in the upcoming draft.
Where are these picks projected to land in April, and what players might a new regime look to target with them?
According to Tankathon , the Colts added the current 82nd pick in the third round, 123rd and 131st picks in the fourth round, the 162nd pick in the fifth round, and the 194th pick in the sixth round.  They also sent the 253rd pick to the Chiefs via Buffalo in the Josh Downs trade.
Despite not having a Round 1 Pick, the Colts are 8th in @tankathon ’s Draft Power Rankings for total pick value. Every team ahead of them has either a projected Top 10 pick &/or multiple Round 1 picks Next GM has a good war chest of picks & cap $ (5th most) to start the rebuild. https://t.co/GJov7a5cuD pic.twitter.com/rkFj6ovs6H
For the 2028 draft, they also added a fifth-round pick from the Seahawks in the Quenton Nelson trade.
Now, in all likelihood these picks will fall somewhere in the range of where they're currently listed; but the situation obviously remains fluid as the season progresses.
The Colts are in the unenviable position of already looking forward to the 2027 NFL Draft. Unfortunately, without a first-round pick, they won't be awarded the chance to take a blue-chip talent at the top of the draft. Still, with the influx of draft picks and projected compensatory picks , Indianapolis has given its future general manager plenty of ammo to maneuver around the draft board.
The wide receiver room is in quite a quandary following the trade of Josh Downs and Keenan Allen . Without a franchise quarterback on the roster or likely to come during the 2027 offseason, Indianapolis would be wise to begin looking to revamp the position group for a potential rookie entering the fold in 2028.
There’s a world where the Colts go sign a Yaya Diaby type and draft a fireballer or two off the edge with Day 2 picks. Then you’ve got a nice little stock of pass rushers that can win in a variety of ways. The defense could be pretty decent in ‘27 with new coaching/vision. https://t.co/oexHUDnrEU
Indianapolis will also enter the offseason with substantial cap space and a chance to give a facelift to a beleaguered defense. Coinciding with this movement, a new defensive play caller and identity on that side of the ball will need to be established.
The Colts have a relatively precocious linebacker room that could use a quality veteran to fortify and instill this new culture. For example, if the Colts were to hire Anthony Campanile, the current Jaguars defensive coordinator, as their next head coach, he could bring along breakout linebacker and upcoming free agent Ventrell Miller.
Whichever direction a new general manager takes, it'll be hard to criticize any approach with the litany of needs the Colts appear to have.
Frankly, it'd be an exercise in futility attempting to project who the Colts may take with any exact pick come April.
Luckily, I keep a cursory list of prospects I've enjoyed watching on tape for one reason or another. You won't see any Jeremiah Smith types, as I've attempted to be realistic given the current consensus on where these guys are expected to be drafted. Information can and will change drastically as the college season rolls on, eventually giving way to the NFL Scouting Combine and various All-Star games.
If you're like me, however, and enjoy the college scouting process, hopefully this list gives you a jumping-off point for your own research into potential future Colts.
The round range is my own projection of where the Colts could look to take that position. A star (*) indicates that the prospect is a personal favorite of mine.

title: Colts Trades Present Massive Opportunities at 3 Vital Positions
full_text:
The NFL trade deadline is officially in the rearview mirror, and the Indianapolis Colts were very busy, given that the franchise is at the beginning of a full rebuild.
The Colts traded off defensive tackle DeForest Buckner (San Francisco 49ers), guard Quenton Nelson (Seattle Seahawks), and wide receivers Josh Downs (Kansas City Chiefs) and Keenan Allen (49ers).
With four key players traded away, it drastically shakes up the defensive tackle, guard, and wide receiver rooms for the Colts for the rest of the 2026 season.
With that in mind, let's look at the pecking order for those three positions for Indianapolis and which players will need to step into the fray as the Colts try to make something out of their 2026 season.
The Colts traded Buckner to the 49ers for a 2027 fourth-round pick. Immediately, this took away one of the best defensive players Indianapolis has had over the last seven years.
However, the Colts felt better about this decision after Adetomiwa Adebawore emerged as a candidate to keep for their rebuild.
This led the Colts to extend Adebawore on a two-year, $35 million deal.
The Colts and DT Adetomiwa Adebawore agreed to terms on a two-year, $35 million extension that includes a $13M signing bonus and $22.5M in new money through 2027. Still only 25, Adebawore has a chance to get back to the market again as he enters his prime. The deal was… pic.twitter.com/D4TVQLVbvO
Through nine games, Adebawore leads the Colts with 4.0 sacks and is second in QB pressures (20) to defensive end Laiatu Latu (23). Adebawore will get eight more games in 2026 as Indy's top man in the defensive trenches.
As for Grover Stewart, he'll resume his position as the Colts' premier run-stuffer. Stewart wasn't traded at the deadline, but there was an offer in place that the Colts didn't execute.
Stewart's contract expires after this year, and it's hard to imagine Indianapolis will re-sign him in 2027, especially after trading Buckner.
Jerry Tillery, Tim Smith, and Kevin Givens will round out the room behind Adebawore and Stewart.
In a lost season where the Colts are gearing up for a refresh next year, it's mostly about Adebawore getting more experience as the undisputed top defensive tackle in the Circle City.
After playing eight illustrious seasons for the Colts, Nelson was traded to the Seattle Seahawks for a 2027 third-round pick and a 2028 fifth-round pick.
Trade! The Colts are sending eight-time Pro Bowl guard Quenton Nelson to the Seahawks for a 2027 third-round pick and a 2028 fifth-round pick, sources tell @ringer @netflixsports . pic.twitter.com/O1EN6vHWSF
Buckner was a big loss for the defense, but Nelson is a future Hall of Famer who was still playing at an elite level upon being traded. However, this gave Indy's 2026 fourth-rounder, Jalen Farmer, the green light to take over.
Offensive line coach Tony Sparano Jr. was one of Farmer's biggest fans during the draft process, and felt that the former Kentucky Wildcat enforcer was a special talent, and made that excitement well-known after he was selected.
It’s officially the Jalen Farmer era in Indianapolis. The #Colts have a new starting left guard for the first time in almost a decade. Lord knows OL Coach Tony Sparano Jr. is excited to get to work. https://t.co/3UctqjGZxD
Farmer hasn't played much this year as the starter, but as expected, he's struggled to fill Nelson's shoes.
Per Pro Football Focus, Farmer has grades of 39.4 overall, 45.7 run-blocking, and 26.8 pass-blocking. He's also allowed seven pressures and three quarterback hits through two games played.
Matt Goncalves remains the undisputed starter at right guard, while Dalton Tucker serves as the swing piece in the room.
The rest of the season is all about Farmer gaining valuable experience to become the left guard of Indy's future.
However, expect him to have big-time growing pains, as he's only 22 and is getting a crash course in what it's like to start in the NFL.
Indianapolis dealt away Downs and Allen, who were both the best wide receivers for the Colts after Alec Pierce was placed on Injured Reserve early in the year with a heel injury.
With Downs and Allen no longer on the roster, Indy's wide receiver corps is incredibly underwhelming, and just might be the worst in the NFL.
This isn't to pile on talents like Laquon Treadwell, Ashton Dulin, and Deion Burks, but when we consider Treadwell, Dulin, Burks, Nick Westbrook-Ikhine, and Anthony Gould have just 27 catches as a whole, it puts things into perspective.
However, this presents huge opportunities for the top three receivers.
Dulin has been mostly a special teams ace in Indianapolis, but now gets a shot to be possibly the top pass-catcher out of nowhere.
Treadwell can get more playing time as a starter than perhaps he's ever seen throughout his 11 years in the league.
Burks will immediately become the top deep threat for the Colts, and will also get work in the slot after the Downs trade.
This offense was already in deep trouble with Downs and Allen on the field, so things could get even more dicey for the passing game and quarterback Daniel Jones.
Regardless, while it gives Dulin and Treadwell the chance as starters, perhaps none of these players will benefit more from the thin wide receiver room than Burks.

title: Colts GM Vacancy Became More Attractive After Trade Deadline
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts ' general manager vacancy looked like a difficult proposition when Chris Ballard was relieved of his duties in October . The team was struggling, the roster was headed for a significant overhaul, and Indianapolis doesn't own its 2027 first-round draft pick.
However, the Colts' activity at the NFL trade deadline has changed the outlook considerably . Indianapolis parted ways with four established starters, accumulated additional draft capital, and created an opportunity for its next general manager to reshape the roster.
There is still plenty of work to be done, but the resources and flexibility now available could make Indianapolis a more appealing destination for potential candidates than it was just a few weeks ago.
One of the biggest selling points of the Indianapolis job is the collection of resources the next general manager will have at his disposal. Between additional draft selections and projected salary-cap flexibility, the Colts have several avenues to begin rebuilding their roster.
Indianapolis currently owns 10 selections in the 2027 NFL Draft, before compensatory picks have been awarded. OverTheCap projects the Colts to receive two more picks , a fith-rounder and sixth-rounder, though that's yet to be confirmed. Still, the prospect of having a dozen selections should be attractive.
Additionally, Indianapolis holds eight more picks in 2028 following its trades. The Colts acquired six total picks in those four transactions while surrendering one seventh-round selection to Kansas City in the Josh Downs deal .
While Indianapolis does not own a first-round pick in 2027 after including its selection in the trade for Sauce Gardner at last year's deadline, the volume of additional selections gives its next general manager plenty of opportunities to fill the roster with players that fit his or her style.
The Colts also have the flexibility to package selections to move up the board or pursue established players through the trade market. No shortage of options with it comes to utilizing draft capital.
There is also the financial component to consider.
Indianapolis is currently projected to have approximately $48 million in salary-cap space for the 2027 season, according to OverTheCap . That figure could change as the offseason approaches, but it gives the next general manager considerable financial flexibility to pursue free agents, retain key contributors and address the roster's most glaring deficiencies.
The quarterback situation could provide another opportunity to create financial flexibility. Daniel Jones currently carries a projected $46.8 million cap hit for 2027, making his future one of the most consequential financial decisions facing the organization. Jones has played nowhere close to the level the Colts paid him to play at, making a parting of ways the most likely outcome in the offseason.
Releasing Jones with a post-June 1st designation would clear up to $38 million in cap space, leaving $86 million in total for the next regime to use at their discretion.
The combination of additional draft capital and significant projected cap space gives the next general manager multiple ways to approach a rebuild. Rather than being restricted to the draft or free agency, Indianapolis can use both avenues to accelerate its roster reconstruction.
Perhaps just as important as the resources available to Indianapolis' next general manager is the freedom to determine what the roster should look like moving forward.
The Colts have already begun their locker room overhaul, but several significant decisions remain. The most notable involves Jonathan Taylor, who surprisingly remained in Indianapolis despite considerable trade interest leading up to the deadline.
Multiple teams reportedly offered a second-round pick or better for the three-time Pro Bowl running back, but Indianapolis ultimately held onto its franchise player. That decision now leaves Taylor's future in the hands of the next general manager.
There is a legitimate argument for keeping Taylor and building around one of the league's most productive running backs. However, there is also a case for moving him while his trade value remains high, particularly with Indianapolis entering a rebuilding period that could extend beyond the remainder of his prime.
Either way, the next general manager will have the freedom to decide what to do with Taylor. He can evaluate his value to the organization, determine whether his timeline aligns with the team's plans and decide whether another trade attempt makes sense.
The same flexibility exists at quarterback.
Jones remains in Indianapolis after the trade deadline, but his long-term future is far from settled. The Colts can evaluate whether he is the right quarterback to lead the next iteration of the franchise or whether it makes more sense to pursue another option through the draft or free agency.
There is also the possibility of giving Anthony Richardson another opportunity, depending on how the new leadership evaluates his future with the organization.
Beyond those two positions, the next general manager will have considerable freedom to determine which remaining veterans fit the team's long-term plans and which young players deserve further opportunities to establish themselves.
That level of autonomy is an important selling point for any potential candidate.
All that said, Indianapolis is certainly not an easy job. The roster has significant deficiencies, the team is coming off a disappointing season and the next general manager will have their work cut out for them to turn the franchise around.
However, the Colts have positioned themselves to offer something that isn't always available to incoming front-office executives: the resources and freedom to build an organization in their own image.

title: Colts Biggest Winners and Losers From 2026 NFL Trade Deadline
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts underwent a significant roster overhaul during the NFL trade deadline, parting ways with four prominent contributors in an effort to accumulate draft capital and reshape the franchise's future.
After trading away defensive tackle DeForest Buckner and left guard Quenton Nelson earlier in the season, Indianapolis dealt wide receivers Keenan Allen and Josh Downs on Tuesday.
The four moves leave considerable holes on both sides of the football, but they also create opportunities for several players who remain in Indianapolis.
Some players stand to benefit from expanded roles and increased responsibilities, while others are left with considerably less support as the Colts attempt to navigate the remainder of a disappointing season.
Here are the biggest winners and losers from Indianapolis' trade deadline activity.
The Colts' decision to trade both Keenan Allen and Josh Downs leaves a wide receiver room devoid of established playmakers, creating an opportunity for Ashton Dulin and Deion Burks to see more involvement in the offense.
Dulin is the more experienced option of the two, having been in Indianapolis since 2019. He's mostly been a special teams asset, but has stepped into a larger offensive role as they years have gone by.
Meanwhile, Burks is the more interesting of the two. He has an opportunity to establish himself as a more consistent contributor and show what he can offer moving forward. The seventh-round pick hasn't seen too many opportunities thus far, logging just nine touches so far, but will have a chance to prove he can be in the mix for the slot receiver job moving forward.
With Indianapolis already looking toward the future, their performances over the remainder of the season could help determine where they fit into the team's plans.
DeForest Buckner's departure created a significant opportunity along the interior defensive line, and few players stand to benefit more than Adetomiwa Adebawore.
Adebawore has already emerged as one of Indianapolis' most promising defensive players, earning a two-year, $35 million contract extension after establishing himself as a legitimate disruptive presence up front.
Now, with Buckner no longer in the picture, an even greater responsibility falls on the young defensive tackle.
Adebawore's first game since signing his new deal demonstrated he can handle that burden. The 25-year-old didn't record a sack, but showcased a multitude of effective pass rush moves and helped influence the pocket numerous times, resulting in teammates finishing the play.
The Colts will need Adebawore to become a centerpiece of their defensive front, particularly as they begin transitioning toward a younger roster. His development was already an encouraging storyline before the deadline, but Buckner's departure gives him an opportunity to take another significant step forward.
Quenton Nelson's departure leaves enormous shoes to fill along the offensive line, but it also opens the door for rookie guard Jalen Farmer to establish himself as a long-term starter.
Farmer has already stepped into Nelson's vacated spot, with a mixed bag of results through two games. Still, moving on from Nelson makes the remainder of the season an important evaluation period for the fourth-round selection.
Replacing a player of Nelson's caliber is an enormous challenge, but the opportunity to gain valuable starting experience should benefit Farmer's development.
With Indianapolis entering a period of transition, the organization needs to identify which young players can become foundational pieces moving forward. Farmer now has an opportunity to make a strong case for himself as part of the team's next iteration along the offensive line.
Grover Stewart's inclusion here is a little different from the other winners, considering his contract expires at the end of the season. His status as a winner hinges significantly on whether or not he signs an extension to be a part of the rebuilding process.
The veteran defensive tackle had been mentioned as a potential trade candidate, and the Colts had offers on the table. However, Indianapolis ultimately elected to keep him, leaving Stewart as one of the most experienced players remaining along the defensive front.
With Buckner gone, Stewart's importance to the defensive line becomes even greater. His ability to provide stability against the run and serve as a veteran presence alongside younger players should be valuable as the Colts navigate the remainder of the season.
Whether Stewart ultimately factors into Indianapolis' longer-term plans remains uncertain, particularly with his contract situation, but he should have an important role to play in the immediate future.
While Daniel Jones remains the Colts' starting quarterback, the circumstances surrounding him have become considerably less favorable.
Indianapolis traded away two of its most productive receivers while also sending away its All-Pro left guard. That's a substantial amount of offensive talent to lose, particularly for a quarterback who has already struggled to find consistency throughout the season.
The Colts haven't exactly surrounded Jones with an abundance of established weapons following those departures, leaving him with fewer reliable options as the offense attempts to finish the season strong. For a quarterback who's best seasons came when he had an adequate supporting cast, the deadline trades greatly hurt his ability to lead an offensive revival down the stretch.
Jones now faces the challenge of producing with a significantly diminished supporting cast while the organization evaluates its direction at quarterback.
Jonathan Taylor might be the biggest loser of the Colts' trade deadline .
For weeks, Taylor was at the center of trade rumors as Indianapolis explored its options ahead of the deadline. Multiple contenders expressed interest in acquiring the three-time Pro Bowl running back, and the Colts reportedly received multiple offers involving second-round draft capital and more.
Despite the interest, Indianapolis ultimately decided against moving him, holding out for a blockbuster return that never materialized.
That decision leaves Taylor in a difficult position. The Colts have made it abundantly clear that they're transitioning toward a rebuild. But Taylor is entering the latter portion of his 20s and remains one of the most productive running backs in football.
There's a legitimate concern that Indianapolis won't be ready to compete for a championship again until Taylor is past his prime. Barring a future trade request or a dramatic turnaround in the team's trajectory, he could spend at least the next two seasons wasting away on a team in transition.
It's difficult to blame Taylor for wanting to remain in Indianapolis, particularly after signing a contract extension in the offseason and repeatedly stating his loyalty to the organization. But the Colts' decision to retain him despite multiple trade offers leaves one of their best players tied to a rebuilding franchise.
Running back's primes are limited, and it's possible Taylor doesn't get anything substantial out of his.
Perhaps nobody was dealt a more difficult hand at the trade deadline than head coach Shane Steichen.
The Colts have traded away four prominent starters, including two foundational offensive players, while also removing a significant talent from their defensive front. The result is a considerably less experienced roster with multiple holes that need to be addressed.
Steichen, already facing an uphill battle to save his job, now faces the challenge of keeping Indianapolis competitive while evaluating younger players and attempting to get the most out of a diminished roster. That's not exactly a formula that will help Steichen stay on as head coach.
With Chris Ballard already dismissed and Indianapolis preparing for a new general manager, Steichen must demonstrate that he's the right person to lead the franchise moving forward.
