title: Grading Colts' NFL Trade Deadline: Fire Sale Provides Solid Start to Rebuild
full_text:
The NFL trade deadline has officially passed, and the Indianapolis Colts made it clear what direction this franchise is heading.
At 2-7 and riding a five-game losing streak, the Colts have spent the last two weeks turning expiring contracts into draft capital while refusing to sell off everyone on the roster.
So, did Indianapolis get enough value? Let’s grade every move.
This is still the one I have the biggest problem with.
Nelson is one of the best guards of this generation, and getting only a 2027 third-round pick and 2028 fifth-rounder feels light. That being said, he was on an expiring contract, and paying him another massive deal at 30 years old probably did not fit where this rebuild is heading.
Not only did he not quite fit into the rebuild's outlook, but Nelson did manage to net the most draft capital for a guard in recent memory. According to Spotrac, via Alex Katson, Nelson is the only traded guard since 2011 to net a third-round draft selection .
I still would have wanted an earlier pick. The difference between what Indianapolis got for Big Q and what other teams have received for All-Pro talent is pretty staggering.
I don’t mind this one nearly as much.
Buckner is 32, was on an expiring deal, and likely would not be the same player by the time Indianapolis is ready to seriously compete again. Getting a 2027 fourth-round pick while sending him back to a contender makes sense.
Allen was on a one-year deal, and Indianapolis turned a 34-year-old receiver into a 2027 sixth-round pick. San Francisco needed receiver help, and the Colts took advantage.
This changed right before the deadline.
Downs requested a trade after the Nelson and Buckner moves, and Indianapolis sent him plus a 2027 seventh-rounder to Kansas City for 2027 fourth- and fifth-round picks.
Considering Downs' poor performances over the last few weeks, I'm surprised the Colts got as much as they did.
For an expiring-contract player who wanted out, that is solid value.
I applaud this front office for not getting taken advantage of here.
Multiple teams were reportedly willing to offer a second-round pick and more, but Taylor is under contract through 2028 and did not request a trade. If nobody wanted to overpay for one of the league’s marquee running backs, keep him.
I’m glad to see No. 28 stay.
Jones has not played well, and Indianapolis reportedly told him before the deadline that he would not be moved. I still believe Jones can look serviceable when the pieces around him are right, but this team has failed to give him that consistency this season.
Adebawore has emerged as one of Indianapolis’ premier young defenders, and locking him up through 2028 gives this rebuild a legitimate piece to build around. He entered Week 9 leading NFL defensive tackles in both pressure rate and pass-rush win rate.
This front office did a solid job turning expiring contracts into picks without getting desperate on Taylor.
I still would have rather kept Big Q, but considering the situation Dodds inherited, I think Indianapolis made the best of a difficult situation.
Michael Greene is a graduate of Indiana University and the Scouting Academy. He's in his first year covering the Indianapolis Colts and NFL, with a unique focus on fantasy football.

title: Instant Grade: Understanding Colts' Decision to Keep Jonathan Taylor
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts were at the epicenter of the 2026 NFL Trade Deadline after they kicked off an early rebuild by firing longtime general manager Chris Ballard .
The Colts subsequently traded franchise pillars LG Quenton Nelson and DT DeForest Buckner for draft capital, which led to a fire sale watch of sorts manned by interim general manager Ed Dodds.
From players on expiring deals to those with multiple years left on their contract, the Colts' roster featured no untouchables, though running back Jonathan Taylor was treated as the next best thing.
After weeks of rampant rumors surrounding the star running back, the Indianapolis Colts have decided to hold onto their star running back as they enter a new era.
Taylor is still one of the league's best running backs and is undeniably the Colts' best remaining player, but was this the right move? Follow along as I break down the decision in question.
The Indianapolis Colts remained steadfast in their pursuit of a Christian McCaffrey-esque return , one that included three current draft picks (2nd, 3rd, and 4th) as well as a future fifth-round pick, for Jonathan Taylor, but the return simply never came calling.
The New York Giants were reportedly the biggest contenders of the sweepstakes in question, as their offer of a 2027 second-round pick, a fifth-round pick, and an unnamed player was turned down, but the Colts stayed firm in their belief in Taylor.
But it wasn't just the Giants who came calling and/or offered similar compensation. Outside of the Giants, the reported interested teams were the Green Bay Packers, Denver Broncos, Minnesota Vikings, Seattle Seahawks, and Cincinnati Bengals.
Furthermore, the Colts had received multiple offers of a second-round pick and more for Taylor over the last week, according to NFL Insider Jordan Schultz .
"But the [Colts] decided that if they ever trade him, it will be in the offseason, when more buyers could be available and a permanent general manager is in place," Schultz reported.
The Colts set a price on a player they valued highly, and when the demand wasn't met, they decided to table talks until at least the offseason.
Will Indianapolis be better off for it? There's certainly an avenue that suggests they make the correct decision, especially considering how quick turnarounds happen in the NFL, but the Colts are embarking upon a massive rebuild, one that likely won't find its footing in time for Taylor's services to matter.
Nothing will change in terms of personnel at the position, but the Colts' immediate outlook at offense looks bleaker than it ever has since Jonathan Taylor joined the team in 2020.
The Colts still have Taylor to lean on for the rest of the 2026 regular season, but considering they've since traded away their best player and blocker across the offensive line, as well as their second and third-best options at wide receiver, and are continuing to roll with Daniel Jones at quarterback, it's hard to imagine a world where Taylor finds sustainable success.
Indianapolis will continue rolling with a two-man backfield of Jonathan Taylor and rookie Seth McGowan for the rest of the year, so even though risking Taylor's health in a lost season is a big chance to take, at least the rookie won't be baptized by fire down the stretch.
Carlie Irsay-Gordon has shown a rather strong process in her first full season as the Indianapolis Colts' principal owner and CEO.
Irsay-Gordon pulled the plug on the past era mere months after she decided to run it back once more with general manager Chris Ballard and head coach Shane Steichen, and this seemingly abrupt move to rip the band-aid off was no easy decision.
Since they lost to the winless Tennessee Titans in Week 5, the Colts have fired Chris Ballard, extended their most promising up-and-coming player (Adetomiwa Adebawore), and have traded four players on expiring deals.
In one month, Irsay-Gordon and Co. have set up the Colts' rebuild via a sound process.
However, the Colts' decision to keep Jonathan Taylor around for the foreseeable future is a questionable one.
On one hand, the Colts were open to trading Taylor. Their decision to ultimately keep Taylor wasn't a case of delusional belief in a player, but rather a strategic attempt to net top-tier compensation while also leaving the door open for the next general manager if demands weren't met.
The issue with this notion is that the Colts are entering a legitimate rebuild that will likely require multiple years to iron out. Not only that, but the Colts are also risking Taylor's health as they prepare to let their new general manager make his/her first big decision.
Taylor would not only have to stay healthy to justify this decision, but he'd also have to perform like the top-tier running back that he is down the stretch to increase, or even maintain, his current trade value.
Given that the aforementioned current-look Colts offense is devoid of talent everywhere else, coupled with the fact that Indianapolis' season is lost, it's difficult to imagine a reality where Taylor can produce to the level we know he's capable of.
Running backs have a shelf life that typically comes calling around ages 27-28, and given that's the range Taylor is in, on top of him playing in arguably the league's worst offense, a regression feels inevitable.
Taylor's recent extension from earlier this offseason puts him under contract through the 2028 season, and since the Colts have already paid him his signing bonus, Taylor's cap hits for the next two seasons are very reasonable.
Providing the next brass with the option to keep Taylor makes the job more attractive on the surface, as they can either roll with a Top 5 running back in the NFL or move him for draft capital.
However, if the next regime decides that an aging running back is a building block of the future, then we already know how the next era will go. Perhaps this will serve as a day-one test for the next general manager, but it still feels like a missed opportunity to start anew.
Jonathan Taylor is still elite, but he hasn't been playing like it in recent weeks, and that was in an offense that has since been depleted even more.
Overall, Irsay-Gordon and Co. have done a good job kicking off the Colts' rebuild in question. Only time will tell if their belief in Taylor will end up hurting them.
Noah Compton is the Publisher of Indianapolis Colts On SI. Noah is from the Indy area and has been covering the Colts since 2022, including stops at FanSided, The Blue Stable, and SBNation.

title: Instant Grades: Colts Get Strong Return From Josh Downs Trade
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts have officially moved on from Josh Downs, sending the 25-year-old wide receiver to the Kansas City Chiefs in exchange for a pair of 2027 draft picks.
Indianapolis will receive a fourth-round pick and a fifth-round pick, sending Downs and a seventh-round pick back to Kansas City.
Trade terms: 4 and 5 for Downs and a 7, per source. https://t.co/vC2Yc7mzlE
It's a strong return for a player who had requested a trade, was approaching the end of his rookie contract, and clearly wanted out of Indianapolis. More importantly, the Colts managed to improve upon the compensation that had initially been circulating around the league.
Here's an instant look at the deal and what it means for Indianapolis moving forward.
The Colts initially placed a third-round valuation on Downs, but reports throughout the past few weeks suggested that interested teams were willing to give up a fourth-round pick at a maximum. Reports indicated that the Colts had a fourth-round pick offer on the table from the Chiefs a week ago.
But rather than immediately accepting that proposal, Indianapolis allowed the market to develop and ultimately secured an additional fifth-round selection, sending a seventh-rounder back for Kansas City to take on Downs' remaining contract.
Downs was unlikely to sign an extension with the Colts in the offseason, so turning him into usable assets for the future was a necessary move to make.
Downs was selected in the third round of the 2023 NFL Draft and established himself as a productive slot receiver during his first few seasons. He recorded 72 receptions for 803 yards and five touchdowns in 2024, demonstrating the ability to become a reliable underneath option in the Colts' passing attack.
However, his production has declined since then. Downs finished his Indianapolis tenure with 33 receptions for 354 yards and one touchdown through nine games in 2026.
There were also growing concerns about Downs' commitment to a struggling team. Since requesting a trade, Downs appeared increasingly apathetic towards the situation in Indianapolis, making a separation the only logical course of action for both sides.
The Colts ultimately turned a disgruntled receiver in the final year of his rookie contract into two draft selections. Getting an additional Day 3 pick on top of the reported fourth-round market is a win for Dodds and the Indianapolis front office.
The only real downside is what Indianapolis is left with at wide receiver. After moving on from Downs and Keenan Allen on deadline day , the Colts have likely the ugliest receiving corps in the NFL. Alec Pierce remains the most established option, but he's been on injured reserve for the majority of the season. After him, there's no remaining proven talent.
Still, that's a relatively minor concern given the direction of the organization. Indianapolis has bigger priorities than maintaining a competitive receiving room for the remainder of a lost season, and the draft capital acquired in these transactions gives the franchise additional resources to address those needs.

Alec Pierce remains the most established option, but he's been on injured reserve for the majority of the season. After him, there's no remaining proven talent.
Still, that's a relatively minor concern given the direction of the organization. Indianapolis has bigger priorities than maintaining a competitive receiving room for the remainder of a lost season, and the draft capital acquired in these transactions gives the franchise additional resources to address those needs.
The Colts couldn't have asked for a much better outcome given the circumstances surrounding Downs' departure.
They secured two draft picks for a receiver who was in the final year of his rookie contract, had requested a trade and had struggled to produce consistently during a difficult season. Indianapolis also appears to have benefited from allowing the trade market to develop rather than settling for the initial fourth-round price tag.
The return is strong, the timing makes sense and the organization can now move forward without another lingering distraction. I'm docking a letter grade solely due to the messy state of the current WR room, but again, that's nothing to stress about in the bigger picture.
In the end, the Colts turned a difficult situation into a productive transaction---exactly what they needed to do at the deadline.

title: Indianapolis Colts Fire Sale Tracker: Analysis, Trades, Rumors, and More
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts will be the center of the NFL world for the foreseeable future.
This is the second consecutive season that Indianapolis will be featured in trade talks at the midway point, but unlike last year, it's not because they're the number one seed in the AFC.
Instead of buying at the deadline, the Colts will be selling.
The 2026 NFL Trade Deadline (November 10th, 4 PM EST) is quickly approaching, and the Colts are amidst a complete teardown of their franchise.
The Colts fired longtime general manager Chris Ballard after they fell to 2-4 in a humiliating loss, and have been active in the trade market ever since as they look to recoup any valuable draft capital they can after Ballard traded away their 2027 first-round pick, as well as their 2026 first-rounder and WR Adonai Mitchell.
It was the beginning of a poetic end, as the last Ballard-led Colts game was a loss to the 0-5 Tennessee Titans, a team that many still consider the worst team in the NFL. Even then, this version of the Colts may very well be the league's worst.
On top of only one playoff win in three appearances, the Colts failed to win the lowly AFC South across 9.5 seasons (2017-2026) under Chris Ballard.
Despite ample evidence to suggest otherwise, Indianapolis Colts' Owner/CEO Carlie Irsay-Gordon decided to bring back both Chris Ballard and head coach Shane Steichen for the 2026 season, referencing their hot start to the previous year as a reason to give them another chance.
The former had been given far too many chances to that point, but to be fair to Irsay-Gordon and her sisters, Co-Owners Kalen Jackson and Casey Foyt, this was the organization's first full offseason under new ownership.
Following the decision to give Ballard and Steichen one last shot in her postseason press conference, Irsay-Gordon said that the "sense of urgency has never been higher" for the GM/HC tandem.
Many didn't believe her, given that she was entering her first full offseason as an NFL Owner/CEO and appeared to be betting on an inevitable collapse, but Irsay-Gordon did what needed to be done, even if it came a bit too late.
In the past 14 days, the Indianapolis Colts have fired longtime general manager Chris Ballard, fallen to 2-6 on the season, and traded away two of their franchise cornerstones.
This article is meant to serve as a one-stop shop for all things Indianapolis Colts-related ahead of the NFL Trade Deadline. I will be updating this story as new information presents itself, so be sure to regularly check back in.
Navigate our trade central (finalized trades, rumors, etc.), future outlook, and more below.
Outside of players still on their rookie contract, as well as some exceptions such as cornerback Sauce Gardner, wide receiver Alec Pierce, left tackle Bernhard Raimann, and a few others, nobody on the Colts roster is safe.
Although the 2026 NFL Trade Deadline is on November 10th at 4 PM EST, the Colts have already gotten a head start on their fire sale.
In order, our trade central will featured finalized trades, a rumor mill, and will conclude with analysis on the team's overall outlook.
A current third-round pick and a future fifth-rounder may seem scoff-worthy at first glance, but when you break down the history of traded compensation for other guards across the league, Nelson's haul starts to make more sense.
Indianapolis' return of a 3rd and a 5th for Quenton Nelson is the most pure draft capital for a guard since at least 2011, per Spotrac. only 4 have netted a 4th: 2013: G. Carimi, 4th 2014: L. Mankins, 4th + player 2021: B. Bredeson + 5th + 7th, 4th 2025: J. Thuney, 4th
I think this is both the best example of why the return for Quenton Nelson isn’t as irresponsible as some are suggesting, and also why the Chris Ballard era needed to end: non-premium positions.
It stings to see any team trade their homegrown future Hall of Famer, but this is the bed the Colts made, and now they must sleep in it.
The Colts' 2026 fourth-round rookie guard Jalen Farmer is Nelson's immediate replacement.
Buckner's departure creates a similar challenge on the defensive line. More responsibility will fall on the remaining interior defenders, including Stewart and Adetomiwa Adebawore.
Not only is the opportunity there, but Adebawore has earned the increased role in question.
After seven weeks, Adebawore is undeniably the Colts' best pass rusher. He is currently tied for second with the most sacks among interior defensive linemen league-wide and leads the team in most major pass-rush statistics.
We've known that Adebawore has some nasty pass-rushing chops, but the biggest development has been his improvement in run defense.
Adebawore has blossomed into a legitimate starting defensive tackle, and it comes at no better time as the Colts have parted ways with their longtime pillar across the defensive line.
However, the Colts' newfound star is on an expiring deal. Adebawore is playing in the final year of his rookie contract, so a big payday is set to come his way.
Update (11/3) : The Indianapolis Colts have signed Adetomiwa Adebawore to a two-year, $35 million contract extension that includes a $13 million signing bonus and $22.5 in new money through 2027.
The Colts had seemingly found their third starting wide receiver for the 2026 regular season after they signed veteran free agent Keenan Allen to a one-year deal late in training camp.
Allen has been productive for the Colts, as his 40 receptions lead the team, and his 351 receiving yards are second only to Josh Downs, another Indianapolis wideout who is likely to be traded ahead of the deadline. He was only meant to serve in a secondary role alongside Alec Pierce and Josh Downs, but the former's aggravated injury forced the 34-year-old veteran into a serious role.
Allen sits at 27th all-time in receiving yards (12,402) and 8th all-time in receptions (1,095) as he moves back out West to the contending 49ers.
The Indianapolis Colts managed to get fantastic value for a wide receiver who is on an expiring deal, has been checked out as of late, and plays a hyper-specific role. Indianapolis had reportedly been looking for a third-round pick in return, but netting two early Day 3 (rounds 4-7) is still a massive win.
After weeks of nonstop rumors, the Colts have decided to keep their most productive player from the Chris Ballard era as they enter their rebuild. An offer of a second-round pick plus additional compensation was not enough to get done, though it probably should have been.
Taylor will be 28 years old and will have two years left on his contract when the Colts enter a new era, and given that their offensive outlook looks even bleaker than it has, it's hard to imagine a world where he can improve the Colts' floor.
The Colts are willing to revisit trade talks for Taylor once the next general manager is in the building, though I doubt they're able to warrant better, if not similar, compensation than they could have at the deadline. I figured the failed Ballard era would have resulted in the Colts going in a new direction as far as roster construction goes, but time will tell if they've made the correct decision.
Update (11/5) : NFL Insider Jordan Schultz : "The belief around the league is that, barring an offer that blows them away, Indianapolis plans to wait until after Sunday’s game vs the Cowboys before revisiting the offers on the table and making the trades that make sense on Monday and Tuesday ahead of the deadline.
ESPN's NFL Insider Adam Schefter confirmed on Halloween that the Indianapolis Colts are officially open to trading Jonathan Taylor and have been active in talks.
Schefter added that the Colts have already received an offer of a 2027 second-round pick along with additional compensation for Taylor's services.

title: Jaguars-Titans Injury Report: Jordan Davis, Jessie Bates Debuts Come With a Question
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars will be ready for their newest faces on defense to hit the ground running once they are settled in ... but will they be ready in Week 10?
The Jaguars' second injury report of Week 10 had new faces Jordan Davis and Jessie Bates as non-participants in practice for the second day in a row, with each player getting back-to-back rest days after the explosive trades that brought them to Jacksonville.
Davis and Bates each spoken to the media this week, with Davis saying "I'm here to do whatever the coaches need me to do," when asked about playing on Sunday against the Tennessee Titans. Bates said he still has to "knock off the plane ride from Spain," after playing there in Week 9 for the Atlanta Falcons, though he also said "I'm ready for sure."
It is worth noting that neither Davis or Bates have had bye weeks to this point, while the Jaguars have already had their bye week in Week 7. If Bates and Davis were to play every game for the Jaguars the rest of the way, each will have played 18 games in the regular-season, which doesn't even account for the likely playoff games that will come later.
There is also the adjustment period in general. Each Davis and Bates are getting crash courses in defensive coordinator Anthony Campanile's scheme, and both will have to be ready to execute at a high level if they are called upon this Sunday.
"I always feel like this, whenever you get a new guy in it’s more just getting the verbiage and everything down. Because that’s really what slows everything down for you," Campanile said on Thursday.
"Once you've got the verbiage and you understand what everything means, I think in every building there are probably a lot of similarities. Things that everybody does, they've all done before, but it's just translating it, and how fast you can get that across to the players and they feel comfortable with it. They can just line up and go play. If you're going out there and you're thinking, it’s super hard to have all your skills, so we're working on getting them to that point right now.”
There does not appear to be as much mystery with fellow new Jaguars defender Davon Godchaux, who the Jaguars acquired from the New Orleans Saints for a conditional future sixth-round pick. Godchaux has practiced for the Jaguars in back-to-back days, which could indicate he makes his debut sooner than Davis and Bates do.
Meanwhile, the Jaguars did have one player who did not participate due to injury: running back Bhayshul Tuten, who has not practiced since sustaining an ankle/foot injury in Week 8 against the Indianapolis Colts.
Tuten ended up playing against the Baltimore Ravens on a short week last week despite not practicing, rushing 12 times for 29 yards and a touchdown while playing a season-low 35.7% of the offensive snaps.
"I think first and foremost, it speaks to his toughness to be able to go out there and do that on a short week. It's tough enough as it is to go out and play on that short week," Jaguars offensive coordinator Grant Udinski said on Thursday.
"It's such a quick turnaround for those guys no matter what position you're at, but he's been carrying the load for us and to turn around and do that is super impressive and it's a credit to him and his values that he places on the team. Kind of a selfless act to be out there and try to give it his best when he might not be 100%.

title: How the NFL Trade Deadline Changed the Jaguars' Defensive Depth Chart
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars defense has a few new faces after the trade deadline, and they should be expected to play roles very, very quickly.
Few people in Jacksonville should be as excited about the Jaguars' massive new pieces as new defensive cooridnator Anthony Campanile ... for obvious reasons.
“Obviously really fired up about it. Any time you get three great players and three great people in the building… So, I couldn’t be more excited about it," Campanile said on Thursday.
"The team itself I think feels the exact same way. They’ve kind of hit the ground running, our three new guys, three new teammates. They’re working really hard, working tirelessly; I can say that. They’ve been in here putting in hours trying to get acclimated and they’ve been everything everyone said they were in terms of the types of guys they are.”
So, what does the Jaguars' defensive depth chart look like now after adding multiple starters? We break it down below.
Starters: Josh Hines-Allen, Travon Walker
Backups: Danny Striggow-Bryan Thomas Jr.-BJ Green II-Wesley Williams
The Jaguars added to quite a few spots over the course of the trade deadline, but the defensive end spot is one that there is no new face. Travon Walker and Josh Hines-Allen are still set to lead the defensive end room, while the Jaguars are set to get BJ Green back from injured reserve sooner than later after they opened his practice window earlier this week. This was a big area of focus ahead of the trade deadline, but the Jaguars are what they are at the spot.
It is clear that Danny Striggow is the No. 3 EDGE and that rookie Wesley Williams is set to contiue to be a healthy scratch. If Green is able to hit the ground running after his injury, then he should be taking a leap over Thomas on the depth chart over the next few weeks. Other than that, this depth chart is as is.
Starters: Arik Armstead, Jordan Davis
Backups: Davon Godchaux-Matt Dickerson-Ruke Orhorhoro-Albert Regis
This is the big change. The Jaguars added two big pieces to the defensive line with Jordan Davis and Davon Godchaux, and they should be expected to play massive roles from the jump. Davis should be able to step right into the Jaguars' nose tackle role after Davon Hamilton's injury, and the Jaguars have a lot of confidence in his ability to contribute as a pass-rusher and not just a run-stuffer.
Behind Davis and Armstead, the Jaguars have some good depth. Godchaux can give them strong snaps as a rotational nose tackle, Matt Dickerson can give them a boost as a nose tackle and three-technique on run downs, while Ruke Orhorhoro is potentially their second-best interior pass-rusher. This is a much, much-improved group.
Starters: Foyesade Oluokun, Ventrell Miller, Dennis Gardeck
Backups: Branson Combs-Jahlani Tavai-Jalen McLeod
The Jaguars are ho-hum at the linebacker room. Ventrell Miller and Foyesade Oluokun  are one of the best linebacker duos in the NFL in terms of pure production. Jacksonville has played the linebacker position perfectly in terms of adding to the room over the years, and the decision to make Ventrell Miller the starter and letting Devin Lloyd walk in free agency.
Starters: Travis Hunter, Montaric Brown, Jourdan Lewis
Backups: Jarrian Jones-Jaylon Jones
The Jaguars are set to have their same cornerback room after the trade deadline, but the entire secondary should be impacted by the Jessie Bates move. I think it is also clear that Jarrian Jones is closer to being a starter than he is a true backup, but there are still only so many players who can be listed as starters. With the Jaguars moves, though, this is a strong room from No. 1 to No. 4.
Starters: Jessie Bates III, Antonio Johnson
Backups: Rayuan Lane-Kaevon Merriweather-Jalen Huskey
This is where some real change has happened. The Jaguars did not trade a second- and fifth-round pick to Atlanta for Bates to not be a starter the second he has been caught up to speed. The more interesting question is what happens on the other spots of the depth chart at safety behind Bates and fellow starter Antonio Johnson. The Jaguars saw Rayuan Lane step in as their No. 2 safety after Eric Murray's injury, so he figures to be the most likely option at the No. 3 spot.
The Jaguars have also used Kaevon Merriweather as a top backup at safety, but he looks like he will most likely be a special teamer moving forward. As for rookie Jalen Huskey, he has been a healthy scratch for most of the season and that will likely be where he is at for game day moving forward throughout the rest of the season.

title: 3 Biggest Questions Facing the Jaguars After Trade Deadline Fallout: Is the Pass-Rush Enough?
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars got better over the trade deadline. In their estimation, they got a lot better.
But even after the Jaguars added some big pieces in the form of Jordan Davis, Jessie Bates III, and Davon Godchaux, there are still questions facing the team as they make their playoff run down the stretch of 2026.
So, what are the biggest questions facing the Jaguars after James Gladstone's trade deadline fireworks? We break it down below.
The Jaguars had three big needs entering the trade deadline : adding help at defensive tackle, safety, and defensive end. The Jaguars certainly checked two of those boxes, with the additions of Davis, Godchaux and Bates expected to make a significant impact right out of the gate. But while the Jaguars did improve their run defense and play-making ability in the secondary, the Jaguars made no moves at defensive end, aside from opening the practice window for second-year defensive end BJ Green off injured reserve.
Jacksonville could see more of a pass-rush upside in Davis than he saw in Philadelphia, where he recorded 9.5 sacks in over 70 games. Davis played in a similar scheme with the Eagles than he will with the Jaguars, so this seems like more of a bet in traits than past production. The Jaguars have been able to generate pressure at a consistent rate all year without a true interior pass-rusher, largely due to their pressure packages and extra blitzers, but there could be a question as to whether the Jaguars' four-man pass-rush is good enough once January comes around.
The Jaguars reportedly were interested in Jets pass-rusher Will McDonald IV, which could imply that they are aware of this need as well. Despite not a ton of sack production over two years, though, the Jaguars have still had a top-rated defense and have won far more often than they have lost. Perhaps that continues now.
The addition of Bates to the back end of the Jaguars' defense will obviously have a lasting impact on the room, with the future looking murky in terms of Eric Murray returning next season. Caleb Ransaw and Jalen Huskey are third-round picks who have not played all that much, which means the future of the safety room right now has to center around Bates and Antonio Johnson. The issue, of course, is that both safeties are in contract years, and the Jaguars now may have to determine which one they bring back.
Perhaps the Jaguars are able to keep both safeties, but you do not see teams drop big deals for multiple safeties in one offseason all that often. The Jaguars could also let one walk and hope to get a compensatory pick back in return after free-agency and then hope that Ransaw, Huskey, or Rayuan Lane are ready to step into the second safety spot.
It is a tough question to weigh. The Jaguars gave up a big trade package to land Bates, who is a ready-made All-Pro safety and is one of the best in the NFL. Letting him walk would seem misguided. On the other hand, Johnson is one of the best young players on one of the NFL's oldest defenses, and he has developed each year under this regime. This could be a tough balance.
The Jaguars opted not to trade Brian Thomas Jr. at the trade deadline, which makes sense considering the Jaguars are in a position to add talent to the roster, not take it away. But the onus is now on the Jaguars to prove that they made the right decision to not use Thomas and his decreasing role on offense as a way to recoup some of the draft picks they dealt over the trade deadline period. Thomas is a real-deal talent, but the Jaguars took a risk by opting to keep him for the rest of the 2026 season.
When it comes to that risk, the Jaguars are also largely the ones who can make it pay off or not. Thomas will have to be at his best when the ball comes his way, which has not always been the case over the last two seasons, but the Jaguars also have to give him chances to make an impact. He hasn't had many of those chances this season, and now the Jaguars must make good on their decision to keep him by increasing those opportunities.

title: Where the Jaguars, Brian Thomas Jr. Must Go From Here After Trade Deadline
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The trade deadline is over, and the Jacksonville Jaguars are ready to look forward.
Looking forward means different things for everyone. The Jaguars as a team have their sights set on Week 10 against the Tennessee Titans , and eventually a playoff push. But for Jaguars wide receiver Brian Thomas Jr., what is ahead could greatly determine his future with the Jaguars after the deadline came and went without him being sent to a new team.
The rumors around a potential Thomas trade swirled for a month-plus after he was benched during the second-half of the Jaguars' 34-31 loss to the Houston Texans in Week 6, but the Jaguars came out of their Week 7 bye with Thomas still as a part of the offense. He saw two targets combined in the last two games (one for a touchdown) but he was still the team's clear No. 3 receiver instead of rookie receiver Josh Cameron.
The Jaguars have always seen Thomas as a team-player, hard-worker, and a valuable piece of their culture and locker room. He is well-liked by the franchise as a whole, as evidenced by his teammates swarming him after his touchdown against the Colts in Week 8. And with the Jaguars clearly looking to add to their talent pool at the trade deadline , it seemed like a Thomas trade was less and less likely the closer the deadline got.
“We have a ton of value when it comes to BTJ. His role and what I imagine his contribution will be down the stretch here is going to be notable," Jaguars general manager James Gladstone said after the deadline on Tuesday. "He's such a good person to work with, such a good teammate, and so I expect a lot of good that comes in what lies in front, knowing that at this point in time, our wide receiver room in particular has got such a range of skill sets at its disposal and those that complement each other really well.
And when you think beyond that, the pass catchers that we have at our disposal when you start working in the tight end group and the running back room, it just allows our offense to be multiple. It allows us to be able to activate guys in different ways and in different games that looks different from one to the next. I think that ability to jump from one to the next is certainly going to benefit us here in the rest of the season and look forward to that being the case beyond.”
In short ... the Jaguars still value Thomas and how his skill-set meshes with the rest of the receiver room, even if it has resulted in just 10 catches for 117 yards and two touchdowns this season -- all  numbers well below what he even accomplished last season in a year that was quite a step back from his rookie season.
Now that the Jaguars opted to keep Thomas on the roster as they look to make their push, there are only a few directions the team, and the receiver, can go.
Simply put, all they can do for the rest of 2026 is to keep chopping away at it with the hopes of the downfield plays eventually coming. Thomas has been targeted on just three deep passes all season, with two incompletions and one interception as a result. The Jaguars' passing game has focused on finding explosives in the middle of the field, an area Thomas is not at his best.
But with the Jaguars turning down the chance to recoup some of their lost trade picks after the Jordan Davis and Jessie Bates moves , Jacksonville has put the onus on themselves to get Thomas more involved. He has rarely been targeted over the last few weeks, and many of his routes against the Baltimore Ravens in Week 9 were hitches or clearout routes, making it the first game of his career he hasn't been targeted in.
But the Jaguars still believe there is value there, whether as a receiver, as a run-blocker, or as a teammate. They must now start to tap into it.
“Yeah, absolutely. I think the guy's just done his job. He comes to work every day and works his tail off, and him and Trevor [Lawrence] are continuing to work together on it, and the time's going to continue to come," Liam Coen said Wednesday.
For Thomas, that means making the most of his oppurtunities. Thomas going on a run during the second-half of the season would do more than just quiet the noise in Jacksonville, but it couldboost his value and appeal to other teams next March when it would make much more sense for a Thomas deal to happen.
Had the Jaguars traded Thomas on Tuesday, they would have been making their roster worse in the middle of a hopeful Super Bowl run. If they do it in March, there could be more teams open to trading, the Jaguars could make more moves at receiver to offset his loss, and they could even have more confidence in Cameron as a true replacement entering his second season instead of in the middle of his rookie year.
Thomas can still benefit from being a Jaguar for the rest of the season. The Jaguars can also still get value for Thomas down the road. But for that to happen, the Jaguars need to give him chances to shine, and he will need to take advantage of them.

title: 5 Bold Predictions for Jaguars vs. Titans: Which New Addition Makes the First Big Play
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- After a frantic start to the week that saw the Jacksonville Jaguars make the biggest moves of this year's NFL Trade Deadline, it is worth remember that the Jaguars do, in fact, have an opponent on Sunday.
The 6-2 Jaguars are set to travel to Nissan Stadium to face the Tennessee Titans in Week 10, their first game since making blockbuster trades for Jessie Bates and Jordan Davis, along with adding Davon Godchaux for a sixth-round pick.
For a Jaguars team that has their eyes set on an AFC South title and a top seed in the playoffs, they are treating the Titans with the same seriousness that they treated the Indianapolis Colts and Baltimore Ravens over the last two weeks.
So, how do we see the Jaguars' Week 10 battle with the Titans playing out? We break it down below.
While it certainly remains to be seen if the Jaguars will actually play any of their new defensive pieces against the Titans, I believe they will. Jakobi Meyers and Greg Newsome each played in their first games with the franchise last season after joining the team during that same week, and I think that means we see the trio make their Jaguars debuts. In the process, I think we see Bates create his first Jaguars takeaway right off the bat.
Cam Ward is far from the most turnover-prone quarterback the Jaguars have played this season; that distinction goes to Daniel Jones. But he is right near the league average in interception rate, and he has made some egregious decisions with the ball over his last two seasons as a starter. This feels like the perfect week for Anthony Campanile to cook some pressure looks up to confuse Ward, and Bates is a natural playmaker. I think we see his impact right away.
The Titans' defense has been ... not very good against slot receivers this season. The Titans rank in the bottom-5 in the NFL against slot targets in each of the following categories: yards per play allowed, yards after the catch allowed, yards after the catch over expectation, and average seperation. The Titans have simply been a mess in the slot, even moving long-time outside cornerback Alontae Taylor to the slot despite signing him in March to play on the outside.
As a result, I think this is a Parker Washington week. He is the clear No. 1 receiver in the offense, and I think he shakes off some inconsistent moments we have seen as of late and has a huge game against the Titans. Washington is due for a big performance, and I think we see it this Sunday against the Titans.
There have been 275 quarterback performances this season. In just 39 of those performances, we have seen quarterbacks throw for fewer than 150 yards. Cam Ward makes up two of those games, a number that is trumped only by Bo Nix and Malis Willis which is, well, not great company to be in as far as productive gunslingers go. Ward has been more productive and explosive as of late and is coming off one of the best games of his career, but I predict the Jaguars limit Ward to under 150.
Ward threw for just 141 yards against the Jaguars in Week 13 a year ago, and the Jaguars limited Daniel Jones and Joe Fagnano to a combined 189 yards over the last eight quarters. The Jaguars' pass defense is clicking, largely due to the work of defensive coordinator Anthony Campanile, and I believe we see it continue this week.
Titans running back Tony Pollard has been on a tear over the last few weeks. Pollard, who has rushed for 246 yards and five touchdowns over the last two games, broke out of a mid-season skid and has been able to average over 4.0 yards per carry in every single game but two this season. While Pollard has been one of the NFL's more impressive runners over the last few weeks, I expect the Jaguars to be ready to bottle him up on Sunday.
Again, I think the Jaguars will play Davis and Godchaux on Sunday. But even if they don't, I do not think the Titans have the offense to keep the Jaguars off-balance enough to run the ball on them. Teams can only run the ball on the Jaguars when the Jaguars are threatened by the early-down pass, and I do not see the Titans having much success there.
The Jaguars have seen Walker Little play really, really well over the last few weeks since stepping into the lineup for an injured Anton Harrison. According to NextGenStats, Little has allowed pressure on just 6.4% of his pass blocks, the fifth lowest rate in the league among left tackles (minimum 100 pass blocks). On his 109 pass blocks, his 87.2% 1-on-1 matchup rate is the highest in the league among left tackles; his 6.3% 1-on-1 pressure rate allowed is the third lowest pressure rate allowed in the league.
“The experience always helps. Confidence is a heck of a thing, and I think he's the one that said it in an interview that humility helped. Where obviously he became our swing tackle, and all that guy has done is just stay the course," Jaguars head coach Liam Coen said on Wednesday. "Like, never got up, too down. He's just very steady. I really like Walker's play demeanor, the look in his eye recently and not taking everything so seriously. He's able to have fun with it. He's out there playing a game that he loves and competes with, but he's playing at a high level right now. He's got confidence, and you can tell.”
Little will mostly draw Titans pass-rusher Jacob Martin, who has had a good year. But after strong showings against the Houston Texans' pass-rush duo in London a month ago and then a dominant outing against Trey Hendrickson last week , I think Little has the edge entering Week 10. He is playing some of the best football of his career right now, and I predict it leads to another shutout.

title: 3 Most Important Things Jaguars' GM James Gladstone Said About Trade Deadline Fireworks
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars are a new team entering Week 10.
The Jaguars were already sitting at the top of the AFC South at 6-2, and that was before Jaguars general manager James Gladstone made trade deadline fireworks with the additions of Jordan Davis, Jessie Bates, and Davon Godchaux on Monday.
Gladstone spoke to the local media Tuesday at the conclusion of the trade deadline to discuss the team's big moves , which saw them trade away a first-round pick, two second-round picks, a fifth-round pick, and a sixth-round selection.
So, what were the most important things that Gladstone had to say? We break it down below.
Is this an all-in move for the Jaguars as they look to push for the No. 1 seed in the AFC in 2026 and potentially beyond? On the surface, the easy answer is yes. The Jaguars could very much be seen as the new version of "eff them picks" that the Los Angeles Rams started a decade ago. Between the Davis, bates, and Travis Hunter trades, Gladstone has now traded three first-round picks and three second-round picks. That is not insignificant.
With that in mind, Gladstone does not believe the Jaguars are viewing it from that lens. Part of it could be because the Jaguars see Davis and Bates as long-term pieces, but part of it could also could be the fact that Gladstone and the Jaguars just do not think along the same lines of, well, any other team in the entire NFL.
“Yeah, I think the idea that this is an all-in move isn't necessarily how I characterize it," Gladstone said. "I characterize it as getting better as a football team and prioritizing getting better as a football team. I look forward to seeing it all come to life and being a part of bringing it to life here this week and beyond. But really that’s the intent behind any decision that we make is what's in the best interest of this team in particular and the organization as a whole moving forward.”
Is this move all-in? That likely depends on perception to a degree. But for as much as the Jaguars believe this isn't pushing all their chips to the middle, it is hard to believe anything but a deep playoff run would be acceptable after Monday's trades.
There is no question what kind of impact that Jessie Bates can have on the Jaguars' defense right out of the gate. He is one of the best playmakers in the entire NFL thanks to his ball skills and instinct, and the Jaguars will need him to be one of their top impact players really from Day 1. With his skill-set and his reputation as a pro, though, there is not much question in terms of what he can offer them in 2026.
With that said, the biggest question after the Bates deal is whether he will be a long-term piece. His contract expires at the end of the season and the Jaguars will need to quickly make a decision as to whether he will be a rental or a key defensive cornerstone to build around for the next few years. We saw a similar situation play out with Jakobi Meyers last week, and the Jaguars quickly managed to make a deal happen there.
So, do the Jaguars have the same plan for Bates that they had for Meyers last season? He was asked that Tuesday, and he gave almost word-for-word the same answer that he gave when asked the same question about Meyers at this time last season.
“I think you can see very quickly that Jesse is a match for all the elements that we appreciate in both a player and a person, and so would love to make sure that Jesse gets his chance to settle in and become a part of this year's team, and then see what comes after it in an organic and natural way," Gladstone said.
All current signs should point to the Jaguars keeping Bates for multiple years beyond 2026. They have to get a deal done first, but they have been here before.
The biggest trade the Jaguars made, in more ways than one, was the move for Jordan Davis. The Jaguars were not afraid to throw a ton of draft picks at the Eagles to land the 26-year-old defensive tackle, and that is the key point here. The Jaguars will of course want Davis to be an impact player out of the gate to help replace Davon Hamilton, but it is also clear that they view Davis as a long-term building block.
Liam Coen and the #Jaguars big new addition pic.twitter.com/8nPVmiwaOs
The Jaguars have said a few times that they believe defensive tackles hit their peak closer to their late-20s than they do when they first get drafted to the NFL. Davis is a young defensive tackle who would fit that mold. That is why the Jaguars truly made the move for Davis; they see him as their long-term answer at defensive tackle instead of hoping a 2027 first-round pick at the position can develop overnight.
“Yeah, that was a major piece to the puzzle. It's a position that ages well," Gladstone said. "Certainly look forward to seeing him integrate here in the early going, while at the same time knowing that it's going to be a longer-term decision that we made with him. And so, making sure that his development over these next few years is something we really think through and plan out. But I think that's certainly a big piece to the why behind it.”

title: Jaguars Winners and Losers After the Trade Deadline: Jordan Davis, Jessie Bates Alter Big Plans
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- Well, it has been quite the week, hasn't it?
The Jacksonville Jaguars were the story of this year's trade deadline , making three trades on Monday and making the biggest trade of the entire deadline by trading a first- and future second-round pick for Philadelphia Eagles defensive tackle Jordan Davis.
The Jaguars, as they have often been under James Gladstone, Liam Coen, and Tony Boselli, were bold, aggressive, and willing to fight against conventional wisdom as they made moves that could cement their case as the AFC's best team in 2026 and beyond.
“Yeah, I think the idea that this is an all-in move isn't necessarily how I characterize it. I characterize it as getting better as a football team and prioritizing getting better as a football team," Gladstone said Tuesday. "I look forward to seeing it all come to life and being a part of bringing it to life here this week and beyond. But really that’s the intent behind any decision that we make is what's in the best interest of this team in particular and the organization as a whole moving forward.”
So, who benefited the most from the Jaguars' flurry of trade deadline moves? And who had their futures, or presents, impacted in the other direction? We break it all down below.
There can not be a happier man in Duval than Anthony Campanile, especially considering the next two months could solidify his case as one of the NFL's top head coach candidates moving into the 2026 hiring process. After Campanile lost two key veterans in one game 10 days ago, the Jaguars have now upgraded nose tackle and safety with legit blue-chip talents who fit the scheme like a glove. He has to be over the moon.
Bates is a perfect fit for what Campanile likes to do, and his ball skills and range should give the Jaguars the ability to continue to be versatile on the back end. Add in his elite tackling ability, and he could be the defense's best player soon. Davis, meanwhile, is one of the few players in the NFL who could do for the Jaguars what Hamilton has done for the last two seasons. Campanile already had a good defense. Now, he should be well on his way to leading a great unit. The Davis and Bates additions are genuine game-changers, and Campanile could very well be leading the AFC's best defense as a result.
In a league where more and more general managers are risk averse because they want to hold onto job security, it is refreshing to see a general manager who is willing to push in his chips. But what I liked the most about what James Gladstone did on Monday was the flexibility he gave the Jaguars beyond just 2026. Many moves made at the trade deadline are short-sighted, but Gladstone's are clearly about the future.
The Jaguars were able to add big pieces like Jessie Bates and Jordan Davis despite having limited cap space because that is how Gladstone made the deals. He paid a big price for Bates, but the Falcons ate most of his 2026 money, and the Jaguars can still easily re-sign him. They basically bought the rights to negotiate with him early for two picks. As for Davis, his cap hits over the next few years are insignificant, and the Eagles are still paying him a pretty penny. Gladstone again bought cap flexibility and talent by leveraging draft picks, which is smarter than just dealing picks for the sake of adding talent.
The Jaguars did not add to their edge group at all during the trade deadline, which bodes well for situational pass-rusher Dennis Gardeck and the rest of the Jaguars' pass-rush depth. Gardeck often serves as the team's No. 3 edge rusher behind Travon Walker and Josh Hines-Allen, but there was a real chance he would lose snaps if the Jaguars added anyone at the defensive end spot. Ultimately, that didn't happen.
This is not to say the Jaguars didn't try. According to SI's Albert Breer, the Jaguars had an offer on the tape for pass-rusher Will McDonald. But no deal was made, and the Jaguars are set to continue to use Gardeck as a key piece of their pass-rush plan across from Hines-Allen and Walker as the season goes on.
The Jaguars have had a need for an interior pass-rusher for some time, and the Jaguars added Ruke Orhorhoro in a trade this offseason with hopes of him helping there. He has been solid, posting multiple pressures more often than not, and he has the second-highest pressure rate among all Jaguars defensive linemen. But had the Jaguars added a player like Christian Barmore or Moro Ojomo, it would have been hard to see a scenario where Orhorhoro would have seen the field very often.
While the Jaguars added two defensive tackles, both players are nose tackles. Neither is an athletic three technique like Orhorhoro and Arik Armstead are, and it is clear the Jaguars will still need that duo to provide some pass-rush from the interior spots. Davis and Godchaux are massive additions, but neither should take many pass-rush reps away from Orhorhoro.
If there are two players whose long-term futures were changed during the trade deadline, it was Eric Murray and Davon Hamilton. Each player already had some questions about their roster spot when it came to 2027, and the Jaguars now have blue-chip players at the safety and nose tackle spots who are ready to take over in 2026 and beyond. There was no guarantee Murray or Hamilton would return as starters, or even return to the roster, before these moves. Now, it is harder to see a scenario where each replicates their roles in 2027.
Hamilton, who is in a contract year, could still sign a deal with the Jaguars before he hits free agency. But the chances of him earning big money to be the Jaguars' nose tackle of the future have likely hit near-zero considering Davis is younger and already under contract for years to come. As for Murray, the Jaguars could easily slot Bates into his spot with a new deal. For that to happen, though, Murray would likely have to be one of several players who gets released for cap space purposes.
The two players who lost the most playing time, or lost a path to future playing time, after Monday's moves were both rookies. Third-round picks Jalen Huskey and Albert Regis have not seen a ton of playing time on defense this year, though Huskey has gotten some snaps in the last two blowouts and Regis cracked the nose tackle rotation in Week 9 after Davon Hamilton's injury. That likely all changes now, though, starting with Week 10.
Huskey was a healthy scratch for the Jaguars at the start of the year when they had a healthy safety room, and he was clearly behind Rayuan Lane and Kaevon Merriweather in the pecking order as the season has gone on. Expect for him to be a healthy scratch once again with Bates added to the starting lineup and Lane and Merriweather pushed down a spot. Same goes for Regis, especially after the Jaguars added not one, but two defensive tackles. The Jaguars could use both players a year from now, but they will likely sit and watch the rest of the season.
The trade deadline came and went and, for the second year in a row, there was no Brian Thomas Jr. trade. This is not to say Thomas' long-term future with the team isn't still murky in terms of 2027 and beyond, but for the rest of this season and the subsequent playoff run, the Jaguars are keeping Thomas on their roster. This was the expected outcome considering where the Jaguars are as a team and where they want to go, even with Thomas' role decreasing over the course of the season.
“We have a ton of value when it comes to BTJ. His role and what I imagine his contribution will be down the stretch here is going to be notable," Gladstone said Tuesday. "He's such a good person to work with, such a good teammate, and so I expect a lot of good that comes in what lies in front, knowing that at this point in time, our wide receiver room in particular has got such a range of skill sets at its disposal and those that complement each other really well.
The fact we saw the San Francisco 49ers give up picks for 2026 Keenan Allen says it all about this…

title: The Jaguars' Move For Jessie Bates Looks Even Better After the Bills' Amani Hooker Response
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars made a big move to add star safety Jessie Bates to their defense on Monday.
Adding Bates was already a massive haul for the Jaguars, even considering the price they paid with a second- and fifth-round selection for the former Pro Bowler and All-Pro. A productive veteran who fits seamlessly with the defense and the culture, making it a move that would be hard to top.
A day later, the move looks even better after a similar price was paid by the Buffalo Bills for their new safety Amani Hooker.
The Bills sent a second-round pick to the Tennessee Titans for Hooker and a fifth-round pick. The late-second round pick is basically a trade down to the early fifth-round, the difference of about 80 picks. In 2026 NFL Draft terms, it is the difference between taking Anthony Hill Jr. in the second and taking Fernando Carmona in the fifth. It is a good bit of ground to give up for a safety while also not getting any of the money relief the Jaguars got in the Bates deal.
Titans are not eating any money on Amani Hooker’s deal in trade to Bills, per source. Buffalo will take on the rest of Hooker’s roughly $4.4 million salary this season. NFL INT leader is under contract for 2 more seasons. 2027 - 10.2 million 2028 - 13.5 million pic.twitter.com/shO8WjIE6P
There are other differences, of course. Hooker will get the "younger" tag, which is technically true by a year. Let's not act like that year exactly serves as a fountain of youth-sized difference, especially considering Bates is still playing at a high level. If we are just comparing their talents today, then Bates has a significantly lower missed tackle rate than Hooker, has more defensive stops, and has similar ball production outside of Hooker having the edge with five interceptions to one.
What is more likely, though: that Hooker has become the NFL's best ballhawk overnight, or that he is having a good year when it comes to the NFL's most volatile defensive stat? Hooker has been a solid player throughout his career, but he has played just one fewer year than Bates and has 11 fewer interceptions and about 47 fewer pass breakups. Bates also has 14 forced fumbles to Hooker's five.
Hooker is having a career year, but he has never been as good as Bates. The only thing he has done better is nab interceptions this season, but last year he had zero. It can be a flukey stat, and should not exactly be the one anyone uses as an argument to compare their talents.
“I can’t imagine that Brandon Beane is overly thrilled with James Gladstone right now." @robertmays , @davehelman_ and Derrik Klassen discuss the steep price the Buffalo Bills had to pay for Tennessee Titans safety Amani Hooker. pic.twitter.com/YNHWb1FeDw
Bates is seen as a top-tier safety for a reason. Hooker is a nice player, too, but he isn't within Bates' tier. Bates is a difference-maker worth paying the high price for, while Hooker seems like the knock-off version who the Bills had to settle for. The Bills needed to add a safety, and they probably should have just done the Bates deal if they were willing to pay this much for Hooker.
The Bills do have Hooker under contract for a few more seasons, while Bates is set to be a free agent at the end of the year. But the Jaguars have already proven they can make these types of trades and keep the player under contract for years to come, and they have given no indications that this isn't the plan with Bates. With how much cap space they should be expected to clear next offseason, keeping Bates should be a non-issue.
The question here is simple. Would the Titans have ever gotten a second-round pick for Hooker without the Bates deal going down? The answer is almost positively no.
As a result, the Jaguars changed the market, and their already-strong deal now looks even better after just a day and some change.

title: Grading Jaguars' NFL Trade Deadline: Jordan Davis, Jessie Bates Moves Are About More Than Super Bowl LXI
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- Just like that, the 2026 NFL Trade Deadline has come and gone.
The deadline ended with the Jaguars making three moves, with each trade coming on Monday. All in all, here is what the Jaguars did:
In short, the Jaguars added Bates, Godchaux, and Davis for a 2027 first-rounder, 2027 second-rounder, 2028 fifth-rounder, 2028 sixth-rounder, and a 2029 second-rounder.
So, how do we think the Jaguars and general manager James Gladstone made out as they look to stake their claim as the AFC's best team? We break it down below.
The Jaguars' path forward is simple: they think they are a Super Bowl team. They should, too, since they are perhaps the only team in the NFL that can boast that they have both a top-5 offense and defense. The Jaguars' offense is in a good place with Trevor Lawrence playing MVP-level football, and the Jaguars have now answered questions at two key positions of need after season-ending injuries to Davon Hamilton and Eric Murray at nose tackle and safety.
By adding Bates, the Jaguars are now putting a former Pro Bowler and All-Pro in a spot that otherwise would have been held by second-year safety Rayuan Lane. Lane has played well in spots this year, but Bates is a massive upgrade. Bates would have even been an upgrade over a healthy Murray, and the price the Jaguars paid is reflected in that. This deal will look different after the season as wekk once we know whether Bates will be re-signed or not.
If the Jaguars traded a second- and fifth-round pick for half a season of Bates, that would clearly be far from ideal. But the Jaguars can easily open up cap space with a few expected releases, and they have shown before that they can add a rental and keep him as a long-term piece. They did it with Jakobi Meyers last year, trading two Day 3 picks for him when he was entering the final two months of his deal. A month later, he signed a three-year extension.
"From everything that we've heard, the guy, the competitor, obviously, but also the person in the community, in the locker room, felt like this was similar to [WR] Jakobi Meyers type of dude, type of competitor, football and personal character. That's why I think it'll only help that room and help that group in the back end continue to provide confidence and communication," Jaguars head coach Liam Coen said Monday, already starting the Bates/Meyers comparisons.
If the Jaguars were to not re-sign Bates, they could be eligible for a compensatory pick based on how next March's free agency plays out. It feels unlikely the Jaguars would look to be big players in free agnecy, but it also feels unlikely Bates would sign a deal worthy of landing a third-round pick four years after he did so the first time. Perhaps they could get a fourth, but that would be in 2028 regardless.
This is a better move for the Jaguars if they re-sign him. My complete expectation is that they will, but a lot of this deal hinges on that factor.
As for Godchaux, there is not a ton to say. Flipping a sixth, likely in 2027 due to the compensatory picks the Jaguars are set to get, for a rotational run-stuffer makes sense. He hasn't had a great year in New Orleans, but he has ties to Anthony Campanile and is a better fit as a pure nose tackle for the Jaguars' scheme than both Matt Dickerson and Albert Regis.
This feels like a neutral move that the Jaguars will likely feel like winners after as long as he contributes to their run defense, but they paid the same cost for him that they did for Daniel Faalele Quinn Ewers. Godchaux can help the Jaguars a lot more this year than a sixth-round rookie could next season or in 2028.
Then there is the big move. The Jaguars sent two premium picks to the Eagles for Jordan Davis, though one of those picks is not set to be due until 2029. The Jaguars, simply, will never, ever been seen as the winners of this deal on paper, in the football community, among insiders and analysts, and whomever else. Accept that now.
The reason why is simple. Trading such a large package of picks for a two-down player would, in most cases, look disastrous. But consider a few factors from the Jaguars' point of view. For one, not all nose tackles are the same, and not all teams value nose tackles like the Jaguars do. Teams with attacking, gap-shooting defenses who are all about creating negative plays on third-down would likely have a much-different valuation on Davis than the Jaguars.
The Jaguars, though, do not live on every down and distance looking for a chance at the quarterback. The Jaguars' entire scheme is based around stopping the run on early downs and forcing 2nd- and 3rd-and-longs for the offense. When that happens, defensive coordinator Anthony Campanile turns up the heat with pressure looks and disguised coverages, the biggest reason the Jaguars have created so many turnovers the past two years.
But to get to third down and force quarterbacks into mistakes, the Jaguars have to win on first and second down. That is why Davon Hamilton was the most important piece of their defense, and that is why his loss to a season-ending injury was such a crushing blow. The Jaguars are the rare team where the nose tackle and run defense set the done for the pass-rushers and defensive backs, and Davis should fit in like a glove.
There is also the fact that the Jaguars have several defensive tackles on expiring deals after 2027. Hamilton's deal is up, and as is Arik Armstead's. So is Godchaux's for that matter. Had the Jaguars not traded the first-round pick for Davis, there is a good chance they would have had to use that pick on a defensive tackle. And that right there might be why they wanted to trade for Quinnen Williams a year ago and for Jeffery Simmons a few weeks ago.
What would the Jaguars prefer? A 26-year-old defensive tackle who should start to now hit his peak, which the Jaguars have said they believe is around that age at the position ... or a rookie who would have to be an impact player right off the bat, despite late-first round defensive tackles ever amounting to that type of player.
By trading for Davis, the Jaguars filled their defensive tackle hole for 2027 and likely beyond. The same can be said about Bates and the safety spot when he gets re-signed. That means these moves not only increase the Jaguars' Super Bowl odds in 2026, but they should increase them entering Week 1 of 2027 as well as long as Bates is retained.
The Jaguars paid a big, big price. James Gladstone will now go through his first three drafts using just one first-round pick. That is a lot of risk. But the reward could be about much more than just this year's Super Bowl. It could be the shot in the arm the Jaguars need to go from good to elite.

title: 4 Jaguars Who Had Their Futures Dramatically Changed After James Gladstone's Flurry of Trades
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars' defense got quite the facelift on Monday.
The Jaguars already had one of the NFL's best defenses entering the final 48 hours of the trade deadline, but general manager James Gladstone gave the unit a significant injection of talent with trades for Jessie Bates III, Jordan Davis, and Davon Godchaux.
While there are still a few hours to go in the trade deadline as of this writing, the Jaguars could be done making moves after their trio of trades to kick off the week. Ifd that is indeed the case, then it is not hard to see how the Jaguars' future plans have changed for a number of vetertans.
So, which Jaguars' future roles look different now that Jacksonville is entering the playoff push with three new faces on defense? We break it down below.
This is the most obvious one. The Jaguars signed Eric Murray to a three-year, $19.5 million deal last March that was always expected to be a short-term floor-raising move as the Jaguars started to put the pieces together. Even before Murray sustained a season-ending elbow injury in Week 8, it felt like from the start of the year that the long-time NFL veteran would be entering what would likely be his final year with the Jaguars. Now that Jacksonville has Bates in the mix , this case should be even more evident.
Yes, Bates is on an expiring deal, but so was Jakobi Meyers when the Jaguars traded for him. It would be surprising to see the Jaguars hand over a second-round pick without already having intentions of re-signing Bates, who will be 30 next season. The Jaguars signed Murray to a three-year deal and made him a starter when he was 31, so why would they hesitate with an All-Pro player who they just gave up picks for?
Re-signing Bates will take cap space , though, and releasing Murray is one thing the Jaguars can do to free some up. Bates is simply on another level as a play-maker than Murray, so the decision should already be made. Murray has been a good soldier for the Jaguars' defense since signing, but releasing him with a post-June 1st designation next year would free up $6.5 million for the Jaguars, while giving them a dead cap hit of over $2.5 million, according to OverTheCap.
This is one that would hurt, but it must be talked about. Davon Hamilton was arguably the MVP of the entire Jaguars defense until he got injured, playing at a Pro Bowl level and putting out the most dominant tape of his career. It seemed like he was hitting his speak as a nose tackle, and it was also happening during a contract year, making it perfect timing for Hamilton. That timing got disrupted in a big way last week when his season ended, though.
The Jaguars did not trade such a big package for Davis with hopes of him being just another cog in their defensive front. He is the new present and future of their nose tackle position, and he is set to be under contract and in Duval for the next several seasons. That spot likely would have continued to belong to Hamilton had he ended the season healthy, and he would have earned it after such a stellar season.
That is not to say there is no chance Hamilton returns now. He is beloved inside the building, and could you imagine a Jaguars depth chart that has Davis and Hamilton as its top two run-stuffers? But it would likely have to be a shorter and less significant deal, and it is at least a question now. Two weeks ago, Hamilton looked like the must-keep of the Jaguars' impending free agents. That has changed a bit now.
With the Jaguars adding Bates and Davis in one day , those are blue-chip players who will have big dollar signs attached to their deals while they are in Jacksonville. Davis is under contract for the next few years while the Jaguars will likely attempt to sign Bates to a deal in the range of three seasons before the regular-season ends. Add in the expiring deal of Parker Washington and a few other key Jaguars, and cap space will be needed.
Two ways the Jaguars can create that cap space? By shedding some contracts of older veterans such as Jourdan Lewis and Patrick Mekari. The Jaguars didn't find replacements for them like they found replacements for Murray and Hamilton, but Lewis and Mekari still offer two clear ways to save money without hurting the on-field product all that much. Lewis has made some big plays for the Jaguars this season but could be slowing down ahead of the final year of his deal, while Mekari has not seen the field this year due to injuries.
According to OverTheCap, the Jaguars would save $8 million in cap if they release Lewis with a post-June 1st designation. Add in another $13 million if they release Mekari, and the Jaguars could create $21 million by moving on from two older players who were likely always going to be short-term stop-gaps to begin with. Add in the Murray move, and that is almost $30 million in cap space freed up.

title: ESPN Matchup Predictor Analyzes Chiefs vs. Falcons Showdown in Week 10
full_text:
After making a statement at Arrowhead Stadium, the Kansas City Chiefs will head back out on the road in Week 10 as the hosting Atlanta Falcons will attempt to play spoiler. KC is looking to build on its blowout win over the Jets in its previous outing.
The Falcons have lost four of their past five matchups but aren't technically out of it given the dire state of the NFC South. As a result, Kevin Stefanski's group is viewing this contest as a must-win if they want to stay in the playoff race. Despite Kansas City's impressive 6-2 record, Andy Reid and Co. have dealt with special teams struggles and offensive inconsistencies. Those issues have put a damper on what has otherwise been a successful start.
Most analysts view the Chiefs as heavy favorites, but what does the ESPN Matchup Predictor forecast? Here's what the computer model expects two days before kickoff.
ESPN Matchup Predictor Chances at Victory: Chiefs 78.1%, Falcons 21.6%.
With nearly a four-in-five chance of coming out victorious, the matchup predictor heavily favors Kansas City this weekend.
Chiefs fans can only take things one week at a time. Until the Broncos lose and give Kansas City an opening, all the Chiefs can do is beat the opponents in front of them.
The biggest storyline of this road clash is the arrival of Josh Downs , who landed with the Chiefs shortly before the trade deadline passed. The shifty slot receiver may not be featured too much out of the gate due to his unfamiliarity with the playbook, but there are bound to be some bright spots in his debut in the red and gold.
Kenneth Walker III is a dynamic weapon in the backfield , but Bijan Robinson is on another level. In spite of poor quarterback play, Robinson is virtually unstoppable in the open field and possesses elite vision as a runner. He has three games in which he surpassed 100 yards this season and is averaging 5.2 yards per carry. Atlanta is unsurprisingly a significant underdog coming into this one, though it really depends on which version of the Falcons show up on Sunday. They were blown out by the Bengals last time out and shut out by the Buccaneers a week prior, but they also hold upset victories over the 49ers and Packers.
The drastic shifts in Atlanta's play have fans scratching their heads, largely due to the play of quarterback Michael Penix Jr. A week after taking home NFC Offensive Player of the Week honors in Week 7, he tossed a career-high four interceptions and failed to get his team a point.
Heading into their final game before a bye, the Falcons are going to throw everything they can at the visiting squad to stay in contention. This is the type of matchup that could see the Chiefs fall into an early deficit if they aren't careful.
