title: These Two 49ers Could Get Cut when Players Return from Injury
full_text:
The San Francisco 49ers opened the practice window for defensive tackle C.J. West and cornerback Nate Hobbs. Both of them could be back on the roster as soon as this week, and if not, they will likely get called up the following week. It raises the question of what the 49ers will do to open roster spots for these two.
The initial thoughts are that adding a cornerback and defensive tackle would mean waiving a player from each spot. Still, they placed Gracen Halton on the IR to add Keenan Allen. They have been thin at defensive tackle as well.
They could cut Sebastian Valdez, who would likely be inactive when West comes back. Valdez will likely make it back to the practice squad. Still, he has flashes during his limited time, and the team needs his depth.
At cornerback, they already cut Jack Jones, who is back on the practice squad. Renardo Green and Deommodore Lenoir are both banged up. Siran Neal is a cornerback but is mostly on the roster for special teams. So, their only outside cornerback depth is Ephesians Prysock. They are not going to cut any cornerbacks to bring Hobbs back.
Two names stand out that are better bets to get released than Valdez. The 49ers should release Brandin Cooks and Khalil Kareem.
At receiver, Cooks had a role, but it is fading. Jordan Watkins produces more, Keenan Allen was added, and Demarcus Robinson is now healthy after returning in Week 9. He was ahead of Jacob Cowing on the receiver pecking order, but Cowing has return duties.
At best, Cooks is the 49ers' fourth receiver. If one of Evans or Samuel can return to the lineup, Cooks would have to be inactive in Week 10. With both likely back soon, his role is phased out.
If the 49ers do not activate West this week, it could give Cooks one more week. However, that should be the swap.
Hobbs is almost definitely coming back this week, and the name to cut is Kareem, who was inactive last week. The 49ers added Kareem when the depth chart was thin. Since then, Nick Bosa and Mykel Williams have returned to the lineup. With Romello Height and Keion White in the mix, his depth is not needed. He will also be easy to bring back to the practice squad.
The first name to get cut when Hobbs gets back is Kareem. When West is healthy, Cooks should get cut.

title: Kyle Shanahan Sounds Off On 49ers Wide Receiver Jordan Watkins
full_text:
San Francisco 49ers wide receiver Jordan Watkins is looking better with each passing week , but it's not just his on-field progress that has impressed head coach Kyle Shanahan.
On the field, Watkins has 10 receptions for 224 receiving yards and one touchdown, and unfortunately, not two after one of his impressive catches was overturned against the Atlanta Falcons.
It's a notable difference from his rookie season, as he missed time in preseason with a high ankle sprain before a calf injury in the regular season, but so far, he has played six games in 2026.
His application and the work he put in when the opportunity presented itself have impressed Shanahan.
"Yeah. I think the more you play, the more success you have, the more confidence you get. I think Jordan's worked through all this and it's hard to just get playing time on our team," Shanahan said to reporters .
"You've got to beat people out. You've got to go ahead of them. Just because you're capable, it doesn't mean that you get it. You've got to beat guys out and he's been close to that, just not quite as consistent as a couple of guys in front of him.
"Got his opportunity with injuries and just the way he attacked it in practice. Some guys, when they don't get their opportunities, they start to make excuses, blame people, listen to social media too much and they don't work quite the same.
"Then their opportunity comes and they're actually worse than what they were two weeks before that. Credit to Jordan, he wasn't like that at all, which takes a mentally strong kid. He kept grinding, kept working and he kept asking what he could do more and to get out there.
"It was, 'Dude, you've just got to be ready when your time's there. You didn't get ahead of those guys in training camp, but that time will come and hopefully you're ready when it comes.'
"He's been more than ready and he's been able to string together a few weeks and he should have more confidence because, yeah, he's earned it."
There's still plenty of development to be made, but the step from his rookie to sophomore year has been a huge leap in all respects.
The next step is to build on the consistency he's shown in recent weeks and continue earning the trust of Shanahan. While he's taken his opportunity with both hands, maintaining that level of performance will be key to earning a more prominent role in San Francisco's offense.

title: 49ers Reportedly Tried to Trade for This Star Receiver
full_text:
It turns out the San Francisco 49ers were listening to fans and pundits over the last month as they tried for New York Jets star receiver Garrett Wilson, per ESPN's Rich Cimini .
The Kansas City Chiefs were also in on Wilson. Unfortunately for the 49ers and the Chiefs, the Jets never entertained them, and understandably so.
Wilson is a core piece of their franchise. He's arguably their best player and is under contract through 2030. They would've needed a significant haul to consider letting him go.
A haul that I question whether the 49ers were prepared to make. In any case, they never stood a chance because the Jets wouldn't discuss it.
The 49ers deserve credit for inquiring with the Jets about Wilson. That is what great franchises do. They make sure to leave no stone unturned with the trade deadline approaching.
Anyone who criticized the 49ers for "failing" to go all in should apologize to them. If they're showing they're willing, but the other team isn't, then there's nothing they can do. It takes two to tango.
The same can be said about their inability to trade for Khalil Mack or any other edge rusher. The Los Angeles Chargers were never going to let Mack go, which is foolish.
It's one thing for the Jets to hold onto Wilson. He's incredible and under contract for the foreseeable future. Mack, on the other hand, is on a one-year deal, while the Chargers are winless.
Mack would've been a great addition for the 49ers, just like Wilson. He would've easily become their best wide receiver on the team. Yes, better than Mike Evans . He's that good.
It's difficult to imagine what kind of deal would've been needed to pull that off. But had they done it, the 49ers would've significantly strengthened their Super Bowl odds.
Still, the idea of adding Wilson is the same as it was before this report emerged. It was never realistic because the Jets weren't budging on him.
It's a moot point. At least the 49ers tried. They tried to go all-in, but if no one else is willing, it can't be helped.
I'd imagine the 49ers pivoted to Keenan Allen after the Jets denied them. They couldn't leave the trade deadline empty-handed when they needed to add a solid route-running receiver.
Again, kudos to the 49ers for aiming high. It would've cost them a fortune to acquire Wilson, but a cost that would've given them strong Super Bowl hopes.

title: 49ers’ Christian McCaffrey Details Harsh Reality of Mike Evans’ Achilles Injury
full_text:
It’s very likely, if not guaranteed, that the San Francisco 49ers will be without star receiver Mike Evans against the Dallas Cowboys.
Evans has been dealing with Achilles tendinitis for the last few weeks. However, it didn’t start that way. Initially, it was simply soreness in his Achilles after his dominant Week 5 outing against the Seattle Seahawks.
He wouldn’t participate in any of the practices for Week 6 against the Washington Commanders, which was concerning. Yet the 49ers saw no issue with it and played Evans anyway, causing his Achilles to worsen.
You would think that the 49ers would know better after they experienced this issue with Christian McCaffrey two years ago. It’s never worth the risk. Now, Evans has been subjected to Achilles tendinitis, an experience that McCaffrey recently shed light on.
Spoiler — it’s a harsh reality.
“It’s tough, man. It sounds like whatever, but it’s a compounding injury,” said McCaffrey. “It can get worse really quickly, and then it can get really debilitating. I had my own experience with it. I hated everything about it.
“Even just waking up is a battle. You walk into the bathroom, it’s a battle. Depending on how bad it gets. I can’t speak for him. I just know it was tough and you’re wondering why? Why the heck did this happen? What is going on? It’s tough. And it takes a long time to come back.”
Talk about words of discouragement. It makes the 49ers look increasingly foolish for playing Evans against the Commanders when he was already dealing with Achilles soreness.
It would’ve been one thing if it was a late December game against a playoff opponent with the No. 1 seed in the NFC on the line. Those are games worthy of risking players.
But not in Week 5 against a 1-3-1 Commanders team at home. It reeked of desperation to play Evans. The only bright side is that the 49ers won that game, but at a premium cost.
They haven’t had Evans for two games, and it’s only going to increase further. No one should be surprised if Evans isn’t seen until December. The soonest I think he’ll be active is Nov. 29 at home against Seattle.
Evans will be needed in that game, but even that feels like a stretch. In the meantime, the 49ers will hope that newly acquired receiver Keenan Allen can adapt to the offense quickly to help shrink the hole.

title: Keenan Allen Trade Could Signal Bad News for 49ers Rookie
full_text:
The San Francisco 49ers trading for Keenan Allen might have a significant impact on every receiver on the depth chart. However, the name that could be impacted the most is rookie De’Zhaun Stribling.
While Mike Evans and Deebo Samuel are both injured, they are expected back in the next week or so. Stribling is on the IR, and his return is not expected until December. Kyle Shanahan clarified before the trade deadline that Stribling would not even return to practice until December.
They would practice December 1 after Week 12, and that would likely be the next time he steps foot on a field. San Francisco would open his 21-day window then. So, it is not a lock he would play that week, or even the next week. He is a rookie who not only has to shake off rust from not playing; he has to join an offense he has not been a part of since Week 1.
It has changed a lot, and he has missed a lot of development time. Plus, a rookie with an injury is not going to be pushed back. So, Week 14 or Week 15 is the more likely return date. The issue with a Week 14 return is that Week 15 is a short turnaround with Thursday Night Football.
That would be a lot to ask Stribling to play for the first time in 13 weeks, then turn around and play again on a short week. It is fair to start to think that if Stribling returned in Week 14, it would be in a limited fashion.
When looking at the skill set of Allen, it matches Stribling far more than Mike Evans or Deebo Samuel. Allen mostly works out of the slot and plays in the intermediate area of the field.
Evans has a 14-yard average depth of target. Samuel is at two this year. Allen is at nine. That is the same depth of target that Stribling had in the preseason. He also was primarily a slot receiver in the preseason, which is where Allen will play when Evans and Samuel are back. Stribling was drafted to replace Jauan Jennings.
The team tried to add Jennings back before settling for Allen. These two have very similar games and work the same portions of the field.
It is starting to become clear that the team added Allen because they do not see Stribling producing much at all to finish the season. If anything, he will not have a role until closer to Week 15.

title: Why Evan Engram Might Have Fit 49ers Offense Better than Keenan Allen
full_text:
The San Francisco 49ers added wide receiver Keenan Allen from the Indianapolis Colts. However, that might have been a backup plan to Denver Broncos tight end Evan Engram, according to Jeremy Fowler from ESPN .
Fowler reported that Engram was on the teams radar as the deadline approached.
“The 49ers looked around for tight end help, and the Broncos' Evan Engram was on their radar,” wrote Fowler. “But they landed on Keenan Allen, who's a bigger receiver and perhaps serves some of the same functions in the offense.”
As Fowler notes, they likely would have served a similar role. Engram is less productive than Allen and would have cost the same, if not more in a trade. Still, as a fit for the 49ers, he might have been a better option.
The 49ers could use a pass catching tight end as much, if not more than a receiver. They lost Jake Tonges for the season in Week 1, and they replaced him with Luke Farrell, who is only a blocking threat.
George Kittle is a great pass catcher, but the tight end room is complete when they can lean into his versatility. With Farrell blocking, and Engram as a pass catcher, they can use Kittle in whatever area they need to complement, or amplify whoever is on the field. It makes Kittle better.
So, Engram would play the same role, but he would complete the tight end room and add to the pass catcher corps.
The 49ers need help at pass catcher, and they are thin at receiver , but they could get healthier in that area soon. Mike Evans, Deebo Samuel and De’Zhaun Stribling are all missing time. They could be back in the next few weeks.
Jordan Watkins started to emerge with those names out, and he is intriguing in year two. They also got Demarcus Robinson back healthy last week. Allen helps, but the wide receiver room could get crowded, and if Stribling returns, his role will be limited.
Engram would have a limited role as well, but at least some threat of him lining up in-line and blocking changes the schematics and opens some things in the Kyle Shanahan playbook that Allen does not.
It makes sense why the 49ers had interest in Engram. The only question is what the difference in cost would be between Engram and Allen.

title: Why the 49ers May Regret Choosing Keenan Allen Over a Younger WR
full_text:
The San Francisco 49ers have announced a trade to acquire Keenan Allen from the Indianapolis Colts in exchange for a sixth-round pick.
On paper, the move makes sense. It gives San Francisco a potential future Hall of Famer for the short term while only costing a sixth-round pick. To be fair, it's about as straightforward a move as you might expect.
That said, the 49ers were linked with multiple other receivers, many of whom were considerably younger. There are a few reasons to suggest San Francisco could end up regretting its decision not to pursue one of those alternatives.
Targeting someone younger could have given the 49ers a potential long-term replacement for Ricky Pearsall . He's entering his third season, and there's no guarantee San Francisco will exercise his fifth-year option following the 2027 season.
Injuries have plagued his career so far, making his long-term future with the team less certain given his lack of availability. His rookie season can be excused, but the injuries suffered over the past two seasons are something the 49ers will have to keep in mind when deciding whether to commit to him long-term.
Allen will likely only be on the roster until the end of this season, but it proves a point about their receiving corps in general.
The vast majority of the receivers playing for San Francisco are already 30 or older. George Kittle, Mike Evans and Brandin Cooks are all 33, DeMarcus Robinson is 32, KhaDarel Hodge is 31, and Deebo Samuel is 30.
Bringing in another veteran does little to address the team's longer-term needs at the position. Sooner rather than later, a massive rebuild will have to be made on offense.
Bringing in someone with Allen's experience is certainly a positive, but there's a legitimate argument that experience shouldn't necessarily outweigh the potential of a younger receiver who has also impressed.
Ultimately, the decision to bring Allen in reinforces the idea that San Francisco is reluctant to part with significant draft capital ahead of what could be an inevitable partial rebuild. That transition could arrive sooner rather than later, making the decision to prioritise a short-term veteran over a younger option all the more questionable.
Can they rely on De'Zhaun Stribling and Jordan Watkins to become the future of the franchise in this position? I'm not so sure. Let's see what unfolds.

title: Why the 49ers Traded for Keenan Allen Instead of Josh Downs
full_text:
It was clear that the San Francisco 49ers wanted to add a wide receiver prior to the NFL trade deadline.
They attempted to acquire Jauan Jennings from the Minnesota Vikings a week ago, but he declined. The 49ers needed to pivot and ultimately brokered a deal with the Indianapolis Colts for 34-year-old veteran Keenan Allen .
It's a bit odd the 49ers went after Allen and not Josh Downs. Not only is Downs younger, but he’s the more explosive and better receiver. He would’ve helped the 49ers stretch the field and delivered a greater impact.
However, the reason the 49ers traded for Allen instead of Downs is simple — he was cheaper. The 49ers sent the Colts a 2027 sixth-round pick for Allen, while Downs went for a 2027 fourth- and fifth-round pick to the Kansas City Chiefs.
Downs is a better receiver than Allen, but he isn’t that much better to justify that haul of draft picks. I had advocated for the 49ers to acquire Downs, but for a fifth-round pick and nothing more.
If the Colts wanted multiple Day 3 picks from the 49ers, then they were right to stand pat. They’re not going to give up multiple picks for a player who will only help them for 8-plus games.
Besides, the 49ers going after Allen means they like his fit over Downs, and it has to do with Mike Evans , who will most likely be out for a few more games with Achilles tendinitis. They’ve lost their go-to receiver for short-yardage conversions.
Allen is one of the best receivers in that realm. On throws under 10 air yards, Allen has caught 31-of-38 targets for 230 yards and one touchdown, the seventh-most yards among wide receivers, per NFL Pro.
Brock Purdy will regain an outlet he can go to quickly for a first-down conversion or around the goal line. Allen can’t dominate with the goal-line fade like Evans, but he’s still a fairly sharp route runner.
He’s probably their second-best route-running receiver now. He can create enough space for Purdy to connect with him. The timing of a route is everything in Kyle Shanahan’s offense, which must have enticed the 49ers to acquire Allen.
Plus, being the wily veteran that he is, it shouldn’t take him that long to get the playbook down, as complicated as it is. All in all, trading for Allen isn’t going to needle too much.
But his addition will help Purdy and the 49ers’ offense enough.

title: Kyle Shanahan Shares Why the 49ers Traded for Keenan Allen
full_text:
Adding a wide receiver became obvious for the San Francisco 49ers when they attempted to trade for Jauan Jennings.
The need for one grew after their Week 9 win against the Las Vegas Raiders. They couldn't continue to trot out Brandin Cooks and Jacob Cowing.
That led the 49ers to trade for Indianapolis Colts veteran receiver Keenan Allen . His addition isn't anywhere close to a significant move, but he will contribute nicely.
However, it's unclear why the 49ers wanted to trade for Allen over anyone else, like Josh Downs. On Wednesday, Kyle Shanahan shared why they traded for Allen and how he fits.
"Trying to get the best receiver you can," Shanahan said. "It always starts with separating, catching the football. He's always been as good as anyone at separating. Always had as good hands as anyone, and then how good he plays without the ball. He's a guy who blocks. He never takes a down off and is extremely competitive. A very smart, aware football player."
The keyword in Shanahan's explanation is "separating." Despite being 34 years old, Allen is still a fairly sharp route runner. After Mike Evans , he's probably the second-best on the 49ers at it.
The 49ers needed someone who could carve out space for Brock Purdy to throw to. They couldn't rely on him to make tight-window throws throughout the game.
Purdy can make some of those throws, but it's not what the 49ers want to do. It isn't a sustainable formula for success. It becomes more likely for drives to get stalled out or, worse, an interception is created.
Allen won't be a downfield threat. That's never been his game, but he will be proficient around 10 yards beyond the line of scrimmage.
Whenever the 49ers need a quick outlet or a short-yardage conversion, they can look to Allen. Purdy now has George Kittle, Christian McCaffrey, and Allen has his trio until Evans returns.
The fit makes a lot of sense for the 49ers. Having Downs would've been nice to stretch the field, but having a player who can separate almost at will fits the 49ers better.
"We were really excited to get him. We think he makes us a lot better," Shanahan said. "Keenan has obviously had an unbelievable career. It was cool to turn on his tape and watch him in Indy and still see the same guy, so we were pumped to get him.

title: 3 Pivotal 49ers Miss First Week 10 Practice vs. Cowboys
full_text:
Surprisingly, the San Francisco 49ers have only three players missing from their first practice of the week. Usually, several players are out.
While the number is low, the downside is that the three players who were held out of the first Week 10 practice against the Dallas Cowboys are pivotal starters.
The first is a usual suspect: Mike Evans . He'll continue to be missing with Achilles tendinitis. He's already missed the 49ers' last two games.
No one should be surprised by his absence. Achilles tendinitis requires ample time for rest and recovery. A few weeks off the field won't make a significant difference.
In fact, 49ers fans should expect him to be missing in action for the next several weeks. Expect him to miss Sunday's game against the Cowboys.
The two new players who are out of practice are starting cornerbacks Renardo Green (back) and Deommodore Lenoir (foot).
Both players suffered injuries in the Week 9 win against the Las Vegas Raiders. Green's injury occurred on his brilliant end zone interception in the fourth quarter when he landed on his back.
It's unclear what the severity of his injury is, but it's enough to keep him out of this week's first practice. The same goes for Lenoir.
It's only one practice, so there shouldn't be much concern yet. However, being without both starting cornerbacks is alarming.
The 49ers will be facing one of the best wide receiver duos in the league on Sunday: CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens. That's assuming Pickens plays.
He missed Week 9 with a hamstring injury. In any case, the 49ers will be in a tough spot without Lenoir and/or Green.
That is what led them to re-sign Jack Jones . He's insurance in case either Lenoir or Green can't suit up against the Cowboys.
The 49ers will have their fingers crossed that it doesn't get to that point. Otherwise, they'll hope their defensive front can make Dak Prescott uncomfortable throughout the game.
That'll be their only way to combat missing two of their skilled starting cornerbacks. The key practice they will need to show up for is on Friday. If not, they will be out.
As for the 49ers who are limited at practice: Deebo Samuel (hamstring), Siran Neal (knee, foot), Upton Stout (shoulder, neck), and C.J. West (knee).

title: Bruce Arians Not Against Returning to Buccaneers Job 'If It Were Open'
full_text:
The Tampa Bay Buccaneers are a long way out from their Super Bowl run. It's only been six years, but since then, the Bucs have had a winning record just twice and have won a single playoff game after winning it all in 2020.
Head coach Todd Bowles has been under fire for some time now following a late-season collapse last year and a 3-6 run at the moment. Bowles took the job in 2022 after head coach Bruce Arians stepped down due to health issues, and since then, Tampa Bay has been up and down.
Arians has been out of the game for a bit, but during a recent podcast appearance with Jordan Schultz, he said that he's now open to coaching again — and that maybe, if his old job were open, he wouldn't be against taking it.
“This is the first time I had the itch again. I had no desire to go back,” Arians said. “After open-heart surgery, I have so much more energy. It's amazing... we'll see what happens."
News: Super Bowl-winning HC Bruce Arians tells me he wants to return to coaching. “This is the first time I had the itch again. I had no desire to go back. … After open-heart surgery, I have so much more energy.” Full interview drops soon! pic.twitter.com/QyNbIYmsyi
It gets more interesting, though. Tampa Bay Times writer Rick Stroud contacted Arians after the clip and asked if he would be interested in returning to Tampa Bay as head coach. His response?
I asked Bruce Arians if he would consider returning to the Bucs. “If it were open, yes,” he said. https://t.co/akaIE1rPTw
Arians is no longer tied to Tampa Bay as a head coach, so no team would have to trade for him. He would be free to pursue any coaching job he would want to pursue, and that would include Tampa Bay's should Bowles be fired at any point before or after the regular season.
Arians is arguably the most successful coach in Bucs history, winning a Super Bowl with the team and netting a .655 winning percentage with 31 wins — the best mark in the franchise.
The Bucs had a strong tenure with Arians, but Bowles hasn't been fired just yet, and Arians would be an older candidate in a league that is increasingly turning toward younger coaches as offense and defense evolve at a rapid rate.
It remains to be seen just how much interest Arians will draw, even from Tampa Bay. For right now, though, the Bucs are 3-6 and resting during their bye week before trying to string some wins together for the remaining eight games of the season.

title: Buccaneers' Most Disappointing Players at Halfway Point of 2026 Season
full_text:
The Tampa Bay Buccaneers were looking to win the NFC South in a big way in 2026, but nine games into the season, they've won just three games.
The Bucs are 3-6, and although they are technically tied for the NFC South lead, they've had some major struggles over the course of the year. They were looking to count on a number of players to help them win this offseason, and some of those players haven't been delivering.
Here are some of Tampa Bay's most disappointing players this season so far:
The Buccaneers were searching for a leading wide receiver after the departure of Mike Evans, and Emeka Egbuka, who the Bucs drafted in the first round a year ago, was primed to take that spot. Halfway through the year, the Bucs are still looking.
Egbuka has been hurt for a few games this year, but even then, he's netted just 31 receptions for 278 yards. The passing game as a whole is brutal at the moment, but he doesn't seem to have the ability to beat his man from rep to rep and make things happen on his own accord.
Egbuka started off strong last year, but now, he's struggled to stand out. For a first-round pick, that's tough.
Another first-round pick, Rueben Bain Jr. will have plenty of time to course-correct. But the Bucs thought they got a steal with Bain in the draft, and so far, that has been far from the truth.
Bain only has two solo tackles across the entire year. He has one sack and one forced fumble, and he has just a 9.9% pressure rate on his pass-rushing snaps, per SumerSports.
Bain has been dropped in coverage a lot and he's still getting used to the NFL level. But the Buccaneers thought they drafted a game-wrecker, and Bain has had very little impact over the first nine games of the year.
Perhaps the most concerning name on this list, Mayfield signed a three-year extension worth $55 million a year before the season started. The move was controversial at the time, and Mayfield hasn't done much to silence his doubters over the first frame of the season.
Mayfield did miss three games with a dislocated thumb injury, but outside of those games, he has played very poorly. He's thrown just three touchdowns to four interceptions (one a pick-six) and has turned the ball over seven total times.
Mayfield's pressure-to-sack ratio is just under 32%, and he has a dropback EPA/play of −0.297 so far this season — dead last among qualifying quarterbacks, per SumerSports. The entire passing offense has been awful in Tampa Bay, and while offensive coordinator Zac Robinson and the wideouts have a part in that, Mayfield is also a fairly big one.
Winfield Jr. has been hurt a lot this season, and he might miss some time again with an ankle injury after leaving the game against the Chicago Bears. Even when he's been in, though, he hasn't lived up to his four-year, $81 million deal.
Winfield has 22 solo tackles, one forced fumble and one pass defended in six games played. His replacement while injured, Ifeatu Melifonwu, has played well in his stead, and Winfield hasn't done much to stand out from him, even when healthy.
The Bucs will look for him to make a bigger impact going forward in the back half of the season.
The Bucs re-signed Riley Dixon this offseason, knowing that he was one of the worst punters across the league last year. So far, that gamble isn't exactly paying off.
Dixon is 31st in the NFL in yards per punt (44.4) and he's dead last in the NFL in net yards per punt (38.4). The Bucs have an excellent defense, but Dixon is doing them no favors with his lack of distance, and his poor punting has hurt the team a few times this year when it came to flipping the field.
The Bucs appear to be rolling with Dixon for the rest of the year, and if Tampa Bay wants to win games, Dixon will have to be much better.

title: Bucs Had Something Other NFL Teams Desperately Wanted Before Trade Deadline
full_text:
Just a few weeks ago, the chances of Jason Licht and Tampa Bay Buccaneers becoming sellers at the NFL trade deadline seemed like more of a certainty than a possibility.
However, back-to-back victories over the Panthers and Falcons — the Bucs' first divisional games of the season — quickly altered the likelihood of that scenario coming to fruition. Not only were the Buccaneers 3-5 and undefeated in the NFC South all of a sudden, but the two teams they were chasing in the standings were no longer out of reach.
Although the Buccaneers were unable to defeat the Chicago Bears on Sunday Night Football less than 48 hours before the trade deadline, Todd Bowles' defense put together another incredible performance that (largely because of the atrocious play of Baker Mayfield ) still wasn't enough to keep the winning streak alive.
However, with the Buccaneers looking like a defensive juggernaut and just one game outside of first place in the division to boot, it wasn't a surprise to see the team stand pat at the deadline in the end.
According to NFL Insider Jeremy Fowler , the Buccaneers had plenty of interest in one of their defensive players.
"The Bucs had strong interest in veteran defensive lineman A'Shawn Robinson, but they rarely trade at the deadline and are still in the NFC South race."
Although there had been plenty of chatter about defensive players like Vita Vea and Yaya Diaby being possible trade candidates when the Bucs' were considered potential sellers, 31-year-old Robinson was the player who other teams were coveting most.
When Robinson was signed as a free agent in the offseason, there wasn't exactly a ton of fanfare regarding the acquisition. However, since joining the Buccaneers, there's no denying that the veteran DT has been one of Bowles' best players.
Beyond bringing a nasty edge to the field and vocal leadership to the locker room, Robinson has been extremely consistent and productive for the Bucs so far. Not only has Robinson produced 24 total tackles, one sack, eight QB pressures, three passes defended and two interceptions, but he's been very good against the run as well.
In fact, Robinson's 88.3 run defense grade is the second-highest among all interior defensive linemen in the NFL. His overall defensive grade is nearly as impressive at 85.8, which is the third-best mark in the league at his position.
It doesn't really matter now, but it's still interesting to learn that Robinson was one of (if not the most) desirable trade targets on the Buccaneers' roster ahead of the trade deadline. That being said, once you dive into the impact he's made on the field for his new team, it's pretty easy to see why.
It's also easy to see why the Buccaneers decided to keep him around. If the team hopes to make a push in the second half of the season to take control of the division and make the playoffs, they're going to need Robinson to play a big part in that. Just like he has so far.

title: Buccaneers' Passing Game Could Be Historically Bad in 2026
full_text:
The Tampa Bay Buccaneers have an electrifying run game that ranks among the best in the league and a suffocating defense that might actually be the best in the league. So why are they 3-6 during their bye week?
The answer is in their passing offense. Tampa Bay's passing offense is last in the league in yards per game (141.9) and yards per pass (5.9). But it goes a lot deeper than that once you dive in to advanced metrics.
This Buccaneers passing offense isn't simply bad — according to success rate, it may be historically bad.
Tampa Bay's is last in the NFL EPA/dropback (-0.297) and 28th in explosive pass rate. But when you take success rate into account, the offense has been dire so far.
Success rate is defined by successful plays. A successful play is typically considered to be 40% or more of the required yards on first down, 60% or more of the required yards on second down and then 100% or more of the required yards on third or fourth down.
Tampa Bay's success rate in the passing game so far this year is a paltry 35.4%. As CBS reporter JP Acosta noted on Twitter, that's only bad, it's the 11th-worst passing offense by success rate since 2010 in Weeks 1-9.
According to @TruMediaSports , these are the 20 worst offenses in the NFL since 2010 through weeks 1-9 when it comes to Passing Success Rate. 4 teams from 2026 being on here is...staggering, and the 2026 Broncos just missed the cut! pic.twitter.com/h94onOVPpx
Obviously, there is still time for this to change for Tampa Bay going forward. The list also, interestingly enough, features three other teams from 2026 — the Los Angeles Chargers at No. 4, the Philadelphia Eagles at No. 6 and the Minnesota Vikings at No. 17.
That shouldn't distract from the fact that, if this trend continues, the Bucs could be a historically bad passing offense. That falls on everyone involved, from offensive coordinator Zac Robinson to quarterback Baker Mayfield and his largely ineffective receiving corps.
The Bucs don't have a ton of time to turn things around, but they'll have to do their best. Every NFC South team currently has three wins at the moment, so the division is all for the taking — and to take it, Tampa Bay will have to get going through the air.

title: Buccaneers Are Wasting One of Their Defense's Best Seasons
full_text:
The Tampa Bay Buccaneers achieved one of their biggest goals heading into 2026 — they boast one of the best defenses in the NFL.
That hasn't been winning them games, though. The Buccaneers are 3-6 at the moment, and despite a weak NFC South keeping the team in the hunt, they've generally struggled throughout the year. There are a few places to attribute those struggles, but the main culprit is the other side of the ball — Tampa Bay's offense has been greatly failing it.
But just how good is Tampa Bay's defense, and just how bad is its offense?
To say that the Bucs defense is playing great football right now might even be an understatement. They're playing some of the best defense in franchise history.
The Bucs defense boasts the best EPA/play in the NFL, per SumerSports (-0.21) and the sixth-best defensive success rate (41.73%). They're first in the league in EPA/dropback (-0.253) and fourth in the league in EPA/rush (-0.141), and they're the seventh best team in the league when it comes to stopping explosive plays of 20 or more yards.
Their real success this season, however, has been turnovers. Tampa Bay leads the league with 16 interceptions, three more than the second-place Green Bay Packers, and they lead the NFL in total turnovers with 21. Incredibly, 12 of those 21 turnovers have come in their last three games.
The Bucs are generating turnovers at an unsustainable rate, so that may dry up at some point. But even so, they have the passing game and running game prowess to suffocate defenses, and that makes them one of the NFL's best units.
This is the unit head coach Todd Bowles has wanted out of his defense all along. It should be winning them games, but it isn't — and that's because his team's other unit is losing them.
Tampa Bay's rushing offense has been inflated a tad analytically due to its incredible rushing efforts against the Carolina Panthers and the Atlanta Falcons, but it remains elite — it's the best rushing offense in the NFL in yards per game, ranks 10th in rushing EPA/play and fourth in explosive rushing plays of 12 or more yards.
That's not the problem. The passing offense is.
Tampa Bay's passing offense ranks dead last in EPA/dropback (-0.297) and 28th in explosive pass rate. The team's quarterback, Baker Mayfield, also ranks dead last among 33 qualified quarterbacks in EPA/dropback (-0.324), ranks 27th in completion percentage (60.6%) and net yards per attempt (5.27) and 30th in passer rating (74.9).
Mayfield also continues to take unnecessary sacks that hurt his team. His 10.59% sack rate is 31st in the league despite facing just the 16th-most pressure.
No wide receiver in Tampa Bay has over 300 receiving yards, and Emeka Egbuka leads the team with 278. Nothing about the pass game works or is even average, and it's dragging the entire team down week after week — especially when the Bucs have to play good opponents.
Tampa Bay needs to figure out its passing game fast if it wants to do anything meaningful in the postseason (should it even get there at all). the Bucs have an excellent defense that can hang with any team, but with a passing offense that can hang with none of them, that defense is largely going to waste.

title: Why Didn't the Buccaneers Make a Move at the Trade Deadline?
full_text:
The NFL trade deadline has come and gone, and the Tampa Bay Buccaneers have completely stayed put.
The Bucs did not make any trades, neither selling off a player nor buying from another squad. General manager Jason Licht and head coach Todd Bowles are confident in what they have — at least including the cost of giving up or trading for a player, anyway — as the pair try to win another NFC South title.
That being said, the Bucs are 3-6 and started the season 0-4 — so why stay put at the deadline? To keep it simple, it's a little complicated.
To go more in depth, the Buccaneers were in a sort of trade limbo.
The Bucs were not good enough at the deadline to buy. There are a lot of problems with this team's offense, from the coaching to the talent, and an extra wide receiver or tight end probably wouldn't fix things. That would also require giving up draft capital — a luxury for teams competing, not for teams with a losing record like the Bucs.
At the same time, though, Tampa Bay isn't quite bad enough to sell. The Bucs are still just a half a game out of the NFC South (and will likely be a game back once the Saints and Panthers play), so they're in contention to win the division, as crazy as it seems.
Selling off a player like Vita Vea or Antoine Winfield Jr. may seem appealing for the long term future, but Bowles and Licht need to win now. To do that, they need all the players they can muster, including the team's aging stars on the roster.
There's also the fact that the Bucs rarely trade in season at all. Licht has done it just once, trading for Jets defensive tackle Steve McLendon and giving up a sixth-round pick. Licht highly values draft capital — perhaps more than any other GM in football — and he isn't interested in shuffling around his players while the season is ongoing.
The Bucs stayed put at the deadline. Now, they have to prove that it was a good idea by winning the division and making the playoffs.

title: Buccaneers Bye Week Update: What Are Tampa Bay's Playoff Chances?
full_text:
The Tampa Bay Buccaneers haven't had the season they wanted.
They started off 0-4, and while they've strung together some wins, they remain just 3-6 heading into their bye week. Normally, that would just about disqualify any team from making the playoffs, but the NFC South is special (derogatory).
As it stands, every team in the NFC South has three wins. The Bucs and the Falcons are 3-6, while the Panthers and the Saints, both of whom have had their bye weeks, are 3-5. The Bucs remain half a game out of NFC South contention, and as the Panthers and Saints play each other, Tampa Bay will likely become one game out of first after Sunday's NFL action.
Despite Tampa Bay's early string of losses and an offense that remains one of the league's worst through the air, the odds are still in their favor to win the division and make the playoffs.
Per The Athletic's playoff simulator , the Bucs still have the best chance to win the NFC South.
The Athletic gives the Bucs a 37% chance to win the NFC South (and a 38% chance to make the playoffs). That's pretty low, but no one else in the division is higher — The Falcons and Panthers both have a 23% chance to make the playoffs, and the Saints have a 16% chance to win the NFC South.
Tampa Bay has largely been kept alive by its weak division, and it likely has the best chance to win that division due to its current division record. The Bucs beat both the Panthers and the Falcons once this year (all while throwing the football just 11 times).
With those two wins already under their belt, they have the best chance to win the division by picking up more of those wins in their next four divisional games — even if they drop other games outside of the NFC South.
The Bucs are on bye while the Panthers and Saints play each other. The Falcons will have a tough task in Week 10 when they host the Kansas City Chiefs at home.

title: Buccaneers Lineman Calls Out Bears’ Jeffery Simmons for Dirty Play
full_text:
The Tampa Bay Buccaneers dropped their Sunday Night Football game to the Chicago Bears 27-24, and with that, they were unable to take the outright lead in the NFC South.
The story of the game was Tampa Bay's considerable number of turnovers on defense, getting five off the Bears, and considerable ineptitude on offense. The Bucs only scored 10 points off of five turnovers, and quarterback Baker Mayfield even threw a pick-six that saw Chicago add seven points to the board.
One of the biggest challenges the Bucs faced was Bears defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons, who Chicago acquired right before the trade deadline. But when asked about him after the game, Bucs tackle Luke Goedeke said that some aspects of Simmons' tool kit have "no place" in the game.
Goedeke told ESPN writer Kalyn Kahler that he thought Simmons was both holding too much and also launching himself at his head at various points in the game.
“I mean, you’re holding me on one, you came right at my head,” Goedeke said . “I mean, that’s always fun. He’s known for it on pass pro, just holding the tackle so that the DE can run free, so I got that twice. So that’s always a good one. But, yeah, just kind of going back and forth. I mean, respect the guy, but some of the stuff he can really take out of his game. It’s just kind of old, to be honest.”
Goedeke elaborated further, saying that the tactics Simmons used during the matchup have no "place in the game".
"There's no reason to just come out on a TE and just drill a tackle in the side of the head," Goedeke said. "[There's] really not a place in the game for that, to be honest with you."
This wasn't the only grievance that the Bucs had with the Bears. Quarterback Baker Mayfield also told reporters that the Bears were calling out Tampa Bay's snap counts during the matchup, which should have been enforced as a penalty if that claim were true.
Bucs QB Baker Mayfield says he doesn’t know what went into the O-line having five false starts Sunday night, though he says the last one came about because the Bears were “barking out the cadence,” which you can’t do. Acknowledges that it’s tough for the refs to call that one,… pic.twitter.com/cMsobPlg1y
Goedeke also isn't even the first Bucs lineman who has had some beef with Simmons. When the Bucs and the Tennessee Titans held joint practice together in 2025, and during that practice, lineman Cody Mauch got into with Simmons after a rep against him.
It’s getting chippy early between Bucs-Titans 👀 Cody Mauch and Jeffery Simmons getting after it with one another leading to both teams having some words. I’ve missed you football. pic.twitter.com/bVCXe9btHd
Despite all of this, though, the Bucs lost that game against the Bears — and their offense floundered while doing so. Tampa Bay has plenty it needs to figure out over the bye week, and it will certainly need to fix some of its offensive woes when it faces off against the Detroit Lions in Week 11.
The Bucs are 3-6 and half a game out of the NFC South lead. They'll have to string together some wins to take the NFC South, and to do that, the offense simply must be better.

title: Grading Every Buccaneers Position Group After Loss to Bears
full_text:
CHICAGO — Another primetime game for the Bucs in the books — but this time, they couldn’t come away with a win.
The Chicago Bears' offense had some sloppy play throughout, with Caleb Williams having a rough night with four interceptions, but poor execution offensively by the Buccaneers meant that they never could really take advantage.
Let’s take a deep dive into each position group and give our report cards out to each one of them. Some of them are not too bad, but some are not too pretty.
It wasn’t a great game from Baker Mayfield. Two interceptions, some off throws, holding onto the ball too late — it just felt like a mess at times. It didn’t help that some of his playmakers couldn’t catch and execute on their own end, either.
Mayfield admitted after the game that turnovers are something he has to clean up, certainly when one of them went straight for six points for the Bears. This offense has to once again turn it around and, it starts with QB1.
Bucky Irving is playing at phenomenal level right now. He's making guys miss, he's hard to tackle and he fights for every extra yard. He’s been the bright spot of this team and the top weapon offensively for weeks. Kenny Gainwell had a big 44-yard play that helped the Bucs get into the red zone.
With solid blocking up front, I thought both running backs took advantage of the holes when they were there.
This group has been a major letdown going into this season.
Injuries certainly aren’t helping, but when the wideouts are on the field, simple catches and important ones alike are being dropped. Ted Hurst got benched after his drop Sunday night. Tez Johnson had two drops, too, but stayed in the game because of his experience.
This group has to do better mixed in with better play from QB1.
This group isn’t much of a threat in the passing game, and I don’t know if it’ll ever be under Zac Robinson. For the most part, the blocking has been the best part of this unit.
There were some targets to Cade Otton in this game, but Mayfield couldn’t hit him on the throws. Blocking surely helps, but the pass-game threat needs to show life here soon.
This unit did the best they could with how well Chicago’s front seven has been playing as of late, certainly with the addition of Jeffery Simmons.
There were holes for Irving and Gainwell and a good amount time for Mayfield in the pocket. Penalties hurt this grade a tad, but overall, play-wise, not too shabby.
Interior Defensive Line: B
I really liked what I saw from this room along with the pass rush off the edge. They were able to get movement up front and get Williams moving into uncomfortable positions. This certainly helped with the four interceptions on the night in the secondary.
For the most part, this group was finding a groove all throughout the night.
Without having Yaya Diaby in the mix, David Walker, Anthony Nelson and Al-Quadin Muhammad had to step up. Luckily, once again, Rueben Bain Jr. continues to grow. He had a huge play tackling Luther Burden III and causing a fumble, which was recovered by safety Ifeatu Melifonwu.
There were a few plays where things went sideways for Alex Anzalone and Josiah Trotter. I noticed from the press box that Anzalone had to call out Trotter on a missed gap assignment that allowed the Bears to get a first down.
Eye discipline was good, though, with Trotter having a few plays rushing after Williams and not allowing for easy dump-offs. Anzalone grabbed his third interception of the season after having two last week against the Falcons.
It wasn’t a pretty start for the cornerback room, primarily for Zyon McCollum, giving up a touchdown and surrendering wide-open Bears players. He turned around his play by grabbing two interceptions, reaching a career season high of four. McCollum's tackling stood out as well, and he's looked strong in that department all season.
Jacob Parrish tipped a ball off Williams' and helped Anzalone have a takeaway, giving Tampa Bay's offense great field position.
Antoine Winfield Jr. left the game fairly early with an ankle injury after colliding with Calijah Kancey on a tackle. Tykee Smith grabbed an interception, and overall, the unit did fine with the help of the Bucs’ pass rush. Melifonwu picked up a fumble in Bears’ territory, allowing Tampa Bay to tie the game.
Overall, this unit played well.
The kickoff team almost gave up a touchdown, but luckily a holding penalty was called, killing that chance. Kevin Knowles, primarily a gunner on punt teams, had impressive plays throughout the game. He was a fantastic addition right before the season began from Kansas City. Chase McLaughlin is Chase McLaughlin — always a trusted source.

title: Overreactions From Buccaneers' Close Loss to Bears
full_text:
The Tampa Bay Buccaneers kept it close against the Chicago Bears, but in the end, they weren't able to get a big win in the Windy City.
The Bucs fell to the Bears 27-24 on Sunday Night Football, dropping them to 3-6. It was a game where Tampa Bay's defense dominated once again, netting five turnovers and holding Chicago's offense at bay for most of the game, but the Bucs were unable to get anything going on offense and they couldn't get the win as a result.
As always, we're giving our overreactions to this matchup — here's how we're feeling after Tampa Bay's loss:
The Buccaneers' offense is a mess almost everywhere (we'll talk more about that later). But perhaps the most pressing need the team has is at wide receiver, and that showed itself in a big way on Sunday night.
Tampa Bay's wide receiver corps had numerous drops on the night — rookie Ted Hurst was benched because he had one, and Tez Johnson had two drops across the night. Once again, tight end Cade Otton dominated the target share with eight of them, and outside of a huge bomb to Johnson that saw him net 76 yards on the night, no other Bucs receiver had over 40.
Chris Godwin remains an ineffective part of the offense despite being on a $22 million deal. Emeka Egbuka was drafted by the Bucs in the first round last year, and he has not looked like a WR1.
The Bucs really, really feel the absence of Mike Evans. They need a definitive WR1 on the team, and they need it badly if the passing game is to repair itself in future seasons.
But for right now, though...
The Bucs have had a strong run game with Bucky Irving and Kenny Gainwell, but that cannot carry the entire offense. The Bears proved that.
Offensive coordinator Zac Robinson's passing schemes have struggled all year, and they've continued to flounder when they've actually been needed. The aforementioned wide receiver issue continues to persist, and on top of all that, Tampa Bay's quarterback hasn't played up to standard at all.
Baker Mayfield is making $55 million a year on his extension, but his pressure-to-sack ratio is just under 32% (that's bad) and he threw a backbreaking interception that went for a pick-six, giving the Bears seven points in a game where the defense was holding them at bay. Mayfield has thrown three touchdowns and four interceptions, and his 32.4 QBR is 30th in the NFL.
The Bucs need the passing game to thrive. It doesn't look like there's a way it gets any better this season, and Tampa Bay will continue to lose games as a result.
Despite all that, though? This defense is elite. They generate more turnovers than anyone else in the NFL, they remain stout against the run and the pass, and they have multiple All-Pro-level players on the team this year who are showing out.
That will be enough to win the NFC South. The Carolina Panthers, Atlanta Falcons and New Orleans Saints don't have offenses half as potent as the Bears do, and Tampa Bay should muster enough wins in their next four NFC South matchups to win the division and make the playoffs.
The team isn't good enough to beat good teams and win a playoff game. But they are good enough to win the division and get there.
And if that happens, the Bucs have an interesting question to ask — What happens next?
