title: 3 Major Storylines to Watch in Titans’ Duel With Jaguars: Draft Buzz Has Hit in Full Force
full_text:
The Tennessee Titans return to action on Sunday for an AFC South showdown with the Jacksonville Jaguars. These two teams are on completely different trajectories right now. The Jaguars are a bonafide Super Bowl contender, while the Titans already have one eye towards a very important offseason.
From this point on, every win should be celebrated as a sign of progress while every loss ultimately gets them closer to potentially landing a true blue-chip prospect in the coming draft.
In fact, that's our first major storyline of the three at hand today: Watching out for replacements and upgrades via the draft process has officially begun.
The obvious name everybody is going wild over is Ohio State WR Jeremiah Smith. He’s clearly best prospect in the draft at a position of need. Unfortunately, they’ll have to lose a lot more games to have a realistic shot at getting him inside their building.
It’s hardly an exaggeration to say that reuniting Smith with WR Carnell Tate could potentially be a franchise-altering moment, especially if QB Cam Ward keeps progressing the way that he has as of late. If the Titans miss out on Smith, they’ll still have several intriguing options at other major areas of need.
Pass rushers Colin Simmons (Texas) and Dylan Stewart (South Carolina) are the two likeliest options given their gaps along the edge. But Notre Dame CB Leonard Moore also happens to be one of the best cornerback prospects in recent memory, so he’ll be in the conversation as well.
The wild card to keep your eyes on is LSU T Jordan Seaton. He’d be a clear upgrade over LT Dan Moore Jr. both short and long term, and it would give the Titans three top-11 picks along the offensive line, including two bookend tackles on each side. That’s the type of pick that can help your young quarterback take the next step, but truthfully, any of those five players would be a welcome addition to the team next spring.
Of course, Week 10 won't be the only game before draft day that helps narrow down the Titans' choices. Beyond draft buzz getting louder, we've got two more in-game stories to keep an eye on.
As you may recall, these two coaches don’t exactly see eye to eye. Prior to last season’s 49ers contest against the Jaguars, Titans HC Robert Saleh was asked as defensive coordinator to talk about what makes the Jaguars such a difficult opponent offensively.
Saleh proceeded to talk about how the Jags had essentially created a unique sign stealing system in which he emphasized that nothing was being done illegally. Despite that clarification, Jaguars HC Liam Coen clearly didn’t appreciate the then-Niners DC bringing that up, and it all boiled over once Jacksonville beat San Francisco 26-21.
Coen appears to blow Saleh off after the game, which then led to an exchanging of words between the two coaches.
At one point, the Jaguars head coach can be heard saying “Keep my name out of your mouth”. Saleh then proceeded to follow Coen as the two continued to shout at each other until the two were eventually separated.
“Keep my name out of your mouth,” Liam Coen and Robert Saleh exchange after Jaguars win. Saleh used the phrase “legal sign stealing” in news conference last week in reference to Coen. pic.twitter.com/yYcjm1oHIP
Both Saleh and Coen have since downplayed the event, but this will be the first time the two of them meet as head coaches of two teams that don’t like each other to begin with. This budding beef between the two head coaches undoubtedly adds a new layer to an already heated rivalry, so it’ll be interesting to see how it all plays out on Sunday.
This is arguably the Titans’ biggest storyline to watch on Sunday. Ward is coming off the first 300-yard game of his career, and many are curious to see whether that was a sign of everything starting to click, or is it simply an unfortunate anomaly.
The Jaguars enter this game as the 22nd-ranked pass defense ( per FOX Sports ), allowing an average of 229 passing yards per game. On paper, this could be a matchup Ward may be able to exploit, especially if Tate is somehow able to play.
Topping 300 yards again would certainly be helpful, but what we really wanna see out of Ward is his improved ball placement, decision-making, processing speed, and overall aggressiveness to be on full display once again.
Nobody is expecting him to be perfect; mistakes are inevitable for any young QB. But how Ward responds to those low moments will be critical for the Titans’ chances on Sunday and going forward.
Shaun is a longtime Titans fan who has years of experience in the field. He missed being on the team beat, and is here to change that. He also writes scripts for EA Sports' Madden games, where fans may have heard his work.

title: Why Titans' Biggest Depth Chart Change After Trade Deadline Comes at the Worst Time
full_text:
When the Tennessee Titans traded Jeffery Simmons before their Week 8 game, DE Jacob Martin stepped up in his absence and leveled three sacks against the Cincinnati Bengals. It was exactly the sort of leading performance Tennessee needed to see from a veteran on the defensive line.
In the secondary, S Amani Hooker came down with three interceptions. His continued dominance looked like a comforting reminder that the defense hadn't been entirely gutted, and that the Titans may be able to have their cake and eat it too with the Simmons trade.
That was true until Tennessee decided to move Hooker at the deadline, too. The draft capital the Titans got in return for both of these players is inarguable - two firsts and a second-round pick - but what is also inarguable is the defense's obviously weakened state.
As a result of Hooker specifically being dealt, second-year S Kevin Winston Jr. will be forced into an even brighter spotlight than before. He entered a starting role opposite Hooker earlier this season, and against the Jacksonville Jaguars in Week 10, the sophomore's role gets bigger.
The issue is: Winston hasn't been fantastic this season, and the Jaguars are a raging, win-now product built for the Super Bowl. The mix doesn't look promising for the home team.
PFF has Winston graded at 56.5 up to this point in his second season. That's good for just 73rd among 100 qualified players at his position. Winston has also yet to come up with an interception this season. Hooker was the only Titans safety with an INT.
The Jaguars have scored 30+ points in their last three contests, and have met that mark in four of their last six contests. Two weeks ago, Jacksonville smacked 42 points on the Indianapolis Colts in a 42-7 win.
It's QB Trevor Lawrence who is leading the way, no less. He's got 18 touchdown tosses on the season (good for fourth in the league), to just four interceptions. This is a Jaguars team, and offense, at the top of their game - Winston is being thrust right into the middle of that in a new way for him.
The Titans are lucky to return CB Marcus Harris after he tweaked his ankle in Week 8, and corners Alontae Taylor and Cor'Dale Flott are both slowly coming into their own. But Hooker was that unit's resident veteran and crux; without him, there exists no clear candidate for a clean takeover.
Winston, in just his second year, has the potential to develop into a reliable centerpiece in time. But his development has come in fits, and the Jaguars are the opposite of a team that could give him a break. It'll be trial by fire for Winston in Week 10, and Titans fans shouldn't expect similar disruption in the secondary to what we saw one game ago.
Lane covers the Tennessee Titans, where he brings an evolving team's journey to fans on a daily basis. A longtime sports fanatic and recent baby blue jersey aficionado.

title: 5 Titans Players Primed for New Roles vs. Jaguars After Trade Deadline
full_text:
The Tennessee Titans traded two of their core defensive pieces during the 2026 NFL trade deadline, defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons and safety Amani Hooker.
Tennessee's trade of Simmons and a 2028 fifth-round pick to the Chicago Bears for two first-round picks and an additional 2027 fourth-round selection was the blockbuster deal of the deadline around the league. However, the Titans also made another major move by dealing Hooker and a 2027 fifth-round pick to the Buffalo Bills for a 2027 second-round pick.
With Simmons and Hooker playing elsewhere for contenders, the Titans will have a few players step into new jobs for the rest of the season. Let's take a look at who will have more prominent roles on Tennessee's defense.
Winston will now step up as the Titans' top safety. The Penn State product has posted 51 tackles, one forced fumble, eight defensive stops, and an 80.3 Pro Football Focus run-defense grade . But Winston must step up in pass coverage and as a leader on Robert Saleh and Gus Bradley's defense moving forward.
As for Adams, the veteran has played under 200 defensive snaps this year, but is now the starter in the back end next to Winston. Adams racked up 36 starts during his four-year tenure with the New York Jets and was a quality player, so the Titans can rely on him not to be a complete liability.
Tennessee has already played a game without Simmons, which was their Week 8 loss to the Cincinnati Bengals. During the contest, Thomas, Horne, and Stackhouse received most of the snaps on the interior.
The rotation may change as the season goes on, but expect all three players to play bigger roles than before still. Thomas will likely step into the starting spot, while Horne and Stackhouse provide viable depth.
Thomas, a former top-five pick, hasn't been a full-time starter in the NFL since his first two years in the league with the San Francisco 49ers. However, the 31-year-old knows Saleh's defense very well and should be able to provide serviceable play in the pass-rushing department and as a run defender.
The Titans will face the Jacksonville Jaguars in their first game after the deadline . We'll see how the defense looks on Sunday, and how the unit responds after the franchise traded its top two players.
Dharya Sharma is a sportswriter from Nebraska who has been covering the Tennessee Titans through his website, SharmSports, since 2023. He is also an NFL and NBA writer for The Sporting News and had a previous stop with Sportsnaut. Follow him on X @SharmSports

title: Would Titans Drafting Jeremiah Smith Crowd the WR Room... or Elevate it to Elite Status?
full_text:
Yesterday, after this year's NFL trade deadline, we circled five names Tennessee Titans fans should be keeping an eye on ahead of the 2027 draft. With two first-round picks therein, general manager Mike Borgonzi is carrying the weight of the Titans' rebuild on his shoulders.
We didn't mention Ohio State pass-catcher Jeremiah Smith for one reason: It would've been too obvious. No team in the league right now isn't at least taking a look at the Buckeyes superstar. Save for a team that could desperately need a QB, Smith would be first off the board for most.
Should that sentiment extend to Tennessee? It appears a little more complicated on the surface. The Titans just took Carnell Tate fourth overall in this year's draft. Tate, a star Buckeyes receiver, has clicked comfortably into the WR1 role as a budding leader in Brian Daboll's offense.
Assuming the 1-7 Titans claim one of the top picks - say, second overall - Smith is more than in the conversation. Is this one worth overthinking for a team trying to fill multiple roles? Maybe, but on the other hand, you've got the sort of talent worth throwing need out of the window for.
Reuniting Smith with Tate would also give the Titans one of the best young WR cores in the NFL, even if that room gets a little muddier in the process.
In his junior year as a Buckeye, Smith has already broken 1,200 yards receiving through nine games. His 14 touchdowns are tied for first in college football, and this season marks the third straight in which Smith has a receiving score for 70 yards or better.
He's a bonafide professional and growing deep threat with the ability to go up and get a 50/50 ball over mutliple defenders. It seems like Smith is doing that every week now.
Drafting Smith would take some touches away from Tate and further complicate a WR room that should've been at least slightly altered at the trade deadline. Calvin Ridley remains competing for touches, and second-year WRs Elic Ayomanor and Chimere Dike are really only starting to carve out their own roles.
That's not even mentioning Wan'Dale Robinson, who was brought in on a $70 million deal to be a cornerstone of the Titans' pass-catching battalion.
Though if that group can embrace sharing the spotlight, and if Cam Ward continues to grow into his role as this team's signal caller, Tennessee would have the chance to end up with something special. It'd be worth a few hard talks to watch the Titans' offense transform overnight.
Lane covers the Tennessee Titans, where he brings an evolving team's journey to fans on a daily basis. A longtime sports fanatic and recent baby blue jersey aficionado.

title: A Great QB Makes All the Difference: How Titans' Matchup vs. Jaguars is a Tale of 2 Rebuilds
full_text:
The Titans’ upcoming Week 10 contest with the Jaguars pits two franchises going in completely different directions against each other.
At 1-7, the Titans made the tough decision to part ways with franchise staples DT Jeffery Simmons and S Amani Hooker in exchange for premium draft capital in hopes of eventually building a more competitive roster sometime in the near future.
Meanwhile, with the Jaguars currently sitting atop the AFC South at 6-2,  decided to go all in with a plethora of deadline deals, acquiring DT Jordan Davis from the Eagles, DT Davon Godchaux from the Saints, and S Jessie Bates from the Falcons.
Pair that with the bold move the Jags made a few years back to acquire CB/WR Travis Hunter in the draft, and it’s clear this is a franchise under GM James Gladstone that isn’t afraid to take some big swings in order to get better.
Moves like the ones Jacksonville has made are simply unrealistic for Tennessee at the moment. Mainly because QB Trevor Lawrence has established himself as a true franchise quarterback for the Jaguars, while QB Cam Ward is still trying to figure things out.
However, it wasn’t always that way. In fact, the two of them had relatively similar starts to their career.
People tend to forget that Lawrence was only 5-20 over his first 25 starts, which is just one more win than Ward has produced through his first 25 starts (4-21). During that time, the Clemson product dealt with a lot of the same things Ward is currently dealing with. Jags head coach Liam Coen wasn't afraid to praise Ward ahead of playing against him this week:
Liam Coen on Cam Ward: “….threw for 300, you know, and you can see that he's just getting more and more comfortable, right? It's a new system. I mean, there's just so many times where we're a little impatient with these things and I think that they're having a good moment of… pic.twitter.com/esVsrAScDZ
Lawrence was surrounded by lackluster talent, a revolving door of coaches, and an irate fanbase that was running out of patience largely due to some of the issues that predated their arrival in actuality.
While this was certainly a rough period for everybody involved, their patience eventually paid off. Things finally clicked for Lawrence once he found some stability in HC Liam Coen, while Gladstone’s bold moves added premier talent for the team to work with. The Jags have now completely turned things around, going 19-6 over his last 25 starts with Lawrence leading the way.
Titans GM Mike Borgonzi and HC Robert Saleh are hoping a similar thing happens in Tennessee. Ward isn’t blameless by any means, but you could argue he hasn’t exactly been set up to succeed as much as he should’ve been.
The Titans are hoping to start changing that reality now that they have a ton of resources at their disposal, including five top-70 picks (in all likelihood) in next April’s draft, along with two first-rounders in 2028.
Tennessee has put itself in a position where it can target premium talent at premium positions throughout the first two days of the event. Trying to rebuild a roster as depleted of talent as the Titans were prior to Borgonzi’s arrival with just one pick in each round proved to be unrealistic.
This team had far too many holes to fix, and not enough picks to do it, which forced them to overpay for average-at-best talent in free agency. Throw in the fact that not all picks pan out, and that’s how this team finds itself in the position they’re still in today despite multiple years of “rebuilding”.
These recent trades will allow the Titans to try to fill at least five positions with top-70 players, including a true blue-chip talent at the top of round one — rumor has it one of WR Carnell Tate’s former teammates isn't half bad. We'll see where WR Jeremiah Smith lands.
But for any of this to matter, the Titans desperately need Ward to follow a similar trajectory as Lawrence’s. Unfortunately, this year is all but over, but that doesn’t mean the groundwork towards getting this thing turned around can’t be set over the final nine games.
The harsh reality is that the Titans probably won’t be any closer to getting this turned around unless Ward finally reaches his full potential.
For everybody’s sake, let’s hope that ends up being the case. And who knows, if everything works out well, maybe a year or two from now we see the Titans evolve into the aggressive franchise that buys players from bad teams instead of being the one on the selling end.
Shaun is a longtime Titans fan who has years of experience in the field. He missed being on the team beat, and is here to change that. He also writes scripts for EA Sports' Madden games, where fans may have heard his work.

title: 5 Draft Targets Titans Fans Must Get to Know After 2026 Trade Deadline
full_text:
The trade deadline, taken with the Tennessee Titans moving DT Jeffery Simmons, saw Nashville's team give up two defensive veterans for two first-round picks and one second-round selection in total. This is a future-facing franchise now more than ever before.
That means Titans fans should be looking into the future, too. As Tennessee prepares to face the division-leading Jacksonville Jaguars out of the bye, holding a 1-7 record, now feels like a proper juncture to begin looking at who could come in to assist this rebuild next.
Now that the trade deadline is passed, we've got five draft prospects that Titans fans should already be getting to know before the event comes to pass next spring. I'm not including Ohio State WR Jeremiah Smith on this list, only because he's at the top of everyone's list.
Could the Titans take a Buckeye pass-catcher two years in a row? Maybe, but I believe the team has more pressing needs that, as of now, we'll focus on addressing.
Dylan Stewart is a name that Titans fans are going to hear a lot over the next four or five months. The South Carolina EDGE may be the best defensive-line prospect in college football right now.
Stewart has been one of the Gamecocks' most reliable playmakers for three seasons now. He's got clean footwork and gets off the snap quickly. This season, Stewart has chalked up two sacks and three forced fumbles.
PFF projects the EDGE as a top-10 pick. If he's available for Tennessee's first selection, he may end up being the favorite to become a Titan.
If it isn't Stewart at the EDGE position, Texas Longhorn Colin Simmons would be next in line. Simmons had 5.5 sacks in one single game against Tennessee earlier this season. Five sacks in one game. He's got 10.5 on the year, and has done so while missing two games.
His speed and disruption off the edge may be unmatched in this draft class. Ankle sprain aside, this is as good as an EDGE prospect gets when healthy.
Whether you'd prefer Stewart or Simmons would come down to a case-by-case basis, but Titans fans should be familiar with both of them prior to the 2027 draft. If the Titans go defense early, either one could pop as high as the second overall pick and nobody would bat an eye.
The only offensive pick on this list, Ole Miss Rebel Kewan Lacy would project as a late first-round selection for Tennessee, whereas the previous two names would likely be slated in the single-digit range.
With Florida star Jadan Baugh likely to be off the board by the time the Chicago Bears' first-rounder falls into the Titans' hands, Lacy would be the only remaining back that high in the pool. Lacy, although he's currently dealing with a left-shoulder injury, is a knockout prospect.
In his healthy 2025 campaign with Ole Miss, the spry back posted 306 carries for 1,567 yards and 24 scores. In limited action this season, he's still managed 388 yards and five touchdowns. With Tony Pollard and Tyjae Spears both entering free agency after this season, the RB position looks to be next up for a reset in the possible case that neither return.
If the Titans go defense with their earlier selection, I'd love to see the front office spin around and try and secure a long-term investment in the backfield. Even if Baugh is off the board, a healthy Lacy would be a great and realistic option.
Another Ole Miss prospect, DT Will Echoles is ranked as ESPN's highest DT on the board. Tennessee could look his (or the next guy's) way if they're after a direct replacement for Jeffery Simmons.
Echoles moves exceptionally well for his size, at 6'3", 315 lbs, and has 2.5 sacks in yet another consistent season for the Rebels. Last year, Echoles finished his 2025 campaign with five sacks and 68 total tackles.
He may not be the most explosive DT in the draft, but the Titans arguably won't find a more reliable, play-by-play pressure cooker from the jump. Echoles would be a solid pickup anywhere Tennessee could get him.
Gilliam is the aforementioned "next guy." He's right up there with Echoles at the DT position for the most part, and on paper, is the more explosive of the two options.
With the Tennessee Volunteers this season, Gilliam has put up an astounding six sacks and two forced fumbles through nine games. This is a massive leap from the half-sack outing he had with the Penn State Nittany Lions in 2025.
Gilliam has ridiculous burst and has come onto the draft scene as fast, if not faster than any other defensive prospect in the nation. He may not have the past consistency to stand on like Echoles, but he could be discussed as an even stronger prospect by the time this collegiate season ends.
A definite player to watch to replace Simmons in the long run.
Lane covers the Tennessee Titans, where he brings an evolving team's journey to fans on a daily basis. A longtime sports fanatic and recent baby blue jersey aficionado.

title: Why the Titans Will Beat the Jaguars in Week 10, Why They Won't, and a Prediction
full_text:
The Tennessee Titans were one of the few teams that saw their bye week crossover with the NFL trade deadline. Fans wouldn't be blamed for forgetting that we've got football this coming Sunday after days on end filled with rumors and breaking news at the end of every sentence.
Not only do the Titans play in Week 10, but they're hosting AFC South-rivals. The Jacksonville Jaguars, one of the most active buyers at the trade deadline, are coming to Nashville to boast their new pickups.
The last time Tennessee faced Jacksonville, the Titans lost 41-7 at the very end of the 2025 season. Cam Ward missed the majority of that game after exiting early with a shoulder injury, and his healthy showing tomorrow is the key to a potential Titans upset.
Ward nearly led Tennessee to a victory over the (now) 6-2 Cincinnati Bengals in Week 8. The Titans falling short 36-43 in overtime was partly due to Ward taking a costly sack late in regulation, but the QB can't at all be blamed for losing a game he kept Tennessee in.
With WR1 Carnell Tate trending toward a return, Ward should have all of his weapons in place to put up another promising game. The Titans even kept RB Tony Pollard at the deadline for Ward's own sake.
Again, Jacksonville bulked up at the deadline - their defense specifically - but Tennessee leaving the offense untouched said loud and clear that this franchise believes in Ward. With a newly-gutted defense, the Titans will be relying on Ward to try and secure the win.
Directly opposing Ward is that new-look Jags defense. In addition to adding All-Pro S Jessie Bates III, Jacksonville also acquired defensive tackles Jordan Davis and Davon Godchaux.
The south-most AFC South team sold off a ton of draft potential to make this happen, but the 6-2 team got a whole lot better as they sprint toward a hopeful Super Bowl appearance. Two out of the next three weeks, the Titans stand in the way.
FOX Sports already had Jacksonville listed as a top 10 defensive team in the NFL prior to these trades. If Tennessee falls short (as is likely expected), it will be because the Jaguars' defense put a stopper in Ward and the offense's growth.
That could be one reason among many, but it seems to be the most relevant by far regarding this specific matchup.
At the end of the day on Sunday, I expect Jacksonville will overwhelm Tennessee. I don't believe it will be in blowout fashion, and this is primarily because of the stable flashes of progress Ward showed in Week 8.
But between their overhauled defense and Trevor Lawrence manning things under center on offense, the Titans are truly facing a championship contender this week. Perhaps the home field will help blunt the blow, as well as the team debuting their Music City jerseys.
I love the jerseys. I like what we saw from Cam Ward in his most recent game. But this Jaguars team has the AFC South in a headlock, and the 1-7 Titans simply don't have enough on paper to climb out of a double-digit projected loss in this one.
Lane covers the Tennessee Titans, where he brings an evolving team's journey to fans on a daily basis. A longtime sports fanatic and recent baby blue jersey aficionado.

title: Why Not Trading Tony Pollard Was Only a Short-Term Fix for Titans' Looming Backfield Issues
full_text:
After weeks of ongoing rumors, the Tennessee Titans have concluded the NFL trade deadline by only trading two players, and neither of them on offense. Two weeks ago, the Titans traded their franchise cornerstone DT Jeffery Simmons to the Chicago Bears. Yesterday, on deadline day, Tennessee traded S Amani Hooker to the Buffalo Bills.
Hooker and Simmons were the Titans' longest tenured players, and arguably the franchise's two best players were dealt. In return, the Titans received two first-round picks, one second-round pick and one fourth-round pick.
One of Tennessee's most anticipated trade candidates was RB Tony Pollard. Fresh off back-to-back performances of at least 100 yards rushing and two touchdowns heading into the week of the deadline.
The timing for Pollard to be traded at peak value seemed better than ever, especially being in his age- 29 season. However, a deal never happened as a result of the Titans wanting to keep Pollard to assist Ward's development, leaving a glaring issue in the backfield that Tennessee will have to face next spring.
In the spring of 2024, the Tennessee Titans signed Pollard, a one-time Pro Bowler in 2022, to a three-year deal worth up to approximately $22 million as the replacement for future Hall of Famer Derrick Henry. Nearly three years later, the Titans haven't resigned him to a longer deal.
Trading Pollard would have saved the Titans $7.25 million in cap space and only would have had to pay $2 million in dead cap, according to Over The Cap . The other two big-name running backs rumored to be on the trade market aside from Pollard were Eagles' Saquon Barkley and Colts' Jonathan Taylor. All three running backs ended up staying put, likely due to teams being unwilling to give up a high price for a position that is widely considered disposable after age 30.
Pollard turns 30 in April.
There was reported interest from the New York Giants and Denver Broncos, according to NFL Insider Jordan Schultz. Ultimately, the Titans decided not to trade their starting running back.
In the spring, Pollard has the opportunity to walk in free agency, which would leave potential draft capital from a team like the Giants or Broncos left behind for nothing. A decision Tennessee's front office may regret with Pollard nearing the end of his prime.
One of the darkhorse candidates the Titans could've traded away at the deadline was backup RB Tyjae Spears. Trading Spears would've made sense of his declining snaps and productions, as well as the franchise's decision to ride out with Pollard at RB1 for the remainder of the season.
However, Spears wasn't traded, and he's set to be another unrestricted free agent in the spring of 2027 with Pollard.
Drafted in 2023, the former Tulane prospect was selected in the third round by the Titans as a backup to Henry. After Henry's departure to the Baltimore Ravens, Spears looked to take the starting role until Tennessee signed Pollard from the Dallas Cowboys.
According to Pro Football Reference , Spears has only started three games in his four-year career in the NFL, serving as a backup for Henry and Pollard in Nashville. In six appearances this season, he has most commonly been used as a pass blocker for QB Cam Ward and a receiving back with limited rush attempts.
However, since Week 6 against the Colts, Spears hasn't seen the field as he deals with a knee injury. If the Titans were ready to trade away an aging Pollard at the deadline for future draft capital, a 25-year-old Spears would get the chance to play significant playing time for the first time in his pro career.
Now, Tennessee has to face Pollard and Spears' expiring contracts, both of whom could be donning new uniforms in 2027. Will someone get brought back, or do the Titans say goodbye to both and try and hit the reset button on short notice?
Isaiah is an award-winning journalist and photojournalist. A graduate from the University of Kentucky, he has previously been published by BloodHorse, KY Insider, and the Kentucky Kernel for multimedia sports coverage. Isaiah is a Tennessee Volunteer at heart bringing his local expertise to Titans coverage.

title: 3 Major Winners, and 2 Losers, From Titans' Defense-Heavy Trade Deadline
full_text:
The trade deadline has officially come and gone for the Tennessee Titans. It was both less eventful than expected and just as impactful as any fan could've hoped it would be.
Defensive studs Jeffery Simmons and Amani Hooker both got moved, while trade suspects Tony Pollard and Calvin Ridley remained in the baby blue and red. It was a defense-heavy deadline with much to talk about for Tennessee moving forward.
Here, we've put together three of the Titans' biggest winners after the cutoff, as well as two losers. Let's dive in to the latter-half outlook for Tennessee after today's shakeups.
According to Jordan Schultz, one of the main reasons Tennessee ending up holding on to Tony Pollard was due to how important he is to Cam Ward's development. As a result of Pollard staying put, Ward is a big winner at the deadline.
Tennessee retaining a piece for the primary reason that he's helpful at Ward's side is a huge sign of confidence in the QB. Ward's Week 8 breakout against the Cincinnati Bengals continues to pay dividends for the progression of his role in the Titans' rebuild.
If you weren't already sure that the Titans continue to believe in Ward as "the guy" moving forward, Pollard being kept should be the period on the end of the sentence.
The scale of Tennessee's rebuild asks (unsurprisingly) for a little more patience from Titans fans. That's like asking for more water from the Grand Canyon.
Jokes aside, the Titans' front office clearly prioritized the new few drafts at the deadline. This is a franchise fully committed to turning the page. With Robert Saleh caught in between a new rebuild and trying to salvage an old one, things look questionable for the current head coach.
It doesn't help that Tennessee traded away arguably Saleh's two best defenders in the process of fast-tracking their rebuild. The defensive specialist has been left to drift without two anchors in his unit, and he may be expected to win sooner than this roster is ready to do so.
Saleh still has plenty of time, but the two trades Tennessee made both make a dent in his armor. The team's 1-7 record obviously doesn't help.
On the flip side from Saleh, general manager Mike Borgonzi is heavily equipped with the assets he needs to continue to hit the mark in the NFL Draft. He doesn't have a flawless record, but WR Carnell Tate and LB Anthony Hill Jr. go down as massive hits.
Now, Borgonzi is set up to capitalize on a vision he had when the Titans hired him in 2025. Mike Herndon pointed out that Borgonzi wanted 12 top-100 picks over a three-year period of time. He's traded this team into a position to accomplish that.
Where those picks end up still matter, and Borgonzi doesn't have infinite slack either. But he goes down as a winner today due to the newly-acquired capital he'll have to build this franchise into a successful one in time.
Naturally, with Pollard sticking around for the rest of his contract year, backup RB Tyjae Spears goes down as a loser today. He came into the 2026 campaign as a clear successor to Pollard's leading role, and has since been outplayed to the point that such a role isn't set for him even when Pollard leaves.
Had Pollard been moved, we could have seen Spears inherit the RB1 spot on a short-term basis with the ability to prove himself afterward. Instead, between the Titans' picks and rookie Nick Singleton behind him, Spears appears to be an afterthought in Brian Daboll's offense.
If he can stay healthy and play well in his limited minutes, Spears may have a chance to reclaim a complimentary role. But with only nine games remaining, he'll go down as a loser at the deadline today.
S Kevin Winston Jr. comes up as our final winner due to the expanded role he'll take on in the secondary with Hooker gone. Winston still has plenty to prove in his second year with the Titans, but he'll get the opportunity to do just that from this point forward.
Winston is recently healthy after missing scattered time with shoulder and quadriceps issues. His ability to play up and stop the run has thus far defined a quiet early tenure in Nashville. The uptick in snaps likely to come for Winston click in with the team's overarching commitment to a younger roster.
Up to now on the season (in six games played) Winston has 51 total tackles and one fumble recovery.
Lane covers the Tennessee Titans, where he brings an evolving team's journey to fans on a daily basis. A longtime sports fanatic and recent baby blue jersey aficionado.

title: Grading the Titans’ Trade Deadline: 2 Best Defenders Dealt, Calvin Ridley Somehow Stays Put
full_text:
The 2026 NFL trade deadline is officially over, and the Tennessee Titans are one of the prominent teams that sold high on their veteran talent.
Tennessee started by trading All-Pro defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons and a 2028 fifth-round pick to the Chicago Bears on October 29. In return, the Titans received a 2027 first- and fourth-round pick , and a 2028 first-round selection.
However, that wasn't the final trade made by general manager Mike Borgonzi. On Tuesday, the Titans shipped off safety Amani Hooker and a 2027 fifth-round pick to the Buffalo Bills for a 2027 second-round pick.
Despite running back Tony Pollard and wide receiver Calvin Ridley also being in trade rumors , both ended up staying put, while Simmons and Hooker are elsewhere. With the deadline now in the books, let's grade all of the Titans' major decisions.
Though cutting ties with a franchise legend like Simmons is a tough pill to swallow , Tennessee received a solid return, and if the front office can hit on the draft picks, the trade will end up laying a nice foundation for the future.
Additionally, the deal makes a lot of sense for Simmons, who will now compete for a championship with the Bears. The four-time Pro Bowler may be the missing piece that elevates Chicago into NFC title favorites.
Hooker is tied for the league lead in interceptions with five and is playing the best football of his career. As a result, Tennessee is selling high on the veteran safety, trading him to a premier AFC contender in the Bills.
By acquiring a second-round pick for Hooker, the Titans now have five projected top-100 picks in April's draft, per Tankathon. Tennessee is conducting its rebuild the right way, and paving the path for a bright future.
According to NFL insider Jordan Schultz, the Denver Broncos and New York Giants were interested in trading for Pollard . However, the Titans decided to retain the 29-year-old running back, which is an understandable move.
Pollard is critical to quarterback Cam Ward's development and has been the engine of Brian Daboll's offense this season. Though Pollard will be a free agent in the spring and Tennessee could've added additional 2027 picks for his services, retaining him to keep the offense afloat and help Ward's progression is a logical course of action.
Ridley has been a complete non-factor for the Titans in 2026, tallying just six receptions for 91 yards in seven games so far. The 31-year-old no longer fits into Tennessee's long-term plans, but his veteran experience and past production could have made a trade possible.
But in the end, Ridley is staying put. His recent incident at the Nashville International Airport may have played a part in rival teams losing trade interest, but Tennessee likely would've only gotten a sixth- or seventh-round pick in return for the former 1,000-yard receiver anyway.
We'll see whether Ridley is able to turn it around in the final nine games, but it's still a bit disappointing that the Titans couldn't move on from him before the deadline.
Dharya Sharma is a sportswriter from Nebraska who has been covering the Tennessee Titans through his website, SharmSports, since 2023. He is also an NFL and NBA writer for The Sporting News and had a previous stop with Sportsnaut. Follow him on X @SharmSports

title: Commanders Winners and Losers vs. Giants: A 24–21 Win They Nearly Gave Away
full_text:
The Washington Commanders gave the New York Giants the ball twice in the final six minutes. Both times, New York had an interception and a chance to put the game away. They couldn't get a first down on either possession. That gave Jayden Daniels one more chance. He found Stefon Diggs for a 32-yard touchdown with 57 seconds left, and Rasul Douglas intercepted J.J. McCarthy to seal the Commanders’ 24–21 win Thursday night at MetLife Stadium. Washington now sits at 3–5–1, two games behind the first-place Giants in the NFC East, with the Bengals coming to town for Monday Night Football in Week 11. The first meeting with the Giants ended in a 27–27 tie after Washington blew a 14-point fourth-quarter lead. This time, the Commanders lost the lead and still found a way back. Here’s who helped, and what nearly cost them.
Sonny Styles Sonny Styles didn’t wait until the fourth quarter to announce himself. Early in the first, he ran through Devin Singletary as McCarthy rolled away and threw it away on third-and-seven. It was the kind of play that makes a quarterback check where No. 52 is lined up before the next snap. He finished with a team-high 13 tackles, but his most valuable work came after Daniels’ interceptions. With New York backed up at its 11, Styles and Deatrich Wise stopped Jameis Winston’s third-and-one sneak. Washington challenged the original first-down ruling, won, and the Giants eventually punted after Winston played the funny-man role again, trying to draw them offsides with his cadence. Following the second pick, Styles dropped McCarthy for a two-yard loss on third-and-three. That stop resulted in Daniels getting the ball at his own 29 with 1:46 left.
Sonny Styles and Arvell Reese just put on an absolute LB MASTERCLASS on primetime. The two rookie LB’s combined for 26 total tackles, 8 stops, and 4 QB hurries 😳🤯 pic.twitter.com/3s2dZ1jzQp
Stefon Diggs A week ago, I was asking where Stefon Diggs was while Washington struggled to find receivers against the Rams. There was no such mystery Thursday. He caught six passes for 83 yards, including a 30-yarder at the two-minute warning in the first half that helped set up Ben Sinnott’s touchdown. The last catch was the one Washington signed him to make. On third-and-four from the Giants’ 32, Diggs beat his man at the line, Daniels found him, and Washington had the lead with 57 seconds left. Ten targets for the night, and a winning touchdown after the offense had wasted two chances to take control.
JAYDEN DANIELS FINDS STEFON DIGGS TO TAKE THE LEAD 🤯 DIGGS AFTER SCORING: “I’M LIKE THAT!” 🔥 (Via @NFL ) pic.twitter.com/FX8PIHEvNb
Ben Sinnott Sinnott entered Thursday with one catch all season. He caught four passes on four targets for 42 yards and a touchdown against New York, giving Daniels an answer at tight end that Washington hasn’t had often enough. His 12-yard catch moved the Commanders to the Giants’ 15 late in the first half. A few plays later, on third-and-goal from the 1, Daniels found him for the touchdown that sent Washington into halftime ahead 10–7. Sinnott then opened the third-quarter touchdown drive with a 24-yard reception. Chig Okonkwo briefly left the game, but Sinnott had already caught a pass before that happened. When I spoke with Vernon Davis about the different roles in Washington’s tight end room , the question was how to get more out of the group as receivers. Sinnott gave the coaches a pretty good answer. Antonio Williams Two targets. Two catches. Forty-two yards and a touchdown. Williams didn’t need much time to change the game, though he probably shouldn’t have had to wait until the third quarter for his first opportunity. On third-and-one at the Giants’ 31, Daniels put the ball in his hands and Williams scored to give Washington a 17–14 lead. His other catch gained 11 yards on the possession after New York went back ahead in the fourth. That drive ended with an interception, but the receiver had done his part. I’ve been arguing that Williams needs a larger role with Terry McLaurin out. Thursday offered another example. If his first target can turn a third-and-one into a 31-yard touchdown, why does it take so long to get him involved? Jayden Daniels Putting Daniels on the winning side isn’t difficult if you look at the result: 23 completions on 33 attempts, 249 passing yards and three touchdowns, plus 28 yards on the ground. He gave Washington the lead three different times. The last one came after the Giants had every reason to think they were done giving him chances. But he nearly ended this game himself. Daniels threw his first interception of the season from the Giants’ 24 with 5:31 remaining, targeting Okonkwo and putting the ball inside where Jevón Holland could take it at the 2. On Washington’s next possession, he forced a fourth-and-two throw toward Okonkwo that Ar’Darius Washington intercepted near midfield. Those were consecutive drives, with the game on the line. On the final possession, a 33-yard pass-interference penalty on a throw toward Treylon Burks moved Washington into Giants territory. Daniels scrambled for a yard, hit Austin Ekeler for five and found Diggs on third down. He made the final answer count. That doesn’t excuse the two decisions that almost kept him from getting that opportunity.
"Just trusting in the process. Just the consistency day in and day out. ... Can't really focus on the outcome, you just gotta stick to the process." Commanders QB Jayden Daniels joins @notthefakeSVP and speaks on the key to keeping the team together and battling each week 🏈 pic.twitter.com/JYwub4RcWQ
Odafe Oweh and Nick Cross Odafe Oweh had Washington’s only sack, getting to McCarthy for a 10-yard loss on third-and-nine in the second quarter. Nick Cross came on the blitz and helped push McCarthy toward him. The Giants punted. Cross finished with six tackles, a tackle for loss and a quarterback hit, and likely could have had a sack to go with his quarterback hurry, but he let up before hitting McCarthy on the play that produced Isaiah Likely’s 66-yard touchdown. We’ve seen Daronte Jones move Cross around the secondary and toward the line of scrimmage . Oweh gets the sack in the book, but Cross showed why Jones keeps sending him toward the quarterback.
Odafe Oweh is up to 5 sacks on the season. This one was schemed up via the Nick Cross blitz. pic.twitter.com/GHcIU0b3l2
Frankie Luvu and Jeremy Reaves The Giants reached Washington’s 16 late in the third quarter, trailing 17–14. Malik Nabers had the ball, and New York was in position to at least tie the game. Luvu punched it out. Reaves recovered at the 20. Reaves also had nine tackles and broke up a pass on New York’s final possession. Washington’s offense went three-and-out after the recovery. It wasted the takeaway, but Luvu and Reaves had already kept points off the board. Rasul Douglas Even after Diggs scored, New York got as far as Washington’s 48. Douglas ended the conversation there, intercepting McCarthy’s third-and-10 throw intended for Nabers with 34 seconds left. He didn’t need a tackle to make the most important defensive play on the final possession. Diggs gave Washington the lead; Douglas made sure it survived.
Brandon Coleman Another false start for Coleman , his sixth this season. That’s tied for the second most in the NFL through Thursday. This one came on Washington’s opening possession, turning second-and-seven at its own 21 into second-and-12 at the 16. Diggs gained four yards on the next play, Rachaad White couldn’t hold a screen on third-and-eight, and the Commanders punted. Coleman’s flag didn’t cause the drop. It turned a manageable second down into third-and-eight after Diggs’ catch. The Commanders had only four accepted penalties for 17 yards Thursday; this is about the same pre-snap mistake showing up again from the same player. title: 10 Commanders Quotes Show Washington’s Close Losses No Longer Count as Progress
full_text:
The Washington Commanders have spent a lot of time talking about how close they are. The 20–13 loss to the Rams left them at 2-5-1, three games behind the New York Giants. After a 27–27 tie in their first meeting , Thursday’s rematch can cut that gap to two games or stretch it to four. Jayden Daniels called it a must win after Sunday's loss. Dan Quinn has avoided that label, but by Wednesday he had little patience left for explanations about new coaches and changing personnel. Lucas Patrick is out , Nick Allegretti is back at center, and the Giants' blitz awaits them again. The week's answers keep coming back to what Washington has to execute: finishing drives, protecting Daniels, defending the Giants' playmakers and getting the late-game details right. From Sunday's postgame interviews through Wednesday's final practice, these 10 quotes show what the Commanders are taking into the Giants game.
Question: How can Washington keep Malik Nabers from beating the secondary deep without letting him pile up yards underneath? “I think that's just—it starts with knocking the run game out, putting them in situations where we know they have to pass the ball. And then, depending on whatever coverage we're taking, understanding what's going to stress our coverage out based off of their concepts, making sure we're all in the right spots. And then from there, just making sure we're tackling him. He's very good with the ball in his hand. He's very elusive, kind of like a running back a little bit. So just being able to get him down when he does have the ball, and of course stay over top, keeping a roof on our coverage.”
Question: Does the possibility of moving two games behind the Giants with a win or four behind with a loss add pressure this week? “You feel the weight of the NFL all the time, right? There's always pressure from, first, a personal standpoint. We have to individually play well and then from a team standpoint. And then you throw media on top and all that, too. Like, there's always pressure from every direction, as you can see. People in contract years, all these little factors that play into it. So no matter what, we're going to have the most pressure on us.”
Question: What has Washington changed to turn red-zone trips into touchdowns instead of field goals? “It's one of the keys that we talked about today, the importance of that, of scoring into the red zone and not having to settle for field goals. So different locations on the red zone, like where shot plays take place compared to crossing ones when you get closer to the goal line, knowing you don't have the distance to go. So having plans to, this is against man-to-man, this is against zone. The decision-making process happens quickly. So how do you recognize what you're seeing and then go attack it? That's what we're working hard on. We've added some extra repetitions for red zone over the last, well now going into the second week of that. That's one of the adjustments that we're making, put the time and the attention on it.”
Question: How do Daniels' suggestions to offensive coordinator David Blough show up in the plays Washington runs on game day? “I think just stuff I don't like throughout the week, he'll take out. Stuff I really do like, he'll call and things like that. So I think that's really where it's shown. And like I say, he's still growing as a coordinator, first-time coordinator, still going through his growing pains and stuff like that. So I just try to do the best I can, just go out there, execute. Doesn't matter what the play call is. It doesn't matter anything. If we got all 11 people going in the same direction, we have a chance.”
Question: With Allegretti returning to center , what challenges come with another switch in the middle of the offensive line? “Yeah, I mean, little nuances and stuff like that, but I still have trust in Nick. We have a really good relationship, and so from that standpoint, I'm comfortable playing next to him.”
Question: After Sunday's Rams loss, how urgent is it to turn the season around against New York? “Yeah. I think next week is a must win.”
Question: How much do a new coordinator, new system and personnel changes explain Washington's late-game failures? “I'd say we're all frustrated. We wanna get to the bottom of that and get the things correct that we want. So I'd say our time on task, there might be new people. Some of the situations, they're not that different and familiar. So we've got to be able to nail these, honestly. That's where we are at the halfway point. And so no excuses on that part. This is part of the gig and how we have to get it done, and we have to get these done.”
Question: What's the difference between playing with urgency and playing desperately? “Desperate is like you're just hoping. You're just hoping. I mean, urgent, like you have a plan ... We need to accomplish it now versus desperate is like, ‘All right, guys, let's just hope. Let's just see what we can do.’ We're not in that stage right now. So definitely urgency.”
Question: Why has Allegretti spoken openly about working with mental-health coaches while dealing with injuries and moving in and out of the lineup? “Just because of how much it helped me. It's one of those things that, as men, we're lulled into this, ‘Don't talk about it. Handle your things yourself.’ And I tried for a long time and I got to a point where it was too much for me. And I'll say probably one of the reasons that I handled the day-to-day here well when I'm not playing is just all the people that were here for me, helped me get the help that I needed. Not just in the locker room, but some coaches, staff members really went out of their way to make sure I was right. “It's a process, obviously. Still working weekly with that, but it's something that in life I never thought I would need to work on. You lift weights, you recover, you work on the football, you watch film, you do all this stuff, but you don't really ever work on the mental health side of things. So really proud of myself and appreciative of my teammates that encouraged me to take that step. Appreciate you asking.”
Question: At what point does saying the Commanders are close to a complete game stop being enough? “I mean, now, right? I mean, what's the point of being close? We eight games in, so either you figure it out or you going to continuously find yourself in the same position having these same conversations, trying to get the same results. So figure it out now. ... It's not time to be trying to figure out, ‘Oh, we're almost there. Almost there. Almost there.’ Either you're there or you're not.”

title: The Commanders Found a Deep-Ball Role for Treylon Burks Worth Keeping
full_text:
The NFL isn't like basketball, where prospects land on depth charts before a wide role gets eventually thinned out, nor is it similar to other team sports like baseball or hockey with their substantially longer seasons of potential opportunities. Development in a game with minimal room to overtake starters and even less leeway to change positional archetypes places an exceptional amount of weight on preexisting infrastructure, with a potentially poor response to a specific environment often getting misconstrued as analysts attempt to understand the players before them.
As we now know, Treylon Burks is one of those players who needed more of a push in a specific direction than he got. The Tennessee Titans hoped he'd become the franchise's playmaker for years to come when they drafted him with the first-round pick acquired in the A.J. Brown trade with the Philadelphia Eagles, but the Washington Commanders have been happy to get consistent production out of him since signing him to their practice squad a little over a year ago.
It's becoming increasingly clear that his ascendance as a go-ball artist has far more to do with his partnership with Jayden Daniels than it does with the X-spot opened up by the down-for-the-count Terry McLaurin. Despite his long path here and his still-incomplete game, he's as worthy of a full-time starting gig as he ever has been, a necessary bright spot during a team-building period that's badly searching for wins.
To be clear, he didn't shift from a disappointing former first-round pick into a relied-upon wideout overnight. It took him most of last year to finally impress Washington and its frustrated fan base. He didn't have much time to build chemistry with Daniels, as the quarterback appeared in only two of the Commanders' 10 final matchups. Burks did, however, enjoy a moment in the sun when he made one of the team's top plays of the season: a fading one-handed touchdown grab against one of last season's top defenses, the Denver Broncos.
#Broncos CB Riley Moss... got Moss'd. Treylon Burks, man. This is incredible. pic.twitter.com/mmK0TeTW4x https://t.co/KZdkroMomU
Though little from that late-season stretch offered any long-term guarantees, he still seemed worth monitoring whenever the Commanders next meant business.
A few months later, when it was time for the squad to whittle its training camp participants down to an inner circle of rotational playmakers, he had 130 yards over eight games to lean on, not much, but enough to convince management that his 13 yards per reception offered some upside as a deep-ball threat, something they lacked outside of the aging and battered McLaurin. Burks himself hadn't exactly been Mr. Perfect Attendance, having yet to make a dozen appearances in a season, with a mere five outings logged during his final year in Tennessee, but his talent made a flier seem worth it.
Washington's play-callers have leaned all the way in on Burks and the long ball, spiking his yards per target to a career-high 10.6 on 22 targets over a half-dozen-game sample size. 19.4 yards per reception also rings in as a high-water mark thanks to the work he's doing after his tough catches, and his average nightly yardage count of 38.8 is within two ticks of the 40.4 mark he'd once peaked at as the Titans' hyped rookie.
Updated WR separation & Catchpoint/YAC Grades pic.twitter.com/mX4vSuk3xm
He's drawing some of the deepest targets at his position, proving a unique enough threat to keep on earning trust from Washington's staff. Following his first target attempt in Week 8 against the Eagles, a bobbled pass he dropped from point-blank range, the Commanders went back to him four more times for 81 yards on three receptions in a successful gamble.
McLaurin's absence after a torn patellar tendon suffered last month has opened a starting spot to complement slot options like Stefon Diggs and Antonio Williams. Daniels has his groove back thanks to a more versatile receiving corps, and his stabilizing presence as a dual-threat creative is proving that Burks may have even more to unlock beyond his role-player status, let alone as a must-deploy ahead of pure reserve options like Luke McCaffrey and Dyami Brown.
Look no further than the Commanders' most recent outing, a Burks-less 20-13 loss to the Los Angeles Rams , for evidence of how much it hurts to lack that extra help. After being left alone with a thin corps of Diggs, Williams, Chig Okonkwo, and surprise hero Van Jefferson, Burks' combination of physical force and finesse will be appreciated when he returns from his foot injury for Thursday's Giants rematch in New York.
With D.C. serving as a "second draft" for the former washout, he's looking almost as deserving of attention as a true rookie like Williams, thanks to his unique skill set. Washington should keep that downfield role for him even when the receiving corps gets healthier. It only took some time to unlock, and the Commanders may have plenty more of that coming as they navigate another messy season.

title: Commanders Power Rankings Fall After Rams Loss, but Dan Quinn Faces a Bigger Question
full_text:
Each week during the regular season, we'll look at what the national media is saying about the Washington Commanders via various publications' NFL Power Polls. With it being Week 10, the chances of winning the division or making the playoffs are starting to look thin. The Washington Commanders followed their best win of the season with another frustrating loss , falling 20-13 to the Los Angeles Rams on Sunday and dropping to 2-5-1. That didn't do Washington many favors with the national media. Six of the nine publications we track each week moved the Commanders down in their latest power rankings, including one writer who had a much different opinion of this team just seven days ago. * Side note: Many have asked whether these polls are helpful, which is a fair question. One way to look at them is as a way to broaden your perspective on what others believe. Not to mention, sometimes it's fun to see the national media guys bump around in the dark, chasing their tails, clueless.
Commanders Power Rankings - Week 9 (Average of 24)
Commanders Power Rankings - Week 10 (Average of 25)
Sports Illustrated - No. 22
Sports Illustrated - No. 28
Note : The table above links each poll to the corresponding publication name. Remember last week when Sports Illustrated's Conor Orr was calling Washington his favorite to win the NFC East? Well, apparently that didn't last long. Orr dropped the Commanders six spots after Sunday's loss, taking them from No. 22 to No. 28. That's quite a turnaround in seven days, although watching Washington stumble through another late-game situation probably didn't help. Oddly enough, ESPN actually moved Washington up a spot despite the loss. WalterFootball still has the Commanders at No. 18, while CBS Sports and Sports Illustrated have them sitting at No. 27 and No. 28, respectively. Hard to find much agreement there, other than the fact that Dan Quinn has some serious work to do. There's something else worth pointing out this week. Six of the nine publications brought up Dan Quinn's job security, which tells you just how much the conversation has changed around Washington. ESPN's John Keim says Quinn's seat could become "white-hot" with another loss Thursday, while NFL.com's Nick Shook believes it's time to start watching for potential coaching changes. Mike Florio at Pro Football Talk went even further, suggesting the mini-bye following the Giants game could be the time to make a move; of course, Florio has repeatedly said Quinn's seat was hot since the preseason. That's a lot of attention on a head coach whose team was being picked by at least one national writer to win the division just a week ago. Quinn certainly hasn't helped himself with some of the late-game decisions we've seen , but Thursday's matchup against New York suddenly carries more weight than just another game in the NFC East standings. The Commanders need a win, and their head coach could probably use one even more. Last week’s Power Ranking Index : No. 24 HIGHEST Ranking: No. 18 LOWEST Ranking: No. 28 Last week’s result : Lost to the Los Angeles Rams 20-13 This week : @New York Giants ESPN had this to say (24th): With their current record, the Commanders are quickly running out of time to stick around in the NFC East. Because they tied the Giants last month, they could earn the tiebreaker with a win. Of course, they would still have to win a few other games down the stretch to make the playoffs. But they'd be alive mathematically. The bigger issue is that if they fall to 2-6-1, coach Dan Quinn's seat will become white-hot. The third-year coach needs to be much better after a 5-12 record in 2025. -- John Keim
CBS Sports had this to say (27th) The heat is getting hotter on the seat underneath Dan Quinn as they move to the final nine weeks. They are pretty much done. — Pete Prisco NFL.com had this to say (26th) Sunday provided yet another discouraging result for a Washington team that still doesn’t take care of the details or handle end-game scenarios well. It’s only the midpoint of the season, but it’s time to put the Commanders on watch for potential coaching changes. They simply don’t have enough to climb out of this hole, not with the way they’re playing. — Nick Shook
Fox Sports had this to say (26th): Jayden Daniels is playing better, which is good, and he tried to pull off a miracle comeback against the Rams. But he just doesn’t have enough horses around him to ride to his team’s rescue anymore. The Commanders have been decimated by injuries, and with shortages at RB and WR, it’s like Daniels is their only weapon. And that’s just not enough against teams like the Rams. Maybe they’ll have better luck at the Giants on Thursday night, but good luck keeping up with the Bengals after that. It’s really already another lost season in Washington. The only question is how long Dan Quinn can survive. — Ralph Vacchiano Sports Illustrated had this to say (28th): I think if there was a team that didn’t need to be the focal point of an end-of-game situational football occurrence gone awry, it would be the Washington Commanders. Alas…   — Conor Orr
Yahoo Sports had this to say (24th): Jayden Daniels set the stakes for Thursday night's game against the Giants, when asked after the team's loss to the Rams whether time is running out to get back in the NFC East race. "Yeah. I think next week is a must-win," Daniels told reporters after the game. He's right. With a win, the Commanders would be two games behind the Giants for first place and hold the tiebreaker, since the teams tied in their first meeting. That's not easy, but Washington wouldn't be dead. If the Commanders lose, they'd be four games back and not have the tiebreaker, which would probably be impossible to overcome. It might not matter because the Commanders aren't very good — they're 20th in DVOA with matching ranks of 20th on offense and defense — but at least with a win they'd have something to keep playing for.  — Frank Schwab Pro Football Talk had this to say (26th) The mini-bye could be the time to bid farewell to the head coach. — Mike Florio The Athletic had this to say (26th) A bad division was there for the taking for Dan Quinn and the Commanders. But they haven’t just found ways to lose (or tie) games. They’ve done it in a comical fashion that has raised questions about Quinn and Jayden Daniels’ game management. — Chad Graff and Josh Kendall Walter Football had this to say (18th) How in the world does Dan Quinn still have a job? I don't understand how this team continuously screws up in late-game situations. One of these debacles is bad enough, but the Redskins keep making the same mistakes and embarrassing themselves.
Put all nine together, and the Commanders land at an average ranking of No. 25.0, down from last week's 23.8. Washington doesn't have much time to worry about what the national media thinks, either. Thursday night's rematch against the New York Giants is coming fast, and another loss would leave the Commanders at 2-6-1 with eight games remaining. At that point, the conversation around this team could look considerably different. We'll revisit these each week and see where the national pulse moves next. title: Commanders News: NFL-Worst on Third Down, Washington Faces the Giants’ Blitz Again | Burgundy Roundup
full_text:
The NFL trade deadline came and went without any moves from the 2-5-1 Washington Commanders . The team apparently had already shifted its focus to its Week 10 opponent, the NFC East-leading New York Giants, who, at 5-2-1, also stood pat at the deadline. With center Lucas Patrick still in concussion protocol, Commanders head coach Dan Quinn confirmed at his presser Tuesday that the team is turning back to Nick Allegretti as the starter . Rookie Matt Gulbin took over for Patrick when he left the Rams game Sunday; Quinn explained after Sunday’s game that Allegretti had been working more at guard, so he went with Gulbin, who had taken the most reps at center. Thursday will mark Allegretti's first start since Week 3 , when he started at right guard. Quinn wants the Commanders to run the ball more, but they keep giving David Blough too few plays to do it. Washington ranks 11th in rushing yards per game and 25th in attempts, while its 31.13% third-down conversion rate is the worst in the NFL . The Commanders converted three of 12 against the Rams and ran only 10 plays in the third quarter. Quinn sees more carries coming from longer drives. Rachaad White and Austin Ekeler won’t get many chances if Washington keeps sending out its punt team after another short series. Quinn said Washington has added extra red-zone repetitions for a second week, so the work started before Sunday’s loss. The Commanders still turned two takeaways in Rams territory into three points and committed three accepted pre-snap penalties. Daniels said he has a say in which plays Blough keeps in the game plan, while acknowledging the first-time coordinator is working through growing pains. They have had those conversations. Thursday is when the offense has to get the details right. Allegretti’s first start back at center comes against a defense that sacked Daniels five times in the October tie. The Giants sent Cover 0 on 10 of his dropbacks late in that game and got three sacks during that stretch. They added seven against Philadelphia on Sunday, three by Arvell Reese. Daniels said Tuesday he needs answers he can check to, including protection adjustments. Allegretti has to get those calls across before the snap, giving Daniels a chance to use them. Washington did not practice Monday and held a walkthrough Tuesday, so both days’ participation listings are estimates. Treylon Burks (foot) improved from a projected nonparticipant Monday to projected limited Tuesday. Terry McLaurin and Dyami Brown remain on IR. Stefon Diggs, Antonio Williams, and Van Jefferson handled the available receiver work against Los Angeles, with Jaden Bradley a possible practice-squad elevation if needed. Tight end Colson Yankoff (knee) and Patrick were estimated nonparticipants for a second day. Chig Okonkwo (hip) and Shy Tuttle (shoulder) improved from projected limited Monday to projected full Tuesday. The Giants held a practice Tuesday, and quarterback J.J. McCarthy (hip) and running back Cam Skattebo (hamstring) were full participants after Monday’s projected limited designations. Abdul Carter (knee/back) and Malik Harrison (groin) stayed limited. Cornerback Colton Hood was added as limited after dislocating a finger at practice on Tuesday.
A month later, Washington has managed only one win since, and will enter the game at 2-5-1 after losing 20-13 to the Rams in Week 9. Commanders head coach Dan Quinn acknowledged the importance of Thursday's game during his presser on Monday: "But what I will say is, like, man, we need this win this week. There’s no doubt." Washington heads to MetLife Stadium this week three games behind the 5-2-1 Giants in the NFC East, where another loss would push Quinn’s team further out of the race.

Mathematically the Commanders remain alive, but with nine games remaining, any realistic hope the team has for a strong finish likely begins and ends vs. the Giants on Thursday (8:15 p.m. ET, Prime Video). A win and they would be two games back with eight to play and own the tiebreaker -- if that eventually mattered.

The problem looked at least temporarily fixed when Lucas Patrick stepped into the role against Seattle . Washington had signed Patrick just 11 days before that start. In that game, right guard Sam Cosmi couldn't go, so it made sense to slide Allegretti over. The next week in London, Patrick stayed at center, and Gulbin slid over to right guard. That signaled Patrick had already taken over for the offseason starter, though Quinn initially called the change temporary before naming Patrick the starter the following Friday.
“I’ve worked with some mental health coaches on that just because it’s a tough process — handling some injuries and being out of the lineup,” Allegretti said Tuesday. “For a long time in my career, I kind of just kept all that to myself. So working through that these last couple of years helped me a ton, and I think it’s helped me day to day just to truly enjoy being here, being in the locker room, regardless of what my role is.”

Heading into the Rams game on Sunday, the Washington Commanders were short on receivers: Terry McLaurin is out for the season, Treylon Burks is out, and Dyami Brown moved to injured reserve. Sounds like a day for Stefon Diggs to shine, right? The problem is Diggs' first catch, a four-yard burner, came with 7:28 left in the third quarter; he wouldn't gain another yard until a five-yarder with 4:41 left in the game. With 52 seconds remaining, they found him again for a 42-yard catch that moved Washington from its own 9 to the Rams' 49 and put the team in position to tie the game.

title: Commanders’ Must-Win Giants Rematch Hinges on Replacing Five Players From the Tie
full_text:
The last time the Washington Commanders and New York Giants played, the game ended in a 27-27 tie after both teams missed chances to win in overtime. That day, Stefon Diggs was inactive, and Jer'Zhan (Johnny) Newton was on injured reserve. Terry McLaurin , Dyami Brown, Daron Payne, Jacory "Bill" Croskey-Merritt, and Javon Kinlaw played; all five are now on IR. A month later, Washington has managed only one win since, and will enter the game at 2-5-1 after losing 20-13 to the Rams in Week 9. Commanders head coach Dan Quinn acknowledged the importance of Thursday's game during his presser on Monday: "But what I will say is, like, man, we need this win this week. There’s no doubt." Washington heads to MetLife Stadium this week three games behind the 5-2-1 Giants in the NFC East, where another loss would push Quinn’s team further out of the race.
McLaurin caught four passes for 62 yards in the first meeting, while Brown played 23 offensive snaps. Diggs gives Daniels another proven receiver against New York, but getting him involved has been an issue of its own. He finished with three catches for 51 yards on 38 offensive snaps against the Rams. “So he’s definitely, like, in the front of our thinking. And so we need him, you know,” Quinn said about Diggs Monday. Washington needs that thinking to turn into completions before it’s chasing the game in the final minutes. Van Jefferson has a much bigger part in this offense now, too. He played just three offensive snaps against the Giants, compared with 36 against Los Angeles, where he caught five passes for 58 yards and a touchdown. Antonio Williams’ workload has grown from 42 snaps in the tie to 52 against the Rams. Jefferson should stay involved even if Treylon Burks returns from the foot injury that kept him out Sunday. He gave Blough another weapon to work with. The backfield has changed as well. Croskey-Merritt ran for 82 yards and a touchdown on 11 carries in the first meeting. Rachaad White and Austin Ekeler handled the running-back snaps against the Rams. I’d get both involved early Thursday and make New York account for them as runners and receivers. Blough has to find production there alongside everything he’s asking of the wideouts.
🚨 TOUCHDOWN COMMANDERS 🚨 BILL CROSKEY-MERRITT IS GONE 💨 Washington takes an early 7-0 lead vs. the Giants! pic.twitter.com/RDAz8I7XNg
Daronte Jones has two substantial workloads to replace up front. Payne played 63 of Washington’s 89 defensive snaps in the tie, while Kinlaw played 56. Payne also recorded a sack and a forced fumble. With both players now on IR , Washington will ask a different group to handle the interior work and create some disruption of their own. Newton’s return to the lineup helps, but his first game back also shows how much work falls on the rest of the rotation. He played 20 defensive snaps against the Rams , while Shy Tuttle played 43, Tim Settle 33, and Ricky Barber 15. I’d keep sharing that work, with Newton’s workload based on what he’s ready to handle. Getting him back gives Jones another option; it doesn’t fill both openings on its own. Blough has to get production from a different supporting cast, and Jones has to make this rotation hold up for four quarters. That’s the job Thursday. Quinn’s staff needs useful contributions from the players available now, with little room left for another game that ends in explanations.
